# Development Notes

> Living document -- kept up to date with tips, processes, and guidance for
> working on WebMS Intra.

---

### Every scheduled job records that it ran (#775, migration 253)

**`Portal\Core\ScheduledJobs` is the ONE place a job's run is recorded and the
ONE place it is read.** `tblScheduledJobRun` holds one row per job: the job's
own address under `cron/`, when it last began, when it last finished, and how
it ended.

Fifteen addresses under `cron/` are called by whatever runs scheduled tasks on
a customer's hosting. Until #775 only ONE left any trace — the mail queue,
through `MailRoutes::jobRan()` — so a portal could silently stop sending
reminders, stop clearing out personal data past its retention period, or stop
taking backups, with no error, no log line and nothing on any page.

**KEYED BY JOB, NEVER BY TOKEN, and that is the whole reason it is a new
table.** `PortalCheck::JOB_TOKENS` lists the eleven tokens, and
`maintenance.cronToken` alone covers FIVE jobs — the mail queue, the retention
sweep, the backup run, the backup check and the health check. Keyed by token,
"the backup has not run for a month" could not be told from "the mail queue ran
a minute ago".

**OVERDUE IS PER JOB (D-070).** One number cannot work: giving statements go
out weekly, so anything loose enough for them would let the mail queue sit dead
for a week, and anything tight enough for the mail queue would complain about
the nightly backup every day. A two-tier split was rejected for the same
measured reason — statements would read as overdue six days in seven, a
permanent false alarm, and **a check that cries wolf gets switched off (#483)**.

**NO RECORD MEANS "NOTHING IS KNOWN YET" (D-071)**, never a warning and never a
backfilled run time. Warning would give every correctly-configured portal a
page of warnings the morning after it upgrades, with no way to clear them but
to wait. Backfilling would write a record saying a job ran when nobody knows
whether it did — inventing evidence in the one place whose purpose is telling
an administrator what is actually true. The never-configured case still has a
real answer, from the token check, which IS knowable from the database.

#### Recording must never be able to stop the job it records

Files reach a customer's server BEFORE anybody presses "Run migrations" (#694),
so these pages are called while the table does not exist. If `began()` threw
then, the mail queue, the reminders and the retention sweep would all stop —
this class would have caused the exact silence it exists to reveal. So
`began()` and `finished()` answer `false` on any cause.

**The cost, said plainly: a recording that fails is silent**, and the page then
says "nothing is known yet" about a job that really ran. That under-claims,
which is the opposite direction from the fault being fixed.

#### THE FAULT THIS SHIPPED FIRST, and it is the lesson

EIGHT of the fifteen pages **exit early** when a setting switches them off, when
another run holds the lock, or when nothing is due. Twelve such paths recorded
a START and no finish — so a job somebody had **deliberately switched off** read
as "started and never finished" on the check page, as a PROBLEM, for ever. **A
job working exactly as configured must never be reported as broken.**

Every one of those paths now records a finish. Which word it records matters:

**THERE ARE THREE OUTCOME WORDS, NOT TWO, AND THE THIRD WAS ADDED FOR A
MEASURED REASON.** A first version had only `ok` and `refused`, so `refused`
was doing two different jobs — "somebody switched this off" and "this ran and
could not do its work". The check page words `refused` as *being called but
switched off*, so **a nightly backup that FAILED would have been reported as
switched off**: untrue in the reassuring direction, about backups. `failed` is
its own word and its own finding.

An unrecognised word is stored as `failed`, not `refused`: it means the caller
is out of step with the class, and `refused` reads as a reassurance nobody has
earned.

#### A broken READ is not "nothing is known yet" either

Both used to answer `NOT_KNOWN`, so a half-applied migration — the table there
but a column missing — reported the reassuring *expected straight after an
update: each one starts being watched the first time it runs*. Nothing was
going to start being watched. `COULD_NOT_READ` is its own answer and a WARNING.

**That also found that the `SHOW TABLES LIKE` guard was doing nothing
observable**: the self-test passed with it deleted, because the `try`/`catch`
answered identically. **A guard nothing can distinguish from its absence is not
a guard.** The one in `state()` now is, and planting `if (true)` in its place
turns F4 red. The ones in `began()`/`finished()` still cannot be — both return
`false` — and that is stated rather than pretended: they are there to avoid
throwing and catching on every call before the migration runs, and to keep "not
there yet" from being answered like "something is wrong".

#### Round 2: the contradiction moved rather than went, and it is PERMANENT

**The all-clear said "Every scheduled job has run recently enough" directly
under a PROBLEM saying seven of them can never run.** Round 1 excluded
token-less jobs from the later findings and subtracted them from the count — and
left the HEADLINE alone, so fault 4's contradiction moved into the all-clear
instead of going.

**And it is the steady state of an ordinary portal, not an upgrade-day
transient.** There are eleven separate tokens, `full_schema.sql` seeds every one
EMPTY, nothing in the installer sets any, and a customer who does not use the
noticeboard push, discipleship or venue agreements leaves those empty for ever.
So the false all-clear was permanent — sitting beneath the sentence that says
"If the clearing-out of personal data is among them, this portal is keeping
records it told people it would delete." That is the reassurance that stops
somebody acting on the problem above it.

**NO FIXTURE COULD REACH THAT STATE, and closing one blind spot had opened it.**
Round 1's own fix for section G's vacuity set EVERY token; H0h/H0i clear one but
leave ten jobs with no record, so `count($notKnown) > 0` suppressed the
all-clear. **The state that was never tested is "some tokens missing AND every
token-bearing job healthy" — which is what a normal portal looks like.**

**Round 2 also found the mail fallback reporting a PROBLEM on a brand-new
portal**, having silently escalated the WARNING it was restoring — and
asserting "the mail job has not run in the last 15 minutes" from a table it
could not read, which is COULD_NOT_READ's own shape one source over.
`MailRoutes::state()` answers `jobLastRanAt` as null both when there is no row
and when the read fails, so "never recorded" and "recorded a while ago" are now
told apart and only the second is said — as a WARNING, with the old page's own
"likeliest reason" sentence restored.

**The customer-facing CHANGELOG still described `refused` as "switched off by a
setting"** — the untruth round 1 had corrected on the page — in the list a
customer reads to decide whether to worry. A document asserting a fix while
restating the thing it fixed is worse than one that says nothing.

**Two of round 1's fixes were pinned by nothing**: the `- count($noToken)`
subtraction (dropping it printed "15 of the 15 recorded a FINISH" where eight
did) and the condition that makes the mail fallback truthful (dropping it gave
every correctly-running portal a PROBLEM on upgrade day, which is what D-071
exists to prevent). Both are pinned now, and the number itself is asserted
rather than only the wording.

**And `gate_refuses()` accepted an `exit` that refuses nothing** — one inside a
closure merely DEFINED in the gate block left the hard gate at exit 0 while an
unauthenticated request wrote the record. The self-test caught it (I1-I6), which
is the right division of labour, except that the gate runs in `pr-security.yml`
(registered) and the self-test in `portal-selftests.yml`, which GitHub has never
registered (#754) — so on GitHub it was guarded by nothing. It requires the exit
at the block's own depth **after round 2 — a design round 3 withdrew and round 4
withdrew again; see the round-4 section below for where it ended up** — and the
block must belong to the gate rather than
being the next one `find()` happens upon. **Three documents had said of round
1's two bypasses "Both closed and planted". One was.**

**And a third missing dependency.** `PortalCheck` gained `ScheduledJobs` in
round 1 and `MailRoutes` in round 2, and both tests that load it require every
class BY HAND. `run()`'s `catch (Throwable)` turns "class not found" into a tidy
"could not run" finding, so the whole check vanishes while the suite looks
healthy. `portal-check-selftest.php`'s section J — "no check reports itself as
unable to run" — is the only thing that notices, and it has now earned its place
three times. **Whoever adds a dependency to a check must add the require in the
same change.**

#### Round 3: the same fault a FOURTH time, in the bucket round 2 created to fix the third

**The all-clear counted, and claimed to speak for, the mail job the page had
just said had stopped.** `$mailStopped` was the only bucket in the loop that
neither suppressed the all-clear nor was subtracted from the count — and round 2
added it in the same edit that excluded the running and token-less jobs.
Measured: four jobs had really finished, the sentence said five, and the "Not
counted here" list did not name the mail job, so it explicitly claimed to cover
the one the warning above it was about.

**The rule, written into the code because three rounds have now broken it: a
new bucket in that loop is not finished until it appears in BOTH the count and
the suppression.** And no fixture reached the state — H0m-H0p2 give the mail job
a record so the fallback never fires, H0q-H0v leave the table empty so
`count($notKnown)` suppresses the all-clear, and "mail stopped and everything
else healthy" fell between them.

**One mechanism, not two.** The obvious fix was to subtract AND suppress, and
the subtraction is provably dead: the count only prints when no bucket is
populated, and then the mail job is not stopped. Measured — dropping it alone
changed no output and no check could tell. A clause that cannot matter makes a
guard look stronger than it is, so suppression does the work and the comment
says which.

**ROUND 2 TRADED A WRONG SENTENCE FOR A VANISHED CHECK.** `MailRoutes::state()`
has no try/catch — `$row ?? [...]` handles "no row" and nothing else — so under
the portal's reporting mode its `prepare()` throws, the exception escapes
`scheduledJobs()`, and `run()`'s catch replaces the WHOLE check with one tidy
"This check could not be completed." Measured on a half-applied upgrade, the
exact state `COULD_NOT_READ` exists for: the page went from "ten jobs can never
run, including the clearing-out of personal data" to that one warning. Round
1's version used `MailQueue::jobIsRunning()`, which catches, so it gave a wrong
sentence and the check survived. **And the comment round 2 added asserted that
this case was handled, which is why nobody would look** — the same shape as the
missing `require`s that commit wrote up, re-created by an uncaught read in the
same edit.

**ONE PAGE, TWO NUMBERS FOR ONE FACT, DIFFERING FIVEFOLD.** The no-token PROBLEM
counted TOKENS (eleven) while the new "Not counted here" sentence counted JOBS
(fifteen), and `maintenance.cronToken` covers five. With only that token empty
the page reported a count of ONE beside "the 5 with no token … each is reported
above". Both are built from one source now, and both count jobs — a token is not
a job, which is the whole reason this package has its own table. **Every fixture
had used a single-job token, where the two numbers coincide**, which is why
nothing saw it; `portal-check-selftest.php` has O6b for the five-job token now.

**And `gate_refuses()` was wrong in BOTH directions, which is the worst pair
there is.** Round 2's depth-1 rule CRIED WOLF on a genuinely refusing gate whose
exits are one level deeper — an ordinary `if/else` on `?json=1` — with a message
asserting something false about the file, in a hard gate that really runs, so a
false red blocks every pull request (#483). And it still passed on
`$log->exit();`, because it text-scanned the reconstructed source and a METHOD
named `exit` reads the same. **`.claude/CLAUDE.md` already records that trap
from #763 verbatim — "`die` as a plain name … only as a METHOD" — and
`php_code_only()` already calls `token_get_all()`, so the token kind was in hand
and thrown away.** The probe marks `T_EXIT` and `T_FUNCTION`/`T_FN` now: a real
exit anywhere in the block, not inside a nested function body. Depth no longer
matters, which stops the crying wolf; the token kind stops the false pass. Three
plants, two of them must-stay-green.

**Three documents still said of round 1's two bypasses "Both closed and
planted".** One was, and round 2's commit message said so while leaving the
sentence standing in both instruction files — which is where the next reader
looks to decide whether the gate is guarded.

**And the count correction was itself inconsistent.** "Nine of the fifteen pages
exit early … those twelve paths" cannot both be true: the twelve live in EIGHT
pages, and nine counts `health.php`, which the same sentence removes from the
early-exit set. In four places, in the comment edited to fix a count.

#### Round 4: a one-line security bypass, and both of this package's tests ran nowhere

**`gate_refuses()` PASSED ON AN ARROW FUNCTION, which restored round 1's fault
in one line.** `fn(): never => exit('Forbidden');` has NO BRACES, so a
brace-depth walk never enters its body and the exit inside it counted as the
gate's own. Measured: the hard gate said OK while the self-test went three red
(I2, I4, I6 — "and NOTHING was recorded").

**It is worse than the fault it restored.** Round 1's bypass only forged the
record. Here an unauthenticated request gets its 403 header and then RUNS ON —
writing `began()` and executing `WebhookDispatcher::retryDue()`, the
outgoing-webhook retry sweep.

**That guard has now been wrong in both directions twice**, and each version was
"verified by planting" the shapes its author had thought of:

| version | false PASS | false RED |
|---|---|---|
| v1 | an exit inside a braced closure | — |
| v2 | `$log->exit();` (a method named exit) | a real exit one level deeper |
| v3 | `fn() => exit()` (no braces) | a braceless gate |
| v4 | `fn() => match (…) { … exit(…) }` (an arrow body with a brace) | `$matches = hash_equals(…)` above the gate |
| v5 | `$bad = !hash_equals(…)`, a cast, a line break | a refusal in an `else` branch, a braceless `else`, an elseif chain, an invoked closure |
| **gone** | — | **the detector is DELETED — the property is behavioural and is now DRIVEN on all fifteen pages (D-065); what remains is a NESTING check, which is the half a source reading can honestly do** | |

v4 marks `T_FN` separately from `T_FUNCTION` and skips an arrow function's body
as the EXPRESSION it is; a braceless gate is read as the one statement that
follows it. Four plants, four must-stay-green.

**AND BOTH OF THIS PACKAGE'S TESTS RAN NOWHERE AUTOMATIC.**
`scheduled-jobs-selftest.php` — named in four documents and in the gate's own
docstring as the guard for everything the gate cannot see, including that one
security property — was in no workflow and not in `tools/run-all-selftests.sh`.
`portal-check-selftest.php` was in `portal-selftests.yml`, which GitHub has
never registered (#754), and also absent from the runner, **which is why that
runner could not see the two missing-dependency breaks that happened in it.**

The runner's own one-liner found three more absent: `clock-change-selftest.php`
(#777's, relied on for twenty-two review rounds) and the two i18n tests
(#763's). All five are in the runner now, and `scheduled-jobs` is in the
workflow with its database created.

**And a failed read was still reported as "nothing is known yet".** Round 3's
try/catch set `$everRan = ''`, so the mail job fell into `$notKnown` — so a
half-applied upgrade got "expected straight after an update: each one starts
being watched the first time it runs", with `'todo' => 'Nothing.'`, while mail
sat unsent. That is word for word the fault `COULD_NOT_READ` exists to prevent,
re-created for one job, **at a LOWER severity than the version round 3
replaced** (a NOTE where round 2 gave a WARNING). It goes to `$unreadable` now.

**`$mailStopped` was a STRING whose emptiness meant two things** — "not stopped"
and "stopped, but its description is empty". Planting an empty `whatStops` made
the warning vanish AND the all-clear return, claiming every job had finished:
the headline fault a fifth time, from a flag a hundred lines from where round 3
removed sentence-matching for exactly that reason. It is an array like every
other bucket now.

**THE RULE ROUND 3 WROTE INTO THE CODE WAS ITSELF THE NEXT FAULT, as an
instruction.** "A new bucket in this loop is not finished until it appears in
BOTH lines" is violated by `$refused`, correctly — a refused run IS a finish —
and a reader applying it literally would remove the all-clear from almost every
portal, because `cron/backup-run` refuses six nights in seven on a weekly
schedule. The rule now states its exception. **And the stated reason for
dropping the subtraction was false**: it said the count only prints when no
bucket is populated, and `$refused` is a populated bucket in exactly that run.
The conclusion held only because of the explicit clause beside it.

**"Corrected in all four places" was false** — three still carried the
impossible pair, including `DEV_NOTES.md` 164 lines above its own correction of
it, and two in the gate's header, in a file the same commit edited.

**And "it has never run and never will" was said about a job that finished
ninety seconds ago** — a token cleared after the job ran, with the row saying so
read by the same method twenty lines later. The alarming direction rather than
the reassuring one, and still untrue on the page whose subject is saying what is
true.

#### Round 5: the gate was wrong both ways for the THIRD version, and the remedy was not a fifth pattern

**`gate_refuses()` v4 passed an arrow function whose body contains a brace.**
`_end_of_arrow()` stopped at the first `{` under a comment reading *"defensive:
never expected"* — and it IS expected, because `match`, a closure and an
anonymous class all sit in expression position. The main walk then resumed
INSIDE that brace with no function recorded, so the exit of a definition nobody
calls read as the gate's own. Five spellings measured, all passing a gate that
refuses nothing; **`fn() => function (): never { exit('no'); };` is v1's fault
verbatim, reached by a new spelling.**

**And it went RED on an ordinary refactor** — the comparison read into a
variable first:

    $matches = hash_equals($expected, $incoming);
    if ($expected === '' || $matches === false) { … exit('Forbidden'); }

v4 decided "braceless" by asking whether the next `;` came before the next `{`,
which is true of that shape. A hard gate accusing correct code of a security
fault blocks every pull request (#483).

**THE ROOT CAUSE, AND THE REMEDY, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THIS SECTION.** There
was **no committed test of the gate**: `grep -rln "gate_refuses" tools/ web/`
returned only the gate's own file. Rounds 1-4 each verified with a throwaway
harness that nobody re-ran — *which is exactly why v4 lost v1's case.*

A fifth cleverer pattern would have produced a round 6.
`tools/scheduled-jobs-gate-selftest.py` will not: it holds **every case from all
five rounds** — twenty-two, ten that must refuse and twelve that must not — and
is a hard gate in `pr-security.yml`. The repository already had this answer in
`tools/api-spec-check-selftest.py`; it simply had not been applied here.

v5 itself steps OVER braces inside an arrow body and locates the gate as the
`if` whose CONDITION encloses the comparison, with one hop through an
assignment, rather than guessing from punctuation. Where it cannot locate the
gate it PASSES rather than accusing — stated as the cost of that choice, because
a false red here stops all work.

**And round 5 found four more documents wrong**, each the same shape:

* `DEV_NOTES.md`'s own v4 row said "— | —" for a version wrong both ways.
* A **third** copy of the stale "Nine pages exit early" survived in the gate's
  `WHAT IT CANNOT SEE` section — the part a reader consults to decide what the
  gate covers — because round 4's search was line-based and that one wraps
  across a line break. **#768 already records that exact trap**: "a line-based
  `grep` that cannot see a phrase spanning two lines".
* "NINE `COMMENT` strings containing ` -- `, one of which this package wrote"
  was wrong in both halves: it is EIGHT and this package wrote none — the one
  it did write was removed four commits later. True when written, wrong in the
  very next commit of the same package, and migration 253's own header said
  eight all along, so two shipping documents disagreed about one count.
* The withdrawn "has never run and never will" still stood as fact in
  `ScheduledJobs.php` and in migration 253's header, quoting a page sentence
  that no longer exists. D-071 has a note rather than an edit, the register
  being append-only.

**The all-clear also claimed an allowance it does not have.** It said "inside
the time expected for that job", and six of the eleven jobs on the 36-hour
default say in their own headers that they are called every 5 to 60 minutes —
so three of them 35 hours late read as "15 of the 15 recorded a FINISH", with
todo "Nothing", while the outgoing-webhook retry sweep was dead. The sentence now
names the four figures and says a job called every few minutes can be hours late
and still count. **The figure is the owner's (D-070) and is unchanged; the
measured fact is put to them as #793**, which is the register's route for a fact
that unsettles a recorded answer.

And `$unreadable` asserted "the place this is kept EXISTS" — true of one of its
two sources and not of the other, since the mail-queue catch takes any
throwable including the table being absent, and `tblMailRouteState` arrives at
migration 216 against this package's 253.

#### Round 6: the detector is GONE, because the property was never one a source reading could answer

**Round 6 found v5 wrong in both directions — the fourth version running — and
then found the shape that settles the design question.** A gate the REQUEST
decides whether to apply:

    if (($_GET['debug'] ?? '') !== '1') {
        if ($expected === '' || hash_equals(…) === false) { exit; }
    }

Every committed guard stayed green, and over real HTTP a request carrying
`?debug=1` was not refused, wrote `began()`, and ran the outgoing-webhook retry
sweep.

**And driving it does not catch that either** — measured, not assumed: with the
wrapper planted, the driven test stayed at 196 of 196, because a wrong token
sent WITHOUT `?debug=1` meets the gate and is properly refused. It is reachable
only by sending the magic parameter, and no test can guess one.

So neither half could do the whole job, and **D-065 is the owner's own rule for
exactly this**: where the property is "this code RUNS", drive it; where it is
"this code LOOKS like this", pin it. The split is now honest:

* **"Does this gate refuse?" is BEHAVIOURAL and is DRIVEN** — section I-ALL
  sends a wrong token and no token to ALL FIFTEEN pages and reads the row back,
  where the old section covered two. `&& false` on a gate's condition fails it;
  so does a missing exit, an inverted condition, and every shape the five
  detectors argued about.
* **"Is the gate NESTED?" is STRUCTURAL and is pinned** — `gate_enclosures()`
  asks what blocks enclose it, and the rule is that each must have been opened
  by `try`, because a `try` cannot decide whether its body runs while an `if`,
  a loop, a `switch` or a function can. Measured across all fifteen: fourteen
  at file scope, `health.php` inside its own `try`, so this is a general rule
  rather than an exception for one file.

`gate_refuses()` and its five versions are **deleted**. The lesson is not that
the fifth pattern was bad: it is that **four of the five versions were wrong in
BOTH directions, which is what a check tells you when it is being asked a
question of the wrong kind.**

**The new check has its own committed test**, rewritten for the nesting rule —
eleven cases then (fifteen after round 7, below), eight that must be refused
and three allowed, with **both counts pinned**, because round 6 showed the previous version's were not: deleting the
two cases that cost rounds 4 and 5 left it printing "20 of 20" and exit 0, the
total being `len(CASES)`.

**Round 7 then found the nesting check wrong both ways — the pattern of this
whole package, one level down — and it was the last round.** Every finding was
in a check, a test or a document, and none in the portal, so under D-064 and
D-066 review closed there; what is left is on issues. The four fixed:

| shape | was | now |
|---|---|---|
| `\hash_equals(…)` at file scope | NO GATE, with a security accusation (false RED) | allowed |
| a bare `{ … }`, `namespace X { }` | refused as "T_BLOCK" (false RED) | allowed: it cannot skip its body |
| `if (…) { $s = "{$x}"; gate }` | the string's `}` popped the `if`: allowed (false PASS) | refused |
| `if (Foo::try()) { gate }` | the method name replaced the `if`: allowed (false PASS) | refused |

The rule now lives in ONE function, `nesting_problem()`, and the gate's test
asks it — it used to hold its own copy, `kind != "T_TRY"`, so it could not have
noticed the rule change at all (#647). Each fix was planted back out and failed
exactly its own case. **Still invisible, and on #794:** the
alternative syntax (`if (…): … endif;`), which opens no brace, and a magic
parameter folded into the gate's own condition or guarding its `exit`, neither
of which nests anything.

**And the all-clear was STILL untrue.** Round 5's replacement named FOUR
allowances when there are FIVE: `cron/import-feeds` has six hours, fell under
"36 hours for the rest", and was told to an administrator as SIX TIMES its real
figure — and the same comment called 36 hours "the longest of them" when eight
days is. **Nothing read a character past "recorded a FINISH"**, so reverting the
whole sentence left every guard green. The figures are now DERIVED from JOBS by
`ScheduledJobs::allowancesInWords()` — typing them out was wrong in two
consecutive rounds — and H0c3 asks for every distinct allowance by name, so a
figure the page omits fails.

Round 6 also found the comment eight lines above the `$unreadable` fix still
asserting "The record is THERE and could not be read", which the comment below
it forbids, both inside round 5's own hunk — and the customer-facing CHANGELOG
still carrying the withdrawn cadence claim, which now states the allowances and
says plainly that a task called every few minutes can be well over a day late
and still read as healthy.

#### Two guards, and what each cannot see

`tools/audit-checks/check_scheduled_jobs_recorded.py` (a hard gate in
`pr-security.yml`) reads the SOURCE with PHP's tokeniser — **not a text search,
because every one of these pages quotes its own token gate in a docblock**, so a
search for `hash_equals` finds the prose. It requires every registered `cron/`
address to be listed and every listed entry to be a real address (both ways),
one `began()` and at least one `finished()` per page with its OWN key, and —
the security property — **the start recorded AFTER the token gate**: a request
with the wrong token that could write there would let anybody on the internet
make a dead job look alive, turning the page from a true report into a
forgeable one.

It states its blind spots (five, counted from the file rather than written here). `finished()` could be moved up next to `began()` and
it would pass. And **one exit path losing its finish is invisible** — because a
page may legitimately hold several finishes, it requires only one. That is the
exact fault this package shipped, so it is planted and recorded green rather
than left implicit. Requiring a finish before every `exit()` was tried and
rejected: the NORMAL end of these pages is also an `exit()`, and ONE
(`health.php`) ends inside a `catch` that RE-THROWS, where recording nothing is
correct.

**That said "two" in four places, and the count was never run.** PHP's
tokeniser finds `T_THROW` exactly ONCE under `web/_apps/cron/`:

    php -r 'foreach (glob("web/_apps/cron/*.php") as $f)
            foreach (token_get_all(file_get_contents($f)) as $x)
            if (is_array($x) && $x[0] === T_THROW) echo basename($f)." line ".$x[2]."\n";'
    health.php line 321

The conclusion survives on the first half alone — the normal end really is an
`exit()` — so this is an overstated piece of evidence rather than a wrong
decision. It is still the shape this repository keeps recording, and it is the
fifth wrong count in two packages.

#### The independent check found four PORTAL faults, and three were reassuring sentences

All three are this package's own headline fault reached from a new direction: a
word or a number carrying more than it can, put in front of an administrator.

**1. The all-clear asserted a finish for a job that was still running.** A run
with no finish yet, inside its own threshold, answered `RECENT` — and
`scheduledJobs()` had no branch for it, so it fell through every test and was
swept into *"Every scheduled job has run recently enough … All 15 of them
recorded a finish"*. Fourteen had. **The cost is not a corner case:** a nightly
backup that dies part-way at 02:00 — the state the whole design calls "the state
worth reporting" — was reported as an all-clear for the next 36 hours, through
the morning somebody would look; and a busy portal's mail job is mid-run often
enough that the false sentence showed routinely. `RUNNING_NOW` is its own status
now, said separately, and the all-clear counts only the jobs it can speak for.
**Why nothing caught it: C4 pinned the CLASSIFICATION and section G drove the
page only with everything finished or one job overdue. No check asked what the
PAGE said in C4's state.**

**2. `refused` was worded as "switched off by a setting" when it means three
things.** The class documented all three — a setting switches it off, another
run holds the lock, or nothing was due — and the page named the first. Every
clause was then false in the commonest state: nothing switched off, the work
being done, and no setting to go and look at. **And it IS the commonest state:**
`backup-run` records `refused` whenever the newest snapshot is not old enough,
so on a weekly schedule the nightly call refuses six nights in seven and on a
monthly one 27 in 28 — so the last outcome on record is `refused` nearly always
and the page told the administrator their backup was switched off, permanently.
The finding now says what is known — the job ran and chose to do nothing — and
lists the three reasons rather than asserting one. Recording WHICH reason needs
a column and every caller to pass it, which is #791.

**3. The one WARNING the page used to give about a stopped mail job was deleted,
and its evidence survives the upgrade.** `tblMailRouteState.jobLastRanAt` has
real history; `tblScheduledJobRun` is empty on upgrade day (D-071, correctly).
Measured against the SAME database, old page and new: the old one gave a warning
with an action, the new one a note saying "Nothing". **The stated reason for
dropping it — "reading both would let one page give two answers about one job" —
does not apply at the moment the new source has no answer at all.** The older
reading is used for the mail queue alone, only while the new record is silent,
and stops the moment it records once.

**4. The overdue sentence asserted a token is set while the finding above it said
the opposite.** `state()` never looks at a token, so one answer contradicted
itself whenever a token was cleared after the job had run. A job with no token is
left out of every later finding, because the token finding already covers it.

#### And the hard gate's one security property was bypassable two ways

Neither was in its blind-spot list, while three documents said it "pins the
security property".

**A gate that EXISTS but does not REFUSE.** Deleting `exit();` from a token block
left `php -l` clean and the gate at exit 0, printing *"with the start after its
token gate"* — while the self-test went to 80 passed, 3 failed, with I2, I4 and
I6 ("and NOTHING was recorded") red. That is an unauthenticated request writing
the record. **This repository had already recorded that lesson twice** (#668's
section D, and `gdpr-coverage-selftest.php`: "Every gate must REFUSE, not merely
exist"). `gate_refuses()` then walked the block and required an `exit` or
`die` inside it — and was later DELETED with its other four versions (round 6,
below).

**`hash_equals(` inside an ordinary string literal.** `php_code_only()` kept
string CONTENTS — while its own docblock said it removed them, which is what
made this invisible to a reader — so one line,
`$why = 'compared with hash_equals( so timing gives nothing away';`, placed
`began()` above the real gate with the gate green, all 66 scripts green and the
self-test at 83 of 83. On `cron/retention-sweep`, the job whose description is
"clearing out personal data past the period this portal said it would keep it".
Contents are blanked now except a `cron/...` key, and heredoc bodies with them.

#### The route list read the schema as raw text

`re.findall(r"'(cron/[a-z0-9-]+)'", text)` over the whole file — in the check
whose own docstring makes the point that a text search finds prose. Measured:
one added comment line, `-- An old address we removed in migration 99:
'cron/old-tidy' is gone.`, made it report a registered job that does not exist
and **block every pull request** until somebody added a `JOBS` entry for it.
`full_schema.sql` is eleven thousand lines of commentary, so that is a question
of when. It also ignored statement kind, so a route removed by a `DELETE` still
read as registered — `seeded_switches()`'s measured fault in #675. Comments are
blanked **tracking quoted strings** (#788's lesson, from this same package),
only `INSERT INTO tblRoutes` is read, and a `DELETE` takes an address away.

`tools/scheduled-jobs-selftest.php` (real MySQL; count the checks from the
file) covers what the
source cannot: section H drives two real pages over HTTP, including a
**switched-off** one, and reads the row back; section I proves a wrong token
records NOTHING. Portal faults were planted and each turned a named check
red — **count them from `tools/scheduled-jobs-selftest.php`'s plant suite, which prints its own total; the figure here was stale within one round** — including the blind spot, one threshold for all fifteen, and
"nothing is known" reported as a warning.

**It drives two of fifteen. The other thirteen are #789**, and that is said in
the file rather than left to be discovered.

### A page that checks the portal against itself (#477, migration 249)

**`Portal\Core\PortalCheck` is the ONE place the checks live**, and
`/admin/check` only draws what it returns. It takes a connection and a site id,
returns findings, and opens nothing of its own.

**It is a different question from the health page, and the two are easy to
confuse.** `/admin/maintenance/health` asks **is the server well** — database
reachable, disk, backups, errors, mail. This asks **is the installation
consistent with itself**. A portal can be perfectly healthy and still have a
menu link going nowhere. Each page links to the other.

**THE BEST THING THIS PACKAGE FOUND WAS ABOUT ITS OWN CHECK, and it came from
planting.** The first `duplicateSettings()` asked "are any settings stored
twice?", because #466 found 479 duplicate rows on every fresh install. The
self-test tried to plant a duplicate and **the database refused it**: migration
187 put a unique key on (`settingKey`, `siteScope`), where `siteScope` is a
worked-out column holding the site number or -1 for an installation-wide row —
because MySQL never treats one empty value as equal to another (#487). With that
key present, a second row is impossible, so the scan was a clause that could not
fire. **The live question is whether the KEY is still there**, which a database
restored from a pre-187 snapshot would not have, and the moment it is absent
#466 is possible again. The check asks that, and keeps the scan only as a
backstop reported when the key is missing — the only state in which it can find
anything. **Reporting "no duplicates found" while the key does the work would be
the false reassurance this whole page exists to end.**

**Ask of every check here: can the thing it looks for still happen?** That one
was a check for a fault the schema already prevents. It is the same shape as a
clause that cannot fail, one level up — in a file whose entire subject is faults
that pass quietly.

**ONE CHECK FAILING MUST NEVER EMPTY THE REPORT.** Each is wrapped, and a check
that could not run says so as a finding of its own. If a thrown query emptied
the page, an administrator would see a clean result and conclude all was well,
which is worse than no page. Section H of the test forces it by renaming a table
the checks read, and requires the others to survive AND the broken one to be
reported as unanswered rather than clear.

**It never prints a fault's own words.** A database message can quote the value
that caused it, and this page is read by an administrator, not a developer. The
area name is enough to find it in the error log. For the same reason the
settings check prints KEYS and never values.

**FOUR THINGS WERE READ FROM MEMORY INSTEAD OF ASKED, AND TWO OF THEM WERE
WRONG ON EVERY INSTALLATION.** Two were caught before the review by calling the
code; two got through to it.

* `DbServer::classify()` returns `headline`, not `label`. Reading `label` would
  have printed an empty sentence on the page with no error anywhere — exactly
  the shape this page exists to catch. Caught by calling it.
* `Site::currentId()` does not exist; it is `Site::id()`. Caught by grepping
  for the definition.
* **The version key.** The check read `portal.version`. The portal records its
  version under `Maintenance::VERSION_SETTING` — `portal.installed_version` —
  and migration 187 **DELETES** the old key. So every correctly-upgraded portal
  was told for ever that it had not recorded its version, and the advice given
  with it could not work: pressing Upgrade writes the key the check was not
  reading. **Worse, the PROBLEM branch could never fire**, because the recorded
  value was always empty — so the stale-version fault the check exists for
  (#466, a portal reporting itself as 0.1.0) was unreachable. **A clause that
  cannot fire, in the check whose own comment congratulates itself on having
  found one.** It passed the self-test only because the TEST wrote
  `portal.version` itself — a test keeping its own copy of the rule, which this
  repository already records as proving nothing. Both now ask the class.
* **The app's page key.** The check read `$meta['route']`. `landing` is the
  page; `route` is only a prefix, and for Expenses, Kids and Worship that
  prefix is not a page at all — `/expenses` does not exist, `expenses/submit`
  does. Both of the portal's own menu builders say so in their own comments and
  resolve `landing ?? route ?? slug`. Reading `route` named those three plus
  `auth` (a core app that is not a destination) as broken, so **the only "needs
  attention" line a correct portal ever showed was noise** — and #483 says a
  check that cries wolf gets switched off, after which it catches nothing. It
  now resolves exactly as `nav.php` does and skips the same list.

**The common thread: every one was a name I was confident about.** None needed
cleverness to find — `grep -n "VERSION_SETTING" web/_core/Maintenance.php` and
`grep -n landing web/_core/apps/*.php` answer both in a second.

**The test must be idempotent, and the first version was not.** A crashed run
left one planted settings row behind; the next run inserted two more, found
three where it expected two, and reported a failure that had nothing to do with
the code. `tidyUp()` runs at both ends, every fixture is prefixed
`zz.selftest` / `zz-selftest` so it can be exact rather than sweeping, and it
also repairs a run that died between dropping the unique key and putting it
back, or between the two table renames. **Proved by running the whole test twice
in a row**, which is the only thing that actually tests idempotence.

**Who may open it is a capability (D-017), not a role in the page.**
`portal.check` ships with `staff` and an organisation may re-point it.
Deliberately not the narrowest gate: what the page shows is what a TESTER is
most likely to hit and least able to describe, so hiding it behind the smallest
possible role would reproduce the problem — the fault visible to the people who
cannot report it and invisible to the people who can.

**THE ERROR WRAPPER IS RIGHT IN PRODUCTION AND IT HID TWO DEAD CHECKS IN THE
TEST.** `run()` catches a Throwable per check so one broken query can never
empty the page. In the self-test, `AppRegistry` and `MailQueue` were never
`require`d — there is no autoloader there — so the Apps and Scheduled-jobs
checks threw "class not found", the catch turned that into a tidy "This check
could not be completed." warning, and section A was satisfied by it. **Two of
the eight checks were never executed and the run was still 32/32. That is how
the Apps fault shipped.** Section J now refuses to let ANY check report itself
as unable to run against a healthy database, because **a silent check and a
dead check look identical** — four of the eight are silent when all is well,
which is right for the page and is exactly what makes J necessary.

`App::db()` falls back to the global `$mysqli`, a seam that already exists, so
the test sets `$GLOBALS['mysqli']` rather than loading bootstrap — which would
start sessions and merge settings it has no use for.

**And the capability was added to the registry and to none of the three lists
in `capabilities-selftest.php` that exist to pin it** — whose own comments say,
in capitals, to add it in the same change. A planted wrong shipped role
(`volunteer` for `staff`) was invisible: 299 passed, 1 failed, identical, and
all 61 audit scripts green. **That is #739's worst finding re-created, in the
package after the one that wrote the rule down.** Fixed; the plant now goes red.

Tests: `tools/portal-check-selftest.php` (42 checks, real MySQL, every finding
planted AND removed, idempotent — proved by running it twice) and
`tools/capabilities-selftest.php` (310). Nothing drives the page over HTTP —
that is #776, and the capability gate is unproved until it exists.

**ROUND 2 FOUND FOUR MORE, AND TWO WERE IN ROUND 1'S OWN CORRECTIONS.**

* **"Nothing is written to the error log" was false for every finding the
  Addresses check can produce.** That check reports a `tblRoutes` row whose
  target file is missing — and that is exactly the branch `Router.php` LOGS
  ("Route target file not found", with the route key and the file). The
  unlogged 404 is the other branch, no route row at all, which produces no
  finding here. The sentence was the page's own justification and it pointed
  the administrator AWAY from the one place that already had the answer.
* **The Apps message covered two branches with opposite consequences.**
  `Router::routeExists()` reads only `routeKey` — it never looks for the file.
  So a missing route row means the menu HIDES the app, while a present row with
  a missing file means the menu DRAWS the link and clicking it 404s. Round 1
  found the original wording ("they appear in the menu and lead nowhere")
  untrue and replaced it with wording true only of the OTHER branch — the one
  the test does not plant. **Each correction was right about the branch it was
  written about and wrong about the other.** They are two findings now, with
  their own advice: one says upload the file again, the other says the app has
  no address.
* **The Help needle was unanchored, and it was live for 2 of the 19 guides.**
  `str_contains($centre, 'help/admin')` is satisfied by
  `help/admin-first-steps`, and `help/calendar` by `help/calendar-imports`.
  Measured: remove the Help Centre's card for the MAIN Calendar guide and the
  check said nothing. Round 1 deleted a clause for being able to silence a real
  finding; **the surviving clause had the same property**. Anchored with a
  look-ahead now, and section N plants it — deriving the sibling pair from the
  tree rather than naming one, so it cannot go stale.
* **The underscore guard was pinned by nothing.** `if (false)` in its place
  left all 42 checks green while the page began reporting
  `api/assets/_coerce`, a shared helper the router refuses by pattern. Sections
  F1-F3 pinned only the WARNING; nothing looked at the NOTE's contents, which
  is where the guard shows. Section M pins it.

**The pattern across both rounds: six of eleven findings were a NAME or a
SENTENCE I was confident about** — `label`, `currentId`, `portal.version`,
`route`, "nothing is written to the error log", "the menu hides it". Not one
needed cleverness to find. Each was one command away.

### One place writes the form token, and the copies were made from each other (#768)

**The rule.** `Auth::verifyCsrf()` replaces the token on every acceptance and
`Auth::csrfToken()` is ONE token per session, so after any accepted post every
carrier on the open page is stale TOGETHER. A page carries it in three places:
`<meta name="csrf-token">` (written by `header.php` on every page), every
`input[name="csrf_token"]`, and every `[data-csrf]` element (the Translate
control). `Portal.writeCsrf()` in `portal.js` is the ONE place all three are
written. Extend that; never write a carrier anywhere else.

**FIVE copies existed and no two agreed how many carriers there are:**
`rememberCsrf()` (meta only), `syncCsrf()` in `event-hub-upload.js` and again
in `report-builder.js` (meta + fields), `storeToken()` in `api-docs/index.php`
(meta only), and `shareToken()` in `portal-translate.js` (all three).

**THE CAUSE IS READABLE IN THE COMMENTS, AND THAT IS THE TRANSFERABLE PART.**
`report-builder.js` says "(event-hub-upload.js precedent)"; `api-docs` says it
follows "the event hub upload widget". **Each new page copied the NEAREST
existing version rather than a shared one**, so the INCOMPLETE rule propagated
and the complete one never did. The shared helper existed throughout and its
own comment said callers should use it "without writing their own copy of
this". **A published helper is a single source of truth only while it is the
BEST copy; the moment it is the worst, its own documentation is an instruction
nobody can follow.**

**The measured cost.** Host Console: publishing a chat prompt rotates the
token; "Send 'We're live'" (#612) sits on the same page in an ordinary form.
Publish, then press — refused, press lost. `go-live-button-selftest.php` could
not see it because it presses the button without publishing a prompt first.
**A test that exercises one control at a time cannot find a fault that needs
two controls in sequence** (#769).

**THE SHAPE IS WIDER THAN THE FIVE COPIES, AND THAT IS WHERE THE LIVE BUGS
WERE.** Looking for "writes some carriers but not all" found five files.
Looking for "spends the page's token and does not hand the replacement back"
found three more, every one of them live: **#770**, adding a passkey — the
handler rotates and returns no replacement, so step 2 reuses a spent token and
the feature cannot work at all; **#774**, push subscription — the script keeps
the fresh token in a private variable, so Save on the notification preferences
page is refused and the member's changes are lost; **#771**, the worship
console — refreshes only after a refusal. **The gate written for this package
is right to pass all three and structurally cannot see them.** Enumerate the
RULE, not the instances of it.

**The return value changed, deliberately — and the first attempt was wrong.**
`rememberCsrf()` used to answer false whenever the page had no meta tag, even
when it had found a token. The first fix made it answer true whenever a token
was found, which made `admin/host-console/event.php`'s own fallback
unreachable: it takes `csrf = Portal.csrf() || csrf; return;`, `Portal.csrf()`
read only the meta tag and answered empty, so it kept the SPENT token where the
old code had kept a fresh one. Two changes fix it together — the answer is now
`writeCsrf()`'s own (was it really stored), and `Portal.csrf()` reads every
carrier, meta first so that no page which has one can behave differently.
**The trap is LATENT, not live:** both pages that branch on it require
`header.php`, which writes the meta tag unconditionally.

**THE GUARD TOOK FOUR ROUNDS AND EVERY ROUND FOUND THE PREVIOUS ROUND'S FIX.**
Findings per round: 6, 4, 5, 4 — none in the original build. Worth keeping:

* **The delegating callers were guarded by nothing**, and three one-edit
  changes killed them with every check green. A call-site pin cannot catch an
  inserted `return;` (#709). Each function's body is pinned — and then round 2
  defeated THAT twice, with a second `function syncCsrf` declaration (the later
  one wins in JavaScript) and a reassignment. **#485 records both spellings and
  says the remedy is to pin the whole file**; I wrote #709's lesson into the
  comment and shipped #485's beaten pattern underneath it. Exactly one
  declaration and no reassignment are now required. The whole-file pin is still
  not used here, because these are large feature files that change for
  unrelated reasons and a pin that goes red constantly gets switched off
  (#483). That trade is recorded, and #773 is the stronger answer.
* **"Has a carrier" and "writes a carrier" are different questions.** Conflating
  them cried wolf on EIGHTEEN correct pages. And "selects a csrf field" plus
  "has a `.value =` somewhere" is not "writes a csrf field" — two true facts
  about one file joined into a false one.
* **FOUR versions of the write detector, three with holes, each "verified by
  planting".** Each planted the forms its author had thought of. v3's own
  comment said *planting one form of a pattern does not test the pattern*, and
  v3 then did it: 48 of 152 lookup × write combinations missed, including
  `for (const f of Array.from(...))`, which is house idiom here
  (`livechat-widget.js`, 12 uses under `web/`). **v4 stopped enumerating
  syntax**: find the statement a lookup sits in, collect every name it binds,
  ask whether any is written. Wrappers, spreads, destructures, `for…of` and
  callbacks are covered without being named. 152/152 and 21/21, no false
  positives.
* **A `//` in raw HTML is not a comment.** The blanker had to become a
  three-state machine (HTML / PHP / script): applying JavaScript rules
  everywhere blanked real code after a URL, and applying HTML rules outside
  `<?php` cried wolf on a `/* */` inside a `<script>`. Both directions wrong;
  model the file.

**AND THE DOCUMENTATION FAILED IN WAYS THE CODE DID NOT.** Rounds 3 and 4 found
almost nothing but untrue comments — several written by earlier rounds to
explain their own fixes. Three worth naming:

* **"The first browser test here" was false.** `tools/layout-audit.mjs` has
  driven Edge over the DevTools protocol since `0186531` (30 October 2026), for
  #569 — the identical technique, six days earlier. Established by
  `grep -rln "remote-debugging-port" tools/`, a command that was not run before
  the claim was written. It even records the node-22 fact that had been called
  unmeasured.
* **A correction applied to one docblock and not its twin 120 lines away** in
  the same file. The instance fixed, the class left open.
* **Verifying a correction with a line-based `grep` that could not see it.**
  The phrase spanned two lines of an f-string, so `grep -c` answered 0 and the
  corrections were reported as applied when three of four had never been
  written — the script had raised `SystemExit` before saving. **A tool
  structurally incapable of finding the thing is not a verification.**

And once, checking whether `layout-audit.mjs` ran in CI, `grep` answered with
**the comment about it written minutes earlier** — #647's shape, nearly turning
a true statement into a false one. Ask for the `run:` line, not the name.

Guards: `tools/audit-checks/check_one_csrf_writer.py` (a hard gate; checks A-F,
failing both ways) and `tools/csrf-carriers-selftest.mjs` (18 checks in a real
browser, nothing installed — it serves its own fixture from node's `http`
module, so it needs neither PHP nor a driver). The browser test proves the
helper; it cannot prove that any given page calls it, which is #773.

### The volunteer photo tier is a real gate now, and that takes photos away (#756, D-047)

**A behaviour change, decided by the owner on 4 November 2026 — D-047 — and not
a tidy-up.** `Photos::userTierRank()` checked for the `volunteer` role and
returned 1; the line immediately below it returned 1 as well, for every
signed-in member, "to keep portals where role rollout is partial functional".
So the gate decided nothing, and had not since `8625b9e`.

The comment beside the fall-through said access was granted "ONLY if you've
explicitly granted them — the role check above gates that". **That was untrue in
the reassuring direction**, which is the shape this repository keeps being burned
by. Asked which of the two was intended, the owner chose the comment.

So the fall-through returns 0, the rung became real, and a real rung is a
capability (D-017): `Capabilities::PHOTOS_VOLUNTEER`, shipping pointed at
`volunteer`, falling open for a global administrator like the rest.

**What it costs somebody:** a signed-in member holding neither tier now sees what
a visitor sees. Nothing shared with everybody is lost — `canView()` lets a
`public` photo through before it asks about rank at all, checked in that method
and in the three pages that read the ladder (`photos/index.php`,
`photos/album.php`, and `canView()` for `view.php` and `serve.php`).

**Hard-coded role gates are down to two**, both taking their key from a row a
customer filled in, so neither is a page gate.

### Why #739 was right to leave it, and why converting it alone would have been wrong

#739 deliberately did not convert this one, and that was correct: making it a
capability while both branches returned 1 would have put a switch on the Roles
page that **cannot change what any member sees** — #671's "a seeded setting that
nothing reads is a lie with a Save button" wearing a capability's clothes. It
would also have **hidden the real question**, which was a product decision and
not a refactor.

**The order matters: settle what the gate should DO, then convert it.**

### Nothing drove the ladder, which is how the no-op survived

Measured with `grep -rln userTierRank tools/`, which answered only
`check_no_new_role_gates.py` — and that reads it as TEXT. No test anywhere called
`Photos::userTierRank()`. That is how a rung that decided nothing lived from
`8625b9e` to 4 November 2026 with a comment claiming the opposite.

It cannot be driven cheaply from the capability test either: the method asks
`Auth::check()`, `App::isAdmin()` and `App::can()`, all of which read the
session. So what is pinned is the fall-through's own value, with comments
stripped. **Both plants were measured:** putting `return 1;` back fails one
check, and bringing `App::hasRole('volunteer')` back fails three here and the
hard gate as well.

**And section O must not be read as proof this changed nothing.** It proves
`photos.volunteer` answers exactly what `App::hasRole('volunteer')` answered,
which is true of the GATE and says nothing about the ladder — before #756 the
line after the gate returned 1 regardless. A note beside the new checks says so,
because reading section O the other way is the "a check that pins a reassurance"
shape.

### Two wording faults found while doing it

`PHOTOS_STAFF`'s `emptyMeans` ended "Albums shared with volunteers … are not
affected — every signed-in member already reaches that tier", which this change
makes false. And a check in the capability self-test was labelled "**twelve**
capabilities are offered", which went red on the thirteenth — the check working,
but **the label was a list named after a number**, the shape #739 recorded as the
one that goes stale. Two things in that file had already been renamed for exactly
that reason and this label was missed; it is named for its job now.

## The erasure review's two races (#735)

*4 November 2026.*

Two guards were backstops no test reached. Both are driven by real code now, in
sections S and T of `tools/erasure-review-selftest.php`.

### "No test can reach this" was a wrong conclusion from a true fact

`GdprEraser::closeRequest()`'s comment said no end-to-end test exercises the
second `whyNotReadyToClose()` ask "because the test harness runs one request at
a time". The fact is true. **The conclusion does not follow**, and that is the
transferable lesson: the thing being described is not two concurrent requests,
it is a row appearing between two points of ONE run — and that run is
sequential. Top check, every step, then the close. Anything that writes a
reviewable row in the middle of it reaches the second ask.

So the question to ask of any "this path cannot be reached" comment is **which
two events have to be ordered**, not how many actors there are. Here the answer
was one actor and one run, and the comment had reasoned from actors.

A database trigger on `tblErasureAudit` provides the write, because every step
of the walk writes a line there. This repository already had the technique:
`tools/password-writer-selftest.php` section H uses a `BEFORE UPDATE` trigger to
reach a state the portal cannot produce on demand.

### What the deleted ask really costs

Measured, not reasoned. With the ask removed, a run over 233 steps reports
`failed: 0`, the request goes to `completed`, and the person's own words are
still in the row. The review's whole purpose is that this cannot happen.

### Why section R could not catch the lock being deleted, and T can

R1 to R4 take the row lock **in the test**. So they prove the database locks,
not that `record()` asks it to — deterministic and vacuous, which is worse than
flaky. Section T never takes the lock on the method's behalf: this connection
holds the row, and the real `record()` runs in its own process and blocks on it.

**A second process is not a convenience here.** The decider under test has to be
blocked while the test carries on, and one process cannot wait on itself. Two
connections driven one after another from one process cannot produce this
ordering, however carefully they are interleaved.

### The harm, read out of `record()` rather than guessed

Without ` FOR UPDATE`, the second decider's in-transaction read is a
consistent-snapshot read taken before the other decider committed. It therefore
still sees the words, carries on, and writes `keep` — and the decision is
written with `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`, so that `keep` lands on top of the other
decision. The record then says the words are still there over a cell somebody
else emptied.

Note what the unique key `uq_errd_item` does and does not do. No part of it can
be empty, so unlike the #487 case it really binds — but `record()` writes with
`ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`, so the key **merges** the second decision rather than
refusing it. The key is not a substitute for the lock, and a reader who checked
only the key would conclude it was.

### How the order is forced

The shape #687 used for the giving-records ceiling: an external session holds
the lock, and the path under test runs against it. This connection empties the
cell **directly** rather than through `record()` — deliberately, because that is
what the other decider's `record('empty')` does to the cell, and doing it by
hand is what lets the lock be held open across the worker's arrival.

Measured three runs out of three with ` FOR UPDATE` deleted: R1 to R4 green,
T2 and T3 red.

### Keep both kinds of check

R5 pins the method's text; T reads its behaviour. Neither covers the other's
half, and the temptation after building T is to delete R5 as redundant. It is
not: T would still pass if `record()` were rewritten to take the lock some other
way, and R5 would still pass if the lock were taken outside the transaction.

### The section written because R was vacuous was itself vacuous at the margins

Found by the independent check, and it is the most useful thing in the package
because it is the SAME SHAPE one level up.

`record()` refuses an already-empty line in **two** places: before its
transaction, where `oneItem()` finds the line is no longer a review item at all,
and inside it under the lock. T2 matched only the word `REFUSED`, so it could
not tell them apart — while its own label asserted the second one.

Measured: with a short sleep the worker returns the FIRST refusal, so **at a
sleep of zero the whole of section T was green in both states, lock or no
lock.** The 1.5-second sleep was the only thing making T non-vacuous, and
**nothing asserted it had been long enough.** With the lock removed, T2 went red
at a sleep of 50ms or more and green at 20ms or less — about a 40-times margin
on this machine, narrower on a loaded runner, and the direction of failure is
FALSE GREEN on the one check that proves the lock behaviourally.

Two changes turn the timing assumption into an asserted premise: T2 requires the
in-transaction wording (`already empty`), and T1b asserts the worker is still
blocked when the line is emptied. **Be exact about which one closes the hole:**
at a sleep of zero T1b still passes, because the worker has not been exec'd yet
and so counts as running; the check that goes red is T2. A first version of
T1b's comment claimed otherwise, which is a claim about a measurement that was
never made.

**The transferable rule: when a test's verdict depends on a sleep, assert the
state the sleep was supposed to produce.** A sleep is a hope; a `proc_get_status`
or a wording requirement is a premise.

### A clause that cannot fail, in the check meant to name a requirement

`mysqli_report(MYSQLI_REPORT_ERROR | MYSQLI_REPORT_STRICT)` makes mysqli THROW
on a statement error — **it takes both flags**, which this repository had to
learn twice (#694 rounds 5 and 6, where "measured, not reasoned" was written
beside a measurement of the wrong code path). So `$db->query('CREATE TRIGGER …')`
never returns `false`, and `S2`'s `=== true` was true whatever happened.

The harm was not the dead check but the DOCUMENTATION resting on it: four places
claimed the `CREATE TRIGGER` requirement was "refused loudly" and "says so at
the point of failure". It said nothing at all — a user without that privilege
got an uncaught exception and a stack trace naming no requirement, with no red
check and no summary line. **A check whose failure mode is an uncaught exception
is not a check that reports; it is a crash with a label.**

### What this still does not prove

Sections S and T drive the CLASSES. Nothing presses two buttons on `review.php`
at once, so what is proved is that `ErasureReview` and `GdprEraser` behave, not
that the page cannot submit in a way that avoids them.

## Installing PHP on your own machine

### Why you need it

The portal is written in PHP, but PHP is not part of this repository — it is a
program that has to be installed on whatever computer you are working on. Two
things stop working without it:

1. **Visual Studio Code cannot check your PHP files as you type.** It shows the
   message *"Cannot validate since a PHP installation could not be found. Use
   the setting 'php.validate.executablePath' to configure the PHP executable."*
2. **You cannot run the same syntax check that the build server runs.** When a
   pull request is opened, the "PR Security Checks" job runs `php -l` over
   every PHP file in `web/`, and a single typo fails the whole build. That is a
   hard gate — nothing merges past it. Running the same check yourself before
   pushing turns a ten-minute round trip into a two-second one.

You do **not** need a web server, a database, or Composer on your own machine
for this. You only need the `php` command itself, so it can read your files and
tell you whether they are valid. The portal is served on shared hosting, which
supplies its own PHP.

### Which version

The project targets **PHP 8.5** and stays backward compatible with **8.4**.
Install 8.5 if your system offers it; 8.4 is fine too. Anything older than 8.4
will report errors on perfectly valid code, because it does not understand the
newer syntax the project uses.

### macOS

The usual way is Homebrew, a package manager for macOS. Check whether you
already have it:

```bash
brew --version
```

If that prints a version number, install PHP with:

```bash
brew install php
php --version          # confirm — expect 8.5.x
```

If `brew --version` says "command not found", install Homebrew first by
following the one-line instruction on <https://brew.sh>, then close and reopen
your terminal and run the two commands above.

Homebrew puts PHP at `/opt/homebrew/bin/php` on Apple Silicon Macs (M1 and
later) and at `/usr/local/bin/php` on older Intel Macs. Confirm which one with:

```bash
which php
```

**If you would rather not use Homebrew**, download a ready-made build from
<https://php.net/downloads> or use MAMP (<https://www.mamp.info>), which bundles
PHP with a web server. MAMP hides its copy of PHP inside the application
folder, at a path like
`/Applications/MAMP/bin/php/php8.5.0/bin/php` — you will need that full path
for the Visual Studio Code setting below.

### Windows

1. Go to <https://windows.php.net/download> and download the **Thread Safe**
   ZIP file for the newest 8.5 release, 64-bit (labelled `x64`).
2. Unzip it to a folder with no spaces in the name, for example `C:\php`.
3. In that folder, copy `php.ini-development` and rename the copy to `php.ini`.
4. Add `C:\php` to your PATH, which is the list of folders Windows searches
   when you type a command:
   press the Start button, type *"Edit the system environment variables"*, open
   it, click **Environment Variables**, select **Path** under *User variables*,
   click **Edit**, click **New**, and enter `C:\php`. Click OK on every window.
5. Close and reopen your terminal, then check it worked:

   ```powershell
   php --version
   ```

Two alternatives, if you would rather not do the above by hand:

- **Chocolatey** (a package manager for Windows): `choco install php`
- **Laragon** or **XAMPP**: bundles that install PHP together with a web server
  and a database. Their PHP lives at a path such as
  `C:\laragon\bin\php\php-8.5.0\php.exe` or `C:\xampp\php\php.exe`.

### Linux (Debian, Ubuntu, Linux Mint)

The version in the standard Ubuntu and Debian repositories is often older than
8.4. The usual fix is Ondřej Surý's PPA, a well-known third-party source that
packages current PHP releases for these systems.

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y software-properties-common
sudo add-apt-repository -y ppa:ondrej/php     # Ubuntu / Mint
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y php8.5-cli
php --version
```

On **Debian** the PPA command above does not apply. Use Ondřej Surý's Debian
repository instead — the current instructions are at
<https://deb.sury.org/> — then `sudo apt install -y php8.5-cli`.

`php8.5-cli` is the command-line build. It is all you need for syntax checking;
there is no need for `php8.5-fpm`, Apache or Nginx.

### Linux (Fedora, RHEL, Rocky, AlmaLinux)

```bash
sudo dnf install -y php-cli
php --version
```

If that installs something older than 8.4, add the Remi repository, which
packages current PHP releases for these systems — instructions at
<https://rpms.remirepo.net/> — then select the 8.5 module and install `php-cli`
again.

### Raspberry Pi

Raspberry Pi OS is built on Debian, so it follows the Debian instructions
above. The version that ships in the standard repository is usually too old, so
use Ondřej Surý's Debian repository:

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y apt-transport-https lsb-release ca-certificates curl
curl -sSLo /tmp/debsuryorg-archive-keyring.deb \
  https://packages.sury.org/debsuryorg-archive-keyring.deb
sudo dpkg -i /tmp/debsuryorg-archive-keyring.deb
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/deb.sury.org-php.gpg] \
  https://packages.sury.org/php/ $(lsb_release -sc) main" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/php.list
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y php8.5-cli
php --version
```

This works on both 64-bit and 32-bit Raspberry Pi OS. On a Pi Zero or an older
Pi the install takes several minutes — that is normal, not a hang.

### Pointing Visual Studio Code at it

Once `php --version` works in a terminal, tell the editor where PHP is. Find
the full path first:

```bash
which php        # macOS, Linux, Raspberry Pi
where php        # Windows
```

Then open Visual Studio Code's settings (**Code → Settings → Settings**, or
`Ctrl`/`Cmd` + `,`), search for `php.validate.executablePath`, and paste that
path in. Typical values:

| System | Typical path |
| --- | --- |
| macOS, Apple Silicon (Homebrew) | `/opt/homebrew/bin/php` |
| macOS, Intel (Homebrew) | `/usr/local/bin/php` |
| Linux / Raspberry Pi | `/usr/bin/php` |
| Windows | `C:\php\php.exe` |

Restart Visual Studio Code. The "could not be found" message should be gone.

Do **not** commit this setting to the repository. The right path is different
on every machine, so it belongs in your personal settings, or in a
`.vscode/settings.json` inside the project folder — which is deliberately
listed in `.gitignore` for exactly this reason.

### Running the same check the build server runs

From the repository root:

```bash
find ./web -type f -name "*.php" \
  -not -path "*/vendor/*" \
  -not -path "*/_libraries/*" \
  -print0 | xargs -0 -n1 -P4 php -l
```

That is character-for-character the command in
`.github/workflows/pr-security.yml`. Silence, or a run of "No syntax errors
detected" lines, means you are clear. Any other output is a real error that
will fail the build, and it names the file and line number.

On Windows, run that command from Git Bash or Windows Subsystem for Linux
(WSL), because `find` and `xargs` are not PowerShell commands. The PowerShell
equivalent is:

```powershell
Get-ChildItem -Path .\web -Recurse -Filter *.php |
  Where-Object { $_.FullName -notmatch '\\(vendor|_libraries)\\' } |
  ForEach-Object { php -l $_.FullName }
```

### What you still cannot do locally

Installing PHP lets you check that files are *syntactically* valid. It does not
let you run the portal, because that also needs a web server, a MySQL 8.0
database, and the credentials in `_auth_keys/` which are never committed. To
exercise the database migrations, use the end-to-end harness described under
**End-to-end migration test (#248)** further down this document — it runs in
CI against real MySQL 8.0.36 and 8.4.11 databases, as two jobs side by side.

## Transcription: a reserved word, a nested form, and a double bill (#276, migration 229)

Four separate faults, each invisible to every check this repository already ran.
Worth reading as a set, because none of them was a typo — each was something that
*looked* finished.

### `fullText` is the reserved word `FULLTEXT`

```sql
SELECT fullText FROM tblTranscript;          -- ERROR 1064
SELECT t.fullText FROM tblTranscript t;      -- fine: qualified
SELECT `fullText` FROM tblTranscript;        -- fine: quoted
UPDATE tblTranscript SET fullText = ?;       -- ERROR 1064
UPDATE tblTranscript SET `fullText` = ?;     -- fine
```

MySQL matches keywords without regard to case, so the camel-case column name is
the keyword. The statement in `Transcription::processQueue()` that **saves a
finished transcript** was written with a bare `fullText = ?` and therefore could
never run. The connection is strict, so `prepare()` throws — **after** the
transcription company has been called and charged. Nothing noticed, because no
page could queue a recording in the first place, so the statement had never been
reached.

Both other readers of the column were fine by accident of style: `transcript.php`
and `stateFor()` both qualify it with a table alias. The schema quotes it.

**Ask of any camel-case column whether its name is a keyword.** `php -l` cannot
see this, and neither can any audit script here — only running the statement can.

### A form inside a form is not a form

The Transcription page's "Process next" button sat inside the configuration
form, with its own `<form action=".../run">` wrapper. HTML forbids nested forms:
a parser that meets a second `<form>` while one is open **drops the tag and keeps
its contents**, so the button's owner became the Save form. Pressing "Process
next" posted the settings, reported "Transcription settings saved", and drained
nothing. It was the only control that could work the queue.

Measured rather than argued about, with PHP 8.4's own spec-compliant parser:

```php
$doc = \Dom\HTMLDocument::createFromString($markup);
$doc->getElementsByTagName('form')->length;   // 1, not 2
```

**Searching the markup cannot find this**, because the markup looks correct. The
check that guards it (`formActionOwning()` in
`tools/transcription-pages-selftest.php`, section K) asks the parsed document
which form owns the button, and a companion check compares the number of `<form`
tags written with the number that survive parsing — so any nested form anywhere
on the page goes red.

### Two writers of one queue state, and only one lock

`queue()` and `processQueue()` both write `tblTranscript.status`. The sweep's
conditional `UPDATE … WHERE status = 'queued'` was right as far as it went and
could not stop this interleaving:

1. `queue()` reads `queued` and decides to re-queue.
2. The sweep flips the row to `processing` and calls the company.
3. `queue()` writes `queued` over it.
4. The next sweep sends **the same audio** and is charged again.

Both now take `SELECT … FROM tblRecording WHERE recordingID = ? FOR UPDATE`
first — the **recording's** row, not the transcript's, because the transcript row
may not exist yet and there is nothing to lock in a row that is not there. The
provider call happens after the transaction is committed: a lock must never be
held across a twenty-five-minute HTTP request.

**Refusing outright was the wrong fix and introduced a worse fault.** Shared
hosting kills long requests without warning, leaving the row at `processing` for
ever, and a flat refusal wedged that recording permanently. Hence
`tblTranscript.startedAt` and `STUCK_AFTER_MINUTES` (120): the refusal is
"processing **and started recently**". `startedAt` is on the server's own clock
to match `queuedAt` and `generatedAt`, and is only ever compared against `NOW()`
on that same clock — so the comparison is right in any zone, and on the two
nights the clocks change a wedged row is freed after 60 or 180 minutes instead of
120. Harmless, and said rather than hidden. (The mail queue stores UTC and is the
better pattern; changing half of one table's columns would have made this
comparison wrong, so it was left alone.)

### What the harness cannot prove, and what was done instead

The HTTP harness runs the built-in server with one worker
(`PHP_CLI_SERVER_WORKERS` unset), so **two requests never overlap** and the race
the lock exists for cannot be created. Removing the lock-based refusal leaves
every behavioural check green — measured by planting it. The same limitation is
recorded for the expense payment race.

So section Q does what is possible: it extracts each method's body with **PHP's
own tokenizer** (a brace-counting walk over raw text has already been caught here
by a `{` inside a log message) and requires the lock, the whole refusal condition
and the conditional claim to still be present; then it proves with **two real
connections** that `FOR UPDATE` really blocks on this engine, with a companion
check that an unlocked read of the same row does not — so the first is about the
lock and not about something else refusing.

**A check on code text knows the guard is written, not that it runs.** Said in
the file, because the first version of that check looked for `stillRunning` and
`return 'busy'` anywhere in the body and stayed green when `&& false` was added
to the condition — the same weakness the QR-service guard had twice.

### Whose money, and whose data

One API key, stored installation-wide, pays for every organisation, and the audio
leaves the server for a third party. So `processQueue()`, `monthSpendPence()`,
`queueStatsFor()` and `recentFor()` are all scoped to one organisation — before
this, pressing "Process next" sent another organisation's audio to the company on
the installation's account, and the recent list showed other organisations'
recording titles.

`Transcription::capFrom()` is the monthly ceiling, built to the #668 rule: the
installation's figure caps the organisation's, read from
`InstallationSettings::layer()` rather than from the merged `$SETTINGS`. **What
actually carries that guarantee is the merge**, not the null test inside it: when
an organisation has chosen nothing, `$SETTINGS` already holds the installation's
figure, so `min` returns it. Resolving null to the built-in default changes no
answer in any reachable state — measured by planting it, which is how an
overstated comment claiming otherwise was caught. The null test stays for the
case of an unmerged array, and the layer the ceiling is read FROM is the thing
section J really pins.
