## Offboarding, erasure and the undo window (#569)

`offboarding/do.php` **files** an erasure request; it never erases inline. There
is ONE audited erasure path — file, confirm, run, with a hash chain over what it
did — and the Erasure requests pages drive it. A second path erasing inline
would be two pieces of code that must agree about 35 tables for ever.

`offboarding.erasureMode` decides when:

- `on_request` (the default) — it waits for a person on Admin, Erasure requests.
- `after_undo_window` — `run_offboarding_erasure_sweep()` in
  `_apps/cron/_retention-sweep.php` runs it once `offboarding.undo_window_days`
  has passed.

**Neither mode erases at the moment of offboarding**, because
`offboarding/rehire.php` exists: erasing destroys what a rehire restores.
Immediate erasure is #663 and was deliberately not built. **Undoing an
offboarding cancels any request still waiting** — without that, the default mode
left a live request to erase somebody who had come back.

### Three things the sweep gets wrong if you write it the obvious way

All three were found by an independent check before this shipped, and all three
are the kind that look fine in review:

1. **Join to the NEWEST offboarding row, not to any row for that person.** The
   first version joined `r.userID = o.userID`, so ANY row satisfied the age
   test. Proved against real MySQL: an offboarding from 2024 that was never
   undone made a request filed TODAY due on tonight's run — while the form had
   just promised the administrator seven days to change their mind. Not exotic
   either: `rehire.php` refuses an undo after the window, so anybody who left,
   returned and left again has an older row with `rehiredAt` still empty.
2. **Claim the request before running it**, with the same conditional
   `UPDATE … WHERE status = 'pending_review'` the staff page uses. Without the
   claim the row stays at `pending_review` for the whole run, so the Execute
   button stays armed and can start a second erasure of the same account; and
   `GdprEraser`'s own "put it back" and "still going" updates match nothing,
   because both look for `processing`. A run that died half way left no sign of
   life at all.
3. **Never log the fault's own words.** An earlier version logged
   `$e->getMessage()` under a comment promising it named nobody — but a database
   or filesystem message can quote the very value being erased, and that error
   row would outlive the erasure by up to a year.

**It cannot honour a per-organisation choice of mode.** `tblOffboarding` has no
organisation column — offboarding is portal-wide — and the mode is read once
from whichever organisation the scheduled request resolved to. An organisation
that saved its own override would not get it. Written down rather than
half-guarded.

### Two options on the form, because the portal does one kind of erasure

`GdprEraser` anonymises where deleting would destroy figures that must survive
and deletes only where that is safe, so "anonymise" and "delete" could never
have differed. `'anonymise'` and `'delete'` are still accepted and still valid
values of `tblOffboarding.dataDisposition`, so old audit rows read as written;
the code treats all three as "erase".

## What a settings default really means (#569, migration 225)

Migration 225 turns a switch on only where `settingValue = defaultValue` — that
is, where nobody has ever changed it. **It cannot tell a deliberate "off" from an
untouched "off"**, because both leave the value equal to the default. Accepted
because this lands before the first usable release.

Each key keeps its own vocabulary (`'false'`/`'true'` for four of them,
`'0'`/`'1'` for eleven) rather than being rewritten to one spelling, because
anything comparing those values as text would change behaviour for reasons
nothing to do with this change.

## `||` is not concatenation in MySQL

A first draft of migration 226 built its guarded `ALTER TABLE` with
`'a' || 'b'`. In MySQL that is **logical OR** unless the server runs with
`PIPES_AS_CONCAT`, so it produced the number `1` and then tried to `PREPARE`
it. Use `CONCAT()`.

## Removing a preference switch is two changes, not one

`notifications-save.php` **rebuilds** `tblUsers.notifyPrefs` from its allowed-key
list and writes the result over the whole column. So:

- Hide a switch and leave its key on the list, and the next save rewrites that
  stored preference to off — for everybody, one at a time, as they each press
  Save. The key must come off the list in the same change.
- Take the key off the list, and the stored value is **dropped** at the next
  save. That is not "left alone", which an earlier version of the comment in
  that file wrongly claimed. It is acceptable only while nothing reads the key.

The same replacing behaviour is why that page and the smaller card on `/account`
have always overwritten each other's keys — #667.

**And removing a feature must not remove the test that guards a past fault.**
Deleting the `/account` card outright broke section F of
`go-live-button-selftest.php`, the only guard proving that saving there does not
throw away a member's other choices (#612). The form was kept, with only its
still-wired switch. Section F's `count($storedNow) >= 15` was then replaced by a
named list of the keys that must survive: the count was only ever a stand-in for
the real property, and a count is exactly what a deliberate change to the number
of preferences invalidates.

## A disabled control is not submitted

Removing GoCardless from the payment picker by marking the option `disabled`
would have been worse than leaving it alone: `payments/save.php` reads
`$_POST['provider'] ?? 'stripe'`, so an installation already set to GoCardless
would have been switched to Stripe by pressing Save for any other reason. It is
shown, enabled and named for what it is.

## What a shared link looks like: the head tags (#569)

`web/_core/templates/head-meta.php` is the ONE place the description, canonical
address, Open Graph and Twitter tags are written. `header.php` requires it, and
so does every page that draws its own `<head>`. Set `$pageTitle` and, where the
page can say something better than the fallback, `$pageDescription`, before
requiring it.

**Why a separate file rather than part of `header.php`.** The pages a stranger
actually sees — the sign-in page, the forgotten-password pages, the public
visitor form, anonymous prayer requests, accepting an invitation, unsubscribing
— all print their own `<head>`, because they must not carry the portal's navbar.
Putting the tags only in `header.php` would have missed exactly the pages whose
preview card anybody is likely to see. Pasting the same twelve tags into each of
those files was rejected: the wording would then exist in a dozen copies, and
the check could only compare copies against each other.

**The canonical rule is a correctness rule, not a nicety.** Both the canonical
address and `og:url` are omitted entirely while
`PortalAddress::visitorCanChooseHost()` is true. With no `site.url` set,
`PortalAddress` falls back to the request's `Host` header, which whoever sent
the request chose; a canonical address built from that announces to search
engines and every preview service that the page really lives at a name an
outsider picked. The description is still written in that state, because it
needs no address.

**`og:image` only when a raster file is on disk.** Every service that draws
these cards refuses SVG and this portal's icons are mostly SVG, so the tag is
written only where the brand in use really has a PNG. Two of seven brand folders
do; the rest are #656. A card with no picture looks ordinary, a card with a
picture that will not load looks broken. `twitter:card` is `summary`, not
`summary_large_image`, because the picture is a square 512 and the wide card
stretches a square into a half-empty banner.

### Do not count the "own head" pages by searching for them

Three reasonable searches written while building this gave **27, 15 and 12**, and
all three were wrong in different ways:

- A file's doctype may sit inside an **e-mail body built as a PHP string**, which
  is not a page head at all. Two of the "missing a title" pages found that way
  were e-mail templates.
- Several pages print their own `<head>` for the main view **and** include
  `header.php` for an error branch, so "own head" is not a property of a whole
  file.

The list that matters is the exemption list in
`tools/audit-checks/check_page_head_tags.py`, which names each exempt file and
why. The exempt ones are PDFs, e-mail previews, kiosk and wall-display screens and
the embeddable widget — none of them an address a person shares. The most
interesting member of that list is `admin/maintenance/backup.php`, the recovery
screen shown when a backup or restore had to leave the portal closed: it is
exempt because `head-meta.php` asks `PortalAddress` and the settings, which
READ THE DATABASE, and that page exists for the case where the database
connection had to be closed. Adding the tags there could break the one page
that says how to reopen the portal.

(An earlier version of this paragraph also listed "the XML podcast feed". It
is not on the list: `recordings/podcast.php` builds its XML as a PHP string
and so never prints a `<title>` the check can see, which means it needs no
exemption. The check itself reported that exemption as stale and it was
removed; the note had not kept up.)

### The check was wrong three times, and planting caught each one

Worth keeping, because it is the same shape as the QR guard (#623):

1. **String literals stripped across the whole file.** HTML attributes carry
   quotes too, so a quote in `content="…"` paired with one inside a nearby PHP
   block and blanked everything between them — including the page's real
   `<title>`. Three pages that genuinely print a title were reported as "no
   longer writes a title", which reads like a tidy-up rather than a fault in the
   check.
2. **Comments not removed before pairing quotes.** An apostrophe in a
   `// we don't …` comment opens a string as far as a regular expression is
   concerned, so every quote after it pairs one out of step. That is why the
   blanking is now a small hand-written scan tracking code, both quote kinds and
   both comment kinds as states, rather than a regular expression.
3. **Asking whether the text `head-meta.php` appears anywhere.** Comment the
   require out and leave the line in place: the page writes no tags and the
   check stays green. It now asks whether there is a **live require**, with
   comments stripped. This is exactly the hole the QR guard had twice.

**And the guard that matters most is on `header.php` itself.** Ordinary pages
write no `<title>` of their own — `header.php` does — so a page-by-page check
never looks at them. Delete the require from `header.php` and hundreds of pages
silently lose their tags while every page-by-page check passes. That is checked
separately and first.

### Why the file-reading check is not enough on its own

`tools/page-head-selftest.php` fetches real pages over HTTP. Building it caught
a case the file-reading check cannot see: `/unsubscribe` **required the partial
and still answered with no tags**, because asked without a token it returns
HTTP 400 and a line of plain text, not a page. That turned out to be a fault in
the test rather than the page, but the same shape — a require sitting in a
branch that did not run — is a real fault the source-reading check is blind to.
Its part E plants the fault of removing the require and fails if the tags are
still there, because a test that cannot see the fault it exists to catch proves
nothing.

**Token-gated pages are not covered by it**, and that is a real gap: accepting
an invitation, resetting a password, confirming an erasure and unsubscribing all
need a seeded record before they draw HTML, which needs real user and
organisation rows because of the foreign keys.

### The pre-push hook

`.githooks/pre-push`, turned on per clone by `tools/install-git-hooks.sh`, which
sets `core.hooksPath`. Per repository on purpose (owner, 5 October 2026): a
global hooks folder overrides every other project's hooks. It runs `php -l` on
the PHP files being pushed and every script in `tools/audit-checks/` — about
eight seconds. It deliberately does not run the self-tests or the migration
harness, which need a database and minutes; a gate slow enough to be resented
gets turned off. `git push --no-verify` skips it and git offers no way to
prevent that, so it guards against forgetting, not against deciding.

## Repeating events, and why the reader was not reused (#569, migration 227)

`Portal\Core\EventRecurrence` works out every date of a repeating event. It is the WRITING half;
`IcsReader` is the reading half, and the two follow **opposite** rules on purpose.

**Nominal against exact (RFC 5545 §3.3.6).** `IcsReader` keeps every occurrence the same EXACT
length, which is right when reading somebody else's calendar: they stated instants and we must not
reinterpret them. The portal's own events store a **wall-clock reading plus a zone**, so "every
Sunday at 10:00" must read 10:00 after a clock change — the NOMINAL rule. Reusing `IcsReader` would
have moved every service by an hour twice a year, and every check would have passed because the
arithmetic was never wrong, only the question.

So the length of each occurrence is carried as **whole days plus a time of day**, never as a number
of seconds (`endShape()` / `applyEndShape()`). An event running 22:00 to 01:00 keeps that shape.

**A month without the date is skipped, not moved.** `dayIfTheMonthHasIt()` asks `checkdate()` rather
than building the date and seeing where it lands, because PHP rolls 31 February into March without
complaining. A silently moved date is the one outcome worse than a missing one. The consequence,
accepted deliberately: a yearly 29 February series makes dates only in leap years, and under a
three-year horizon that is ONE date. Raising `calendar.repeat.maxYears` to four is now a real answer
to that, which is part of why the number was worth making a setting.

**Each date is a COPY of the row just inserted**, with only the start, end, slug and series changed
(`INSERT … SELECT`). The column list is the one this handler already built for the first event, so an
occurrence carries every field the first one does and a column added to the form later is copied
without anybody remembering to come back. Both new statements carry `AND externalFeedID IS NULL`:
`FeedImporter` is the ONE writer of an imported event (#514), and a portal-owned clone of somebody
else's event is something no feed refresh would ever tidy up.

**A rule belongs to a SERIES, not an event.** That is how `tblRecurrenceRules` has always been
shaped, and it is why `calendar/export.php` could already collapse a series-with-a-rule into one
`VEVENT` with an `RRULE`. Nothing had ever written a rule, so that code had never run; writing one
made that path live without changing it.

**THE RULE ROW IS A PUBLISHED PROMISE, NOT A RECORD OF THE REQUEST.** This is the single most
important thing on this page, and the first version got it wrong in two ways that the independent
check measured:

- Both stop fields left empty — which the form invites — stored no count and no end date, so the
  feed sent `RRULE:FREQ=WEEKLY` with **no COUNT and no UNTIL**: a forever-repeating event in every
  subscriber's calendar, while the diary held five dates.
- `repeatCount=400` posted past the form stored 400, so the installation **published** a 400-date
  series having capped that organisation at five. A limit that holds for `tblEvents` and not for
  what the installation publishes is not a limit.

So `maxOccurrences` is written as the number of dates **actually created**, and `endDate` is
deliberately NULL. Both are needed: `export.php` prefers `UNTIL` over `COUNT` when both are present,
and an `UNTIL` taken from the request would overshoot a series our own ceiling had stopped. The
asked-for end date is therefore not kept, which costs nothing a subscriber can see — `COUNT` pins the
series exactly — and is the only arrangement where the two cannot drift apart.

**And only the fields that apply to the frequency are written.** Writing them all regardless was the
other fault. A weekly series stored `dayOfMonth = 3`, meaningless for a weekly rule. Worse: the form
shows every box at once on purpose (no JavaScript), so "every month, the same date" with a weekday
box also ticked is the ORDINARY case — and it stored both, while `export.php` prefers `dayOfWeek`,
publishing "every Monday of every month" against one date a month in the diary. An nth-weekday
pattern stores only the FIRST ticked weekday, because that is the only one the generator uses.

**THE INVARIANT, AND WHERE IT IS ENFORCED.** A pattern may be published only while it produces
exactly the dates the reader can see. **The authoritative check is in `calendar/export.php`**, at the
one place a rule is used: `$patternStillTrue()` expands the stored rule from the first row of the
series' whole run and requires the result to equal that run exactly — the starts, the ends, and the
nine columns the published entry renders.

That is the third design, and the first two were wrong in a way worth recording. Rounds 1 and 2 put
the enforcement in the SAVE HANDLER — remove the rule whenever the handler knows it has stopped being
true. Round 3 showed that cannot work: **attaching an ordinary one-off event to a repeating series,
two clicks on the event form and nowhere near the repeat code, left a public event that appeared in
nobody's subscribed calendar at all** (the collapse skips every other row of the series), and moving
one occurrence made the feed advertise a date that had never existed. A writer cannot know about every
later edit. The reader can always ask.

**Comparing counts is not enough** — measured. Moving one occurrence leaves the count unchanged, so a
counts-only guard published a pattern containing a date the diary had never held. Expanding and
comparing catches an added row, a removed row, a soft-deleted row and a moved row with one test.

**TWO FILTERS HAD TO BE TOLD APART, and conflating them cost a round.** The first version compared
against `$events` — the rows already in hand. Safe, but the whole-calendar download carries only
events from today on, so a series that had already begun could never match its own pattern and every
ongoing weekly service went out one date at a time. That is exactly the series somebody most wants as
one entry. The owner chose on 29 October 2026 to make it work.

- The **time** filter ("from today on") is about what this download carries. It must NOT stop a
  pattern being used: the pattern covers past dates too, and a subscribed calendar showing them is
  ordinary.
- The **visibility** filter is about what this reader may know. It MUST stop it: a series holding an
  event they may not see would otherwise be published as a count covering a date they were never
  allowed to know about.

So `$seriesRunForViewer()` reads the series' whole run under the request's own visibility rule and
status filter, with no time filter, and the master entry takes its start and end from that run's
first row rather than from whichever row this download happened to reach first. Starting it at the
first future row while counting the whole run would advertise dates past the real end of the series.

**The privacy half had no check of any kind until a planted fault found it**, and neither did the
audit script — `check_event_visibility.py` was satisfied because the rule's name appeared in a
comment nearby. Checks N17–N20 close it by making one occurrence members-only and reading the public
feed.

`EventRecurrence` is the same class that created the dates, so this is not a second implementation to
keep in step; it is the one implementation asked the same question twice.

**The save handler still does its three parts**, as a tidiness measure rather than the guarantee —
each was a measured fault in its own right:

1. **The event just inserted is MOVED onto the pattern's first date** when the typed start does not
   satisfy the pattern. `array_slice($dates, 1)` assumed date 0 was that event; it only is when the
   two happen to agree, and the form lets them disagree in one click because the weekday boxes are
   independent of the date above them. Measured: a Wednesday start with Thursday ticked threw away
   the first Thursday and left the diary holding a Wednesday the pattern never produces — and the
   rule then advertised a date the portal did not have. Keeping both was rejected: no single `RRULE`
   can say "this Wednesday and then every Thursday".
2. **A rule is written only for a series this request created.** `export.php` reads a series' rule
   with `ORDER BY ruleID LIMIT 1` and then skips every other event of that series, so a stale or
   second rule row would publish the old pattern and make the new dates vanish from every
   subscriber's calendar. Joining an existing series therefore DELETES its rule and writes none.
3. **The rule is withdrawn if any date failed.** `maxOccurrences` is bound before the copies run,
   so it is the number GENERATED; after the loop, a mismatch between that and the rows created
   removes the rule entirely. A series with a hole in it cannot be described by one pattern (#670).

**The week does not start on the same day in both halves.** `EventRecurrence` counts "every other
week" from SUNDAY (`weeklyStarts()` walks from the Sunday beginning the first occurrence's week, and
its day numbering is 0 = Sunday). RFC 5545 §3.3.10 defaults `WKST` to **Monday**, and `WKST` matters
only for a weekly rule whose interval is above 1. So "Sunday and Wednesday, every fortnight" — an
ordinary church pattern — put six dates in the diary while the feed described a different six, three
of them wrong. `export.php` now emits `WKST=SU`, and only where it can matter. Declaring what the
portal did was chosen over changing which dates a fortnightly series produces.

**Two gap cases, not one.** A start in the missing hour moves forward and its end moves with it
(fix: `shiftedBySameAmount()`). Separately, an END that lands in the missing hour is itself pushed
past the gap, because it used to keep a reading that does not exist.

**Do not overstate that second one** — the first draft of this paragraph did, in both directions, and
the independent check measured it false. The instant and the length were always correct: a stored
`01:30` resolved to 02:30 BST, sixty minutes after a 00:30 start, which is exactly what the stored
`02:30` resolves to now. And the occurrence is **not** really longer than its siblings; it only looks
an hour later on the clock — the same "appearance only" distinction the calendar reader already draws
at its check I34f. What was genuinely wrong is the fictional text, and that is reason enough: this
portal's rule is that wall-clock times compare **as text**, so a reading no clock ever shows sorts and
compares against readings that do, and reads back as a different value from the one written. A
maintainer who believes the occurrence is "really longer" will try to pull the end back an hour,
which reinstates the fictional reading. Check I08 asks the general question: every reading the class
produces must exist in the event's zone.

**What the feed still cannot do (#670), stated precisely.** There is no `EXDATE` and there are no
`RECURRENCE-ID` overrides, so the feed cannot send "this series, except that one date moved". What it
does instead is stop sending the series as a pattern at all and list every date on its own. So a date
cancelled, moved, lengthened, renamed or re-described **is** reflected in a subscription — accurately,
just verbosely. Nothing is hidden and nothing is invented.

**The published entry IS the series' first occurrence**, not merely dated like it: its identifier,
link and last-changed time come from that row too. An earlier version took only the dates and
justified the rest with "`$patternStillTrue()` has required every rendered field to be identical" —
untrue on EVERY collapse, because `uid` comes from `eventID`, `url` from `eventSlug` and
`lastModified` from `updatedAt`, none of which can match across a run. The measured consequence was
an entry identified by one occurrence and dated at another, whose identifier changed every time a
date passed, and which went out under two different identifiers from the two export addresses — a
delete-and-re-add in a subscriber's calendar every week. Taking all five from the run's first row
makes the entry coherent and the identifier stable. Checks Q07–Q09.

One consequence worth knowing:

- **A column the calendar file does not render may differ across the rows without stopping the
  collapse** — the hero image, and `locationWebURL`. None of that reaches the file. Keep the list
  honest if the renderer ever carries more: it has already been wrong once, naming the **map
  position**, which the file does render as a `GEO` line. Measured: a moved pin on one occurrence
  was published for every date. The two coordinate columns are compared now.

*(An earlier version of this section also said "a series stops being tidy about a week after it
begins", because the whole-calendar feed carries only future events and the guard then compared
against those. That was true of the design before the owner's decision of 29 October 2026 and is
false now — see the paragraph above on telling the two filters apart. It was left standing beside its
own correction, which is exactly the contradiction these notes warn about four lines further down.)*

The earlier version of this paragraph said a cancelled or moved date was "not reflected in an outside
subscription". That was true of the first two designs and is not true now; it was left standing beside
its own correction for a while, which is exactly the contradiction these notes exist to prevent.

### The three ceilings, and who may loosen which

`calendar.repeat.maxOccurrences` and `calendar.repeat.maxYears` are settings, not constants. Three
tiers, each unable to loosen the one above it:

| Tier | Where | Who sets it |
|---|---|---|
| `HARD_MAX_OCCURRENCES` 1000, `HARD_MAX_YEARS` 10 | `EventRecurrence` | nobody — a release changes it |
| the installation's setting | `tblSettings`, `siteID IS NULL` | a global administrator |
| the organisation's setting | `tblSettings`, real `siteID` | that organisation's administrator |

**The installation's value CAPS the organisation's; it is not overridden by it (#668).** The
effective number is the smaller of the two. One installation may serve many organisations and the
two levels **may be different people**, so this is a boundary between parties and is enforced in the
save handler, not by the `max` on the input. A number above it is refused with the reason and
recorded, never quietly clamped.

**A ceiling needs a ceiling.** A series is created inside ONE web request on shared hosting under
whatever time limit the host sets, every date is an `INSERT … SELECT`, and there is no bulk undo. A
request that runs out of time half way leaves a series partly made. Hence `HARD_MAX_*`.

### Four things that were got wrong first, each caught by a check rather than by reading

1. **The third global that never arrived.** The installation-wide layer began as
   `$SETTINGS_INSTALLATION`, a global beside `$SETTINGS`. `Router.php` does
   `global $mysqli, $SETTINGS;` before loading a page and **those two are the only things a page
   inherits** (`.claude/rules/app-pages.md`). So the form and the settings page both read an empty
   array, concluded the installation allowed the built-in defaults, and an organisation's 500-date
   series sailed past an installation limit of 6. The layer now lives behind
   `Portal\Core\InstallationSettings`; widening the two-variable rule was rejected, because that
   rule is load-bearing. Caught by checks K01, K02 and K05 of the page test.
2. **"Not chosen" resolved to the built-in default**, which then capped the installation: with the
   default at 3 years, an installation raising its horizon to 4 handed back 3, because `min(3, 4)`
   is 3. An installation could lower a limit but never raise one. `rawRepeatPair()` now answers null
   for "this layer has not chosen", which is a different thing from choosing the default. Caught by
   H04 of the generator test.
3. **An endless rule reported nothing.** A weekly rule with no end produced 157 dates with
   `capped = false`, so a diary that stopped in 2029 looked complete. `lastAllowedDate()` now returns
   the SENTENCE to show rather than a yes/no, because the sentence has to name the number of years
   and that number is a setting.
4. **The form printed a renamed constant.** Making the ceiling configurable renamed
   `MAX_OCCURRENCES` to `DEFAULT_MAX_OCCURRENCES`; `_event_form.php` still printed the old name, so
   **every create form raised a fatal error.** `php -l` cannot see an undefined constant and the 51
   generator checks never touch the form. Only the HTTP test caught it, which is the whole argument
   for having one.

### What the tests cover, and what they cannot

- `tools/event-recurrence-selftest.php` — 60 checks, **no database**: the patterns, both clock
  changes in three zones (one of which changes on a different date), the hour that does not exist,
  skipped days, both ceilings, and the installation-caps-organisation arithmetic.
- `tools/event-repeat-pages-selftest.php` — 126 checks over **real HTTP against a real database**:
  the form is served, posted, and the rows read back. **Renaming `repeatFrequency` on the form fails
  A03 and nothing else** — measured, not assumed, because every other section posts the field names
  itself. A03 reads the names out of the save handler rather than listing them, so there is no third
  copy to keep in step. (Do not stretch that into "A03 is the only check that catches a renamed
  field": H02 pins `repeatCount`'s own attributes and A04 pins the five frequency values, so those
  two names are covered twice. It was written the wider way first and the independent check caught
  it.)
- **Neither can test two people creating the same series at once.** The built-in server runs with
  one worker, so two requests never overlap and such a test would pass on broken code.

## Backups a customer can keep (#569, migration 228)

`DbBackup` writes a snapshot as a FOLDER under `web/_backups/`: one `.jsonl` file per table, and
`_manifest.json` written last. Right for the server, useless for somebody who wants a copy
elsewhere. Three pieces were added.

### `Portal\Core\BackupArchive` — the ONE place a snapshot becomes one file

Built on **libsodium's `secretstream`**, not on anything hand-rolled. That primitive exists for
exactly this job: a long file encrypted in pieces where each piece is authenticated AND tied to its
place in the order, so a file cannot be truncated, reordered or spliced without the read failing. A
"encrypt each block and add a checksum" version was considered and rejected — chunked authenticated
encryption has a short list of ways to be subtly wrong and this gets all of them right.

The file is: a plaintext JSON envelope line (format, snapshot, key mode, salt, Argon2 costs — nothing
secret, because an import must know what to ask for before it can ask), then libsodium's 24-byte
stream header, then length-prefixed chunks. The entry list is INSIDE the encrypted part, so a file's
contents cannot be identified without the key.

**Nothing is ever held in memory.** Packing walks the folder and writes in 64 KB pieces; there is no
temporary archive. A 6 MB table packs and unpacks with no measurable growth, which check F03 measures
rather than asserts.

**Four things it refuses, and all four were found by planting or by an independent check rather
than by reading:**

0. **An entry that declares more bytes than follow it.** This **hung** — 100% CPU, for ever.
   Reproduced: an entry line saying `{"bytes":1000}` followed by five bytes in one FINAL chunk. The
   end-of-stream test required no entry to be pending, so the one case that mattered fell straight
   through it, nothing more could be pulled, and the loop span. On a host with a time limit that
   burns a web worker until it is killed, and the half-unpacked folder was left behind too, because
   `unpack()`'s clean-up lives in a `catch` that never ran. The "cut short in the middle of a file"
   message was dead code for the same reason. Check C11, in a child process with a timeout, because a
   hang cannot be observed from inside the process that is hanging.

1. **A chunk length is bounded.** The four bytes giving it are read BEFORE anything is
   authenticated — they have to be, because they say how much to read — so a hostile file can claim
   any size. Without the bound, `fread($handle, 2147483647)` is a **memory-exhaustion fatal, not an
   exception**, so nothing in-process can catch it: check C08 runs the unpack in a CHILD PROCESS and
   asks whether it refused cleanly or died. The first version of that check sat in-process, the plant
   killed PHP, and the output read exactly like a test that had not run.
2. **The FINAL tag is required.** The closing line arrives inside the encrypted stream so it is
   authentic, but libsodium's FINAL tag is a separate statement that nothing follows. A planted
   packer that never emitted it passed all 36 checks, which made the class header's claim that FINAL
   "proves the file is whole" untrue at the time.
3. **A name with a slash or a dot-dot** is refused outright rather than cleaned up: the portal never
   writes such a name, so one in a file means the file is not ours.

**The key-work costs are bounded, and that bound is the one check an attacker needs no key to
reach.** The envelope is plaintext and unauthenticated — it has to be readable before any key
exists — and the Argon2 cost in it is paid BEFORE the stream is authenticated, so anybody who can
touch the file sets the work and any typed key starts it. Measured on a good file with only the
envelope rewritten: 2 GB of key work took 3.2 seconds, 16 GB took 30.8, and **1 TB never returned**.
Argon2 asks the operating system for that memory directly, so PHP's `memory_limit` does not apply and
on shared hosting it is the customer's account that pays. `MAX_PWHASH_MEM` is 1 GB (libsodium's own
SENSITIVE preset) and `MIN_PWHASH_MEM` 8 KB — a floor as well as a ceiling, because a file claiming
trivial work would make guessing the typed key cheap. Checks C12, C12b, C12c.

A docblock here said the envelope was "never acted on" while the code beneath it acted on the salt
and the costs. It cannot not act on them — they are what turn a typed key into the key. What makes it
safe is that changing either produces a different key and the stream then fails to authenticate, plus
the bound above. Corrected.

**Two guards are honestly unprovable and say so in the code:** the check that a file did not change
size while being packed (staging it means altering a file's length while another process is half way
through reading it), and the download's clean-up on a **cancelled** download. A check was written for
that second one and **passed with both guards removed**, because the page test's snapshot is small
enough that the server finishes the answer before the test's client gives up — so no cancellation was
ever staged. Staging one honestly needs a database big enough to still be streaming, which is minutes
of runtime on every pull request. Both are defensive, believed right, unproven, and labelled.

### `_backups/incoming/` is NOT a snapshot, and that cost real data

`DbBackup::listSnapshots()` lists **every** folder in `_backups/`. The import page creates
`_backups/incoming/` and tells the customer to put files there — so it appeared on the Backup page as
a row reading "Unfinished — not a backup" **with a Delete button beside it**, and
`isSnapshotName('incoming')` was true, so Delete accepted it and removed the folder and everything in
it. That may be the only copy of the database somebody has just brought back after losing their
server, and the row actively invited the press. Reproduced against the real class by the independent
check.

`DbBackup::NOT_SNAPSHOTS` is now the ONE list of reserved folder names, consulted by
`isSnapshotName()` (so no action from a browser can name one) and by `listSnapshots()` (so it never
appears). Before adding a name, ask whether it is a folder somebody might legitimately want to
restore or delete through the page.

### A download, and why it is a POST

The key is typed in, and a key must never travel in an address — an address reaches the access log,
the browser history, the `Referer` of the next request and any proxy between. So the key is posted
and the file is the answer to that POST. The cost is that the browser cannot resume an interrupted
download, which is the right trade.

**It packs to a file before sending a byte.** Once bytes have gone the answer cannot be taken back,
and the browser would save a part file with no way of knowing. A part backup is worse than none,
because somebody keeps it believing it is a copy of their data. It costs disk briefly; the
alternative costs correctness.

### An import that does NOT restore

Two steps, on purpose. The import unpacks; putting it back is the existing Restore with every guard
it already has, including `WHOLE_DATABASE_ONLY`. One press would mean a second path writing over a
live database, and that path would have to agree with the first about every guard for ever.

Named `imported-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS` from the moment of import: it cannot collide with what is there, it
is obvious which came from outside, and `prune()` only removes `upgrade-…` so an imported backup is
never tidied away by the scheduled job.

**Two ways in, because the obvious one cannot be relied on.** `upload_max_filesize` and
`post_max_size` are commonly 2–64 MB while a real database backup is larger, and a customer on
shared hosting usually cannot raise them. So the page reads both limits and SAYS what the server will
take, and the `_backups/incoming` folder route has no limit at all.

### The scheduled job

`cron/backup-run`, called daily by the hosting company's scheduler whatever the setting says; how
often a backup is really taken is decided in the job, so changing the setting does not mean editing a
scheduler entry the customer may not reach.

**Whether one is due comes from the snapshots themselves**, not a stored "last run": a backup taken
by hand counts, a failed run cannot push the next one a whole period away, and restoring the database
cannot confuse it. `DbBackup::isTakenHere()` is the ONE place that decides whether a snapshot was
taken here or imported, and both this job and `prune()` ask it — an imported snapshot must not count
as evidence that the current database has been saved, and without that an import silently suppressed
the next scheduled backup (measured by section N of `tools/backup-page-selftest.php`).

**Four faults this work had, all found by running it and none visible on the page:**

- the loop in `BackupArchive::readEntries()` **hung** on a file asking for more bytes than it
  carried (above).
- the Argon2 cost was taken unbounded from an unauthenticated envelope (above).
- `_backups/incoming/` was listed as a deletable snapshot (above).
- the download's temporary file survived a cancelled download, and two comments said it always did
  not.
- the job read `takenAt`, `name` and `deleted` — **none of which exist**. It would have taken a
  backup every single run (an age of null reads as "due"), told nobody which one, and reported
  nothing tidied. The project's own rule is to check a name against the thing that uses it.
- it only caught exceptions, but `snapshot()` answers `success: false` for an ordinary failure — so a
  backup that simply did not work would have been reported as taken, the worst possible outcome for a
  backup job.
- an imported snapshot suppressed the next scheduled backup.
- **two of the "an administrator of one organisation cannot do this" checks were passing for the
  wrong reason**: the Backup page refuses a non-global administrator before rendering anything, so it
  carries no form token for them, and the request was refused by the FORM TOKEN rather than by the
  gate under test. Planting the gate away left all 174 checks green. The checks now take a token from
  a page that administrator can load, and assert it is non-empty so they cannot go hollow again.

### Tests

- `tools/backup-archive-selftest.php` — 47 checks, **no database and no web server**: the round trip
  byte for byte (raw bytes and an empty file included), both key modes, a wrong key, a wrong key
  file, a tampered byte, a truncated file, a missing FINAL tag, an impossible chunk length, a
  path-climbing name, a miscounted entry list, a failed pack leaving no file, and that the file
  carries no name, table name or key in the clear.
- `tools/backup-page-selftest.php` — extended to 181 checks over real HTTP: the schedule saves and
  refuses nonsense, the download round-trips through the real pages and is opened again by the class,
  the import appears and unpacks, an imported snapshot is listed and REHEARSES a restore successfully,
  both gates refuse an organisation's administrator and record it, and the job's token, not-due, due
  and prune behaviour.

## Repository vs Server Structure

The Git repository root contains documentation and CI/CD config. **All deployable
code lives inside `web/`.**

> **The server side of this diagram described a layout that no longer exists**,
> until it was corrected on 27 October 2026 (#637). It showed the three channels
> sharing one base folder, with `public_html`, `public_html_dev` and
> `public_html_beta` beside each other — the arrangement where a deploy of one
> channel could overwrite another's code, last push winning. **Each channel now
> has a folder of its own**, and the web address points at `admin_html` inside
> it. `README.md` holds the current deploy table and is the place to check first.
> The domain below is **one customer's set-up, shown as an example**: no address
> is built into this product (#500).

```
Git repo root (NOT deployed)          Server: <one channel's folder>/
├── .claude/                           ├── _core/
├── .github/workflows/deploy.yml       ├── _vendor/
├── CHANGELOG.md                       ├── _sql/
├── DEV_NOTES.md                       ├── _auth_keys/    (server-managed)
├── README.md                          ├── _libraries/    (server-managed)
└── web/ ─── contents deployed ──────► ├── _uploads/      (server-managed)
    ├── _core/                         ├── _apps/         (app controllers, #159)
    ├── _apps/        (#159)           ├── _backups/      (server-managed)
    ├── _vendor/                       ├── _includes/
    ├── _sql/                          ├── _functions/
    ├── _lang/                         ├── admin_html/    (the staff pages)
    ├── _install/                      ├── _install/
    ├── _includes/                     ├── _lang/
    ├── _functions/                    ├── private_html/
    ├── _libraries/ (gitignored)       ├── public_html_landing/
    ├── public_html/                   └── public_html_redir/
    │   ├── auth/
    │   ├── dashboard/
    │   ├── expenses/
    │   ├── help/
    │   └── settings/
    ├── private_html/
    ├── public_html_landing/
    └── public_html_redir/
```

The `_` prefix on every server-side dir is a naming convention: any dir
that starts with `_` is **above the web server's document root** and cannot be
reached over HTTP. Only the channel's web folder is web-accessible.

The repo holds **one** `public_html/` source tree, and the deploy mirrors it into
the channel's own folder. **The old destinations `public_html_dev/` and
`public_html_beta/` beside a shared `public_html/` are gone** — see the warning at
the top of this section and the deploy table in `README.md`. There is still no
per-channel front controller in the repo. Note also that the channel is decided in
exactly one place, `Portal\Core\Channel`: never work it out from a folder name in
code, and never type `public_html` into a path (use `PORTAL_WEBROOT`).

**Key rule:** when referencing paths in PHP code, use `PORTAL_ROOT` and related
constants (defined in `bootstrap.php`). When referencing paths in Git/CI, prefix
with `web/`.

## Deployment Model

WebMS Intra uses a **three-branch SFTP deployment model** modelled on the
iHymns pipeline. Only `web/` is synced; the active branch decides which
public web root the upload lands in.

| Branch  | Channel    | Where it lands on the server                     | Auto-bump rule       |
| ------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------ | -------------------- |
| `alpha` | alpha/dev  | its own folder, named by `SFTP_PATH_ALPHA_DIR`    | PATCH (always)       |
| `beta`  | beta       | its own folder, named by `SFTP_PATH_BETA_DIR`     | Conventional Commits |
| `main`  | production | its own folder, named by `SFTP_PATH_LIVE_DIR`     | none on `main`       |

### Remote layout: one folder per channel (rewritten by the workflow package, #499)

Each channel has a folder of its own, named by `SFTP_PATH_ALPHA_DIR`,
`SFTP_PATH_BETA_DIR` or `SFTP_PATH_LIVE_DIR` inside the base folder
`SFTP_PATH_ROOT_DIR`. **Point the channel's web address at `admin_html` inside its
folder.**

```text
SFTP_PATH_ROOT_DIR/
└── <the channel's folder>/
    ├── admin_html/            ← from web/public_html/
    ├── _apps/                 ← from web/_apps/      (#159)
    ├── _core/                 ← from web/_core/
    ├── _install/  _lang/  _sql/  _vendor/
    ├── _libraries/dompdf/     ← fetched at deploy time by tools/download-dompdf.sh
    ├── _auth_keys/            ← created once if missing, then never touched
    ├── _uploads/              ← the same
    └── _backups/              ← the same
```

**THIS REPLACED A SHARED BASE, and that is the point of the change.** All three
channels used to share one base folder: only `web/public_html/` went to a sibling of
its own (`public_html/`, `public_html_beta/`, `public_html_dev/`) and every code
folder went to the shared base **from every branch — last push wins**. So deploying
alpha overwrote live's `_core`. Nothing warned anybody; it was simply how it worked.
Each channel now has its own copy of everything, and the deploy refuses a folder that
does not look like that channel's own.

### Workflows

- `deploy.yml` — push to alpha/beta/main, or manual dispatch. PHP-lint, fetch
  pinned dompdf, SFTP via lftp (SSH key first, password fallback).
- `version-bump.yml` — push to alpha or beta. Alpha always bumps PATCH; beta
  uses Conventional Commits (BREAKING/`!:` → major, `feat(` → minor, else patch).
- `changelog.yml` — push to alpha or beta only (NOT main — the ruleset
  on main blocks the bot's direct push). Appends per-branch sections to
  `CHANGELOG.md` from commit messages since the last `v*` tag. Entries
  propagate to main via the normal beta → main merge.
- `package.yml` — merge into `alpha`, `beta`, `rc` or `main`, or a manual
  run. Builds the installation zip and checks it. For `main` it publishes a
  GitHub Release, for `rc` a pre-release; for `alpha` and `beta` the zip is
  only a download on the run. A manual run never publishes, whatever the
  branch. **It replaced `release.yml`**, which made a Release when somebody
  pushed a `v*` tag by hand; such a push now gets a run that says it
  published nothing, rather than silence. Publishing waits on a repository
  variable, so nothing is published until that is switched on.
- `auto-merge-alpha.yml` — PR opened or synchronised against `alpha`. Enables
  GitHub native auto-merge, then dispatches BOTH `deploy.yml` and
  `package.yml` after the merge. The bridge is required here because GitHub's
  *native* auto-merge IS attributed to `GITHUB_TOKEN`, which doesn't trigger
  downstream workflows. Manual UI merges on `beta` and `main` don't need a
  bridge — the `push:` event from a human-attributed merge fires normally.
  **Anything new that is supposed to happen on a merge into `alpha` needs a
  line here too.** The package bridge was missed when `package.yml` was
  written (found by its independent check, 14 October 2026, added 27
  October): `package.yml` listens for a push to `alpha`, that push never
  happens, and the proof is that `version-bump.yml` — which fires on the same
  event — has raised the version on `alpha` twice in the branch's whole
  history. The bridge's failure is deliberately swallowed with a warning,
  because `gh workflow run` cannot find a workflow until its file is on the
  default branch, and a hard failure there would lose the deploy dispatch.
- `portal-selftests.yml`, `mail-selftests.yml`, `calendar-selftests.yml` — every
  pull request, with no path filter, which is why these are the ones that can be
  made required status checks. The self-tests that need only PHP run in one job;
  the rest run against a real MySQL, on 8.0.36 and 8.4.11. Before this, most
  self-tests ran nowhere but a developer's machine.
- `backup-selftest.yml`, `e2e-migrations.yml` — a pull request **that touches the
  files they are about**. They still run and a red one is still visible, but
  **a path-filtered check must never be made required**: GitHub has no "required
  only when it runs", so the branch rule would wait for a report that never comes.
  `package.yml` has no `pull_request` trigger at all, so the same goes for its
  jobs. (The first draft of the owner's required-checks checklist named all three
  and would have locked `main`, `beta` and `alpha`; its independent check caught
  it on 27 October 2026.)
- **Not every test runs automatically**, and nothing in the workflows says so:
  `tools/page-scripts-selftest.php` (#625), `tools/qr-selftest.php` (#623) and
  seven of the 32 scripts in `tools/audit-checks/` are named in no workflow. Two of
  those seven are the tripwires added for #625 and #622. Tracked as #637.
- **The Psalm job was removed** (13 October 2026). It installed Psalm in a
  temporary folder, Psalm stopped with "Could not find any composer
  autoloaders", the step swallowed that with `|| true`, wrote an empty report
  and went green. A check that cannot fail is worse than none, because it
  looks like a pass. The names "PHP Static Analysis" and "PHP -l lint" were
  kept on purpose: a branch rule finds a required check by its job name.
  With Psalm gone, **no code-analysis check in this repository can turn a run
  red** — `codeql.yml` still runs but keeps `continue-on-error: true`,
  because Code Scanning is not switched on and the upload half of that step
  would fail on every pull request. The owner chose on 26 October 2026 to
  keep it that way and say so plainly rather than hide it.
- `pr-security.yml` — runs on every PR against alpha/beta/main. PHP lint
  (hard gate), gitleaks secrets scan, heuristic anti-pattern scan (checks
  9-22), and — as its own step, so it is never skipped by the heuristic
  scan's early exit — the foreign-key target check (#552, check 23).
- `calendar-selftests.yml` — runs on every PR against alpha/beta/main. Runs
  the four calendar self-tests (#514) that used to depend on somebody
  remembering to run them by hand. Three of the four (event visibility,
  feed resolver, feed importer) each get their own throwaway database,
  built from `full_schema.sql` in a MySQL 8.0.36 container GitHub starts
  beside the job and removes, data included, when the job ends; the
  fourth, the calendar reader self-test, needs no database at all.
- `e2e-migrations.yml` — the end-to-end migration test harness (#248). Runs
  on PRs and on pushes to alpha/beta/main, in both cases only when
  `web/_sql/`, the harness folder or the workflow itself changes, plus
  manual runs. Runs the
  harness's seven phases and its three data checks three times, as three jobs side by side, on
  MySQL 8.0.36, MySQL 8.4.11 and MariaDB 11.4.13.
- `repo-config-audit.yml` — weekly + on PRs touching `.github/workflows/`.
  Detects orphaned required-status-check rules (see gotchas section).

**Three of the descriptions above have not yet been observed for real on
GitHub.** `calendar-selftests.yml`, `pr-security.yml`'s check 23, and
`e2e-migrations.yml`'s MySQL 8.4.11 job were all added on the
`claude/alpha-wip` branch, which has not yet been opened as a pull request.
The first two run on a pull request (the calendar self-tests can also be
started by hand, once that file reaches the default branch). The migration
test runs on a pull request or when alpha, beta or main is updated — in
both cases only when certain files change — and can be started by hand;
none of that has happened yet. The present tense above
describes what each is BUILT to do, not something already seen on GitHub's
own machines. What was proved instead is local, and some parts, such as how
GitHub starts and removes the database container, can only be proved on
GitHub. The local proofs ran on this Mac, in throwaway MySQL 8.0.36 and
8.4.11 containers, and on a Linux machine built to match GitHub's runner
(Ubuntu 24.04, the same PHP 8.4 packages GitHub's `setup-php` step
installs). That last proof found a real fault. On a machine whose PHP lacks
seven old Windows time-zone names, the calendar reader self-test's own
"L4" check used to fail. Whether GitHub's runner lacks them was never
verified, because it did not need to be: the fault was in the portal's own
committed data, not in any one machine. It is tracked as issue #557 (high
priority) and is now fixed: `tools/generate-windows-timezones.php` converts
every zone it writes to its CURRENT spelling and refuses rather than fall
back to an old one, the committed list was regenerated, and a new self-test
check ("L6" in `tools/ics-reader-selftest.php`) stops an old spelling
creeping back in unnoticed. See the CHANGELOG's `fix(calendar):` entry for
issue #557.

### Day-to-Day Workflow

1. Branch off `alpha` for new work.
2. Open a PR against `alpha` → auto-merge fires once checks pass.
3. When `alpha` is stable, open a PR from `alpha` → `beta` for wider testing.
4. When `beta` is stable, open a PR from `beta` → `main` for production.
5. **Nothing more to do: the merge into `main` publishes the release.**
   `package.yml` works out the version from `web/_core/version.php`, makes the
   tag itself and publishes `webms-intra-<version>.zip` with its checksum.
   Pushing a `v*` tag by hand publishes nothing any more, and the tag still
   counts as taken, so do not do it. If the run is red because "The version
   number was not raised", raise the number and merge again.

   A release candidate works the same way on the `rc` branch, which does not
   exist yet: a merge there publishes `v<version>-rc.<n>` marked as a
   pre-release.

### Manual Deploy Override

`Actions → Deploy via SFTP → Run workflow` accepts an override target
(`alpha` / `beta` / `main`) that bypasses the branch-based mapping for a
one-off deploy.

### Commit flags

- `[skip ci]` — skip every workflow on this commit
- `[deploy all]` — force a full re-sync regardless of change detection

## CI/CD Secrets Setup — Step-by-Step

Configure these once when bringing a fresh repo (or a new server) online.

### 1. Generate the SSH deploy keypair (preferred over password)

On your local machine:

```bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "webms-intra-deploy@github" \
  -f ~/.ssh/webms_intra_deploy -N ''
```

Produces:

- `~/.ssh/webms_intra_deploy`     — private key (goes into GitHub secret `SFTP_KEY`)
- `~/.ssh/webms_intra_deploy.pub` — public key (goes onto the DreamHost server)

### 2. Authorise the public key on DreamHost

DreamHost panel → **Users → SFTP Users → [deploy user] → Manage Users**,
paste the contents of `~/.ssh/webms_intra_deploy.pub` into **Authorized Keys**.

Verify from your laptop:

```bash
ssh -i ~/.ssh/webms_intra_deploy -p 22 <SFTP_USER>@<SFTP_HOST> 'pwd; ls'
```

### 3. Set the GitHub repo secrets

> ⚠️ **Three names in this step were RETIRED by the deploy rewrite (#499, #500).**
> `SFTP_LIVE_PATH`, `SFTP_BETA_PATH` and `SFTP_DEV_PATH` used to be listed here as
> required. They are now on `RETIRED_SETTINGS` in `tools/deploy/resolve-settings.sh`:
> setting one only produces a warning, and the deploy will refuse for want of the
> base folder. The table below is the real list. **Every value is an example of one
> customer's set-up, not a default** — nothing in this product has a built-in address.

| Setting                | Secret? | Required | Example value |
| ---------------------- | ------- | -------- | ------------- |
| `SFTP_HOST`            | secret  | yes      | `iad1-shared-XX-XX.example-host.com` |
| `SFTP_USER`            | secret  | yes      | `dh_abcd1234` |
| `SFTP_PATH_ROOT_DIR`   | secret  | yes      | `/home/dh_abcd1234/portal.example.org` — a FULL path to the base folder |
| `SFTP_PATH_LIVE_DIR`   | secret  | yes      | `public_html` — **a NAME inside the base folder, never a path** |
| `SFTP_PATH_BETA_DIR`   | secret  | yes      | `public_html_beta` |
| `SFTP_PATH_ALPHA_DIR`  | secret  | yes      | `public_html_dev` (the alpha branch deploys the dev channel) |
| `SFTP_PORT`            | secret  | no       | `22` if omitted |
| `SFTP_KEY`             | secret  | one of   | the whole private key file (preferred) |
| `SFTP_PASSWORD`        | secret  | one of   | the SFTP password (used only when `SFTP_KEY` is unset) |
| `SFTP_ENABLED`         | variable | yes     | must be **exactly** `true` — four small letters, no spaces or line breaks. Anything else means "work it out but upload nothing", which is how you take a dry run. |
| `ADMIN_BASE_URL_LIVE` / `_BETA` / `_ALPHA` | variable | no | the staff address the health check uses; empty means skip that check |

A channel may have its own login and its own base folder instead
(`SFTP_HOST_LIVE`, `SFTP_USER_LIVE`, `SFTP_KEY_LIVE` or `SFTP_PASSWORD_LIVE`,
`SFTP_PORT_LIVE`, `SFTP_PATH_LIVE_ROOT_DIR`, and the same for `BETA` and `ALPHA`).
**A channel's own login is all or nothing:** if any one of its five login settings is
set, its host, user and key-or-password must ALL come from that channel's settings.
Nothing is borrowed from the shared login, because "a new host with the shared user"
would sign in happily and then write the shared base folder's path onto the wrong
server, and that cannot be told from a deliberate choice by looking at the values.

```bash
# Replace every value with your own. None of these is a default.
gh secret set SFTP_HOST           --body 'iad1-shared-XX-XX.example-host.com'
gh secret set SFTP_USER           --body 'dh_abcd1234'
gh secret set SFTP_PATH_ROOT_DIR  --body '/home/dh_abcd1234/portal.example.org'
gh secret set SFTP_PATH_LIVE_DIR  --body 'public_html'
gh secret set SFTP_PATH_BETA_DIR  --body 'public_html_beta'
gh secret set SFTP_PATH_ALPHA_DIR --body 'public_html_dev'
gh secret set SFTP_KEY            < ~/.ssh/webms_intra_deploy
# optional:
gh secret set SFTP_PORT           --body '22'
gh secret set SFTP_PASSWORD                       # prompts (keeps it out of shell history)
# not secret, and nothing uploads until this one says exactly "true":
gh variable set SFTP_ENABLED      --body 'true'
```

---

### 3b. Where the deploy puts things (#493, #499, #637)

**Sections 3b and 3c used to be here — 365 lines describing an arrangement that
was planned, replaced, and then left in place behind a warning saying "do not
follow this".** They are deleted rather than annotated, which is this
repository's rule: where something no longer applies, delete it instead of
explaining that it no longer applies. A superseded instruction behind a warning
is still an instruction, and somebody setting up a server reads the table, not
the warning above it.

**What they got wrong, so that nobody reinstates them:**

* They described **one shared base folder** with `public_html/`,
  `public_html_beta/` and `public_html_dev/` as siblings, last push winning.
  Each channel has had a folder of its own since `c61211e` (27 October 2026),
  with the staff pages in `admin_html` inside it and nothing shared.
* Six of their setting names are retired and read by nothing:
  `SFTP_PATH_LIVE_ADMIN_DIR`, `SFTP_PATH_LIVE_PUBLIC_DIR`,
  `SFTP_PATH_BETA_ADMIN_DIR`, `SFTP_PATH_BETA_PUBLIC_DIR`,
  `SFTP_PATH_ALPHA_ADMIN_DIR` and `SFTP_PATH_ALPHA_PUBLIC_DIR`. They sit in
  `RETIRED_SETTINGS` in `tools/deploy/resolve-settings.sh` (line 207), which
  warns and carries on.
* **3c's standing warning was false.** It said "do not deploy until the #493
  work has landed. The deployment does not yet know about `admin_html/`". It
  does: `STAFF_WEB_DIR_DEFAULT='admin_html'` at
  `tools/deploy/resolve-settings.sh:129`, overridable per run with
  `DEPLOY_STAFF_WEB_DIR`. A warning that tells somebody not to deploy, months
  after deploying became safe, costs real time.

**Where the truth lives now**, and only in these two places so they cannot
disagree:

* `README.md` → "Branches and where they deploy", which was corrected in the
  same package.
* `.github/workflows/deploy.yml`'s own header, "WHERE THINGS GO, INSIDE ONE
  CHANNEL'S FOLDER", and `tools/deploy/resolve-settings.sh`, which is the one
  place that decides where files go and refuses when it is unsure.

**Read the workflow, not a copy of it.** That is the lesson #637 is really
about: every one of the fourteen wrong statements it uncovered was a document
describing correct machinery inaccurately, and each had been read as true for
weeks.

### 4. Enable the kill switch

```bash
gh variable set SFTP_ENABLED --body 'true'
```

While `SFTP_ENABLED != 'true'`, all deploy runs no-op.

### 5. Repo settings (one-time UI clicks)

1. **Settings → General → Pull Requests → Allow auto-merge** = ON.
2. **Settings → Branches → Add rule** on `alpha`, `beta`, and `main`:
   - Disable allow-deletions
   - Disable allow-force-pushes
   - (Recommended) Require status check on `main`

### 6. Verify

```bash
gh workflow run deploy.yml --ref main
gh run watch
```

### Rotating the SSH key

1. Generate a new keypair
2. Add the new public key on DreamHost (don't remove the old yet)
3. Update `SFTP_KEY` in GitHub
4. Trigger a manual deploy to confirm
5. Remove the old public key from DreamHost

## dompdf at deploy time

Expense PDF generation depends on dompdf in `_libraries/dompdf/`. The library
is **not** committed to this repo — `tools/download-dompdf.sh` fetches the
pinned version at deploy time and the lftp mirror uploads it as part of the
shared `web/` sync. Update the pinned version by editing `DOMPDF_VERSION` in
that script.

For local development:

```bash
bash tools/download-dompdf.sh
```

The script is idempotent — re-runs skip if the right version is already present.

---

## Per-site branding flow

The portal supports per-site visual branding via `tblSites` columns. Site
admins can override the brand colour, logo and favicon per-site without
touching code.

### Data model

`tblSites` columns relevant to branding (see migration `037_site_favicon.sql`):

| Column         | Type         | Purpose                                          |
| -------------- | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `siteName`     | VARCHAR(255) | Display name used in nav, page titles, footer    |
| `logoPath`     | VARCHAR(500) | Header logo URL/path (any image format)          |
| `faviconPath`  | VARCHAR(500) | Browser-tab favicon URL/path; NULL = default     |
| `primaryColor` | VARCHAR(7)   | `#RRGGBB` hex; default `#5e6ad2` (Linear indigo) |
| `copyrightOrg` | VARCHAR(255) | Footer copyright holder                          |

### How a value flows from DB to UI

1. `Site::loadSiteRow()` selects the row into a class-level cache. (It is
   private, and reached through `Site::init()`; this line named it
   `loadCurrentSite()`, which no code has ever had.)
2. `Site::branding('color' | 'logo' | 'favicon' | 'name' | …)` returns the
   relevant column.
3. `web/_core/templates/header.php` reads `Site::branding('color')`,
   derives `--portal-primary-rgb` (R,G,B) from the hex, and **inline-
   styles** the `<html>` element:

   ```html
   <html data-bs-theme="light"
         style="--portal-primary: #5e6ad2; --portal-primary-rgb: 94, 106, 210;">
   ```

4. `web/public_html/assets/css/portal.css` defines the design tokens
   inside `:root`. Because the `<html>` inline style has higher
   specificity than `:root`, the per-site primary wins. The derived
   variants (`--portal-primary-hover`, `--portal-primary-active`,
   `--portal-primary-subtle`) are auto-derived from the primary via
   `color-mix()` and shift along with it on any browser that supports
   color-mix (Chrome 111+, Safari 16.2+, Firefox 113+). On older
   browsers, the literal indigo hex fallbacks defined in `:root` apply.
5. `header.php` also renders `<link rel="icon">` from
   `Site::branding('favicon')`, with `/assets/images/favicon.ico` as the
   fallback.

### Admin UI

Umbrella admins manage all sites at **`/admin/sites/`**. The "New / Edit
site" modal has form fields for `siteName`, `siteKey`, `hostPattern`,
`logoPath`, `faviconPath`, `primaryColor` (color picker), `copyrightOrg`,
`timezone`, and active status.

The save handler at `web/public_html/admin/sites/save.php` validates the
primary colour as `#RGB` or `#RRGGBB` and falls back to the indigo default
on invalid input.

### Defaults for white-label deploys

`tblSites` ships with the global "WebMS Intra" defaults. New sites
inherit `#5e6ad2` until the admin sets their own brand colour. Logo and
favicon default to `/assets/images/logo.svg` and
`/assets/images/favicon.ico` respectively.

### "Powered by &lt;product&gt;" footer attribution

When a site uses CUSTOM branding (any branding field differs from the
ACTIVE product brand — see "Two-layer brand model" below), the footer
renders a small "Powered by &lt;product&gt;" attribution after the
copyright line, where `<product>` resolves via `Site::productName()`.
Sites running the active product brand defaults don't show it — the
copyright line already names the product.

Detection (`Site::usesCustomBranding()` in `web/_core/Site.php`):

- `siteName` differs from `Site::productName()` (active product name
  resolved from `product.name` setting / `PORTAL_PRODUCT_NAME_DEFAULT`
  constant / `Site::DEFAULT_SITE_NAME` cold-start fallback), OR
- `logoPath` differs from `Site::DEFAULT_LOGO_PATH`
  (`'/assets/images/logo.svg'`), OR
- `primaryColor` differs from `Site::DEFAULT_PRIMARY_COLOR`
  (`'#5e6ad2'`, compared case-insensitively), OR
- `copyrightOrg` is non-empty (default is NULL), OR
- `faviconPath` is non-empty and differs from the default favicon path

Admins disable attribution globally via the `branding.hidePoweredBy`
setting in `/settings/` (set to the string `'true'`). Default is
`'false'`, so attribution is on out-of-the-box for custom-branded
deploys.

Markup lives in `web/_core/templates/footer.php`; styling is in the
`.portal-powered-by`, `.portal-powered-by-prefix`, and
`.portal-powered-by-mark` rules in `portal.css`. The mark class is a
hook for future hyperlinking when the product landing page exists.

The same detection ALSO drives a `<meta name="generator" content="<product>">`
tag in `web/_core/templates/header.php`. This is the standard SaaS / CMS
attribution mechanism — invisible to humans, picked up by site analysers
like Wappalyzer + "View page source" + browser dev tools.

---

## Two-layer brand model (issue #296)

There are TWO independent branding layers in the portal. They compose
top-down at render time.

```text
┌─ Layer 1 — PRODUCT (system) ────────────────────────────────────┐
│   Set ONCE at install via the installer's Step 1.5 picker.       │
│   Lives in tblSettings (siteID=NULL) as product.* + portal.industry. │
│   Drives: <meta name="generator">, footer "Powered by …",        │
│   X-Powered-By header, PWA manifest name/description,            │
│   installer wizard heading + footer.                             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                       ▼ overridden by ▼
┌─ Layer 2 — TENANT (per-site, already shipped) ──────────────────┐
│   Set per-site via /admin/sites/<id>/branding.                   │
│   Lives in tblSites columns + `branding.*` settings.             │
│   Drives: page chrome (siteName, logo, colour, favicon),         │
│   copyright org, "Powered by …" visibility opt-out.              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Resolution rule everywhere**: tenant override > product default >
hardcoded constant.

### Why two layers

Tenants already had `branding.*` (Linear-style per-org skin). Adding a
SECOND layer above lets the same codebase ship as different sub-brands
without forking — `WebMS Intra` for the generic install, `ChurchMS` for
church installs, future `SchoolMS` / `CharityMS` etc. for other verticals.
Tenant branding stays decoupled; an install branded as `ChurchMS` can
still be deployed for `Mill Road SDA Cambridge` and the latter wins in
the chrome.

### Product brand presets

Defined in `web/_core/brand-defaults.php` as a `return [...]` array keyed
by `portal.industry` value (`generic`, `church`, `school`, `nonprofit`,
`community`, `small-business`). Each preset declares `name`, `tagline`,
`publisher`, `assetFolder`, and a human `displayLabel` for the installer
dropdown.

The file is **bootstrap-free** — it cannot reference any class, function,
or constant from elsewhere — so the installer (which runs before the
framework loads) can `require` it the same way the runtime does.

### Resolution helpers

| Helper | Reads from | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Site::productName()` | `App::settings('product.name')` → `PORTAL_PRODUCT_NAME_DEFAULT` → `DEFAULT_SITE_NAME` | header meta, footer mark, X-Powered-By, manifest |
| `Site::productTagline()` | `App::settings('product.tagline')` → `PORTAL_PRODUCT_TAGLINE_DEFAULT` | manifest description, installer subtitle |
| `Site::productPublisher()` | `App::settings('product.publisher')` → `PORTAL_PRODUCT_PUBLISHER_DEFAULT` | footer copyright |

The `PORTAL_PRODUCT_*_DEFAULT` constants are seeded in `bootstrap.php`
from `brand-defaults.php`'s generic preset, so they're already valid
strings before `$SETTINGS` is loaded.

### Picking the brand at install time

The installer wizard's **Step 1.5 — Organisation Type** (encoded as the
string `'1.5'` in URLs, alongside the existing `'2.5'` data-choice page)
shows a dropdown of preset display labels. The chosen industry key is
stored in `$_SESSION['install_industry']`; all subsequent steps display
the matching brand. After `full_schema.sql` runs, Step 3 INSERTs the
preset's `name` / `tagline` / `publisher` values plus the industry key
into `tblSettings`.

### Changing brand post-install

The brand is fully reversible: admins can edit `portal.industry`,
`product.name`, `product.tagline`, or `product.publisher` via
`/admin/settings`. Changing `portal.industry` does **not** auto-rewrite
the other rows — the admin may have customised them. Re-seeding is a
manual SQL exercise if a full preset reset is wanted; documented as a
v1.x follow-up.

### Per-brand assets

Per-brand asset folders live at
`web/public_html/assets/images/brandkit/assets/<assetFolder>/{icon,icon-192,icon-512,logo}.svg`
(moved from the original `assets/images/brands/<assetFolder>/` path
during the WebMS/ChurchMS brand-kit drop — `manifest.php` and
`header.php` both resolve from `brandkit/assets/` today; `assets/images/brands/`
no longer exists). The brand-aware `manifest.php` controller resolves the
active preset's `assetFolder` and serves icons from there; it falls back
to the top-level `/assets/images/{logo,icon-192,icon-512}.svg`
placeholders if the per-brand file isn't present (belt-and-braces —
every preset directory that exists today does have the full set).
All six presets (`generic`/`webms-intra`, `church`/`churchms`,
`school`/`schoolms`, `nonprofit`/`charityms`, `community`/`communityms`,
`small-business`/`businessms`) now have distinct artwork (#306) — see
FEATURES.md's "PWA install prompt + manifest shortcuts + sub-brand
starter artwork" section for what's designer-finished (WebMS, ChurchMS —
outlined-vector wordmarks) vs. functional-starter (the four newer
presets — `icon*.svg` are full-quality hand-drawn-equivalent emblems on
the same token structure, but `logo.svg`'s wordmark line is set in a
system-font stack pending a designer pass).

### Where the brand is NOT applied

By design, these surfaces stay as `WebMS Intra` regardless of preset:

- PHP `@package WebMS Intra` / `@author MWBM Partners Ltd` doc-tags —
  these document code authorship, not user-facing branding.
- `error_log('[WebMS-Intra] …')` server-log prefixes — codebase identity
  for operators reading logs, not user-facing brand.
- `robots.txt` — comment header is brand-neutral so the static file
  can be served without going through a PHP controller.
- ~~`openapi.json` `info.title`~~ — no longer true: this now IS
  brand-aware via `openapi.php` + `api-spec.json` (#307, see "Deferred
  follow-ups" item 2 below).

### Deferred follow-ups from the brand-layer PR (#297)

Tracked as separate issues; called out here so they don't get lost
between PRs.

1. **Distinct sub-brand artwork** — ✅ **done (#306)**. All four
   previously-placeholder presets (`school`/`schoolms`,
   `nonprofit`/`charityms`, `community`/`communityms`,
   `small-business`/`businessms`) now have their own
   `assets/images/brandkit/assets/<assetFolder>/{icon,icon-192,icon-512,logo}.svg`
   set — the resolver needed no code changes, exactly as anticipated
   here. Remaining gap: each new `logo.svg`'s wordmark is system-font
   text, not the WebMS/ChurchMS kits' outlined vector glyphs — a
   designer pass on that one file per preset is still open (tracked
   in-repo, not a fresh GitHub issue — see each `logo.svg`'s own
   `<desc>`).

2. **`openapi.json` brand-aware conversion** — ✅ **done (#307)**. The
   spec now lives at `web/_core/api-spec.json` with
   `web/public_html/openapi.php` rewriting the `info` block per the
   active brand before emitting, routed via `tblRoutes` — the exact
   pattern anticipated below stayed accurate.

3. **`prayerRequests.*` → `prayer-requests.*` setting-key naming
   standardisation** — drift dating to the original prayer-requests
   app (PR #129). Every other app uses kebab-case slugs as setting
   prefixes (`prayer-requests` is the directory name, `tblRoutes`
   key, app slug). The setting key is camelCase. A migration would
   rename the rows in `tblSettings` AND update the three handlers
   that read `App::settings('prayerRequests.*')`. Mechanical work;
   only deferred because it touches a wide-blast-radius app and
   isn't urgent enough to bundle into this PR.

Each is filed as its own GitHub issue with `for consideration` label
so the per-item decision happens later. Search the issue tracker for
"deferred from #297" to find them.

## Theme modes + colour-blind palette

The portal and the standalone installer support three theme modes and an
opt-in colour-blind safe palette. Both are user-level preferences stored in
`localStorage` (per-device, per-browser).

### Theme modes

- **Light** — light surfaces, dark text (the design's default visual)
- **Dark** — dark surfaces, light text (`[data-bs-theme="dark"]` overrides)
- **Auto** — follows the OS `prefers-color-scheme` and live-updates if the
  system flips

Click the half-stroke circle icon in the navbar to cycle through the modes.
The icon updates to indicate the active preference (sun = light, moon =
dark, half-stroke = auto). Persisted as `localStorage.portal-theme` =
`light` / `dark` / `auto`. Missing key defaults to `auto`.

The same control exists in the standalone installer at `/install/` (top-
right of the page). Its tokens mirror `portal.css` and are kept in sync
manually.

### Colour-blind safe palette

Opt-in toggle (`localStorage.portal-cb` = `on` / unset). When enabled,
the eye icon in the navbar shows as active and the semantic colours
(success, danger, warning, accent) shift to a palette from Wong (Nature
Methods, 2011) that's distinguishable for deutan + protan colour
blindness (~95 % of CB cases):

- `--portal-success`: default `#16a34a` (green) → CB `#009e73` (bluish-green); dark CB `#5dd1a8`
- `--portal-danger`: default `#dc2626` (red) → CB `#d55e00` (vermillion); dark CB `#ff8a4d`
- `--portal-warning`: default `#d97706` (amber) → CB `#e69f00` (orange); dark CB `#ffc04d`
- `--portal-accent`: default `#06b6d4` (cyan) → CB `#56b4e9` (sky blue); dark CB `#7fc6f0`

Primary stays untouched — it's the site's identity colour and is
user/site-set (see "Per-site branding flow" above).

**Accessibility note:** CB-safe tokens reduce the risk of mis-reading
status colours, but **colour alone should never be the only signal**.
Components that convey state (badges, alerts, validation messages)
should also use icons or text labels. The PR template's security
checklist already mentions this for new UI work.

### Dyslexia-friendly reading mode (#46)

A third opt-in toggle (`localStorage.portal-read` = `on` / unset), applied
as `<html data-portal-read="on">` and wired identically to the CB toggle
(FOUC script → nav button → `portal.js` `initReadToggle()`). When enabled,
`[data-portal-read="on"]` in `portal.css` swaps the body font to a clean
system sans-serif stack (`Verdana, Tahoma, "Trebuchet MS", …` — no web font
is fetched, so it stays CSP-safe and adds no network cost) and applies wider
letter/word spacing, ~1.6–1.7 line height and left-aligned (never justified)
body text. These choices follow the **British Dyslexia Association Style
Guide (2023)**. It composes with the theme and CB toggles — all three can be
on at once. The nav button uses the `fa-book-open-reader` icon; the help
page `/help/getting-started` documents it for end users.

### Flow

```text
localStorage  ──FOUC script──▶  <html data-bs-theme="..." data-portal-cb="..." data-portal-read="...">
                                       │
                                       ▼
                              portal.css token / rule overrides
                                       │
                                       ▼
                              all components inherit
```

The FOUC script runs synchronously in `<head>` before first paint, so
the chosen theme + CB mode are applied with no flash. portal.js (and
the installer's inline JS) then wire up the toggle buttons and listen
for `prefers-color-scheme` changes when in `auto` mode.

### Where to find the code

- `web/public_html/assets/css/portal.css` — token blocks for light,
  dark, CB-safe (and dark + CB-safe combined)
- `web/_core/templates/header.php` — inline FOUC script reading
  localStorage and applying the attrs
- `web/_core/templates/nav.php` — theme + CB toggle buttons
- `web/public_html/assets/js/portal.js` — `initThemeToggle()` (cycles
  light → dark → auto), `initCbToggle()` (on/off), `initReadToggle()` (on/off)
- `web/_install/index.php` — installer mirrors the theme + CB controls inline
  (it's standalone, can't load portal.css/portal.js; the reading-mode toggle
  is portal-only for now)
