### The guard against over-reaching guarded nothing, because no fixture was ordinary enough

The fix above needed a check in the opposite direction: if the rule ever
over-reached and called ordinary calendars incomplete, `FeedImporter` would
refuse to remove anything from any calendar, for ever, silently. Check I7d was
written for that, and its comment said so.

**It guarded nothing.** Measured on 28 October 2026: of the fifty-six fixtures
in `tools/fixtures/ics/`, **not one held a correctly closed nested block.** No
`END:VALARM` anywhere. No `BEGIN:VTIMEZONE` anywhere. The only `BEGIN:VALARM`
was the deliberately unclosed one added that same day. I7d read `basic-utc.ics`,
which is `VCALENDAR` → `VEVENT` → end: no nesting at all.

An independent check proved the cost by narrowing the pop to the two blocks the
reader cares about — the sort of tightening a later reader would write:

```php
if ($last === $block && ($block === 'VEVENT' || $block === 'VCALENDAR')) {
```

**All 345 checks passed.** Meanwhile ten of thirty-four well-formed shapes
flipped to `complete = false`: a realistic Google export, any event carrying a
reminder, `VTODO`, `VJOURNAL`, `VFREEBUSY`, `X-` components. Nearly every
calendar anyone would really subscribe to. Every refresh of every one would have
taken the "incomplete" branch for ever, and nothing would have said why.

`nested-blocks-closed.ics` is now a deliberately ORDINARY calendar — a
`VTIMEZONE` with `STANDARD` and `DAYLIGHT`, and an event with a `VALARM`, all
properly closed. With it, the same plant fails I7d at once.

**The lesson is about fixture sets, not about this rule.** A suite of
fifty-six files can still have a hole the shape of "the normal case", because
fixtures get written to pin faults and every fault is unusual by definition.
When a check exists to prove something ORDINARY still works, go and look at
whether any fixture is actually ordinary.

### A check whose comment claimed more than it delivered

C13's comment said it pinned the "exact rather than nominal" duration rule (RFC
5545 §3.3.6) and would catch an interval taken from `diff()`. The same
independent check restored that `diff()` route and **all four C13 checks
passed.** The 2027 London change is at 01:00 on 28 March, the moved occurrence
runs 02:30–03:30, and none of the three occurrences spans a transition — so
exact and nominal give the same answer for that fixture.

What C13 really pins is narrower: all three occurrences are 3,600 seconds, so
the one that moved did not lose or gain an hour in the moving. I26 and I29 are
what pin exact-versus-nominal, because their series genuinely cross a
transition, and they are the checks that caught the planted `diff()`. The
comment now says that. An overstated guarantee is worse than none.


### The replacement comment was wrong in the same way as the one it replaced

Worth recording as a pattern, not an anecdote. `generateStarts()`'s docblock
said "the clocks going BACK need nothing special here" — wording that waved away
a real fault and stopped reviewers looking. The replacement described the fault
but got its reproduction wrong: it said an event "whose start lands in the
repeated hour" comes out zero-length.

**That reproduction gives the right answer.** A series whose `DTSTART` is in the
repeated hour is correct throughout, because the first date goes through
`readDateTime()` exactly as a one-off does. The fault is in the SECOND OR LATER
date of a series, generated by `generateStarts()`. Measured:

| series | result |
| --- | --- |
| weekly 01:30, DTSTART 2026-10-25 (first date on the reading) | correct, 3,600 s throughout |
| weekly 01:30, DTSTART 2026-10-18 (25 October falls on it) | **25 October is 01:30–01:30, zero** |

So a reader following the comment would have built the first shape, seen
01:30–02:30, and concluded there was nothing to fix — the same outcome as the
"needs nothing special" wording, reached by a different route. #653's title said
"starting in" too, so the issue did not rescue it; both are corrected, with the
mistake recorded on the issue rather than quietly edited away.

**The general lesson: when a comment describes a fault, check that the
reproduction it implies actually reproduces it.** A comment that sends somebody
to the wrong experiment is worse than one that says nothing, because the wrong
experiment comes back green.


## The hour that happens twice, settled (#653, 28 October 2026)

The forward direction — the hour that does not exist — was settled on
23 September 2026 and pinned by check C13. The backward direction was not, and
this is the record of settling it.

### What was wrong

`Portal\Core\IcsReader` turned a repeating date's clock reading into a moment by
carrying the recurrence cursor's own UTC offset forward. On the night the clocks
go back, Europe/London runs 01:00–01:59 twice, so a reading of "01:30" names two
moments an hour apart. The cursor gave the EARLIER of the two. A one-off at the
identical reading went through `makeDate()`, which gives the LATER. **The portal
answered the same question two different ways depending on whether the event
repeated.**

Because an occurrence's end is its start plus its exact length (RFC 5545
§3.8.5.3, the owner's decision of 23 September 2026), a start resolved an hour
early pushed the end onto a reading an hour short. Measured against the
committed class:

| series in `TZID=Europe/London` | the date on 25 October 2026 | should read |
| --- | --- | --- |
| daily 01:30–02:30 | `01:30 → 01:30`, **zero** | `01:30 → 02:30` |
| daily 01:30–05:30 | `01:30 → 04:30`, **three hours** | `01:30 → 05:30` |
| daily 01:30 + `DURATION:PT1H` | `01:30 → 01:30`, **zero** | `01:30 → 02:30` |

The four-hour row is the one that says what the fault really was. Issue #653
reported only the zero-length case, which reads like a rounding oddity. It is
not: **a date starting in the repeated hour read an hour short, and zero is what
that looks like when the date was an hour long to begin with.** The instants
were right in every case — only the readings were unreadable.

### The fix, and why it sits where it does

`IcsReader::laterOfARepeatedReading()` is the ONE place that decides what such a
reading means: **the LATEST moment that carries that reading**, worked out from
the zone's own transitions. Check I34c pins that the repeating and one-off paths
agree on the stored readings.

An earlier version of this note said the two agreed "by construction", because
the function rebuilt the reading exactly as `makeDate()` does. That stopped
being true — see the next section, which is why — and it was an overstated
guarantee even while it held: `makeDate()` still takes PHP's own pick, so in the
Americas a one-off's *instant* is the earlier one while a series date's is now
the later. What they agree on is the stored **readings**, which is what is kept
and shown, and that is now a measured claim rather than an architectural one.

**It is called from `buildOccurrence()`, and it cannot move earlier.** The
identity of a date within its series, `recurrenceKeyFor()`, is the start turned
into UTC — so the two moments sharing "01:30" have *different* keys
(`…T003000Z` and `…T013000Z`). That key is matched against the `EXDATE`s and
`RECURRENCE-ID`s in the customer's own file, and it is **stored on the row** as
`externalRecurrenceKey`. Resolving the reading before the key was built would
rename every such date, so on the next refresh the importer would see the
renamed date as new, add it, and remove the one already there — losing anything
attached to it. Check I34b pins that the key is unchanged, which makes that a
testable claim rather than a promise in a comment.

An earlier version of this paragraph also said "a skipped date would stop being
recognised". **That is backwards**, and it was measured: an `EXDATE` written with
the event's own `TZID` keys through `readDateTime()` and so ALREADY fails to
match a series date on this reading, so moving the resolution earlier would make
that form START matching. Only a UTC-written `EXDATE` naming the earlier instant
matches today, and that is the one that would break. The stored-key reason above
is correct and is enough on its own. (The `TZID` form not matching is a real
fault of its own — the form Google, Apple and Outlook all write — filed as
**#654**.) It was corrected in the code comment and the `.OpenAI` mirror in the
first fix round and missed here, which round 2 caught: a correction applied to
three of four places leaves a note contradicting the code it documents.

### The fix shipped HALF-DONE, and only an independent check saw it

**`new DateTimeImmutable($text, $zone)` does not give the later of two
ambiguous moments.** The first version of the fix was built on the belief that
it does. PHP/timelib takes the first matching offset in the zone's own type
table, and that is standard time in Europe, Australia and New Zealand but
**daylight time across the Americas**. Measured on PHP 8.5.11 / tzdata 2026.3:

| zone | reading | PHP gives | which of the two? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Europe/London | 2026-10-25 01:30 | GMT | the later |
| Europe/Berlin | 2026-10-25 02:30 | CET | the later |
| Australia/Sydney | 2027-04-04 02:30 | AEST | the later |
| America/New_York | 2026-11-01 01:30 | EDT | **the EARLIER** |
| America/Chicago | 2026-11-01 01:30 | CDT | **the EARLIER** |
| America/Santiago | 2027-04-03 23:30 | −03 | **the EARLIER** |

So the first fix was a **no-op in New York, Chicago, Los Angeles, Havana,
Santiago and the Azores**, and #653 stayed live there. Swept across fifteen
zones, one backward transition each, the middle date of a daily hour-long
series:

```
Europe/London        01:30 -> 01:30   0s SHORT   (old)    01:30 -> 02:30  OK (new)
Europe/Berlin        02:30 -> 02:30   0s SHORT            02:30 -> 03:30  OK
Australia/Lord_Howe  01:30 -> 02:00  30m SHORT            01:30 -> 02:30  OK
Pacific/Chatham      03:15 -> 03:15   0s SHORT            03:15 -> 04:15  OK
America/New_York     01:30 -> 01:30   0s SHORT            01:30 -> 02:30  OK
America/Santiago     23:30 -> 23:30   0s SHORT            23:30 -> 00:30  OK
Atlantic/Azores      00:30 -> 00:30   0s SHORT            00:30 -> 01:30  OK
```

**America/Santiago is the zone this repository already uses as its non-European
test zone** in `tools/import-notifier-selftest.php`. The fault was shipped into
it and every check passed, because `tools/ics-reader-selftest.php` hard-codes
`$orgZone = new DateTimeZone('Europe/London')` and every I34 fixture is written
in London.

The repository's own time-zone rule says to "test them in a zone that actually
changes". That was done. **What was needed is one clause further on: a zone that
resolves the OTHER way.** Check I34i now reads a New York series directly, plus
Australia/Lord_Howe for a thirty-minute change so that nothing assumes the
change is an hour.

The fix no longer borrows PHP's answer. It takes every offset in force near the
moment from `DateTimeZone::getTransitions()` and keeps the latest instant whose
reading matches, which is why it is indifferent to how big the change is. A
cheap pre-filter — the offset a day either side — means the transition array is
only built on the day or two a year it can matter.

### And a THIRD time, in a new place: `setTimestamp()` is not safe either

The rewrite scanned the zone's transitions and built one candidate instant per
offset — with `$local->setTimestamp(...)`. **`DateTimeImmutable::setTimestamp()`
does not reliably set the instant it is given.** On an object carrying a named
zone, PHP converts to the wall clock and resolves again, so when the instant
asked for is itself inside a repeated hour it snaps back to PHP's
first-matching offset. Measured in America/Metlakatla:

```
$local->setTimestamp(1446373800)                      -> 1446370200  (01:30 PST)
(new DateTimeImmutable('@1446373800'))->setTimezone()  -> 1446373800  (01:30 AKST)
```

So the candidate built for the later offset came back as **the input instant**,
never newer, never chosen — and the function collapsed to PHP's own pick again.
A sweep of every zone PHP knows, 1900 to 2050, against an exhaustive reference
(every offset the zone has ever used, keep the latest whose reading matches)
found it wrong in **81 zones** at one reading per transition, **82** at three,
and **88** with the independent check's denser sampling. With the candidate
built from its instant: **0**. The count depends on how densely you sample, so
it is quoted with its sampling rather than as a fact about the world.

**Most affected cases were pure base-offset moves** — standard time on both
sides, a country changing its clocks for good — but **not all**, and an earlier
version of this note said "every one", which was untrue and made the failure
mode sound narrower than it is. Measured: 10 distinct transitions in 7 zones had
summer time in force on one or both sides (`Atlantic/Azores` 1942-45,
`America/Santiago` 1946, `America/Montevideo` 1974, `America/Cancun` 1998,
`America/Argentina/San_Luis` 2008, `America/Iqaluit` 1942, `Antarctica/Palmer`
1965). The only property they share is that PHP's internal table resolves those
two offsets the wrong way round, and it is unpredictable from the zone:
`Asia/Almaty` 2024 works, `America/Metlakatla` 2015 does not.

**And today's data DOES hold such a move after 2025** — `Africa/Casablanca` and
`Africa/El_Aaiun` go +01:00 to +00:00, standard time both sides, on
20 September 2026, and on tzdata 2026.3 that is the last transition either has.
An earlier version of this note said there were none, which was false. The
conclusion survives for a reason that version never gave: **PHP happens to
resolve those two zones' repeated hour to the LATER**, so the broken code was
right there by luck. No customer is wrong at this moment because of how the data
falls, not because of anything the code guaranteed. Base-offset moves land every
year or two (Mexico 2022, Greenland 2023, Kazakhstan 2024, Morocco 2026), and
the next one PHP resolves the other way would have made #653 live again in that
zone, silently. A member importing a 2022 Ciudad Juárez calendar reads an hour
short today.

**I34i was not enough to catch it, because every zone in it changes for summer
time.** Check I34j uses America/Metlakatla's 2015 move, and planting
`setTimestamp()` back confirms I34j is the only section that fails. The
committed test passed 363 of 363 with the fault in place.

The same unsafe construction was in the cheap pre-filter and is fixed there too.

### A vacuous check, caught in writing it

I34j was first written with a third check that asserted WHICH of the two moments
was chosen, joined by `||` so that it would pass. Both branches were measured:
the first can never pass (rebuilding the reading goes through PHP and gives the
earlier instant on correct and incorrect code alike) and the second compared the
reading with itself and was always true. It passed on everything and tested
nothing, and it was deleted rather than patched.

The reason it could not be made to work is the limit this section is about: **a
stored reading does not record which of the two moments it names.** The only
observable difference is the stored END reading, which is what I34j's two
surviving checks assert.

**An assertion joined by `||` so that it will go green is not an assertion.** If
a check needs an alternative branch to pass, find out which branch is carrying
it before believing either.

### A FOURTH fault, and this one stored wrong times: the length

Found by round 3. `$lengthSeconds` was measured between the two moments
`readDateTime()` returned — and `readDateTime()` resolves an ambiguous reading
with PHP's own pick, the EARLIER one across the Americas. So on the night the
clocks go back a `DTSTART` of 01:30 in New York was read as EDT while its
`DTEND` of 02:30 was read, unambiguously, as EST, and **subtracting the two
absorbed the clock change**: a one-hour event measured 7,200 seconds.

That part was pre-existing — the second and later dates of such a series were
already stored two hours long. **What this package added was worse**: #653 moved
the START to the later moment while the inflated length stayed, so the first
date and the one-off became wrong too. Measured in `America/New_York`, file says
01:30 to 02:30:

```
before #653   01:30 -> 02:30,  01:30 -> 03:30,  01:30 -> 03:30
with #653     01:30 -> 03:30,  01:30 -> 03:30,  01:30 -> 03:30
now           01:30 -> 02:30,  01:30 -> 02:30,  01:30 -> 02:30
```

The fix is in `prepareEvent()`: **both ends are resolved the same way before the
length is measured.** That makes every zone answer as `Europe/London` already
did — which is also why no London check caught it, and why check **I34k**, in a
zone that resolves the other way, is the only thing that does. The all-zone
sweep does not see it either: it tests the resolution rule, not how a resolved
start is used.

Two comments had to be corrected with it, because both stated a guarantee the
code had stopped keeping: that a `DTEND` length "lands on precisely the moment
the file stated", and that a one-off "is not affected by the choice either way".

### Faults five and six, both found by round 4, both about the LENGTH

Round 3's length fix was right for every ordinary shape — round 4 swept all 419
zones, 1900-2100, comparing old and new stored lengths, and every difference was
the fix removing an absorbed clock change. But two things were wrong around it.

**Five: half the fix could be deleted and nothing noticed.** Resolving only the
`DTSTART` and leaving the `DTEND` raw passed **all 368 checks AND the all-zone
sweep**. The behaviour really does change — a `DTSTART` of 00:30 with a `DTEND`
of 01:30 in New York (start unambiguous, end IN the repeated hour) becomes a
one-hour series there while its Europe/London twin stays two hours, which is the
exact zone inconsistency the fix exists to remove. Worse, the comment beside the
code **named I34f as the guard**, and I34f's fixture is Europe/London, where both
calls are no-ops. It could never have seen it. Check **I34l** now does, in New
York, and asserts the ordinary night's length as a number because that is the
date that tells the two behaviours apart.

The sweep cannot help here and its own header says why: it tests the resolution
rule, not how a resolved pair is used.

**Six: an event could LOSE ITS END ENTIRELY.** When the start is a READING and
the end is an INSTANT — `DTSTART;TZID=America/New_York:20261101T013000` with
`DTEND:20261101T060000Z`, which RFC 5545 permits — resolving the
start to the later moment (06:30Z) pushes it past an end of 06:00Z. The resolved
pair stops making sense, the code fell through to "no length at all", and the
event was stored as `01:30 → 01:30`, shown as a start time only, **with no
warning**.

**The released code was already wrong on this shape, differently**: it stores
`01:30 → 01:00`, an end BEFORE the start. Measured against a released-equivalent
copy. An earlier version of this note said the released code stored
`01:30 → 02:00`, which was untrue in the direction that matters — it made the
released behaviour sound fine when the shape was already broken, so the fallback
repairs a pre-existing fault as well as a self-inflicted one. (That version also
quoted "6,822 readings of the shape"; the figure could not be reproduced,
because counting readings of a shape depends entirely on the sampling — three
reasonable samplings give 7,959, 3,411 and 4,548 — so it is dropped.)

The length now falls back to the FILE's own pair when the resolved pair is
incoherent: 05:30Z to 06:00Z, a plain thirty minutes. The stored start stays the
resolved reading, which is right — it is only the length that has to come from
the file, because the file gave an instant and an instant cannot be re-resolved.
Check **I34m**.

### Fault seven: the FOURTH `setTimestamp()`, in the one place nobody looked

`buildOccurrence()` built the END as `$startLocal->setTimestamp(...)`.
`$startLocal` is now the RESOLVED (later) start, so an event **shorter than that
night's change** has its end inside the repeated hour too — and `setTimestamp()`
snaps it back to PHP's first-matching offset, the earlier pass. The clamp then
turned an end-before-start into **no length at all**: a fifteen-minute event
stored as `23:30 → 23:30`, no warning. **The released code stored it correctly,
so this was a regression.**

The comment sitting directly on the fault said "`setTimestamp()` keeps the zone,
so the answer is still written in the organisation's own time" — true about the
ZONE and silent about the INSTANT, which is the part that matters. This class
documents the `setTimestamp()` trap at length in `laterOfARepeatedReading()`;
this call was simply never revisited.

24 zones, 17 transitions after 2000: the nine Argentina zones (2004), Cambridge
Bay and Santo Domingo (2000), Caracas (2007, a thirty-minute change), Ciudad
Juárez (2022), Eirunepé and Rio Branco (2013), Metlakatla (2015 and 2019). The
`DURATION` route was never affected. It could only collapse the end onto the
start, never store a plausible wrong length. Check **I34n**, which is the only
thing that catches it — the all-zone sweep cannot, because it tests the
resolution rule and not how a resolved start is used.

### One consequence that is deliberate and member-visible, so the owner should see it

A series whose **first instance's `DTEND`** is the ambiguous reading now stores
**every later date two hours long** where the released code stored one. Measured
in `America/New_York`, file says daily `00:30 → 01:30`:

```
released   00:30 > 01:30,  00:30 > 01:30,  00:30 > 01:30
now        00:30 > 01:30,  00:30 > 02:30,  00:30 > 02:30
```

This follows correctly from the exact-length rule (RFC 5545 §3.8.5.3, the
owner's decision of 23 September 2026) plus resolving both ends, and it is what
Europe/London already did. But on an ORDINARY night the stored pair no longer
matches the file's own readings, and Google, Apple and Outlook would all show one
hour. The exposure is narrow — the series must START on the change night — and it
is recorded here because it is member-visible from now on and was not an
explicit decision, only a consequence of two that were.

### Three untrue statements in the class's own doc block

All three were in the paragraph that is supposed to say what the code cannot do,
which is the worst place for them.

- *"Reading both back in the organisation's zone … gives the full length"* — true
  in Europe/London, false in the Americas, where PHP resolves the ambiguous
  reading to the earlier and the same stored pair reads back an hour shorter.
  I34f's own comment already said it was a property of that one zone; the doc
  block stated it generally.
- *"LOOKS an hour short"* — it is short by the SIZE OF THAT NIGHT'S CHANGE: an
  hour almost everywhere, thirty minutes in Australia/Lord_Howe, and more in
  some historic data.
- *"It does not make the repeating and the one-off path produce the same
  INSTANT"* — they DO, because both go through the single call in
  `buildOccurrence()`. Measured by reading the I34k calendar with UTC as the
  organisation's zone, which exposes the instant: both come out 06:30Z. This
  paragraph had now been wrong in **both** directions across successive rounds —
  first claiming agreement "by construction", then denying agreement that
  exists. The narrow true version is that `makeDate()` alone gives PHP's pick,
  and this function is what both paths then pass through.

### The sweep reported PASS over nothing

Its own header calls that "worse than no sweep", and then it did it: planting an
empty offset list in the reference gave `ambiguous: 0`, no mismatches, **PASS and
exit 0**. The rename tripwire covered only one of the two ways to get there.
There is now a floor — fewer than 2,000 ambiguous readings REFUSES with exit 1,
against 145,265 today — so "nothing went wrong" and "nothing was tried" can no
longer print the same word. Two more of its header's claims were untrue and are
fixed: "or made public" (`method_exists()` is true whatever the visibility, so
making it public changes nothing) and a USAGE line still saying `--dense` takes
"minutes".

### A trap that moved into the test

The first version of I34i's length check measured a stored pair by rebuilding
each reading in America/New_York. **It failed on correct output**, reporting
7,200 seconds for an hour-long event, because PHP reads `01:30` back as EDT
there. The trap the whole section is about had simply moved from the code into
the check.

Lengths in these checks are now measured with `st_clockSeconds()`, which reads
both texts in UTC — plain arithmetic on the readings, which is what a member
sees. The 7,200-second round trip is itself pinned by a check, so that nobody
"fixes" the stored data to suit a naive re-read. It is also a reason event times
are compared as **text** in this portal (#604).

Note what this does to a claim made elsewhere: "the portal reads a stored
reading back by resolving it in the organisation's zone, which takes the later
of two" is true in Europe and false in the Americas. I34f's recovery of a full
7,200 seconds is a property of Europe/London, not a general one.

### The other regression the fix shipped first, and what caught it

The first version took the ORGANISATION's zone and judged every reading in it.
That is wrong, and not subtly: **a `DTSTART` ending in `Z` states an instant, not
a reading.** There is nothing to resolve, and rebuilding such an event's London
reading and taking "the later one" moved a real event an hour LATE.

Every one of the 357 checks in `tools/ics-reader-selftest.php` passed. What
caught it was part G of `tools/feed-importer-selftest.php` — which needs a MySQL
container and a web server — on an event written `003000Z`.

The fix is to judge the reading in the zone it was WRITTEN in (the event's own
`TZID`, the floating zone, or UTC). That makes a `Z` time a no-op for the
plainest of reasons: **UTC has no clock changes, so it has no repeated hour.**
Check I34h now guards this in the test that needs no database, and planting
proved it is the SOLE catcher of that mistake.

### Two leftovers that look alike and are not

Calling both "the known limit" — as the first draft of these comments did —
would send the next reader to fix the wrong one.

| | what it is | is the data right? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| end falls in the repeated hour (I34f) | `00:45 → 01:45` for a two-hour date **looks** an hour short | **Yes.** Reading both back in the organisation's zone uses this same rule and gives the full 7,200 s. The fix for the appearance is to show the offset, not to change what is stored. |
| the file stated instants in `Z` (I34h) | `00:30Z → 01:15Z` stores as `01:30 → 01:15`, end before start | **No.** Read back, that pair is **minus 900 s**, and the true 45 minutes cannot be recovered. Nothing at this layer can fix it; it needs an offset stored beside the reading. |

Part G of the importer's self-test pins the second shape too, and asserts only
that the end reads earlier than the start — never anything about the length.
That restraint is now explained rather than merely observed.

### A PHP trap, and why a plant "passed"

A plant meant to resolve the reading the EARLIER way used `modify('-1 hour')`.
**PHP applies that to the WALL CLOCK**, so on a moment reading 01:30 GMT that
night it gives 00:30 BST — a different reading. The plant fell through its own
condition, changed nothing, and passed all 357 checks. That looked exactly like
a hole in the checks and was not.

The genuine earlier instant with the same reading is
`setTimestamp(getTimestamp() - 3600)`. Same family as the `diff()` trap recorded
above: hours are exact, clock arithmetic is nominal, and the two part company
twice a year. **Plant with the operation you mean, and prove the plant landed by
its effect, not by the fact that you wrote it.**

### Which check catches what

Measured by planting all five plausible mistakes, not assumed:

Re-measured after I34j and I34k were added, because two rows had quietly
stopped being true — a table presented as a measurement has to be re-run when
the thing it measures changes.

| planted mistake | caught by |
| --- | --- |
| the fix removed altogether | I34, I34c, I34d, I34e, I34i, I34j, I34k |
| trusting PHP to resolve the reading, instead of scanning the transitions | I34i, I34j, I34k |
| building a candidate with `setTimestamp()` (the third no-op) | **I34j alone** |
| the length measured from the UNRESOLVED pair (the fourth fault) | **I34k alone** |
| assuming the change is exactly an hour | **the Lord Howe check in I34i alone** |
| the cheap pre-filter returning too often, so ambiguity is missed | I34, I34c, I34d, I34e, I34i, I34j, I34k |
| the transitions window narrowed to nothing | I34, I34c, I34d, I34e, I34i, I34j, I34k |
| dropping the `format() === $text` guard on a candidate | C13, I29, I34f |
| `st_clockSeconds()` re-resolving in the zone instead of UTC | the I34i clock-length check alone |
| the reading judged in the organisation's zone | **I34h alone** |
| `setTimestamp()` in the cheap PRE-FILTER only | **no self-test check at all** — only `tools/ics-zone-sweep.php --dense`, which is why that now runs on every pull request |
| resolving only the `DTSTART`, leaving the `DTEND` raw | **I34l alone** (and nothing at all before I34l existed — it passed 368 checks and a clean sweep) |
| resolving only the `DTEND` | **I34k alone** |
| dropping the file's-own-pair fallback (the end is lost) | **I34m alone** |
| the sweep's reference emptied | the sweep's own ambiguous-reading floor |
| that, AND the floor removed | **nothing — PASS over nothing**, so the floor is load-bearing |
| the resolution method renamed | the sweep REFUSES, exit 1 |
| the END built with `setTimestamp()` in `buildOccurrence()` | **I34n alone** — and by nothing at all before I34n existed, the all-zone sweep included |
| only the zero length "fixed" (nudge an end equal to its start) | **I34d alone** among I34's own checks (also I34h, and K1/K5, because a zero-length date is a legitimate shape elsewhere) |
| resolved before the recurrence key is built | I34b, with I34, I34d, I34e |
| resolved to the EARLIER moment | the line checks. I34c's *agreement* check passes, correctly: the choice is made in one place, so both paths move together and still agree. Agreement and correctness are two different claims. |

Tests: **I34 to I34n** of `tools/ics-reader-selftest.php` — six new fixtures for
the London cases, and three calendars built inline for the zones that need a
different organisation zone (America/New_York, Australia/Lord_Howe,
America/Metlakatla), because `st_read()` always reads in `$orgZone` and
`$orgZone` in that file is Europe/London. Part G of
`tools/feed-importer-selftest.php` is what makes the `Z` case end-to-end.

**The all-zone sweep IS committed and DOES run**, as
`tools/ics-zone-sweep.php --dense`, on every pull request. The first draft of
this paragraph argued the opposite — that it "took about a minute" and so did
not belong in a per-pull-request job. **Measured: 419 zones, 334,240 readings,
145,265 of them ambiguous, in 1.4 seconds.** That guess was wrong by two orders
of magnitude and was about to leave the only instrument that catches two of the
three no-ops sitting in a drawer, which is precisely what #646 was about.

Two things about it worth keeping:

- **`--dense` is not optional.** Light sampling starts at 1900 and tries four
  readings per transition, and it misses the PRE-FILTER form of the third
  no-op entirely: the readings that expose that one sit a whole DAY apart, at
  the 1867 Alaska, 1892 Samoa and 1899 Rarotonga moves across the date line
  where the clocks went back a full 86,400 seconds. Planting it was caught by
  `--dense` and by nothing else — not the light sweep, not any of the 368
  checks in the self-test.
- **It reaches a private method by reflection**, so it pins an implementation
  detail. It therefore REFUSES, loudly and with exit 1, if that method is
  renamed, rather than sweeping nothing and reporting success.


## A clock-change test that went red by itself (#652, 28 October 2026)

`tools/import-notifier-selftest.php` asked PHP's time-zone data for two
Europe/London clock changes **in the twelve months from today**, and tested both.
Run on 28 October 2026 that window held exactly one (28 March 2027), because the
next (31 October 2027) fell three days past its edge. Four checks went red with
nothing wrong anywhere in the code.

**It is a five-day window, recurring irregularly — not the months the issue
estimated.** Measured day by day over the 1,095 days from 25 October 2026, the
old shape finds fewer than two changes on **20** of them, in four windows for
the two zones N8 uses:

```
2026-10-25 .. 2026-10-29   Europe/London
2028-04-02 .. 2028-04-06   America/Santiago   <-- a latent fault nobody had hit
2029-03-25 .. 2029-03-29   Europe/London
2029-09-02 .. 2029-09-06   America/Santiago
```

(and 2028-09-24..28 and 2029-04-01..05 for Pacific/Auckland, which only
`ordinaryDay()` uses, where it is harmless.) From 30 October 2026 the window
reaches 31 October 2027 again and the test goes green by itself.

So the issue's "will keep failing until roughly the end of March 2027" was
wrong, and so was the first version of this very paragraph, which said "exactly
five" days — a figure that was both too low and internally inconsistent with
the two five-day ranges it then listed. An independent check caught it. Each
window is five days; there are four of them in three years, not one a year.

The fix is to count from a FIXED date, `CHANGE_NIGHT_ANCHOR` (1 January 2027),
whose twelve months hold two changes in each of the three zones used. Nothing
needs the changes to be in the future: `ImportNotifier::run()` is handed the
moment to pretend it is, so the whole of that section happens in 2027 whatever
today's date is. The new shape finds two changes on all 1,095 days.

Two details worth keeping:

- **The four nights are written out BY HAND in the test** (London 28 March and
  31 October 2027; Santiago 3 April and 5 September 2027). Every check in the
  section derives its night from PHP's data, so if a government moved a change
  and a data update followed, they would all still pass while testing a
  different night from the one the comment names. Deriving the expected dates
  from the same data would only prove the data agrees with itself.
- **The "fewer than two changes" branch now reports SKIPPED, not FAIL.** If a
  country abolishes its clock changes there is nothing wrong with this portal
  and the check simply cannot be made. Reporting FAIL for that is how a check
  gets switched off, and then it catches nothing.

Checked for elsewhere: `tools/held-texts-selftest.php` already asks for two
years and says why; `tools/mail-queue-selftest.php` uses 400 days;
`mail-pages-selftest.php`, `sign-in-limits-selftest.php` and
`giving-retention-selftest.php` span a whole calendar year. The notifier was the
only one asking for two changes inside 366 days of now.


### The API description had never been executed against the code (#641)

`web/_core/api-spec.json` is served to customers' developers by `/api-docs/`. Until 30 October 2026
nothing compared it with the handlers, and the drift was invisible from either file alone: you have
to hold both at once. `tools/audit-checks/check_api_spec_matches_code.py` does that, and it is a
hard gate in `pr-security.yml`.

**What it found on the day it was written:** 17 reachable endpoints absent from the description,
two more documented only under their REST address while the text denied their legacy address
existed, one handler whose switch was never seeded, and four seeded switches with no handler.

**Reachability comes from the router's own rules, not from a list.** `ApiRouter::dispatch()` requires
exactly three path parts and checks the last two against `^[a-z0-9\-]+$`. The check uses that same
pattern, so `_apps/assets/api/_coerce.php` — shared code that `create.php` and `update.php` require —
is excluded by the very convention that already makes it unreachable. **A hand-written list of "files
that are not really endpoints" would need a new line for every helper somebody added, and would go
red on the day they forgot.**

**The `api/v1/` facade has to be resolved, or the check cries wolf.** Four tables in `ApiRouter`
(`V1_RESOURCES` plus the create/update/delete name overrides) decide which handler a REST address
lands on. They are read out of the file, with comments stripped first so a commented-out resource
cannot be read as live. Without this, `noticeboard/save` and `leadership/assign` would have been
reported as documented-but-missing. A `**Legacy alias:**` line is also counted as documentation,
for the 40 legacy addresses described that way inside the v1 operation that shares their handler.

**That second part is NOT load-bearing, and the first version of this note claimed it was.** It said
ignoring aliases would report 28 undocumented endpoints against a true figure of 19. Measured against
the check's own sets, `aliases - targets` is EMPTY and removing the parse leaves the check green: an
alias line sits inside the v1 operation that already resolves to the same (app, action) pair, so it
can never contribute a pair `targets` lacks. The 28 came from a different model that did not resolve
the facade at all. The parse is kept for the one case it would catch — an alias naming a pair no v1
path resolves to — and the false measurement was caught by the independent check, which is the point:
an overstated guarantee is worse than none, including in a comment justifying a check.

**The three named lists fail BOTH ways.** `UNREACHABLE_ON_PURPOSE`, `UNSEEDED_ON_PURPOSE` and
`ORPHAN_SEEDS_ON_PURPOSE` name each known-and-deliberate state with its reason. Something unlisted is
a new fault; something **listed but no longer true** is also a failure, because a named exception that
has stopped describing anything is worse than none — it is believed. That is the exact shape that bit
the end-to-end migration harness on 29 October 2026, when three of its exceptions had quietly stopped
being true and nobody was told, because the workflow that would have said so only runs on a pull
request.

**What the check deliberately does not do.** It compares which addresses exist, not whether what the
description says about them is true — a documented parameter the handler ignores, a response field
never sent or a wrong status code all pass. The one exception is the "Legacy alias: none" sentence,
and that works only because it happens to be a claim about an address. It also does not try to
work out which HTTP verbs a handler accepts: that is decided at run time by `ApiAuth::requireMethod()`,
which `PORTAL_API_V1` deliberately relaxes, and guessing it from the text of a file would be wrong in
both directions.

**Five endpoints do not use the portal's envelope, and that is now written down.** `worship/state`,
`worship/advance`, `livestream/ping`, `push/subscribe` and `push/unsubscribe` answer their own flat
JSON, set none of `ApiResponse`'s security headers, and some open CORS to any origin on purpose
because they serve an embedded player on other people's sites. **`worship/advance` and the two push
endpoints return the replacement form token as a TOP-LEVEL field, not `meta.csrfToken`** — the
operator's console is drawn once and posts repeatedly, so without carrying it forward every control
works exactly once.

**Three comments stated guarantees the code had forgotten to implement** — the #645 shape, and worth
reading as a set because none of them would fail a test:

- `livechat/api/prompt-publish.php` said "pasting curl with the bearer-token-or-session would also
  work". A bearer key is accepted only by `ApiAuth::requireWrite()`/`requireRead()`, and the file
  calls neither.
- `tours/api/active.php` said it offered only tours whose version is at or below the running
  `PORTAL_VERSION`. Nothing in the file reads `PORTAL_VERSION`; the `ORDER BY` takes the highest
  version there is, so a tour seeded for a later release would be offered. A real gap, left as it
  stands because fixing it changes which tour people see.
- `noticeboard/api/save.php` and `noticeboard/api/upload.php` said their `App::isSiteAdmin()` check
  "fails closed for bearer keys too". The condition is `ApiAuth::source() === 'session' && …`, which
  **skips** the test for a key rather than failing it closed. The behaviour is the house convention —
  a key's authority is its scope, and **eight files** under `web/_apps` contain that same test (nine
  occurrences; `users/api/create.php` has two, which is how an earlier draft of this note said
  "nine handlers") — but the justification was the opposite of what the code does.

### A form that saves installation-wide must not prefill from the merged array (#674, 30 October 2026)

`$SETTINGS` is already merged by the time a page runs. So a box filled from `App::settings()` shows
the OPEN ORGANISATION's value, while a Save handler writing `settingKey = ? AND siteID IS NULL`
writes the INSTALLATION's. **The failure needs no mistake:** a global administrator opens the page
while in an organisation that has its own row, sees that row's value, presses Save without touching
anything, and it is now the installation's — for every organisation on it.

`Portal\Core\InstallationSettings::layer()` holds the installation-wide rows alone and is what such
a form must read. `admin/settings/repeats` and `transcription.monthCapPence` already did, which is
what made the inconsistency on the rest of that page visible.

**It is fifteen admin forms, not one.** `tools/audit-checks/check_install_wide_prefill.py` finds them
by pairing a page that writes with `siteID IS NULL` against the other pages in its own folder.
Fourteen are on a pending list so the check can gate immediately; `--strict` fails while any remain.
They are not fixed in one sweep because each page needs reading field by field — a page may
legitimately show a merged value BESIDE an installation one — and changing fifteen pages on a guess
is how a sweep adds more faults than it removes.

**Two things about the check are worth keeping.** It requires a `<form>` on the page, because a
runner, an OAuth callback or a webhook handler in the same folder reads the merged value *because it
needs the effective value to work* — measured, five such files would otherwise be reported out of
nineteen (the first draft of this note said twenty-one), and a check that cries wolf gets switched
off. And it skips a page that reads the
installation layer **at all**, because a page that has reckoned with the two layers often reads both
on purpose: the fixed transcription page reads the layer for its boxes and the merged array once more
to REPORT a difference. **The check reported that fix as a fault before that term existed** — it was
telling somebody to undo the correction. The cost, stated in its header: a page fixed for one field
and not another now passes.

**Four things the independent check found, and the first is the one to remember.** **A test that
pins one field out of nine is one guard and eight unguarded fields:** section S originally checked
`provider` alone, and putting the merged read back on `language` and `batchSize` left all 149 checks
passing. It now pins every box the form submits, each with a different installation and organisation
value, so a wrong box names which layer it read. **Reading the layer for an OPERATIONAL question was
a new fault, not a fix:** judging readiness on it made the page say "no transcription company is set
up" and disable the button while a posted run would have worked, because `run.php` reads the merged
value — so the boxes now show the installation's settings and anything describing what a run WILL DO
reads the merged one. **The check's write pattern was wrong twice**, believing one spelling existed
where three savers insert straight into the column, and counting a `SELECT … siteID IS NULL` as a
write — which produced a false accusation against a page whose paired saver only reads. **And its
list of limits omitted two blind spots, one hiding a live instance:** a read through the inherited
`$SETTINGS`, and a page that is its own saver, which `maintenance/backup.php` is.

**The harm is demonstrated, not argued.** Section S of `tools/transcription-pages-selftest.php` puts
the old merged read back and watches the installation's provider change from `openai` to
`assemblyai` on a Save that touched nothing. S06 then removes the organisation's row and requires the
new notice to disappear, so the notice cannot be one that is simply always shown.



### Five replies that described the inside of the envelope as the whole reply (#641, 30 October 2026)

`events/list`, `events/detail`, `noticeboard/list` and both Event Team Hub operations declared their
payload as the 200 body. Every one of those handlers answers through `ApiResponse::success()`, which
wraps what it is given in `{status, data, meta}` — so the description told a reader to find `eventID`
at the top level when it is at `data.eventID`, and the event itself at `data` when the handler nests
it at `data.event`. **This is the quiet kind of documentation error: every field name is right, and
every path to it is wrong.**

`PaginatedListResponse` was deleted rather than corrected. It described flat paging and an array
called `items`; its only user nests paging under `data.pagination`, calls its array `events`, and
sends `hasNext`/`hasPrev` that it never declared. **A schema that documents a reply nobody sends is
worse than no schema, because it looks authoritative** — and this project's rule is to delete what no
longer applies rather than explain that it no longer applies.

**The `Allow` examples are now computed, not written — at the second attempt.** The first edit
added the computed example beside the stale one rather than replacing it, so all 48 held two
contradicting values and the note claiming they were fixed was false while that stood. Found by the
independent check. **An edit that adds where it meant to replace is worse than no edit: the original
fault survives and a claim that it is gone arrives beside it.** All 48 said `GET, POST`. The real header comes
from `ApiRouter::v1AllowHeader()`, which inspects the handler files on disk, so it differs by
resource — the noticeboard really is `GET, POST`, while events is `GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE`,
prayer requests has no DELETE, and expenses and leadership have no PUT or PATCH. Each example is now
derived the same way the router derives it.

**NOTHING GUARDS ANY OF THIS, and that is worth knowing before trusting it.** The two checks
compare which addresses exist and whether every property has words. **Neither can tell whether a
declared response shape matches what the handler sends, whether a status code is documented, or
whether an example is stale** — `check_api_spec_matches_code.py` says so in its own header. The
independent check proved it by planting three part-3 regressions at once (an `Allow` example reverted
to `GET, POST`, a real `429` deleted, and the noticeboard array put back as the whole body) and both
checks stayed green. These corrections were made by reading handlers and they will go stale the same
way the originals did; catching that would need a test that calls each endpoint and compares the
reply with its schema, which no harness here does.

**And a measurement trap, which is the most reusable thing here.** Working out which endpoints a
bearer key can reach, the first pass searched each handler for `ApiAuth::requireWrite`. It returned
46; the answer is 45. The extra was `livechat/api/prompt-publish.php`, which this same package had
just given a comment saying a bearer key **cannot** reach it — and the comment contains the call's
name. Stripping comments with PHP's tokenizer gives 45. It is exactly the shape that has bitten the
audit checks repeatedly: **searching for the text of a call finds the text, not the call.**

### The API description's own schema, and why its validator is hand-written (#641, 30 October 2026)

`web/_core/api-spec.schema.json` describes the shape `api-spec.json` must have, and
`tools/audit-checks/check_api_spec_schema.py` executes it. It is deliberately **not** a copy of the
OpenAPI 3.0 meta-schema: it covers the subset this portal uses and enforces the house conventions a
general validator would know nothing about — above all a `description` on every property and every
parameter.

**Why the validator is written out by hand instead of using a library.** There is no `jsonschema`
on the development machine, and every other script in `tools/audit-checks/` uses the standard
library only. A check that needs something the machine has not got cannot be run before pushing,
which is exactly what #646 was about. So the keywords the schema uses are implemented in the check,
in about 150 lines.

**The honest cost, and the guard on it.** That validator is not a conformant JSON Schema
implementation, and it would **silently ignore** a keyword it does not know — which would quietly
turn part of the schema into decoration. `UNDERSTOOD` is the list of keywords it implements, and the
check **fails when the schema uses one outside that list**, so the failure is loud. The schema's own
`$comment` records the same contract from the other side.

**What writing 286 descriptions actually found.** The descriptions were written from the handlers,
not from the field names, and the pattern worth knowing is how often a limit does not refuse:

- **Money is in two different units** depending on the app. Assets are in **pence** (`89999` is
  £899.99); expenses are in **pounds and pence** (`12.50` is twelve pounds fifty). Nothing in the
  data says which, and there is no currency field on an expense claim at all.
- **Many limits quietly change a value rather than refusing it.** Most asset strings are shortened
  to fit; `limit` is brought inside range; an asset's `currency` falls back to `GBP`; a category or
  parent that does not resolve becomes null; an unrecognised `priority` or `visibility` becomes the
  default. Each of those is now stated, because "max 150" reads as "151 is refused" and it is not.
- **Two fields replace rather than add.** An attendance breakdown and the noticeboard's poster list
  are both whole-state: sending an empty list wipes the breakdown, or hides the whole board.
- **`licenseKey` is write-only and cannot be cleared** — blank means "leave it alone".
- **An identifier that is easy to get wrong**: leadership's `assignmentID` is the assignment, not
  the role, and the role goes on existing after it is used.

**Three untrue statements corrected.** `format: date-time` claims RFC 3339, which a plain database
timestamp with no offset is not. `PaginatedListResponse` describes a shape **no handler returns**;
its only user nests paging under `data.pagination` and calls its array `events`, and also sends
`hasNext`/`hasPrev`, which the schema never declared — so the schema now says so rather than leaving
it to be found. And `Asset` was referenced by nothing while the prose pointed readers at it; it is
now used by the four endpoints that return it, stating that `list` gives a subset and `detail` gives
four fields the shape does not declare.

**What the independent check found, because it is the shape this kind of package fails in.** Nine
real problems, every one a statement that was untrue rather than anything broken. Three are worth
carrying:

- The `AssetCreate` summary still said `currency` refuses a bad value, while the field's own new
  description said that summary had been corrected. **The file documented a fix that had not
  happened** — worse than the original error, because it reads as settled.
- A shared parameter description is only as true as its least similar endpoint. The `limit` text
  said to read a page total; four of the eleven endpoints carrying it send no totals at all.
- An example chosen to make a rule memorable has to be checked like any other claim.
  `DocumentCreate.isPublished` offered `False` as a value meaning true. The handler lower-cases
  first, so `False` is the one value that means false.

**And two things about the validator.** `oneOf` shared `allOf`'s loop, so it meant "every branch"
rather than "exactly one". Nothing in the schema used it, so nothing was wrong — but the file
claimed to implement everything it listed, and **the `UNDERSTOOD` guard catches a keyword that is
MISSING, never one implemented wrongly**. That is why the selftest now runs the validator directly
against 35 keyword cases in both directions: an end-to-end plant can only reach keywords the
description happens to use, and neutering the validator's `enum` test left both the check and the
selftest green. Finally, **a `$ref` with a sibling `description` is ignored by OpenAPI 3.0
tooling** — the version this document is pinned to — so a caveat written beside a reference never
reaches a reader. Wrapping the reference in `allOf` is the idiom that renders.

**A counting lesson, again.** Three traversals gave 181, 274 and 286 undescribed properties. The
check's independent implementation also says 286, which is the first time two separate
implementations have agreed — that agreement is the reason to trust the figure, not the figure
itself. And adding checks moved the "38 audit checks" line in two instruction files twice in one
day, so that line now names no number and says how to count them.

## Ten checks and two tests that ran nowhere (#646, 28 October 2026)

Found while wiring up a new check for #640, after an independent review pointed
out that the new check was not in any workflow. Measuring that turned up a much
larger gap: **ten of the scripts in `tools/audit-checks/` and two of the
`tools/*-selftest.php` files were invoked by no workflow at all.**

Every one of them guards something that was found broken at least once. That is
why the script exists. So the position was: twelve correct guards, none of them
running, over faults that had each happened before.

### The measurement, before and after

| | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Audit checks on disk | 36 | 36 |
| …invoked by a workflow | 26 | **36** |
| Self-tests on disk | 53 | 53 |
| …invoked by a workflow | 51 | **53** |

### The one that mattered most

`check_2fa_gate_order.py` guards the sign-in bypass fixed on 27 October 2026,
where four two-factor gates granted an identity before the check that earns it,
so `?redirect[]=x` made `Auth::safeRedirectUrl()` throw while `user_id` was
still set — PHP wrote the session at shutdown and the next request saw somebody
fully signed in who had never been asked for a code. On the password form, that
needed nothing but the victim's password.

The note beside that fix is explicit that **two** checks are needed because
neither catches the other's half: this script watches the ORDER, section Z of
`two-step-selftest.php` watches the BEHAVIOUR, and **reversing the order alone
is invisible to the self-test** — measured at the time, not assumed. So the half
that would catch a re-reversal was the half that ran nowhere.

Proved both directions: with the fix in place the check passes; with the
`unset()` moved back below the redirect in `web/_apps/auth/login/index.php`, it
fails and names the file and both line numbers.

### All ten as hard gates, and why that was safe to do

The owner's instruction was "hard gates where green". All ten pass on the
current code, so all ten went in as gates with `if: always()` and no `|| true`.
That last point matters: this repository has already had a check "documented as
always-blocking" that could never fail the build because of a `|| true`, which
is why the account-change guard now runs twice.

`check_no_hardcoded_domains.py` is left as it was — non-blocking, because it
carries a pending list and `--strict` is what fails on it.

### Four faults in the wiring, and two of them only a runner could have found

An independent check of the wiring found four. They are worth listing because
three are general traps, not one-offs.

1. **The QR test needed `gd`, which no workflow here had ever asked for.**
   `tools/qr-selftest.php` refuses outright without it — "this PHP has no gd
   extension, which this TEST needs to read PNG pictures" — and exits 1, so the
   step would have turned the job red and checked nothing. It passed locally
   because this Mac's PHP has gd. **No green run proved gd was present**: it is
   not in `setup-php`'s default set, not one of the five `setup-php` steps in
   this repository listed it, and no other test here uses it. The classic shape
   — the developer's machine has what the runner does not — and the only cure is
   to ask what the test needs rather than whether it passes here.
2. **A step id beginning with a digit.** `id: 2fa_gate_order`. Ids must start
   with a letter or underscore, and `steps.2fa_gate_order.outcome` is not valid
   expression syntax either, so nothing could ever read its result. The downside
   was the whole of `pr-security.yml` being rejected, which would have taken out
   every other check with it. It was the only such id in any workflow here.
3. **A count in a comment that was already wrong.** The header said "thirteen
   tests that need no database" when there were fourteen — missed when #640 was
   wired — and this change made it fifteen while correcting two *other* counts
   four lines below. Re-counted from the file: fifteen PHP tests plus two that
   need no PHP.
4. **A fallback that could not work.** The `qrencode` install step had no
   `continue-on-error: true`, so a failed `apt-get` failed the job and the next
   step's "run it without part Q" branch would have printed its warning into a
   run that was already red. It failed *closed*, so nothing was hidden — but the
   graceful degradation the comment described was impossible, and a transient
   apt hiccup would have reddened a hard-gated job for an unrelated reason.

### Two things local validation caught before any of that

1. **Twelve step names were silently truncated — the twelve written in this
   change.** A `#` preceded by a space starts a comment in a workflow file, so
   `name: Role keys (hard gate, #646)` parsed as `Role keys (hard gate,`.
   Existing names such as `Foreign-key target check (#552, …)` survive only
   because their `#` follows a bracket with no space. All twelve are now quoted.
   Worth knowing because the failure is invisible unless you parse the file.
2. **The counts in the workflow's own header comment.** It claimed a number of
   database-backed tests and of throwaway databases; both were re-counted from
   the file rather than adjusted by arithmetic (25 tests, 23 databases — they
   differ because two tests use the second and the loose server).

Both were found by parsing the workflow files locally with Ruby's YAML reader.
There is no `actionlint`, `yq` or `pyyaml` on this machine, but Ruby is present,
and one line of it parses every workflow and counts the steps — well worth doing
before a push rather than discovering it in a run.

### What is NOT proved

#646 asks for each check to be proved running **by pushing a branch with a
planted fault and watching it go red**. That needs a push, which is the owner's.
What is proved here is: every step exists as the YAML parses it, none is skipped
by its own condition, none has an escape hatch, each check passes on the current
code, and three of the ten refuse the exact fault they guard.
## 37 deprecated cURL calls, and the one that is not deprecated (#673, 30 October 2026)

`curl_close()` has done nothing since PHP 8.0. The handle stopped being a
resource then and became an object, freed when it goes out of scope. **PHP 8.5
deprecates the call**, so every one of them writes a `Deprecated` line to the
error log.

The portal called it **37 times across 15 files** — `Payments` eight times,
`Translation` five, `Zoom` and `Transcription` four each, `Sms` and
`AiAssistant` three, `Geocoder` twice, and one each in `Hymnal`, `Qr`,
`ErrorMonitor`, `AssetRegister`, `WebhookDispatcher`, `What3Words`,
`CloudflareStream` and the Integrations page. So talking to a payment provider,
sending a text, starting a Zoom meeting, geocoding an address, transcribing a
recording or translating a string each added a line to the log that said
nothing.

**Not every outside call the portal makes, and saying so would overstate it.**
`SafeFetch` (every fetch of an address a person typed, calendar imports
included), `WebPush`, `MailerGoogle` and `Auth` had already removed theirs, so
sending a push and sending mail never wrote one. An earlier draft of this
section said "every outside call" and listed push among them; the independent
check caught it, and it is the #487 shape — a claim about the blast radius that
is wider than the fault.

**Why that is worth a package rather than a tidy-up.** The error log is where a
real fault is found. Hundreds of deprecation lines per hour is how the one line
that matters gets missed.

### Four files had already worked it out

`SafeFetch`, `WebPush`, `MailerGoogle` and `Auth` had removed the call and left
a note saying why. `SafeFetch` also does `unset($handle)` inside its retry
loop, which is a real need — the variable is reused — and not the same thing as
closing it. The other fifteen now carry the same short note in place of their
first call.

### The issue's own figures were wrong

#673 said 43 calls across 19 files. **Six of those lines were the comments in
those four files**, each mentioning `curl_close` to explain why there is no
call. Counted with PHP's tokeniser: **37 calls, 15 files.** Searching for the
text of a call finds the text, not the call — the same lesson as #641.

### `curl_multi_close()` is NOT deprecated, and that matters

Measured on PHP 8.5.11 rather than assumed, because getting it wrong in this
direction is what makes a check unusable:

| Function | PHP 8.5 | Guarded |
|---|---|---|
| `curl_close()` | deprecated since 8.5 | refused |
| `curl_share_close()` | deprecated since 8.5 | refused |
| `curl_multi_close()` | **no notice at all** | allowed, not flagged |

A check that refused all three would report a call PHP is perfectly happy with.
A check that cries wolf gets switched off, and then it catches nothing.

### The tripwire, and why it does not search text

`tools/audit-checks/check_no_curl_close.py` asks PHP's own tokeniser through
`php -r`. A text search would report **all 21 comment lines, across 19 files,** that
mention `curl_close` under `web/` as faults — it was 6 before this package, and
this package added the other 15 notes itself, so the figure more than trebled in
the same change (an earlier draft of this sentence still said six). Count it
rather than trusting the number here:
`grep -rn curl_close web --include="*.php" | wc -l`. A text search would also hit
and would also report `$fn = 'curl_close';` — a string, not a call. Hand-rolled
comment stripping has been got wrong three times on this project: an apostrophe
in `// don't` puts every later quote out of step. So the tokeniser is used
rather than re-implemented.

**It must accept TWO token types, and the first version accepted one.** PHP
tokenises a bare `curl_close` as `T_STRING` but a fully-qualified
`\curl_close` as `T_NAME_FULLY_QUALIFIED`. Reading only `T_STRING` made the
check report **clean on a real, live deprecation** — proved by planting
`\curl_close($ch);` into `Zoom.php`, which is `namespace Portal\Core;`, as are
**fourteen of the fifteen files this package changed** (the fifteenth,
`web/_apps/admin/integrations/index.php`, has no namespace). That spelling is
not a curiosity: it is ordinary style in namespaced code. **This is the most
likely way the fault comes back, and the guard that exists to stop it was blind
to it.** A name that still holds a `\` once the leading one is stripped —
`\Vendor\curl_close` — is a different function and is deliberately allowed, so
the fix does not cry wolf.

**Two claims in the first draft of this section were wrong, and the second
review round caught both.** They are recorded because each is a shape this
project keeps hitting:

* **"every file under `web/_core/` is `namespace Portal\Core;`"** — false.
  It holds **190** PHP files: **105** are `namespace Portal\Core;`, **15** are
  `MWBM\Mail`, and **70 declare no namespace at all** (everything under
  `_core/apps/`, `_core/templates/`, `_core/partials/`, plus `bootstrap.php`,
  `version.php`, `brand-defaults.php` and a few more). The substance survived —
  fourteen of the fifteen changed files really are `namespace Portal\Core;` —
  but the sentence as written was a sweeping claim nobody had counted.
* **"php-cs-fixer's `native_function_invocation` writes `\curl_close(` by
  itself"** — DROPPED, not corrected, because it cannot be settled here. That
  rule's default `include` is `@compiler_optimized`: roughly 39 functions the
  Zend compiler special-cases, and `curl_close` is not among them. So it holds
  only when the rule is configured `@all` or `@internal`. There is no
  php-cs-fixer on this machine (no `vendor/`, no `.php-cs-fixer*`, which is
  consistent with "no CLI, no Composer"), so the claim rested on nothing that
  had been run. **The argument never needed it.**

**And one fold in the check cannot be pinned by any test, which is said out
loud rather than papered over.** The scan lowercases both the list of refused
names and each token it finds. The token side is now pinned by three cases
(`CURL_CLOSE`, `\CURL_CLOSE`, `Curl_Close` — all real deprecations, since PHP
function names are case-insensitive), and removing it correctly turns the
selftest red. The *list* side is a no-op, because `REFUSED` is already
lowercase: removing it was measured and changed **not one hit**. The review
round reported its removal as an unguarded fault; it is not a fault, it is a
plant that changes no behaviour, and believing such a plant is how a check gets
"fixed" for a problem it never had.

It has **no exemption list**, deliberately: there is never a reason to call
these, and a list would need a line per caller and go stale the first time
somebody forgot.

**It fails rather than passes when it cannot run.** A missing `php`, a
tokeniser that answers nothing, or a scan that reads zero files is a failure,
not a pass — that is the #646 lesson, where twelve guards looked wired and ran
nowhere.

### What it cannot see, and how both directions were proved

A call assembled at run time (`$fn = 'curl_' . 'close'; $fn($ch);`) is a
variable call, not a named one, so the tokeniser does not report it. Nothing
here does that.

`--selftest` runs **17 cases**. Thirteen exercise the scan: a plain call, a
`curl_share_close`, a fully-qualified call, one inside a namespace and a
fully-qualified share must all be refused; a comment, a doc block, the name in
a string, `curl_multi_close`, a **method** of the same name, `\Vendor\Http\curl_close`
and a relative `Vendor\curl_close` must not; and an apostrophe before a real
call must still be caught.

**Four exercise `main()` itself, and that was added because the first
`--selftest` could not see the half that matters.** The independent check
showed that changing `if len(hits) == 0` to `>= 0`, or deleting the vacuity
guard, left **all** the scan-level cases green while the check reported clean
on a tree holding a real call. The untested half was precisely the half a
one-character edit could neuter. `main()` now takes its root as a parameter so
the selftest can call it and assert its exit code: 1 for a real call, 1 for the
backslash form, 0 for a clean file, 2 for an empty folder. Both mutants are now
caught.

A third small fault of the same family: moving the `--selftest` dispatch out of
`main()` while changing its signature meant `--selftest` silently ran the
ordinary check and reported success. It is dispatched from `__main__` now, with
a note saying why.
## An event status the column never had, and the row that vanished (#676, migration 230, 30 October 2026)

`tblEvents.status` is `ENUM('draft','published','cancelled','postponed')`.
Three writers allowed **`archived`** — a word the column has never had — and
omitted **`postponed`**, which it has:

| File | Shape |
|---|---|
| `web/_apps/events/api/create.php` | inline list; falls back to `draft`, never refuses |
| `web/_apps/events/api/update.php` | list **assigned to `$validStatuses`**; answers 400 |
| `web/_apps/calendar/manage/import.php` | inline list; row-level error |

### The cost depended entirely on the server, and that is the point

Both halves measured on MySQL 8.0.36, not reasoned about:

**Strict** (every connection since #593, 12 October 2026):

```
INSERT INTO t (status) VALUES ('archived');
ERROR 1265 (01000): Data truncated for column 'status' at row 1
```

A 500 to the caller. Nothing stored, so nothing wrong in the database.

**Not strict** (any installation older than #593):

```
SET SESSION sql_mode='';
INSERT INTO t (status) VALUES ('archived');     -- accepted
SELECT CONCAT('[', status, ']') ...  ->  []     -- status = '' is TRUE
```

An ENUM keeps the empty string in its **index 0, "invalid" slot**. It is not
one of the four words, so **no status filter can find it**:
`WHERE status = 'draft'` and `status IN ('published', …)` both miss it.

**Be precise about the damage — the first draft of this section was not, and
the independent check caught it.** It said the event was "invisible on every
screen" and "cannot be found, edited or deleted through the interface". Neither
is true. `calendar/manage/index.php:190` builds its conditions as
`['e.isDeleted = 0', 'e.siteID = ?', 'e.externalFeedID IS NULL']` and adds a
status condition **only when one is chosen**; its badge at `:455` is a `match`
with a `default` arm, so nothing throws. The event **is** listed, **is** in the
count, and **can** be opened, edited and deleted there — it shows a grey badge
with a blank label, and opening it preselects Draft, so a Save repairs it by
hand. Measured: of 130 places that read `tblEvents`, **86 never mention status
at all**.

What is actually wrong is narrower and still worth repairing: a status no
filter matches, a blank badge in an administrator's list, and a value the
column itself calls invalid.

And `postponed` could not be set **through the API or the importer**, while the
API returned it in `Event.status`. It has always been settable from the
ordinary admin event form (`_event_form.php:83`) and the series bulk editor
(`series-edit.php:121`) — saying "through any route" was wrong.

### Migration 230 repairs, it does not restore

Every such event becomes `draft`. The owner chose that on 30 October 2026
because it **never publishes anything** and never asserts an event was
**cancelled** — it hands the event back to an administrator, visible to them
and not to members, which is the closest guess at what somebody sending
`archived` wanted. It also matches what `create.php` already does with a word
it does not recognise.

**What was intended cannot be recovered.** MySQL stored the empty string, not
the text it rejected. There is no schema change: the column was right and the
code was wrong, so the migration is a data repair and
`full_schema.sql` carries only its mark.

### An untrue comment that would have been a 500

`admin/calendar/moderate.php`'s header said **"Reject = status='archived'"**.
The code has always written `draft` (line 68, with `isPublic = 0`). Had it done
what the comment said, **every rejection of a submitted event would have been a
500.** An overstated comment is bad; a comment describing a crash the code
avoids is worse, because somebody will one day make the code match it.

### The tripwire was wrong twice, and planting found both

`tools/audit-checks/check_event_status_matches_column.py` reads the ENUM out of
`full_schema.sql` and compares it with every allow-list, every status written
straight into an events statement, and the API description.

**Version 1 cried wolf 14 times.** It checked every file under `web/_apps` that
merely *mentioned* `tblEvents`, and every one of the 14 was false:
`status = 'confirmed'` is an **RSVP's** status, `'pending_review'` an **erasure
request's**, `'processing'` the **retention sweep's**, and
`service-plans/save.php`'s list of `draft/published/archived` is the **service
plan's** status, whose column really is `ENUM('draft','published','archived')`.
Several of those files only JOIN to events. **"The file mentions the table" is
not "this writes the table's column"** — it is now scoped to files holding an
`INSERT INTO`/`UPDATE tblEvents`, AND half B looks for a literal only inside a
400-character window after such a statement.

**Do not credit the scoping with all fourteen.** Measured on the shipped check:
removing the file scoping alone brings back **one**, not fourteen, because the
window already puts an unrelated `status = 'confirmed'` out of reach. The two
changes went in together and the narrower window does most of the work. An
earlier draft of this section credited the scoping for all of it — the same
shape as the #641 "28 versus 19" figure, a number carried into the record that
the artefact does not support.

**Version 2 read only lists written INLINE** inside the `in_array` call. But
`events/api/update.php` — one of the three files this issue is about — assigns
`$validStatuses = [...]` first. So it was **never examined**, and putting
`archived` back into it left the check **green while it printed "3 allow-list(s)"
checked**. False assurance is the worst failure a check can have, and only
planting the fault found it. It now reads both shapes, and the count went 3 → 4.

**A third fault was in a test fixture, not the check:** a case meant to prove an
unrelated status far from the events write is ignored used 120 comment lines as
padding. The tokeniser strips comments, so the padding vanished and the case
went red. When a fixture needs distance, pad with code.

Its `--selftest` is **17 cases**: both list shapes, correct and faulty; comments
and doc blocks that mention `archived`; the concatenated `UPDATE` shape that
`moderate.php` uses; a bound `?` that is not a literal; and **five cases in the
cry-wolf direction** — another table's column, a service-plan list, an RSVP
status beside an events JOIN, an unrelated list, and a distant statement.

**What it cannot see**, stated because an overstated guarantee is worse than
none: a status chosen at run time and bound; a list built by concatenation or
read from a setting; a list holding neither `draft` nor `published`, since that
is how it recognises one; and a literal status inside an `INSERT`'s `VALUES`
list. That last was checked rather than assumed — all four
`INSERT INTO tblEvents` statements name `status` in their column list and bind
it with `?`, so the shape does not occur today.

## An install script that both seeds and deletes cannot be read with one regex (#675)

**30 October 2026.** `check_api_spec_matches_code.py` decided which API endpoint
switches a fresh install holds with a single `re.findall` over
`web/_sql/full_schema.sql`:

```python
set(re.findall(r"'api\.([a-z0-9\-]+)\.([a-z0-9\-]+)\.enabled'", text))
```

That file does not only seed. It **folds old migrations in**, deletions
included. Migration 186 removes four `api.expenses.*` switches for handlers that
are not in this repository, and the fold-in puts that `DELETE` *after* every one
of their `INSERT`s. A key written inside the `DELETE` matched the regex exactly
as a key inside an `INSERT` does, so the check counted four rows as seeded that
no installation has held since migration 186.

**Read this out of a loaded database, not out of the SQL.** The same lesson as
the generated-column one below. Loading `full_schema.sql` into MySQL 8.0.36 and
asking gives three rows — `api.expenses.create.enabled`,
`api.expenses.delete.enabled`, `api.expenses.list.enabled` — and nothing else
beginning `api.expenses.`. Reading the file gives seven.

**Crying wolf was the harmless direction. The dangerous one is the opposite.**
The check also asks whether every handler on disk HAS a seeded switch, because
without one `ApiRouter` answers 403 to everybody. A handler whose switch is
seeded and then deleted is exactly that case — genuinely unreachable — and the
old reading called it seeded and passed. Measured rather than argued: append

```sql
DELETE FROM `tblSettings` WHERE `settingKey` IN ('api.events.create.enabled');
```

to the install script and the old regex still answers `('events', 'create') in
seeded == True`, for an endpoint that now answers 403 to every caller. That
plant is committed as part of `tools/api-spec-check-selftest.py`.

The fix is to apply the two statement kinds **in file order**: a key in an
`INSERT` adds, a key inside a `DELETE` span removes, and a later seed brings a
row back. Nothing there understands SQL and it does not need to — the keys are
plain quoted literals and the only question is which statement each sits inside.
What it still cannot see is written in the function: a `DELETE` matching by
`LIKE`, by a subquery or by anything other than the key in full; a row written by
application code; and an `UPDATE` changing a value, which is correct to ignore
because an administrator may switch any endpoint off.

**The same shape applies to routes**, and for the same reason: `full_schema.sql`
removes `tblRoutes` rows as well as adding them, so `page_routed_handlers()`
honours deletions identically.

## A file in an `api` folder is not necessarily an API endpoint (#675)

Found in the same package, and it is the part most likely to catch somebody out
again. `web/_apps/expenses/api/export.php` is in an `api` folder, so every
reasonable assumption is that `ApiRouter` serves it at `api/expenses/export`. It
does not — or rather, it would, but that address answers 403 because
`api.expenses.export.enabled` is deliberately not seeded.

The file is reached through the **ordinary page router**. `tblRoutes` holds

```
expenses/api/export  ->  expenses/api/export.php
```

and `Router::dispatch()` resolves a target under `PORTAL_APPS` first, so the
address `expenses/api/export` loads that same file. **At that address neither of
ApiRouter's two gates applies**: not the per-endpoint `api.{app}.{action}.enabled`
row, and not the app's own API-folder switch from `AppRegistry::API_FOLDER_APPS`.
Two fewer gates than the folder name implies, on a file whose own header comment
still calls it an "endpoint".

Three consequences worth keeping:

* **A check that walks `_apps/*/api/*.php` and assumes ApiRouter is wrong.** That
  is what made #675 report a live, working CSV download as a dead handler.
* **An audit of "who can reach what" must read `tblRoutes` too**, not just the
  switch table. There is exactly one such file today; `check_api_spec_matches_code.py`
  check I names it and fails both ways, so a second one has to be a decision.
* **Searching for the wrong address finds nothing, and nothing reads like
  nothing-to-fix.** #675 said "nothing links to it" on the strength of
  `grep -rn "expenses/export" web/`. The link says `expenses/api/export`. This is
  the same shape as the `tblActivityLog`/`tblActivityLogs` miss recorded above:
  check a name against the thing that actually uses it.

## A harness that fetches a fresh token cannot test a token being spent (#675, #634)

Small, and it invalidated a check I had just written. The point of
`Auth::verifyCsrfWithoutSpending()` in the Expenses export is that the approvals
page's approve/reject form is built from the same token, and `verifyCsrf()`
**replaces** a token whenever it accepts one — so downloading the list used to
stop the next approval from working.
