The obvious test is: download, then approve. Written with the harness's own
`post()` helper it **passes on the broken code**, because `post()` reads a fresh
token off the page before submitting — a reasonable thing for a harness to do
and completely wrong here. Measured by planting the spending call back: the
`post()` version stayed green.

The real sequence is **one page load, one token, two uses of it**: the person
opens the approvals page, presses Export, then presses Approve on the form that
page had already drawn. The check now captures the token once and posts it
directly, and planting the regression turns both of its halves red.

## My fix for that regex was wrong in the same silent direction, and one character decided it (#675)

Worth its own note, because the lesson is not "parse SQL properly" — it is that
**a docstring claiming a limitation is harmless is the thing to check hardest.**

The rewritten `seeded_switches()` applied seeds and deletions in file order, and
found the end of each `DELETE` statement with `text.find(";", …)`. Its docstring
said:

> "A DELETE carrying one inside a literal would end the span early, and the keys
> after it would read as seeds — **the over-reporting direction, not the silent
> one**."

That sentence is false, and the independent check found it. Keys read as seeds go
into the "present" set, so a handler that exists on disk stops being reported as
unseeded — which is check G passing on an endpoint that answers 403 to every
caller. The *exact* fault the rewrite existed to catch.

It does not even need a string literal. A `--` comment is enough, and comments
like this are this file's own style throughout. **These two statements differ by
one character**, and the first passed while the second correctly failed:

```sql
DELETE FROM `tblSettings`
-- these are gone; nothing reads them any more
WHERE `settingKey` IN ('api.events.create.enabled');

DELETE FROM `tblSettings`
-- these are gone and nothing reads them any more
WHERE `settingKey` IN ('api.events.create.enabled');
```

`read_install_script()` now scans the file once, tracking whether each character
is in code, a quoted literal, a quoted identifier or a comment. Comments are
blanked to spaces of the same length so every offset still lines up, and only a
semicolon found in *code* ends a statement.

Three things that fell out of doing it properly:

* **A key quoted inside a comment is no longer read as live**, which fixed a
  second finding of the same check: removing the `expenses/api/export` route row
  while leaving `-- used to be routed as 'expenses/api/export.php'` behind made
  the check go green on a handler that had genuinely become unreachable. Writing
  that comment is the natural thing to do when removing a route.
* **`#` starts a comment in MySQL, but not inside a literal.** The install script
  seeds colours such as `'#0f766e'`; a scanner that did not know this would blank
  the rest of those lines and lose whatever followed.
* **`--` only starts a comment when followed by whitespace or end of input.** The
  file is full of `-----` rules inside comments, and `a--b` is not a comment.

Both faults are now committed plants in `tools/api-spec-check-selftest.py`, which
is why they are safe to forget.

## A setting written at the wrong LEVEL, and the check that went blind to its own fix (#677)

**30 October 2026.** `admin/settings/organisation/save.php` wrote nine `org.*`
keys and `portal.support.email` with `siteID` NULL — the row every organisation
uses — on a page called Organisation settings. The fix is ordinary: each
organisation holds its own, migration 231 copies the installation's values down,
and `$upsert()` takes the level as an argument **with no default**, because a
default is the same mistake waiting for the next caller.

Three things from it are worth keeping.

### Ask whether a field ARRIVED, never what it contains

The page disables the portal-address box for anybody who may not change it, and
**a disabled control is not submitted at all**. The first version of the handler
guarded only *who may send* that field and then wrote the result regardless:

```php
$checked = PortalAddress::check($text($_POST['portalAddress'] ?? ''));   // '' when absent
$upsert($db, PortalAddress::SETTING, $checked['address'], null);         // writes ''
```

`PortalAddress::check()` accepts empty as "no address", so an ordinary
administrator saving their **support** address cleared `site.url` **for every
organisation** — after which every e-mailed link is built from whatever host the
next request arrives at, which a visitor can choose (#500). Found by the new
section O of `access-pages-selftest.php` on its first run, not by reading.

This is the #667 shape again — a `disabled` control that would silently have
switched a payment provider — and it is the second time in a month. The rule:
where a form holds fields at two different levels, or for two different kinds of
person, each write is conditional on **`array_key_exists()`**, not on the value.

### A check can go blind to exactly the shape of its own fix

`check_install_wide_prefill.py` finds savers by looking for a literal `NULL` in
an `INSERT INTO tblSettings (… siteID …) VALUES (…)`. Passing the level as a
bound parameter stopped it matching, so the file stopped being a saver and **the
whole folder stopped being examined.** Proved by planting one key back to
installation-wide: nothing noticed.

That is the worst possible direction, because binding the level **is the pattern
the fourteen pages still on its pending list should adopt.** Each one fixed that
way would quietly leave the check's view, and the pending list would have emptied
while the coverage emptied with it — a list of fixed pages and a check guarding
nothing.

The cure is the house pattern: a named list, `LEVEL_CHOSEN_AT_RUN_TIME`, each
entry saying which keys go to which level and why the merged-prefill fault cannot
arise in the sibling page, failing **both** ways. **Measure before adding a list
like this:** exactly two files under `admin/` have that shape and no literal-NULL
write as well (twenty have both, so the ordinary branch still covers them), which
is what makes a two-line list proportionate rather than a fifty-line chore
nobody maintains.

### A `\b` in a non-raw Python string is a BACKSPACE

Writing that new regex into the check with a generator script whose own literal
was not raw turned `\bsiteID\b` into `\x08siteID\x08`. The check parsed, ran,
reported no problems, and **could never match anything**. Python warns about
`\s`, which is left alone; it does not warn about `\b`, which is a real escape.
The symptom was a detector that found 0 files where a standalone test of the same
pattern found 2. `grep -c $'\x08'` over a file is the one-line check.

### What is NOT recorded anywhere else

`renderBase()` runs **before** `MailQueue::add()`, so an e-mail's footer — and
therefore its support address — is rendered in the request that created the
message, with that organisation's merged settings. A queued message keeps the
right one. Nothing had to change in `Mailer` or the queue for the support address
to become per-organisation, and that is why.

## A per-organisation setting with a fallback has three traps, and I hit all three (#677)

**30 October 2026.** Making `portal.support.email` per-organisation "with a
fallback to the installation's value" sounds like one line of work. It is three
separate decisions, and getting any of them wrong is invisible on the page.

### 1. An empty value is not the same as no row

The merge falls back to the installation's row **only when the organisation has
none**. A stored empty string is a value, and it wins. So an organisation that
had ever cleared the box would have masked the installation's support address
for ever, with no way back from the page — which is not "falling back" at all.

Clearing the box therefore **deletes the row**. Said another way: for a setting
with a fallback, "empty" has to mean *inherit*, and the only way to express
inherit is the absence of a row.

This was traced from a real failing assertion in
`portal-address-selftest.php`, whose part H sets the installation's address and
then reads the Help page — and got "no support e-mail address has been set up"
while the installation had one.

### 2. A form that saves one level must not prefill from the merged array

This is #674 mirrored, and it defeats the thing the migration was careful about.
The box showed the merged value — the organisation's own, or the installation's
where it had none. Save wrote the organisation's row. So an organisation with no
row of its own would open the card, see the installation's address sitting in the
box, press Save without touching anything, and now hold **its own copy** of it.
The hosting provider changes the installation's address later and it reaches that
organisation never again.

One press of Save per organisation produces exactly the outcome migration 231
refuses to cause by copying rows down. The box must show **only what this
organisation has set**, with the inherited value beside it as words.

Note that `check_install_wide_prefill.py` cannot see this direction: it looks for
merged-prefill plus an installation-wide *write*. Here the write is
per-organisation and the harm runs the other way.

### 3. `$SETTINGS_INSTALLATION` is not available in a page

The settings loader really does keep it beside `$SETTINGS` — and **a page
inherits only `$mysqli` and `$SETTINGS`**, which is the standing rule in
`.claude/rules/app-pages.md`. Reading it in an app page gives `null` every time.

The symptom was perfect: the help text silently took its "the installation has
no address to fall back to" branch and told administrators the opposite of the
truth, on a page that rendered without a warning. `InstallationSettings::layer()`
is the supported reader. Caught by a check in section O, not by review.

## A test that only deletes what it borrowed leaves the fixture poorer (#677)

Section O of `access-pages-selftest.php` needed four known installation-wide
values, so it deleted whatever was there and inserted its own. At the end it
deleted again — and those four rows are **seeded by `full_schema.sql`**, so the
database was left without rows a fresh install has.

Two things make this worth a note rather than a shrug:

* The suite's own closing clean-up check could not see it. That check compares
  the keys recorded by its `setting()` helper, and this part wrote with raw
  `q()`, so the run reported every check passing while the fixture decayed.
* The next test to run against that database inherits the damage, and the
  failure will look like that test's fault.

Read the rows first, put exactly those back — including "there was no row",
restored by leaving none — and assert it, which is now the last check of the
part.

## A shared template is the right place for a thing every page needs — pick the one already required (#680)

**30 October 2026.** The browser-tab icon links lived in `header.php`. A page
that draws its own `<head>` never reaches that file, so it had no icon — and
with none a browser falls back to `/favicon.ico`, which no file and no address
answers. That was live on the **sign-in page**, the first page any visitor sees.

The tempting fix is a new partial, `head-icons.php`, required by both. The
better one is to put the links in **`head-meta.php`**, because:

* every own-`<head>` page **already requires it**, and
* `tools/audit-checks/check_page_head_tags.py` **already fails a page that does
  not**, naming the 13 exemptions one by one.

So the class closes with no new thing to remember and no new list. A new partial
would have been a second thing for the next own-head page to forget.

Two details that make it work rather than nearly work:

* The links go **outside** the sharing-tag block in that file. Those tags are
  skipped when there is no trustworthy whole address to put in them (a canonical
  built from a host the requester chose points search engines at a name an
  outsider picked); an icon needs no address and belongs on every page either
  way.
* `$siteFavicon` and `$brandIconPath` are taken with **`??=`**. `header.php`
  works both out at the top of itself, before requiring the partial, so an
  ordinary page reuses its answer and an own-head page gets it worked out there.
  One copy of the resolution chain, two entry points.

**And check the direction you did not change.** Moving the links out of
`header.php` is one require away from being a regression for *every* page in the
portal rather than a fix for a few. Section F of `page-head-selftest.php` checks
an ordinary page still carries the icon (F04) as well as the sign-in page (F01),
and when the original fault is planted F01 and F02 go red while F04 stays green
— which is how you know the two checks are testing different things.

**A guard on a shared template has to read what is PRINTED.** The first version
of the new check read the raw file for `rel="icon"`, and passed on the link
commented out inside `<?php /* … */ ?>` — every character still there, nothing
served. Measured by planting, not reasoned about. It now reads
`printed_markup()`. That is the third time in this repository a guard has been
satisfied by text that never runs (the QR host function, #623; a commented-out
`require` in this very check), so treat "the text is present" as evidence of
nothing.

## A limit where 0 means "no limit" is the largest value, not the smallest (#668)

**30 October 2026.** `min(merged, installation)` is the whole rule for a limit
an organisation may tighten but not loosen, and it is correct — the merged value
already is the organisation's own where it has a row and the installation's where
it has not, so no query is needed to tell the two apart.

Zero breaks it, and it is not a corner case: several of these settings use 0 for
"keep for ever" or "no limit". Compared as a number it passes every limit,
because 0 is less than everything.

**Converting it in the handler is worse than not converting it.** The first
version of this work converted only the POSTED number, in the one page, and the
independent check broke it in both directions within minutes:

* an installation that chose 0 — "keep for ever", which its own form offers —
  got a ceiling of **0**, so every organisation save was refused, **including a
  tighter one**. Thirty days was refused on an installation that allowed for
  ever. And because the refusal ends the request before all three writes, the
  organisation could not change its other two settings either.
* an installation that chose 3650 — ten years, the most its form offers — let an
  organisation store 0 and keep the data **for ever**, which is strictly longer,
  because `3650 > 3650` is false.

So the rule is stated once, in `SettingLimit`, read at **both** levels, and it
cannot be expressed as arithmetic: **"for ever" is allowed only when the
installation itself allows for ever.** Everything else is compared as days, with
for-ever standing in as the hard maximum.

Two consequences for a page:

* **"What is the ceiling" and "may this organisation choose for ever" are
  different questions**, and a page needs both. A box with `min="0"` offers
  for-ever whatever its `max` says, so offering it where the installation forbids
  it is a control whose own Save refuses it — the #675 fault.
* **Never prefill a value the box's own `max` forbids.** An organisation that
  chose 1000 days while that was allowed would be shown `value="1000"` against
  `max="90"`, and the browser then refuses to submit the whole form — a dead Save
  button with only a tooltip to explain it, taking every other setting on the
  page down with it.

## Four ways a text check passes on a gate that does nothing (#668)

Section D of `setting-limit-selftest.php` reads the save handler as text, because
sections A to C exercise the rule and cannot tell you a handler still calls it.
Asking only whether the text is PRESENT passed on all four of these, each planted
on its own and each measured:

```
if (false) { … }                     the whole gate off
if ($refusal !== '' && false) { … }  the condition weakened
refusal logs, never exits            it records "nothing was saved", then writes
refusal clamps: $days = $allowed     it silently shortens instead of refusing
```

The third is the worst, because the activity log actively lies. The second is the
shape `.claude/CLAUDE.md` names twice — and this file walked into it anyway,
which is the argument for planting every time rather than trusting the warning.

What closes it: pin the **whole condition** with a pattern, require the refusal
block's own text to contain `exit();`, and require it NOT to assign to the number
on the way past. Note `preg_match('/\$days\s*=/')` matches `$days === 0`, so an
assignment test needs `=(?!=)` — that one failed on correct code first.

And a text check still cannot prove the behaviour. This page has no HTTP test at
all; `event-repeat-pages-selftest.php` K06–K08 does exactly that for the repeats
page, and this handler deserves the same.

## Check that a planted fault actually applied (#668)

Third time this month. A plant removed `"    exit();\n"` from a block that had
been sliced to END at the newline — so the string never matched, the file was
unchanged, the test passed, and the plant was recorded as "not caught" when it had
never been tried. The fix to the check it was testing was real and needed; the
evidence for it was not.

`assert` that the thing you meant to break is actually different afterwards. A
plant that silently does nothing produces the most expensive kind of result: a
guard believed to be unnecessary.

## Five shapes that hide a setting key from a search (#668)

**30 October 2026.** Judging #668's 32 candidate settings meant answering "what
reads this, and what writes it" for each. A plain search for the dotted key
answers neither reliably. Five shapes, every one of them met in this repository:

| shape | example |
|---|---|
| a nested read | `$SETTINGS['chat']['maxBodyChars']` |
| a prefix query | `MailQueue` reads `LIKE 'mail.queue.%'` |
| **a constant** | `AnonymousCheckins::RETENTION_KEY` |
| a differently-scoped array | `$settings['maxUploadMb']` in `photos/upload.php` — the dotted path is gone by then |
| seeded and read by nothing | `forms.responseRetentionDays`, `webhooks.maxRetries` (#686) |

The third one is the expensive one: `attend.detailRetentionDays`, the live
breach #668 named, appears **nowhere as a literal** in the page that writes it.
A tripwire built on literals would have passed on the very fault it was built
for.

The fourth cost me a false claim. I reported **four** settings as seeded-but-unread
and two of them were read — in a comment on the issue, before checking the last
segment on its own. Search for the **last segment** as well as the whole key
before calling a setting dead, and for a `LIKE` on its prefix.

## A check that cries wolf gets switched off, so measure the false alarms (#668)

`check_limit_settings_capped.py` asks which files can create a per-organisation
settings row and whether any writes a limit-shaped key without capping it. Its
first version produced four findings, **two of them false**, and both false ones
were pages that write `siteID NULL` only and are global-administrator-only —
they cannot cross the boundary the check is about at all.

The cause: it asked whether the `VALUES` list **contained** a placeholder.
Every such INSERT does — `VALUES (?, ?, ?, NULL, NOW())` contains three. It now
pairs the column list with the values list and looks at what sits in the
`siteID` **position**.

Two more faults in the same check, both found by planting:

* **It did not recognise the worked example.** `EventRecurrence::installationAllows()`
  is the first reader built to this rule, and the check reported it as a fault
  because it only looked for `SettingLimit::`.
* **It found nothing at all** until adjacent string literals were joined. The
  house style builds a statement as `'INSERT INTO t (…) ' . 'VALUES (…)'`, so
  `INSERT … VALUES` never appears in one literal — and the one file the check
  exists to account for is written exactly that way. A pattern spanning the two
  matches nothing, the check reported zero writers, and then called its own
  exception list stale.

The general lesson, which #668 states and this proved twice: **count the false
alarms before wiring a check in.** Two out of four would have been enough for
somebody to stop trusting it, and then the real fault is unguarded.

## Two readers of one setting must not disagree about what will happen (#668)

`MailQueue::ownNumberCheck()` caps its four numbers against the installation by
reading the installation's own row directly, **not** by asking `SettingLimit`,
and that is deliberate rather than an oversight.

The queue reads these numbers with a single `LIKE 'mail.queue.%'` query because
a scheduled job sends for **many** organisations and cannot use the request's
merged settings — there is no "current organisation" in a job. If the check that
decides whether a value may be SAVED asked a different reader from the one that
decides what the job DOES, the two could disagree, and an administrator would be
told their number was accepted while the job used another. A little duplication
is the cheaper mistake.

The three-tier rule is identical either way: lower is always allowed, higher
never, and a hard range in code caps both.

## A save-time cap is not a cap (#668)

**30 October 2026.** `MailQueue::ownNumberCheck()` was taught to refuse a value
above the installation's. That stops somebody **choosing** one. It does nothing
about a row already stored, and three ordinary things leave one:

* it predates the check (the per-organisation feature shipped with #592);
* somebody wrote it with direct SQL;
* a **whole-database restore of an older backup** brought it back — and that is
  the supported route, because a one-table restore of `tblSettings` is refused.

Measured by the independent check: the installation's rows said 7 and 48 while
the job used 365 and 720 for an organisation whose rows were already there. So a
failed message's body sat on the installation's disk for a year on an
installation that had chosen a week.

Worse than the gap itself, the comment beside the new check **justified** reading
the installation's row *there* precisely so that the save test and "what the job
does" could not disagree. They disagreed, in the one direction the rule is about.
A justification that the code does not honour is the #645 shape: a comment
stating the guarantee the code forgot to implement.

`numbers()` — the reader the job uses — now takes the smaller of the two as
well. The check and the job agree because they do the same thing, not because a
comment says they do.

## The precise rule for "does this setting name look like a limit" (#668)

Three versions, and the first two were wrong in opposite directions. Both were
measured against the same twelve keys.

**Too narrow** — a regex anchored on the last segment with a capitalised word
list missed five real limits: `mail.queue.keepFailedDays` (the capital F stopped
`[a-z0-9]*Days$` matching — and that is the key the whole package is about),
`giving.retention.years` (lower-case `years` never matched `Years`),
`transcription.monthlyMinutes`, `offboarding.undo_window_days` and
`venues.renewal_lead_days` (snake_case).

**Too wide** — substring matching on every segment found `min` inside
`venues.reminder_roles`, `count` inside `org.address.countryCode`, and the
*namespace* `retention` inside `giving.retention.hold`, `.confirmed`, `.scope`,
`.countryCode` and `.yearEnd`. Six settings that are not limits, reported beside
the one that is.

**Right**: take the **last segment only**, split it into words on camelCase
boundaries and underscores, lower-case them, and match **whole words** against a
list. Both halves are load-bearing — the last segment stops the namespace
deciding, the whole word stops "reminder" being a minimum.

The cost, stated rather than hidden: a limit whose last segment uses a word not
on the list is invisible. That is a list to extend when one turns up, not a
pattern to loosen.

## Every number in the argument can be wrong while the argument is right (#668)

The tripwire's docstring justified its own design — "scoped to the files that can
write a per-organisation row, because a list of that size is maintainable" — with
three figures: **31 files**, of which **one** names a limit-shaped key, **directly**.

Measured with the check's own functions: **seven** files (five under `web/_apps`,
two under `web/_core`), of which **four** name a limit-shaped key, and the one it
was thinking of is a **constant**. 31 is close to the number of files containing
*any* `INSERT INTO tblSettings` (32), of which all but seven write `NULL`.

The design was right. Every number offered in support of it was wrong, which is
the worst way to be right: a reader who checks one figure and finds it false has
no reason to trust the conclusion. **Measure the numbers you put in a comment
with the same code the comment is about** — it took one short script here.

## A seeded setting that nothing reads is a lie with a Save button (#671)

`/admin/maintenance/offsite-backup` had six seeded settings, a form, a permission
rule narrower than the page's, a refusal written into the activity log, and a
read-only mode for a site administrator. All of it was careful, and **nothing in
the repository read any of the six values.** The sync script used the variables in
its own copy on the server; its header said so, and so did the setup guide. Only
the page was silent, so the page was the one thing that lied — and it lied with a
success message: "Off-site backup settings saved."

**How to find this shape.** For every key a page writes, search the whole
repository for a reader, and count the ones that are not the page itself:

```bash
grep -rn "backup\.offsite" . --include="*.php" --include="*.sql" --include="*.sh" \
  | grep -v "full_schema.sql\|103_offsite_sync.sql\|offsite-backup"
```

That printed nothing. The three remaining mentions of `offsite` anywhere under
`web/` were two comments citing the page as a precedent for a time limit, and one
link from the help page.

**Why it survived so long:** every automatic check passed. `check_schema_seed_parity.py`
is happy — the keys are seeded in both places. The route exists, the file exists, the
form posts to the right address, the permission check is right. **Nothing anywhere
asks whether a setting is READ.** A tripwire for that is a real possibility and is
not built: the hard part is that a legitimate setting may be read only by a shell
script, a scheduled job, or a file that is not deployed.

## A bridge from the database to a shell REFUSES; it never escapes (#671)

`tools/offsite-backup/read-offsite-settings.php` hands six settings to a bash
script. Three of them end up on a command line. A settings box is free text.

The rule written into that file, and worth keeping: **a value that does not match
its pattern is not printed at all.** The script then uses the value in its own file
and prints a `WARNING` naming the setting. Nothing is cleaned up and passed on,
because an escaped destination is still a destination nobody chose, and what is
being sent is the whole database.

What makes the `KEY=value` format safe without `eval` on the far side: every value
is checked against a pattern containing no newline, no space, no quote and no shell
character, so stored text cannot add a second line or a second key. The bash side
re-checks every value anyway — two guards, because the bash one is the one that
would have to hold if the bridge were replaced or edited on the server. The patterns
on the two sides are kept deliberately identical so they can be read side by side;
two guards that differ are worse than one.

One thing measured rather than assumed: **bash does not re-read the content of a
variable it has expanded**, so a dollar sign or a backtick inside a value is not
dangerous in `"${VALUE}"`. The patterns are still narrow, for readability rather
than for safety. A **leading dash** is the real hazard, and it is refused
separately: `rclone` and `mail` would both read one as an option rather than a value.

## A fixed path to the portal is wrong on every real server (#671)

`log-offsite-result.php` began with:

```php
require __DIR__ . '/../../web/_core/bootstrap.php';
```

It is copied to `<portal>/_backups/`, so that resolves to
`<parent-of-portal>/web/_core/bootstrap.php` — correct **only when the portal's
folder is literally named `web`.** It is in a checkout of this repository, which is
where it was tested; it is not on a customer's server, where the deploy mirrors the
CONTENTS of `web/` into a folder the customer names (the `SFTP_PATH_…` secrets).

Measured on 30 October 2026 rather than reasoned: from a folder named `portal-live`,
`realpath()` of that path is `false`.

**The consequence is the part worth remembering.** The recorder stopped before
writing anything, so `tblOffsiteSyncLog` stayed empty on every real installation,
and the off-site page showed "Last sync: never" and "No runs logged yet" however
many copies had really been sent — **and a failed run was equally invisible**, since
a failure is recorded through the same file.

**And it had already been found.** `docs/offsite-backup-setup.md` said: "A run is
recorded **only when the portal's folder is called `web`**. On any other folder name
the copy is still sent, but the page shows nothing for it. *Tested (19).*" So it was
observed, measured, written down as a limitation — and not treated as a bug. Writing
a fault down accurately is not the same as deciding what to do about it, and a
limitation that no customer could ever avoid is a bug.

Both files now look for `_core/bootstrap.php` in the two places either can be
(copied to `<portal>/_backups/`, or run from `tools/offsite-backup/` in a checkout)
rather than assuming a name.

## Stripping comments before a text check, and the two opposite ways it bites (#671)

The off-site page has to answer "does the copy of the sync script on THIS server
obey these settings?" The script is copied by hand and never deployed, so the page
cannot assume it is current.

It checks the mechanism, not a version label: the bridge file must exist, and the
script must have a non-comment line assigning `READ_PHP` **and** a non-comment line
calling `php "${READ_PHP}"`. A `@version` line is a claim; a customer editing the
file keeps the claim and changes the behaviour.

**Why the comments must be stripped.** The script NAMES the bridge several times in
its own prose, explaining what it does and cannot do. So a plain search for that
name, or for `READ_PHP`, is satisfied by a script whose call has been **commented
out** — exactly the state the check exists to catch. Section O of
`backup-page-selftest.php` plants that state and the page catches it; with the
comment-stripping condition replaced by `false === true`, **four checks in that one
section fail and no others**, so the stripping is load-bearing and the plant is pure.

**The same technique failed the opposite way in the same package.** A check in
`offsite-settings-selftest.php` asserts the recorder no longer uses the old
`'/../../web/_core/bootstrap.php'` path. The first version searched the whole file
and failed — because the fix's own comment **quotes the old line on purpose**, to
stop somebody putting it back. There the naive search called a fixed thing broken;
on the page it would have called a broken thing fixed. Both are the same mistake:
asking the text a question only the code can answer.

## A comment claimed a refusal the code never made, and only running it decided (#671)

The bridge's "how many copies to keep" reader carried a comment saying `"8.5"` and
`"08"` were both refused, "rather than rounded or read as base eight". The code
refused `8.5` and **accepted `08`**, returning 8 — `/^[0-9]+$/` matches a leading
nought. The self-test's own expectation was written from the comment, so the test
caught the comment rather than the code.

Accepting it turned out to be right, and the reason is worth keeping: the danger
that made `08` worth refusing was **bash reading it as base eight**, which the
script's own note records costing a whole silent tidy-up. That danger is gone
through the bridge, because what the bridge prints is always a canonical decimal
with no leading nought, and the script reads it with an explicit `10#` as well. So
the fix was to the comment and the test, not to the behaviour — but which of the two
was wrong was not knowable by reading either.

## access-pages-selftest.php cannot run beside anything on the same MySQL server (#689)

Running four CI-wired self-tests at once against one MySQL container, each with its
own database, gave `access-pages-selftest.php` **332 passed, 2 failed**. Alone,
against the same already-used database: **334 passed, 0 failed.**

It counts the portal's account look-ups out of `mysql.general_log`, which is **one
table for the whole server**, narrowed only by `thread_id <> CONNECTION_ID()`. So
every statement any other test's connection runs — on any database on that server —
is counted, and the two strictest checks go over.

**The owner's rule of 12 October 2026 allows packages that share no files to run
side by side with their "own named containers and ports". This is the case that
shows a shared database SERVER is not enough separation, even with different
database names.** And it fails in the dangerous direction: two failures that read
exactly like a real regression in whatever you are checking, with nothing in the
message pointing at another process. Re-run a surprising failure alone before
believing it.

## A pattern with no "s" drops the WHOLE flag, not the rest of the line (#671)

`log-offsite-result.php` read its arguments with:

```php
if (preg_match('/^--([a-z\-]+)(=(.*))?$/', $arg, $m) === 1) { $args[$m[1]] = $m[3] ?? ''; }
```

Without the `s` modifier, `.` does not match a newline. The instinct is that a
multi-line value would be **truncated at the newline**. It is not: the `$`
cannot be reached, so the WHOLE pattern fails, the `if` is never entered, and
**the flag is not recorded at all.** Measured: a multi-line `--output` stored
NULL; the same text on one line stored fine.

So `tblOffsiteSyncLog.output` was NULL for every run ever made, because a run's
log is never one line. The column looked unused rather than broken.

**Why it mattered more than a missing log.** Since #671 the settings bridge
REFUSES a value it will not put on a command line, rather than escaping it — and
a `WARN` line is the only thing that says which setting was refused and why. The
only place those lines were kept was that column. So a mistyped destination left
no trace anywhere an administrator could reach, while the page said the settings
were in force. Splitting at the first `=` has no such trap: the name is checked
on its own, and the value is whatever follows, newlines and all.

## A refusal is only a safety feature if somebody is told (#671)

The design rule "refuse rather than escape" is right, and it was half-built. The
bridge held a bad value back correctly, the script used its own value correctly,
and **nothing an administrator could see said so** — the warning went to a column
no page read and to a hosting panel's e-mail. So the portal showed one
destination and the copy went to another, which is the fault #671 was raised
about, one step along.

Two things make a refusal honest, and both are cheap: say it where the value is
TYPED (the page asks the same question through `Portal\Core\OffsiteSettings`, so
a typo is caught at Save), and say it where the RUN is reported (the page now
lists each run's warnings, the newest prominently). Asking the question in two
places was the alternative, and was rejected: two guards that can drift apart are
worse than one.

## Adding a "succeeded but did nothing" path invalidates every reader of the exit code (#671)

The sync script gained a skip path: switched off on the page, it sends nothing,
records `skipped`, and **exits 0** — deliberately, so a hosting panel does not
e-mail a failure every week for a feature somebody turned off.

`offsite-backup-run.php` read only the exit code. So it answered "Off-site sync
completed in 1s." in green for a run that packed nothing, encrypted nothing and
sent nothing. Before the skip path, exit 0 really did mean a copy had gone.

**And that was the state of every fresh installation**, because
`backup.offsite.enabled` is seeded `'0'` — so the first thing an administrator
did after setting the feature up, pressing "Run now" to check it, told them it
had worked. When you give a program a new way to succeed without doing its job,
every existing reader of its exit code is now wrong; find them in the same change.

## Check a page's claim against the FALLBACK, not the happy path (#671)

The page said, in bold: **"Switched off, so nothing is being sent."** It was
written while thinking about the normal case, where the script asks the portal and
obeys. It is false in exactly the cases that matter, and the proof was in this
package's own setup guide: the script's documented fallback, when it cannot reach
the database or `php` is missing from the scheduled job's path, is the `ENABLED`
value inside the script file — which ships as **send**, on purpose, so that a
database problem does not quietly stop somebody's backups.

So the page denied something the same package documented. The lesson is narrow
and reusable: when a design has a fallback, every sentence about what the system
will do has to be read twice — once for the normal path and once for the
fallback — and the sentence has to be true of both, or say which it describes.

Two more of the same shape were found in one review: the banner claiming an empty
"Recent runs" means nothing was sent (recording is allowed to fail without
failing the run), and "each of those three cases prints a WARNING" when a setting
with no row stored prints nothing.

## Blanking a value you cannot use turns "we cannot tell" into a decision (#671)

The length guard in the bridge was first written to blank any over-long value and
let the normal rules handle it. That is wrong for two of the six settings, and
dangerously so for one: an **empty alert address is a real choice** meaning "do
not e-mail", and it has to be able to override an address left in the script
file. Blanking an over-long address would therefore have silenced failure e-mail
on the administrator's behalf, from a value they never set.

The fix is to MARK the value as unusable and let each value's own block decide
what leaving it out means — because "leave it out" means something different for
a destination (keep the file's), an alert address (keep the file's, never
"silence") and `enabled` (anything that is not exactly `1` is off, which is the
safe direction).

## A very large setting value aborted every backup, and blamed the wrong line (#671)

The settings boxes have no length limit — `settingValue` is MEDIUMTEXT — and the
bridge's rclone pattern happily matches 200,000 letters and a colon. The script
read the bridge's first line with `printf '%s\n' "${SETTINGS_OUT}" | head -n 1`.
At about 128 KB on macOS, and about **64 KB on Linux** (which is the real
target), that overflows the pipe: bash prints `printf: write error: Broken pipe`
and, under `set -o pipefail`, the whole run stops **before anything is packed**.

The recorded row then read `A step failed near line 399` — which is a closing
`fi`, not the failing line, because the `ERR` trap records `LINENO` at the point
the trap fires — and advised checking the destination for a partial copy when
nothing had ever been sent. Every scheduled run failed the same way until
somebody edited the box.

Two guards now, and **they are not interchangeable** — the first version of
this note implied they were, and the self-test's author disproved it. The class
refuses anything over 256 characters, and the script takes the first line with
`${SETTINGS_OUT%%$'\n'*}`, which is string handling inside bash with no second
process and cannot break that way.

**But the script's fix alone does not keep the backup working.** Measured on
31 October 2026 by raising `OffsiteSettings::MAX_LENGTH` and leaving the script's
fix in place: the run gets past the settings step and `rclone` refuses the
200,000-character remote instead — "Failed to create file system for
destination" — so the run still fails and no copy is sent. The pipe fix stops a
confusing failure; the length ceiling is the only one of the two that keeps a
copy going out. Worth stating because "we fixed it in two places" invites the
assumption that either would do.

A related precision, from the same check: an over-long ALERT ADDRESS is held
back twice over, because `filter_var` refuses a local part beyond about 64
characters anyway. So the length branch is belt and braces there, and raising
the ceiling does not make a 300-character address acceptable. Both facts are now
written beside the code, because a reader of the first version would have
concluded the opposite of each.

## "The newest row" is not "the row this run wrote" (#671)

`offsite-backup-run.php` runs the sync script with `exec()` and then has to say
what happened. It asked:

```sql
SELECT status FROM tblOffsiteSyncLog ORDER BY logID DESC LIMIT 1
```

Nothing in that ties the answer to the run just made. So "this run recorded
nothing" really meant "the table has never held a row", and the check built on
it worked **only on a fresh installation** — the one case where the fault cannot
be seen. Measured on 31 October 2026 with one older `success` row on file and a
stand-in that recorded nothing: the page answered "Off-site sync completed in
0s." in green, for a run that packed nothing and sent nothing. Equally, a
`skipped` or `failed` row from last week would have decided this week's message.

The same misreading was already in the fallback insert beside it:
`if ($exit !== 0 && $mostRecent === null)`, where `$mostRecent` meant "any row
that has ever existed" — so on an installation with any history, a failed run
that never reached its own logger recorded **nothing at all**.

The fix is a high-water mark: read `MAX(logID)` BEFORE `exec()`, then ask only
about rows after it. 0 when the table cannot be read, which makes every row
"after" it — the safe direction, because the page may then quote an earlier run
but can never claim a copy went when no row exists.

**The testing lesson is the sharper half.** The first version of this section
emptied the log table before pressing the button, so every check passed on the
broken code. A test that starts from a clean state cannot see a bug whose cause
is state that was already there. The check that pins it now (O11b) is
deliberately the only one in that section an empty table cannot satisfy.

## One rule, four copies: how a shared range drifts apart (#671)

The two "copies to keep" figures were bounded in four places by the time the
package was finished: the save handler's `max(1, min(52, …))`, the display
clamp, the `min`/`max` on the input boxes, and the bridge that hands the figure
to the shell script. Each was added for a good local reason, and nothing was
wrong at any moment — but changing a constant would have left three of them
behind, and the input's own `max` is the one that silently stops the **whole
form** submitting when a stored value is outside it (#668).

All four now read `Portal\Core\OffsiteSettings`. Worth noticing how it
happened: the class was created to stop the PAGE and the BRIDGE drifting, and
two more copies were left in place in the same file, because they did not look
like the thing being fixed.

---

## Changing a repeating series' pattern (#669)

### The design, and the one choice everything else follows from

A repeating series here is **not** one row with a rule attached: every date is an ordinary
`tblEvents` row, and `tblRecurrenceRules` only *describes* them so `calendar/export.php` can
publish one repeating entry instead of twenty. So changing a pattern means adding, moving and
removing real event rows, each of which may have somebody's attendance or a booked room hanging
off it.

`Portal\Core\SeriesRepattern` is the ONE place that decides what such a change would do. It takes
facts and returns a plan; it opens no connection and runs no query, so the whole decision is
testable without a database **and** the page that previews it cannot disagree with the handler that
applies it — they are handed the same plan object.

**The choice that makes the rest safe: a date the new pattern still wants is UPDATED IN PLACE,
touching only its start and end.** It is never deleted and re-created. That single decision is what
keeps a hand-changed title, venue, description or poster safe *without the comparison having to
detect those changes at all* — they are simply never written. The only hand edit left to catch is a
changed **time**, which is exactly what `patternStart` answers. Re-creating instead would also
destroy every attached record through the CASCADE rules, for a date the person expected to keep.

**Pairing is by the DAY, never by the time.** All four things #669 asked for fall out of that one
rule: a time shift pairs every date with itself and re-times it; weekly→fortnightly leaves half the
days unpaired and removes them; extending leaves new days unpaired and adds them; shortening removes
the tail. No special case per operation.

### "Edited by hand" is worked out, not remembered

Migration 232 adds `tblEvents.patternStart` — the moment the pattern produced that date, as a
reading of the event's own clock. Equal to `startDateTime` means nobody moved it. Same shape as
`externalRecurrenceKey` for imported events, and for the same reason: **a comparison cannot be
forgotten by a new writer, and a flag can.**

`updatedAt` cannot do this job, and it is the obvious wrong answer: it carries
`ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, so `calendar/manage/series-edit` already moves it on rows nobody
edited by hand — one bulk status change would report a whole series as hand-edited.

**It is deliberately NOT backfilled, and the reason runs both ways.** Setting
`patternStart = startDateTime` for every existing series date would *claim* every one of them is
untouched, hand-moved dates included, and the first pattern change would then move exactly the dates
the column exists to protect. But leaving it empty would normally make the feature useless on every
existing installation — #671's first lesson, that a fix which only works on a fresh installation is a
fix for the one case where the fault is invisible. It does not here, because an unrecorded date falls
back to re-generating the series' **current** rule and asking whether the date is one of its dates.
So empty means "ask the rule", not "give up", and a date is only left alone for want of an origin
when there is no rule row either (a real state: the create handler deletes a series' rule when
ordinary dates join it).

**The recorded origin wins over the rule when both could answer**, and that case is pinned by a
check. Somebody who moves a date *onto* another of the pattern's dates has still moved it; the rule
would say "untouched", and the honest answer is "a person did this".

### A foreign key is not how every table says it — the worst fault in this package

`ATTACHMENTS` was first built from the schema's `FOREIGN KEY` declarations, and the audit script
beside it said in its own docstring: *"A table that points at an event WITHOUT a foreign key.
Nothing in this schema does that today (checked)."* **That claim was written without checking and it
was false.** Asked of a loaded database, two tables name an event with no constraint at all:

| Table | Column | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| `tblEventRSVPs` | `eventID INT NOT NULL`, `uq_event_user (eventID, userID)` | Every member's going / maybe / no answer. One of the things the owner's decision names out loud. |
| `tblZoomMeeting` | `eventID INT NULL` | Written by the seeded `/calendar/zoom-create`. |

So the list that exists to protect records missed the most sensitive table in the set, and the page
offered to remove a date while every member's answer sat against it, with no reason shown.

**And be precise about `'no rule'`, because the first version of this note was not and the difference was MEASURED on MySQL 8.0.36 rather than reasoned about.** This page SOFT-deletes, and no ON DELETE rule fires on an UPDATE — so all three values behave identically here: every attached row survives, pointing at a date nobody can see. That is the real harm and it is the same for all 34 tables. The rule only decides what a later real DELETE does, and only then is 'no rule' the worst (CASCADE takes the rows, SET NULL blanks the link, no key leaves a reference to nothing). Giving the soft-delete consequence as the reason for a claim that holds only under hard deletion welded two scenarios together.

The check now looks for the `eventID` **column**, which is what "points at an event" actually means,
with one real exclusion: a table whose own `AUTO_INCREMENT` primary key is called `eventID` is not
pointing at anything (`tblWebhookEvent`). Verified the right way round afterwards — the constant
against `information_schema` on a loaded database, 34 and 34 with nothing missing either way — rather
than against the SQL text the check itself reads.

**The lesson is not about foreign keys.** It is that a safety list keyed on the *tidier half* of a
schema looks complete and is not, and that writing "(checked)" in a comment is not checking. Ask the
database.

### The attachment list is the dangerous shape

`SeriesRepattern::ATTACHMENTS` names every table with an `eventID` **column** — **34 of them** — with the plain words for what a row in it means. It is the only thing stopping a pattern
change from hiding a date that carries a register.

It is the worst possible shape for a safety list, because **it looks complete whatever is in it**.
Add a table with an `eventID` key and say nothing, and its rows become invisible to the page: the
first pattern change afterwards hides the dates they hang off, nothing fails, and nothing is logged.
`tools/audit-checks/check_series_attachments_complete.py` is what makes the constant trustworthy —
a hard gate that fails BOTH ways (a table missing from the list, and an entry naming a table that no
longer points at an event; the second direction is how the migration harness's own exception lists
went stale unnoticed).

**Two parsing traps in that check, both found by getting them wrong first.** A foreign key is not
always inside its own `CREATE TABLE`: `tblAttendanceSessions` gets its `eventID` key through an
`ALTER TABLE` in the file's tail, and a parser that walks back to the nearest `CREATE TABLE`
attributed it to whichever table was created last — reporting `tblEvents` as pointing at itself AND
missing `tblAttendanceSessions` entirely, wrong in both directions at once. And comments must be
stripped before anything is matched, or a commented-out key counts as live (#675's lesson).

Asking the tables is **one query per table across the whole series**, not one per date: a 200-date
series would otherwise need six thousand queries. The table names come from the code constant, which
is what makes building the statement text from them safe; the event numbers are still bound. **A
table that will not answer stops the page** — carrying on without it would make every date it
protects look unattached.

### Two numeric-key traps, one of which took the page down

**`(string) $value` on a numeric array key is load-bearing.** The "which week" dropdown looped over
`['1' => 'First', '2' => 'Second', …]`. PHP turns a numeric array key into an **integer**, and with
`declare(strict_types=1)` handing an int to `htmlspecialchars()` is a TypeError, not a quiet
conversion.

What that looked like is the part worth remembering: the page rendered its heading, its explanation
and most of its form, threw there, and the error handler printed the footer — so the response was
**HTTP 200 ending in a perfectly ordinary `</html>`, with the preview silently missing**. `php -l`
cannot see it and no audit script here can either. Only asking for the page found it. The `===`
comparison against a posted string needs the same cast, or nothing is ever pre-selected.

### The rule row, and why it is usually withdrawn

`export.php` collapses a series with a rule into ONE repeating entry and then **skips every other
event of that series**. So a rule that over-promises does not merely look untidy — it sends every
subscriber dates the diary does not hold AND hides the ones it does.

A rule may therefore survive a repattern only when the series afterwards holds **exactly** the dates
the new pattern makes. In practice that means a series with no past dates and nothing left alone, so
the usual outcome is: old rule removed, no new one, subscribers see each date on its own. That is the
#670 decision applied to this page, and it is said in plain words in the success message rather than
left for somebody to notice. `export.php` has its own `$patternStillTrue` guard, so this is the
second of two defences — but it is the one that stops a false rule being *written*, and a stored
falsehood that one reader happens to catch is still a stored falsehood.

### The confirmation is checked against the preview, and the gap that hid

The confirmation posts a fingerprint of the previewed plan; the handler works the plan out again and
compares. If the series moved in between, the change is refused and the new preview shown — the
person agreed to a *specific* list of changes. An **empty** fingerprint is refused too, because
`hash_equals('', '')` is true: the shape of the OAuth `state` hole of 27 October 2026.

**The gap planting found, and it is the most useful thing in this package.** Removing the "did they
press the confirm button" test altogether — `$confirmed = $isPost === true` — failed **nothing**.
The fingerprint check was quietly doing both jobs, because the only request in the test that carried
a fingerprint was one that also confirmed. That matters because the hidden fingerprint field sits
inside the **same form** as the pattern boxes, so a real browser pressing "Show me what would change"
a second time posts it and does *not* post `confirm` (the name of the other button) — under the
planted code, that second preview would silently apply the change. Checks R11b and R11c exist for
exactly that request. **A guard that is never exercised alone is not covered, however many checks
pass around it.**

### Four more faults the independent check found, each with its own shape

1. **A soft-deleted row keeps its address for ever.** `uq_event_site_slug (siteID, eventSlug)` covers
   hidden rows, so a day this page removed and later re-added collided on the unique key: the whole
   change rolled back, the administrator was told "Something went wrong … please try again", and
   retrying could never cure it. It was **intermittent**, because the first version built the address
   from the date's position in the add list, which changes between runs. The address is now asked of
   the database, probing for a free one, bounded at 50 tries — and that probe deliberately reads
   **every** row including imported and hidden ones, because the unique key does not care who owns
   them. Narrowing it to portal-owned rows would reintroduce the collision; there is a comment saying
   so, because the visibility audit script flags that query and the honest answer is "this needs no
   guard", not "add one".

2. **A copy inherits history that cannot be true of a new thing.** The dynamic INSERT took every
   column of its template but four, so extending a run whose next date had been cancelled by hand
   created new dates that were **already cancelled**, carrying that date's cancellation reason and the
   name of whoever cancelled it. Two kinds of harm from one line: wrong data, and privacy — the copy
   also duplicated `submitterName` and `submitterEmail`, a member of the public's name and e-mail,
   onto rows they had nothing to do with, and **`GdprEraser::catalogue()` clears neither column on
   `tblEvents`** (checked, not assumed), so those copies could not have been erased on request. The
   rule that came out of it: **when you copy a row, list the columns that describe one instance's own
   history and clear them.** A status of `cancelled` or `postponed` means "this particular occurrence
   is not happening", which cannot be true of a date that did not exist until now, so those map to
   `published`; `draft` and `published` describe the series and are inherited.

3. **An overstated guarantee, again.** `followsPattern()` compared the START only, while the class
   docblock promised "the only hand edit the comparison has to catch is a changed TIME". A move writes
   the start **and** the finish, so both are hand-editable — and a service lengthened by hand from one
   hour to three was silently shortened again, reported as "re-timed" rather than left alone. That is
   the owner's rule 2 broken by a comment the code had not implemented. `patternEnd` now records the
   finish and both are compared. Its companion fault matters as much: **a move must write both**, or
   every date the page re-times reads as hand-edited next time and the page quietly stops working
   after one use.

4. **The remedy was a link that did not work.** The only thing the page offers for a date it refuses
   to touch was `?eventID=`, and `calendar/manage/index.php` reads `$_GET['edit']` and reads `eventID`
   nowhere. The repository's own "name things by the right identifier" trap, in the one place the
   feature hands the problem back to a person — and nothing in 202 checks looked at an `href`.

### Four checks that were vacuous, and how each was found

All four passed while the thing they named was broken. Planting found every one; reading found none.

- **Two were satisfied by a row the change never touched.** "The series keeps a rule" and "that rule
  promises four dates" were both true of the rule row written when the series was *created*, so they
  passed while the page wrote nothing at all. Fixed by capturing the pre-change `ruleID` and requiring
  a different row.
- **One pinned a value on a change that never altered it.** The recorded finish was checked after a
  pattern change that re-timed nothing, so leaving `patternEnd` stale on a move passed. Moved to the
  one change that really re-times four dates and gives them a new finish.
- **One removed the wrong dates.** The slug-collision check shortened a series whose removed dates had
  been created by the *save handler*, whose addresses have a different shape (`<slug>-2`, `<slug>-3`)
  from the page's. Those cannot collide with anything the page builds, so the old position-based
  address passed all 226 checks. The series has to be **extended first** — which is what gives two
  days an address this page built — then shortened, then extended again over the same days.

**The general rule, which is worth more than the four cases:** for each guard, ask what request
exercises it *with the other guards satisfied*. Removing the "did they press confirm" test failed
nothing because the plan fingerprint absorbed it — the only request in the suite carrying a
fingerprint was one that also confirmed. A guard never exercised alone is not covered, however many
checks pass around it.

### Tests

- `tools/series-repattern-selftest.php` — 60 checks, no database, no server. The refusals are the
  point: a test that only ever proves dates get moved proves almost nothing. Its section I checks the
  class really has no dependencies (no query, no connection, no settings, no logger, **no clock of its
  own** — the caller passes the moment in, which is what keeps every case exact and stops the class
  reading the server's zone instead of the event's).
- Section R of `tools/event-repeat-pages-selftest.php` — 72 checks over real HTTP, reading the rows
  back out of the database. It needed a third account: both existing ones are administrators, so
  nothing could have proved the page refuses anybody.
- **Two checks there passed for the wrong reason at first** and had to be tightened: "the series keeps
  a rule" and "that rule promises four dates" were both satisfied by the rule row written when the
  series was *created*, while the page was broken. The pre-change `ruleID` is now captured so the new
  row must be a different row. A check satisfied by a row the change never touched is not a check.
- **Not covered:** two administrators changing one series at the same moment. The harness runs the
  built-in server with one worker, so two requests never overlap and such a test would pass on broken
  code. The attachment list **is** re-asked inside the transaction before anything is hidden, which
  closes a different and more likely window — an administrator confirming while a door steward marks
  attendance — but nothing here holds a lock on the series, and no test can prove either way.

## A check can name the right file and still guard nothing (31 October 2026)

Three self-tests were red on the committed tree, found only by running the whole set by hand. The
interesting part is not the three faults — it is the two ways the *fix* to one of them passed on
broken code, both found by planting and neither by reading.

### What the check is for

`tools/gdpr-coverage-selftest.php` pins which pages may call
`GdprEraser::fileRequest($siteId, $userId, true)` — the third argument means "already confirmed", so
no e-mail link is needed and the request lands straight in an administrator's queue. In
`after_undo_window` mode the daily sweep then carries it out with nobody looking. Getting this wrong
destroys somebody's personal data.

The #569 offboarding work added a third such caller, `_apps/offboarding/do.php`. It is legitimate: it
needs a signed-in administrator of the organisation that is open, a POST with a valid form token, and
`AccountGuard::check()`. So the right answer was to name all three callers **and pin those gates**,
because what earns the third one its flag is its gates, not its name.

### The two ways the first attempt passed on broken code

**1. Matching the `if (...)` line does not pin the refusal.** The check contained
`str_contains($code, 'if (App::isAdmin() === false) {')`. Emptying the block —

```php
if (App::isAdmin() === false) {
    // the refusal deleted; the condition left exactly as it was
}
```

— left every one of the 68 checks green, with any signed-in member able to offboard anybody. The same
for `AccountGuard`, which is #518 reintroduced. This repository had already learnt that exact lesson
in #668, whose section D passed on four disabled gates; a check that matches a condition and not its
body is the same fault wearing different clothes.

**2. `basename()` is not an identity.** Callers were listed as `do.php: Site::id(), $userId, true`.
Moving the call into a brand-new, completely ungated `web/_apps/zzplant/do.php` was therefore
indistinguishable from the gated one — and the gates were read from a hard-coded
`offboarding/do.php` path, so they still looked present. `do.php` is a generic name. The two
basenames in the version before this one happened to be distinctive, which made keying on the name
*look* safe without ever being safe.

### What it looks like now

- Callers are named by their **path under `web/`**. The folder the walk starts from is kept in a
  variable so the path is cut where the walk began — taking `strlen(realpath(...))` instead cuts the
  wrong number of characters, because the iterator hands back the path as it was given
  (`tools/../web/…`) and `realpath()` is shorter.
- Each gate must be present **and must refuse**: from the end of the gate's own anchors, an `exit`
  must come before the next `}`.
- The three gates must appear **in order**. Nothing checked that before, while a comment claimed it.
- The source is **masked**, not merely stripped of comments: every string literal becomes a run of
  `x` of the same length. `$codeOnly()` leaves literals alone, so a `}` inside a message, or the word
  `exit` inside one, would answer the walk's question falsely in either direction. Keeping the length
  means the shape of a condition is still recognisable.

Seven planted faults, all caught, every file restored byte-identically.

## A test can compare a page with itself and still fail (31 October 2026)

`mail-pages-selftest.php` and `sign-in-limits-selftest.php` both compare the page a person lands on
after asking for a password-reset link, across four cases: an address with an account, an address with
none, a mail server that refuses, a certificate that has expired. If those pages differ, a stranger
can find out which addresses have accounts. Both tests were failing.

The pages were **dumped and diffed** rather than reasoned about, and the only difference was one
attribute: `nonce="…"` on the inline script `web/_core/Asset.php` writes to fall back to a local copy
of a library. That script arrived with #625. `App::cspNonce()` is `bin2hex(random_bytes(16))` — 32
hex characters, where the helper stripped 64. So the portal was right and the test was comparing
noise.

Two things worth keeping:

- **Strip by name, not by widening the pattern.** Accepting 32 hex characters as well as 64 would
  have blinded the comparison to any real difference of that length, and plenty of identifiers here
  are 32 hex. Matching `nonce="[0-9a-f]+"` cannot match anything else. Proved by planting a 32-hex
  value that is *not* a nonce on the same page and watching it still be caught.
- **A plant that prints nothing proves nothing.** A second plant meant to simulate a real leak read
  a session key that does not exist, so it printed an empty string and the check stayed green. That
  is an invalid plant, not a gap in the check. A genuine end-to-end leak plant is awkward here
  because the handler deliberately answers *before* it looks the address up (#580), so at redirect
  time it does not know.

### And a clause in the same test that could never fail

"The ELEVENTH try is refused, even with a REAL link: the password is not changed and the link is not
used up" looked the stored link up by `hash('sha256', $link)`. The portal stores
`hash('sha256', 'reset-link-utc:' . $token)` through `Auth::resetLinkFingerprint()`. The row was
never found; `null['usedAt']` is null; the clause passed on a row that did not exist, raising a PHP
warning nobody read. It now calls the portal's own function and requires the row to **exist** —
writing the prefix out in the test would be a second copy of the portal's rule, which is the same
fault one step further on.

## Two fixes of mine that looked right and were not (31 October 2026)

Both from the #692 package (a date a pattern change adds now arrives as a draft). Neither was found
by reading; the first was found by planting and the second by `git show`.

### 1. A fix that cannot work, because the page had already consumed what it needed

A new check asked for the message the pattern-change handler writes — "N date(s) added as drafts" —
on the page it redirects to, `calendar/manage/series-edit.php`. It came back "(no message shown)".

I concluded the page had never printed the message it was given, wrote that into a long comment, and
added a read of the session plus a block to print it. **The claim was false.** `git show HEAD` on
that file shows one read of `flash_msg` and one block printing it, and it had always worked. What my
"fix" did was add a **second** read before the page's own — and because the first read `unset`s the
message, the page's own block then had nothing to print. So I broke a working page while believing I
was repairing it, and the check went on failing, which looked like confirmation.

**The actual cause was my own test, twice over.** It first read the message from the wrong page: the
repattern page itself reads and unsets `flash_msg`, so opening that page consumed the message before
the check could see it. Corrected, it then built the address by passing the handler's own `Location`
straight to a helper that prefixes the organisation's part — joining two already-built addresses, the
exact #536 trap — so the request landed somewhere with no message at all. Both failures print the
identical "(no message shown)".

Three things worth keeping:

- **Before claiming a page has never done something, look at the committed version.** Two seconds of
  `git show HEAD:<path>` would have stopped the whole detour. A backup taken *after* your own first
  edit is not evidence about the original; mine showed two reads and I read that as "the page is
  odd" rather than "I did that".
- **"No message shown" has at least three causes** — the message was never set, something consumed
  it first, or you are looking at the wrong page — and they are indistinguishable from the symptom.
  Probing both ends (where it is set, where it is read, with `session_id()` on each) separated them
  in one run after an hour of reasoning had not.
- **A duplicate read of a one-shot value is a silent breakage.** `unset($_SESSION['flash_msg'])` is
  destructive by design; a second reader anywhere earlier in the page wins and the later one shows
  nothing, with no error.

### 2. Why the draft decision needed three checks, not one

`tblEvents.status` already defaults to `draft`, so the code change is one line. What is easy to get
wrong is everything around it: the preview must say the dates will arrive as drafts *before* anything
is written, and the message afterwards must say they did. Without the second, somebody presses the
button, reads "2 date(s) added", and goes looking for them on the public calendar where they are not
— a message that is not untrue and still misleads.

Those two sentences live in two different places in the page and either could be deleted on its own,
so each has its own check (S15b, S15c). The status check is written `=== 'draft'` rather than
`!== 'cancelled'`: the weaker form passes on either answer, and the status is the whole of what #692
changed.

### And two more untrue sentences in the same package, both caught by the independent check

Worth adding to the two above, because they are the same shape — a confident sentence nobody had
measured — and because one of them I had already written into three documents.

**"Anybody subscribing to this calendar now sees one repeating entry."** The message said this
whenever the repeat rule row was written. The rule row is decided on the series' dates alone, which is
right. But `calendar/export.php` reads a series' run with `AND e.status = 'published'` and collapses
it into one `VEVENT` only when those published rows match the rule's expansion. Once the added dates
are drafts they never can, so a subscriber sees one entry per date — the literal opposite of the
sentence, for exactly the change just made. Before #692 the added dates inherited `published` and the
two agreed. **A sentence can be true for years and be falsified by a change three files away.** The
message now has three answers and names how many drafts are holding it up.

**"Publish them one at a time."** I wrote that in the preview, in a code comment and in `FEATURES.md`,
and raised an issue (#696) for the bulk control I assumed was missing. The handler redirects to the
series' **bulk edit** page, which already lists every date including drafts with a tick-box each and a
bulk `Status` control. So the facility existed, on the very page the administrator lands on. **Before
writing "you cannot do X yet", open the page they are sent to.** #696 is closed as not planned.

## The rows a restore cannot put back (#694)

Added 31 October 2026. The behaviour is in `CHANGELOG.md`; this is what somebody
changing the code needs to know, and what the tests cost to get right.

### The fault, exactly

A snapshot written before 27 October 2026 has no `whole_database` flag in its
manifest, so `DbBackup::restoreAll()` holds the three
`WHOLE_DATABASE_ONLY` tables back. It still replaces `tblSites` and `tblUsers`.
Two of the three are their children with `ON DELETE CASCADE`:

    tblSettings.siteID        -> tblSites.siteID    ON DELETE CASCADE
    tblTotpBackupCodes.userID -> tblUsers.userID    ON DELETE CASCADE

`tblMigrations` has no foreign key at all, so it can never go this way.

**A one-table restore cannot cause it either**, and I first said on the issue
that it could. `restoreTable()` builds `$pointedAtBy` and refuses any table
another table points at, telling you to restore the whole snapshot instead. The
mechanism was corrected on the issue before any code was written. This is a
whole-database restore from an old-form snapshot, and nothing else.

### Why the rows are read early and written late

`readRowsACascadeWouldTake()` runs **before** any table is emptied;
`holdRescuedRows()` runs **after** every table is back. That order is the whole
design, and it is not an accident of style:

* The holding table may itself be in the snapshot. Writing the rescued rows
  before the restore would see them deleted again by the restore of that very
  table.
* Both happen inside the restore's own transaction, so a restore that rolls back
  takes the kept rows with it — the rows were never lost in that case, and a
  holding table full of rows that are still in their own table would be worse
  than useless.

The price of keeping them in memory for the length of one restore is
`CASCADE_RESCUE_MAX_ROWS` (20,000). Past it, **nothing** is kept and the warning
says how many there were: keeping some would read as keeping all of them. **That
path is not exercised by any test**, and proof 27's header says so.

### Four traps, each of which cost something

1. **`EXTRA LIKE '%GENERATED%'` is not how you find a generated column.** MySQL
   puts `DEFAULT_GENERATED` in `EXTRA` for any column declared
   `DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`. My first version of `putHeldRowsBack()` used
   that test, so `tblSettings.updatedAt` was read as generated, left out of the
   INSERT, and re-stamped by the database with the moment of the put-back. The
   row was back, with the right key and the right value, carrying the wrong
   "last changed" date. `columnFacts()` already reads `GENERATION_EXPRESSION`
   and its comment already warned against exactly this; I wrote a worse copy
   beside it. **Read the class before adding a helper to it.**
2. **"Did any row go back" is not "did THIS row go back".** The mark was written
   `if ($mark !== false && $put > 0)`, which marks every row as put back the
   moment one succeeds. A row that could not go back would have stopped being
   offered — the single thing this feature exists to prevent.
3. **A row that cannot go back has more than one possible reason, so do not
   assert one.** The likeliest is that its organisation or person is not in the
   restored database. But a row that is *already there* fails the same way, and
   the two cannot be told apart from the insert's failure. The page says
   "the likeliest reason is…", never the reason.
4. **The holding table is not there before migration 233 has run**, and files
   reach a server before anybody presses "Run migrations". Every reader asks
   `holdingTableExists()` first (`SHOW TABLES LIKE`, as
   `Newsletter::demoRegisterExists()` does and for the same reason: a blanket
   try/catch would hide a broken connection behind "nothing is being kept").
   The restore then proceeds and the warning says the rows could not be kept —
   because refusing a restore would block a recovery at the one moment somebody
   is recovering, which is worse than the loss this issue is about.

### What the tests taught

**`brs_checkSame()` is why trap 1 was found.** Every weaker check passed: the
row existed, its key was right, its value was right. Only comparing every value
of every table saw the date. Proof 27's comment says so, so nobody reduces it to
a row-exists test.

**Proof 27 derives its row counts from the database, never types them.** A fresh
install already holds per-organisation settings rows — migration 231 (#677)
copied each organisation's address down — and that is exactly the change #690
showed had quietly broken two tests that had hard-coded "none". The baseline
count is read from the pristine database, which is independent of the code under
test.

**Two existing proofs had to be mended, not excused.** Proofs 6 and 17 cause
this cascade, so they now leave rows in the holding table, and `brs_reset()`
compares the whole database. `brs_clearHeldRows()` returns the count and each
caller **checks it was not nothing** — a silent sweep would go on passing the
day the rescue stopped working, which is the shape of dead check this project
has been caught by before.

**One claim of mine in the code comments was false and a test caught it.** The
comment said the new warning replaced the older "N table(s) that are NOT in this
snapshot were changed as well". It does not: both are printed, the older one
covers every table outside the snapshot including the ones that cannot be
rescued, and proof 6 now pins both sentences, because pinning one would pass
with the other deleted.

### What the independent check found, and the shapes behind it

Five real problems, all in work that had already passed every test it had. Each
is a shape worth recognising again.

**A describing sentence that is narrower than the thing it describes.** The words
naming the lost settings rows listed four address fields. The rescue takes every
row with a `siteID`, whatever its key: `attend.detailRetentionDays`,
`giving.retention.years` and the four `mail.queue.*` numbers are all
per-organisation. **Seven** files under `web/` can write such a row — see the
next section for how I got that number wrong twice. So the sentence could name four address fields to somebody
whose retention periods had gone, at the worst possible moment. The cure was two
parts: make the sentence general, and give the page the **keys** out of each kept
row. A settings key says what a row IS without being a value, which is the line
to draw — `nameInsideHeldRow()` returns the key and the JSON is never returned
at all, so no caller can print a stored value by accident.

**A comment that invents a column, and takes a check down with it.** Two comments
said a kept `tblTotpBackupCodes` row carried its owner's e-mail address. That
table is `(codeID, userID, codeHash, isUsed, usedAt, createdAt)`. So two clauses
of the privacy check searched a page for an address that could never be on it,
however broken the page was. The check still had working clauses, so it was not
wholly vacuous — but **a clause that cannot fail makes a check look stronger than
it is**, which is worse than leaving it out.

**"Nothing deletes it" plus "it is kept for ever" is a privacy decision nobody
made.** `discardHeldRows()` takes only waiting rows and the card lists only
waiting rows, so a row marked as put back was unreachable and permanent — a
second copy of a code hash or a setting value, growing with every restore and
travelling into every later snapshot and off-site copy. Four documents said the
rows "wait until an administrator clears them", which was true of waiting rows
only. `rowJson` is now emptied in the same statement that sets `putBackAtUtc`.
The test for it counts `COUNT(rowJson)` against `COUNT(*)` **and** checks the
other columns are still there, because emptying the whole row would destroy the
audit trail instead of the copy.

**Asking "is it on the list" when the question is "is it being put back".** The
rescue skipped any table not in `$heldBack`, and `$heldBack` is built only from
