names the manifest itself holds. So a snapshot that simply did not contain
`tblSettings` — an imported one, or a hand-edited manifest — restored `tblSites`,
let the cascade wipe every per-organisation row, rescued nothing and printed no
#694 warning. **No existing check could have caught it**, because every fixture
was a genuine old-form snapshot, which contains all three tables. Section F of
proof 27 is the check, and what makes it decisive is that its snapshot still
*says* it covers the whole database: nothing is held back, so the old reading
would rescue nothing. This is the same lesson as I7d (#645): when a check exists
to prove something ordinary works, make sure some fixture is actually ordinary —
and its mirror, when a fix is positioned to close a shape, check it closes the
whole shape.

**Returning the same answer for two different facts.** `discardHeldRows()`
answered 0 both for "this portal keeps no rows for that table" and for "none was
waiting", so the page said `0 kept row(s) for <anything you posted> discarded.
They cannot be recovered.` and wrote the posted name into the activity log as
though it were a real table. It answers -1 for the first now, and
`DbBackup::keepsRowsFor()` is the one public test both writers and the page ask.

### Round 3, and the two shapes that only showed up because the earlier fix worked

**A real lock makes new paths reachable, so the fix needs the handling the
broken version never did.** Round 2 moved the `FOR UPDATE` read inside the
transaction, which is what finally made it a lock. Round 3 then found that
`prepare`, `bind_param`, `execute` and `get_result` sat *outside* the `try`.
Under `mysqli_report(MYSQLI_REPORT_STRICT | MYSQLI_REPORT_ERROR)` every one of
them throws — and **it takes BOTH flags**, which I got wrong twice. Measured on
the STATEMENT path (`prepare()` on a missing table), PHP 8.5.11:

| flags | result |
|---|---|
| `MYSQLI_REPORT_ERROR` | returns false, raises a warning, no exception |
| `MYSQLI_REPORT_STRICT` | returns false, **no warning at all**, no exception |
| `STRICT \| ERROR` | throws `mysqli_sql_exception` |

`ERROR` is what makes a statement error get reported; `STRICT` turns a reported
error into an exception. **A CONNECT error is reported whatever `ERROR` says**,
which is why `STRICT` alone throws there — and that is exactly the measurement I
first made and then generalised to statements. **Measuring the wrong code path
and writing "measured, not reasoned" against the conclusion is worse than
reasoning**, because the next reader has no reason to doubt it. So a throw
escaped the method with the transaction open and the statement unclosed — and
the newly reachable case was exactly the one the lock exists for. With the lock
genuinely held, a second administrator pressing the button now **blocks**; the
page has already called `TimeLimit::atLeast(900)`, so PHP will not cut it off
first, and at `innodb_lock_wait_timeout` (50 seconds by default) `execute()`
throws ERROR 1205. Outside the `try` that gave a bare 500 instead of the honest
message, and — worse — `Logger::db()` hands back the *same* connection, so the
`tblErrors` row was written inside the still-open transaction and rolled back
when the connection closed. **The fault left no record anywhere.** The read is
inside the `try` now, with a `finally` that frees and closes on every path.

**A correction recorded in six documents was applied in one.** Round 2 wrote
that `"unused" two-factor codes was wrong in five places` and that
`"address rows"` understated what the cascade takes. Round 3 found both
uncorrected wordings still in: the in-app help page, migration 233's own header,
section 18 of the eraser test, `CHANGELOG.md`, `.claude/HANDOFF.md`, and — on the
very line that recorded the correction — `.claude/CLAUDE.md` and its `.OpenAI`
mirror. **A document that asserts a fix while stating the thing it fixed is
worse than one that says nothing**, because the next reader stops looking. The
help page mattered most: its own comment says it is said there "because this is
the page somebody opens when they are about to put a backup back", so it was the
one sentence a customer reads *before* deciding whether to accept the loss, and
it understated it.

**And a check made only of absences passes when the thing stops happening.**
Section P's new log check asserted that the posted table name was *not* in the
activity log and that the event type was *not* `BackupHeldRowsPutBackFailed`.
Delete the `$record()` call entirely and it stayed green, under a name claiming
"the refusal is recorded WITHOUT the posted name". The positive clause comes
first now. Same family as #668's section D and the `&& false` lesson: pin what
must be true, not only what must not.

**What I did about it, and why it is not a committed check.** After round 3 I
swept the whole package myself for every wording the three rounds had declared
untrue — a short script over `git status --porcelain`, matching each banned
phrase and treating a hit as a *live claim* only when the surrounding 200
characters did not also read as a recorded lesson. It found a **seventh**
instance, in `FEATURES.md`, which round 3 had not named. Zero after fixing it.

That sweep is a technique, not a tripwire, and it is deliberately not in
`tools/audit-checks/`. The banned-phrase list is specific to one package's
history, it would need curating for ever, and the "is this a live claim or a
recorded lesson" test is a heuristic on surrounding prose — exactly the shape
#668 warns about, because a check that cries wolf gets switched off and then
catches nothing. **The rule worth keeping is the habit: when a round tells you a
sentence is untrue, grep the whole working tree for that sentence before
reporting it fixed, and count the places.** Round 2 said "wrong in five places"
and fixed one.

### Round 5, and the refactor that should have come three rounds earlier

Three more: the wrong account of which `mysqli_report` flag makes mysqli throw
(it takes BOTH — see the table above; and the "correction" I made in this round
was wrong too), in four
documents, after the two code comments had been corrected a round earlier; a
pronoun defined later in its own sentence; and a refused discard logged under the
same event type as a successful one.

**The lesson is the refactor, not the three faults.** The sentence an
administrator reads had grown to ninety lines and nine nested ternaries, and four
of the six wording faults rounds 2-5 found were inside it. Every one was a
ternary in the middle of a clause: a rehearsal saying "nothing replaced them", "1
setting(s) ... were removed", "1 of them is being kept" about one row, "Any of it
that existed ... if it was created since is not". **None was findable by any
check, because nothing judges how an assembled sentence reads** — and a test that
pins a substring of it will happily pin a substring of nonsense.

`DbBackup::cascadeWarning()` now holds eight complete sentences, keyed by the
three facts that choose between them. The rule it encodes: **when a sentence is
built from branches, spell out the whole sentence for each branch.** A reader can
check eight sentences; nobody can evaluate nine nested ternaries over eight paths
in their head, which is why five rounds of review kept finding faults in it.

Print the output of anything like this before changing it. The sixteen outputs
here were printed by calling the real method through a small harness that pulls
the method and the constant out of the file and evals them, so no wording was
transcribed by hand — transcribing is how you check the sentence you meant to
write rather than the one that is there.

### Round 6: measuring the wrong code path

The most useful thing in this whole package. I wrote that `MYSQLI_REPORT_STRICT`
is the flag that makes mysqli throw, and put "measured, not reasoned" beside it.
The measurement was real. It was of a **connect** error, and the sentence was
about four **statement** calls. Measured properly, `prepare()` on a missing
table, PHP 8.5.11:

| flags | result |
|---|---|
| `MYSQLI_REPORT_ERROR` | returns false, raises a warning, no exception |
| `MYSQLI_REPORT_STRICT` | returns false, **silently** — no warning, no exception |
| `STRICT \| ERROR` | throws `mysqli_sql_exception` |

`ERROR` is what makes a statement error get reported at all; `STRICT` turns a
reported error into an exception. A connect error is reported whatever `ERROR`
says, which is why `STRICT` alone throws there — and why the easy measurement
looked conclusive.

**The lesson is not about mysqli.** "Measured, not reasoned" is only worth
writing if the measurement is of the thing the sentence is about. Written against
a conclusion drawn from a neighbouring code path, it is worse than reasoning,
because it removes the next reader's reason to doubt. Before attaching it, ask
which code path the claim describes and whether that is the path you ran.

`web/_core/bootstrap.php`'s own comment had carried the same untruth since long
before this package. Correcting it meant touching one file outside the package's
list; that is declared rather than buried, because the alternative was leaving
the wrong explanation in the one place everybody looks it up.

### Round 6: a sentence wrong in both directions, and a branch nothing reached

The sentence telling an administrator what their backup might still hold has now
been wrong twice, in opposite ways: first hedging on whether the snapshot
*contains* the table while saying nothing about row currency, then hedging on
currency while *asserting* presence. The second was false for exactly the case
the package had just added coverage for — a snapshot that does not contain the
table — and false in the reassuring direction. **When a hedge has two conditions,
write both; a hedge that covers one and asserts the other is not a hedge.**

And half the eight sentences — the whole `canKeep === false` branch — were
reached by no check, which proof 27's own "what this cannot show" list had failed
to mention. Section G reaches them by renaming the holding table to a name
outside `tbl%` and taking the snapshot afterwards, because an un-upgraded
database has no holding table *and no snapshot containing one*. It caught two
faults of mine in its first two runs, both in the test rather than the portal —
which is what a test exercising a genuinely new branch should do.

## Carrying the kept rows through a restore (#697)

#694 gave the portal a holding table for rows a restore could not put back.
`tblRestoreHeldRows` was then an **ordinary** table, so the next whole-database
restore emptied it and filled it again from the snapshot — and a snapshot taken
*before* some rows were kept holds none of them. The waiting rows went, and a
waiting row is the only copy of itself anywhere outside the snapshot being
restored from. The same silent loss #694 exists to stop, one door along, and it
shipped inside the fix for it.

**A warning is not a fix, and this is the clearest example of why.** The first
version said so, before and after, naming the count and telling the
administrator to deal with the rows first. But the only person who ever reads
that sentence is somebody mid-recovery, which is the condition #694's own
reasoning says not to rely on — the owner's "no timer" decision rests on exactly
that point. A sentence that has to be acted on at the worst moment of somebody's
week is a design that has chosen to fail quietly.

### The fix is the mechanism that was already there

Read the waiting rows before anything is emptied; write them again after every
table is back. The same read-early, write-late order as the cascade rescue, and
for the same reason: the holding table is **itself in the snapshot**, so
anything written earlier is emptied again when that table's turn comes.

### `WHOLE_DATABASE_ONLY` guards the one-table button, and almost nothing else

Adding `tblRestoreHeldRows` to that list was option 4 on the issue: refuse a
one-table restore of it, which would otherwise throw away every waiting row with
no carry to save them. That is what it does.

**It was also written up as having a second effect, and that was wrong.** The
claim was that an old-form snapshot — one that does not say it covers the whole
database — now leaves the table alone, "so it cannot write over kept rows at
all", which inverts the danger compared with #694. It is a **no-op for every
snapshot a customer can have**:

    git log -S"whole_database" --format='%h %ci' -- web/_core/DbBackup.php | tail -1
      b7496b7 2026-10-27 18:19:23 +0000
    git log --format='%h %ci' --diff-filter=A -- web/_sql/233_restore_held_rows.sql
      ac1b19e 2026-10-31 17:26:43 +0000

A snapshot with no flag predates the flag; the holding table arrived four days
later. Such a snapshot **cannot contain it**, so there was never anything to hold
back. The only whole-restore case the addition changes is a modern snapshot
somebody has edited the flag out of — which is precisely what the flag was added
for, and is now section G of proof 28.

**An old-form snapshot was already safe for a simpler reason: the table is not in
it.** So is any snapshot that does not contain it, old or modern. The carry is
needed by a snapshot that *does* contain it.

**How the wrong claim survived: the fixture could not exist.**
`brs_legacySnapshot()` writes a snapshot in the old form by reading every live
`tbl%` table — so it cheerfully produced one containing `tblRestoreHeldRows`. A
check was built on it, four documents described the second effect, and the
customer-facing help page was changed from a true sentence ("leaves three tables
alone") to a false one. Caught by the independent check, which restored a genuine
one and read the answer. **This is the #645 lesson exactly: when a check exists to
prove something ordinary still works, check that the fixture is actually
ordinary.** `brs_legacySnapshot()` now omits the table, with the dates in a
comment above it.

That is also why proof 26 earns its keep. Its one-table refusal loop iterates
`WHOLE_DATABASE_ONLY`, so removing a name from the list does not make that loop
fail — it simply stops testing it. The explicit
`array_keys($list) === ['tblMigrations', …]` pin is what catches a deleted name,
and planting proved it: the list check failed and the eleven refusal checks went
on passing.

### Recognising a row you are about to insert again

A snapshot taken *after* a row was kept holds that same row, under the same
number, so the carry cannot simply insert everything. Each carried row is looked
up by its own `heldID` first:

| what is at that number | what happens |
|---|---|
| nothing | written back **with** its original number |
| the same row | left alone — the snapshot's copy *is* this row |
| a different row | written back under a **new** number |

"The same row" compares `tableName`, `siteID`, `userID` and `heldAtUtc`, and
deliberately **not** `rowJson`. Two separate reasons, both load-bearing:

- A row already put back has had its copy **emptied** (#694 does that in the
  same statement that marks it). Comparing the copy would call it a different
  row and re-offer something the restored database says is finished.
- `rowJson` is a **JSON column**. MySQL rewrites what it stores — keys reordered,
  a space after each colon — while MariaDB's `JSON` is an alias for `LONGTEXT`
  and rewrites nothing. A text comparison therefore means two different things
  on the two engines. This is the same trap as the `rowJson LIKE '%"userID":…'`
  clause that could never fail in #694's eraser test.

The third row of that table is reachable in production whenever the snapshot came
from a database whose numbering ran differently — an imported snapshot, or one
taken after rows were discarded and others kept. Proof 28 reaches it by making
one waiting row carry a number the snapshot already uses, and planting the
fallback away turns the whole restore red (the duplicate-key insert throws and
the restore rolls back, which is the honest direction and exactly what the
`RuntimeException` promises).

### What is deliberately NOT carried

A row that has **already been put back** is history: it records that a row was
kept and returned, and its copy of the data was emptied when it went home.
Putting a database back to an earlier moment is supposed to put its history back
with it. Proof 28 checks that those records go, so the decision cannot be
reversed by accident — and the judgement itself is written beside
`readWaitingHeldRows()`, because no check can tell you whether it is right.

**What that costs, stated rather than glossed.** No data goes: a put-back row's
`rowJson` is already empty and the row itself really is back in its own table.
What goes is the **audit trail** — the record that somebody returned those rows,
from which snapshot and when. An earlier draft of this section said "nothing is
lost that the restored database does not itself account for", which is too strong:
the restored database does not account for that.

### The rehearsal writes, and that is not new

A rehearsal (`restoreAll($path, true)`) runs inside the transaction and rolls it
back, so "a rehearsal changes nothing" has always meant "no value survives it".
`holdRestoredMail()` and `holdRestoredTexts()` already wrote inside one.

**One thing a rehearsal does leave behind, measured by the independent check:** an
INSERT that is rolled back still consumes an AUTO_INCREMENT number, so a
rehearsal that reaches the clashing-number branch leaves the next `heldID` one
higher. Harmless, and invisible to `brs_checkSame()`, which compares values —
which is why proof 28's claim is now "left every value of every table as it was"
rather than "changed nothing at all". The carry runs in a rehearsal too, deliberately, because a rehearsal that
skipped it could not tell an administrator the carry would fail — which is the
one thing a rehearsal is for. `holdRescuedRows()` is still skipped on a
rehearsal; it writes rows only a real restore has business keeping.

### The independent check's round on #697, and the one finding worth memorising

Eight real problems, and **seven of the eight were about what the package said
about itself** rather than what it did. The mechanism survived every attack: the
waiting rows came through a modern snapshot, an old-form one, a snapshot that did
not contain the table, a rehearsal, a failed restore and an un-upgraded database.

The one that was not about wording is the one to remember. **Narrowing
`sameHeldRow()`'s identity from four columns to `tableName` alone left all thirty
of proof 28's checks green while a real waiting row was silently lost** — the
restore reported success, printed no carry warning at all, and the row was gone.
Three quarters of the identity was guarded by nothing, because the only fixture
that reached the clash branch made its two rows differ in `tableName`, which is
the one column a narrowing keeps. Section E now has **one sub-case per column**,
each differing from the snapshot's row in exactly one of `siteID`, `userID` and
`heldAtUtc` with the same `tableName`, so any proper subset of the four fails.

**The general shape: a fixture that differs in several ways at once tests only the
first thing the code looks at.** It is the same family as "a check that exists to
prove something ordinary still works needs an ordinary fixture" — in both cases
the fixture quietly decides how much of the code is reachable, and nothing says so.

Four smaller lessons, each a repeat of one already written down:

- **"All N" of a number that counts a subset.** `carriedWarning()` was handed the
  count of rows *written again*, not the count waiting, and said "All". With four
  waiting and two in the snapshot it told an administrator "All 2 rows kept for
  you". Say what the number counts.
- **A hedge that covers one condition and asserts the other.** For the third time
  in two packages. `tooManyToCarryWarning()` asserted the rows were "no longer
  offered on the Backup page" from a branch that reads no rows and cannot know.
- **A clause that cannot fail, in the package that wrote the lesson down.** The
  new check in section P forbade a phrase that was never on that page, under a
  label claiming it proved the page "does not still say the opposite".
- **A claim about history with nothing behind it.** The changelog said the Backup
  page's card "used to say the opposite". The card said nothing; the package added
  the paragraph. One `git show HEAD:` would have caught it.

### Round two of the check on #697: two behavioural faults, and a one-server blind spot

Six more real problems. Four were wording again; two were behaviour, and both
were measured rather than argued.

**The carry did not run at all on a server with `lower_case_table_names = 1`.**
That setting decides whether MySQL treats two names differing only in capitals
as one table, and on a server set to 1 every name `SHOW TABLES` reports comes
back lower case. `readWaitingHeldRows()` asked
`in_array('tblRestoreHeldRows', $replacing, true)` — case-sensitive — so the
answer was false and the restore behaved exactly as it had before #697. Measured
on `mysql:8.0.36 --lower-case-table-names=1`: one waiting row before, none
after, `success=true`, **no warning of any kind**.

The same run showed **#694's cascade rescue inert beside it**, for the same
reason and in the same loop. So the root is older than this package.
`isWholeDatabaseOnly()` has compared with `strcasecmp()` since it was written,
*because* `lower_case_table_names` is a server setting — which means the two
halves of one class disagreed about what a table is, and the tables were still
held back while neither protection fired. `DbBackup::namedIn()` compares a name
against a list of names, and `DbBackup::forTable()` fetches an entry out of an
array KEYED by table name.

**Fixing the five `in_array` sites was not enough, and I wrote "all five sites
use it" in four documents before anyone checked.** The next round measured what
that cost, and it is the sharpest lesson in the package:

- **An array subscript is the same comparison written another way.**
  `$facts['tblRestoreHeldRows']` and `self::REMOVED_COLUMNS[$table]` went on
  matching exactly.
- **Making the carry RUN without fixing the subscript turned a silent loss into
  a BLOCKED RECOVERY.** `columnFacts()` keys its answer by
  `information_schema`'s own `TABLE_NAME`, lower case on such a server, so the
  subscript found nothing, `carryWaitingHeldRowsThrough()` threw "the shape
  could not be read", and **every whole-database restore and every rehearsal was
  refused while any row was waiting** — naming the wrong cause, because the
  shape had been read, just under another key. The only route to it was #694's
  rescue *succeeding*. This file elsewhere refuses to create exactly that
  condition: "refusing it would block a recovery at the one moment somebody is
  recovering".
- **`$restored` was a fourth server-reported list**, holding two PRE-EXISTING
  faults of the same shape: restored mail was not held and restored held texts
  were not recorded as not sent. Their own docblocks say what that costs —
  "three waiting messages came out as six copies when this was run", and a text
  sent "a SECOND time, to somebody's phone and at the customer's cost".

**A fix is not finished when the shape you first noticed is gone.** Ask what
other shapes do the same job: a subscript, `===`, `array_search`, `isset`, a
`switch`. The check's header now lists the ones it still cannot see.

**The blind spot is the part worth keeping.** Every self-test in this repository
runs one database server, set to 0, where names match exactly. So **no test here
can see this fault return** — a correct guard over a fault that has already
happened, with nothing able to run it. That is the #646 situation, and the answer
is the same: a tripwire. `tools/audit-checks/check_table_name_comparisons.py`
fails on a case-sensitive `in_array()` against a server-reported list, *and* on
`namedIn()` ceasing to exist or ceasing to use `strcasecmp()` — because without
that second half the first is satisfied by deleting the comparison altogether.
Four plants, including the function commented out whole, which is the shape that
fooled the QR check twice.

**The ceiling lost everything it existed to protect.** Past
`CASCADE_RESCUE_MAX_ROWS` the carry held nothing and let the snapshot's older
copy of the list replace the lot: 20,001 waiting rows in, **zero** out, measured
with the real class — while the Backup page and the help page both promised that
putting a backup back could not lose them. That is "check every page claim
against the FALLBACK, not the happy path", broken in the package that cites it.

The fix is not a bigger ceiling. The decision moved **before** the transaction,
and past the ceiling the holding table is **not put back at all** — the rows stay
exactly where they are, everything else in the snapshot goes back, and the answer
says so. It reuses the mechanism `WHOLE_DATABASE_ONLY` already provides, and the
ceiling is now decided in exactly one place, because two readers of one limit is
how #668's save-time cap came to disagree with its job.

### Three smaller lessons from the same round

- **An absolute promise is as wrong as an undercount.** Fixing "All N rows" (a
  count of a subset) produced "Every row that was waiting is still waiting",
  which one branch breaks by design: a row the snapshot records as already put
  back stops waiting, because the restore honours that snapshot's history. The
  sentence now speaks only of the rows it wrote again.
- **A plant that cannot change behaviour proves nothing.** Adding `putBackAtUtc`
  to `sameHeldRow()`'s identity looked inert — all checks green — but the lookup
  does not *select* that column, so both sides were null and the comparison was
  unchanged. Reversing the decision properly takes two edits, and only then does
  the new section E2 fail. A green run after a plant is evidence only once you
  have shown the plant reaches the code.
- **A fix for "the fixture differs in several ways" can itself be incomplete.**
  Three sub-cases were added for four identity columns, all sharing the
  snapshot row's `tableName`, and the claim "any proper subset fails" was written
  anyway. `['siteID', 'userID', 'heldAtUtc']` is a proper subset and passed.
  There is a sub-case per column now; the `tableName` one is declared synthetic,
  because the two kept-row shapes cannot differ in the table alone.

### Round three on #697: a fix that made things worse, and why one server is not enough

Five more. Two were behaviour, and the worst was **mine, introduced by round two's
fix**.

**Fixing half of a case-sensitivity fault is worse than fixing none of it.**
Round two made the five `in_array()` comparisons ignore capitals, so on a server
with `lower_case_table_names = 1` the carry started running. It then threw,
because the line that hands it the table's shape was still an exact lookup:

    $facts['tblRestoreHeldRows'] ?? []

`columnFacts()` keys that array by `information_schema`'s own `TABLE_NAME`, which
is lower case there. So the carry took its "the shape could not be read" branch,
which stops the whole restore — and **every whole-database restore, rehearsal
included, was refused while any row was waiting.** The only way to reach it was
#694's rescue *succeeding*. A silent loss had become a blocked recovery, which is
the one condition this file elsewhere refuses to create: *"refusing it would block
a recovery at the one moment somebody is recovering."* The message named the wrong
cause too — the shape had been read, just under another key.

**An array subscript is a comparison written another way.** That is the sentence
to keep. `DbBackup::namedIn()` compares a name against a list; `forTable()`
fetches an entry out of an array keyed by table name. `REMOVED_COLUMNS[$table]`
was the same shape, and `$restored` was a **fourth** server-reported list holding
two **pre-existing** faults: restored mail was not held, and a restored held text
was not recorded as not sent. Their docblocks price them — "three waiting messages
came out as six copies", and a text sent "a SECOND time, to somebody's phone and
at the customer's cost".

**"All five sites use it" is what let it survive.** That sentence went into four
documents after round two, and it is exactly the kind of claim that tells the next
reader to stop looking. A fix is not finished when the shape you first noticed is
gone: ask what else does the same job — a subscript, `===`, `array_search`,
`isset`, a `switch`.

### What this cost in verification, and the standing conclusion

**The repository's own harness cannot test this.** Run
`tools/backup-restore-selftest.php` against a server with the setting on and it
fails in its *own* checks, which compare table names exactly (`in_array((string)
$table, $real, true)` against `SHOW TABLES`, and `unset($cut['tables']['tblSettings'])`
on a manifest whose keys are lower case). Those failures are MOSTLY the test's — and the word "mostly" cost another round.
One of them came out of the real class (`putHeldRowsBack()`'s own "the shape of
... could not be read"), so a blanket "the failures are the test's" buries
exactly the finding that matters. Sort them one at a time.

So the behaviour was verified by driving the class directly against a server with
`--lower-case-table-names=1`: the restore succeeds, the waiting row survives,
restored mail is held, the held text is recorded. Then each of the three fixes was
planted away in turn and reproduced its exact fault — the refusal, the silently
lost row, the unheld mail. **The guard against regression is therefore an audit
script, not a self-test**, and proof 28's header says so rather than implying
cover it does not have.

### The gate that passed on broken code, twice

`check_table_name_comparisons.py`'s first version was bypassed two ways, both
measured as reaching the code:

- it required the `in_array()` call to be **followed by** a comparison, so
  `$isThere = in_array('tblX', $list, true);` escaped it;
- it listed the **haystack** variables it knew about, and `$restored` was a fourth.

It now anchors on the **needle** — a `'tbl…'` literal — and matches the call's own
parentheses, so neither the haystack's name nor what follows the call matters.
That also cured a cry-wolf: matching haystack names by substring turned it red on
an ordinary `in_array($column, $orderedColumns, true)`, and #668's rule is that a
check which cries wolf gets switched off.

Its second half asked whether the **word** `strcasecmp` appeared in the helper's
body. `$how = 'strcasecmp';` satisfied that while the comparison used `===` — the
`check_no_outside_qr_service.py` lesson word for word, in a check written by
somebody who had just read it. It now requires a **call**, with comments and
string literals masked first.

### Round four on #697: fix the CLASS, not the instance

Four more. Three rounds in a row now, the same single class of fault has been
fixed one instance at a time, and each round found another instance:

| round | the instance fixed | what the next round found |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | five `in_array($name, $list, true)` calls | `$facts['tblRestoreHeldRows']` — a subscript |
| 3 | that subscript, and `REMOVED_COLUMNS[$table]` | `columnFacts()[$table]` in `putHeldRowsBack()` |
| 4 | that one, and the check now flags the shape | — |

**The round-4 instance was the worst of the three.** `putHeldRowsBack($table)`
receives a name that `keepsRowsFor()` has just required to match `CASCADE_RESCUE`
exactly, so it carries the **source's** spelling; `columnFacts()` keys its answer
by the **server's**. On a server with `lower_case_table_names = 1` the lookup
found nothing and the method returned before touching a row — while
`discardHeldRows()`, which needs no shape, worked perfectly. So the Backup page
offered a kept row, drew both buttons, and **only the one that throws the data
away worked.** "Put it back" always failed, naming the wrong cause.

**The rule took a fourth round to state correctly, and the wrong version is the
more interesting half.** Round 4 wrote: *a table-keyed array is safe only where
both sides came from the server; the fault is an index that came from the
source.* That is wrong in **both** directions, and the counter-examples are both
inside this package:

- **It clears a real fault.** `REMOVED_COLUMNS[$table]` was the second of the
  three faults. Its index comes from the restore's loop over the **manifest** —
  the server's own names — while its keys are typed in the source. The rule
  calls that combination safe. Measured: every key in a manifest written on a
  lower-case server is lower case.
- **It condemns three correct sites.** `CASCADE_RESCUE[$table]` is indexed by a
  source name and capitals really do matter there (`keepsRowsFor('tblsettings')`
  is false, by design) — and that is correct, because the array's own keys are
  source-typed too. `forTable()` would be the wrong fix.

**The true rule: a table-keyed lookup is safe when BOTH SIDES COME FROM THE SAME PLACE, and unsafe when one side is folded by the server and the other is not.** Keys typed
here indexed by a name typed here is safe. Keys from `information_schema` indexed
by a name from `SHOW TABLES` is safe on one server, with the cross-server residue
as #698. One of each is the fault. That version classifies all four known
instances, all three `CASCADE_RESCUE` sites and #698 correctly.

**The shape of the mistake is worth more than the rule.** A rule written to
generalise a fault, from the fault's own symptoms, will describe the instance you
happened to see. Both halves of this one had to be tested against the OTHER
known sites before it was worth anything — which is what the fifth round did and
the fourth did not.

**And a sentence of mine made it worse twice.** Round 2 produced "all five sites
use it"; round 3's correction produced "`forTable()` is now the ONE way". Both are
the kind of claim that tells the next reader to stop looking, and in this codebase
"the ONE place" is a standing promise with real weight. The second was written
*while correcting the first*.

### The gate asked a narrower question than the one it exists to answer — twice more

`check_table_name_comparisons.py` was bypassed by two one-token regressions, each
shown to reach the code:

- **`strcmp` inside `forTable()`.** The check pinned `namedIn()` alone, although
  its own header named both helpers as the remedy. It pins both now.
- **`in_array('tblX', $list)` with no `true`.** The check required the third
  argument to be `true`. A loose `in_array` over strings is **just as
  case-sensitive** — PHP's `==` between two non-numeric strings compares them
  exactly — and dropping `, true` is the likeliest way the regression returns.
  Any `in_array()` of a table name now fails it.

A new check D flags a `columnFacts()` subscript by shape. **The first version of
that sentence said the round-4 instance "could not recur silently", and two lines
disproved it** — assigning `columnFacts()` to a local first walked past check D
entirely, and the independent check measured it reproducing the fault with every
check green. Check E now follows exactly one assignment, and only inside the four
held-row methods, because applied to the whole file it reported FIFTEEN safe
sites. The helper bodies are pinned WHOLE rather than by the presence of a
`strcasecmp` call, because `strcasecmp(...) === 0 && $table === (string) $name`
is a real call and is case-sensitive again.

**Five versions of one check now, and the arc is identical to
`check_no_outside_qr_service.py`: each version asked something narrower than the
question it exists to answer, and only planting found the gap.** What finally
stopped it was giving up on detecting arbitrary shapes and pinning the two
helpers' entire bodies — the literal form of this repository's own "pin the WHOLE
condition" rule. The cost is that any edit to either helper fails the check,
which is the point: it forces the change to be deliberate.

**What it still cannot see is listed in its header rather than implied away** — a
needle in a variable, a needle built by concatenation, more than one assignment,
a `columnFacts()` array passed to another method, and anything outside
`DbBackup.php`.

### A check that pins a reassurance makes the untruth load-bearing

The warning added in round 3 to stop a silent disappearance ended "Nothing has
been lost: this snapshot holds the row in its own copy of the table it came
from." The code never looks at whether the snapshot holds that table. Two
measured counter-examples: a snapshot containing the holding table but not
`tblSettings`, and an ordinary sequence where the waiting row held the **last**
copy of a setting value and afterwards it was in no table and no kept row.

Worse, section E2 **required** those words, so the check held the untruth in
place — and the proof's own fixture is one of the worlds where the sentence is
false, which is why it never noticed. The sentence now says only what is known
(the snapshot records the row as put back, so it is no longer offered) and where
to look, and the check requires the reassurance to be **absent**.

## The giving-records ceiling (#687), and what two check rounds cost

The feature is small: an optional ceiling on `giving.retention.years`, settable
installation-wide or by an organisation for itself, off by default. Two
independent check rounds found **nine** real problems in it. Seven were mine;
one was pre-existing (#700) and one was a test counting rather than naming.

### The claim that justified the design was false

#668's standing rule is that **a save-time cap is not a cap**, because the job
that clears records reads the stored figure. #687 does not cap in the reader —
deliberately, because this figure is a statutory retention period and shortening
one behind a customer's back can be unlawful and cannot be undone. The
justification was that two save-time gates keep `years <= ceiling` true by
construction, and that **the only way past them was hand-written SQL or a
restored backup.**

That sentence was in five places, and it was wrong. The gate compared against the
request's **settings snapshot**, taken at start-up by `bootstrap.php`, while the
other gate read the database live. Two ordinary web requests were enough:

    request A starts (snapshot: no ceiling)
    request B sets the installation ceiling to 7      -> accepted
    request A saves 50 years, confirmed               -> accepted
    a fresh request: ceiling 7, stored figure 50, confirmed

Measured by the first check round, reproduced in **60 of 60** simultaneous pairs.

**The lesson is about the sentence, not the race.** "The portal cannot reach this
state" is precisely the claim that stops the next reader looking, and it was the
stated reason for not capping in the reader. Where a design rests on a claim
about what cannot happen, that claim has to be measured.

### Closing it, and proving it closed

Both gates now re-read the ceiling **live** and take `FOR UPDATE` on the
installation's own settings row, inside the transaction that writes — the rule
the four money writers follow (#647). `capFromDatabase()` is the authority for
every refusal; `capInForce()`, which reads the snapshot through `SettingLimit`,
is for drawing the page only.

The second round proved it rather than accepting it: **116 genuinely simultaneous
pairs, 0 of 116** above the ceiling; both orders forced with an external session
holding the lock, each path blocking about five seconds and then refusing; and —
the part that matters — **removing just ` FOR UPDATE` brought the original end
state straight back.** That plant is what distinguishes "the lock closes it" from
"the live read closes it", and without it the conclusion would have been a guess.

### The gate was never too weak — only too eager

Three separate false refusals, each of which looked like safety:

- It gated `$years`, which is the typed figure **or** the country suggestion. So
  with a ceiling in force and an empty years box, **switching the hold on was
  refused** — the one control that stops records being cleared — and the message
  said "that number was not saved" about a number nobody had typed.
- Moved after the suggestion, it still ran before the **un-tick** branch was
  decided, so clearing the years box with the tick left on (how the page draws
  it) was refused, while the identical end state saved if the administrator also
  unticked by hand.
- It judged the organisation's **own** ceiling even when the save did not change
  it, so an own ceiling the installation had later been lowered past blocked the
  hold, the year end, confirming and a plain Save — over a number the
  organisation never raised and the page itself had prefilled.

The gate now runs after rules 1 and 2, on `$yearsOwn`, which by then is exactly
what will be stored; and the own ceiling is judged only when it **changes**,
which is #667/#677's rule: ask whether the field changed, not only whether it
arrived.

### #668's prefill fault, reproduced under the comment citing it

Both number boxes were prefilled above their own `max` — the ceiling box because
`max` was the installation's ceiling, the years box because `max` was the ceiling
in force while a stored figure can legitimately exceed it. #668 names this in so
many words: *"must never prefill a value its own `max` forbids — the browser then
refuses to submit the whole form."* Measured in headless Edge: `rangeOverflow`,
no submit event at all. For the years box that meant **the only way to use the
page again was to shorten a statutory retention period**, which is the one thing
the feature exists to avoid forcing on anybody.

`max` is the hard maximum on both boxes now, and the handler is the boundary —
which it has to be, because anything can be posted.

### And one of my own edits deleted working code

Moving the gate "to after rules 1 and 2" was done by cutting the text between my
own block and an anchor below it. **Rules 1 and 2 was what lay in between**, so
the confirm logic went with it: seventeen checks failed across three self-tests,
none of them about the ceiling. The whole-suite rule (#695) is the only reason it
was caught.

**A slice between two markers deletes whatever is between them.** The same method
had already silently duplicated a block in an audit script earlier the same day.
Replace exact text, or insert before an anchor; if a slice is unavoidable, print
what it removes and read it before writing the file.

## A preference that was saved and read by nothing, while the push obeyed its own (#666, #616, #683)

*1 November 2026.*

**The fault, and why it survived so long.** `cron/event-reminders.php` sent an
event reminder to everybody who had answered "going". It read no notification
preference for the e-mails at all. The word `notifyPrefs` appeared exactly once
in the whole file — in a comment, about the companion **web push**.

**Be exact about how little the switch did, because the first draft of this
section was not, and the independent check caught it.** That draft said the
switch "was saved, honoured for the companion push, and ignored by the mail",
and the same clause reached four other documents and two code comments. It is
false. `git grep -n eventReminders 8810a06 -- web/` finds only the two account
pages that WRITE the key and draw its tick-box — each a view and a handler, so
four files — plus two schema column comments: **no reader anywhere in the
portal.** Quote the command with its `-- web/` filter; without it the output is
wider than the sentence claims. The push is gated on a different key entirely —
`pushServiceReminders`, shown on the page as "Service reminders" — so a member
who switched "Event reminders" off went on getting both the e-mails and the
push. The sentence was wrong in the direction that flatters the old code, and it
replaced a comment that had been right: the block deleted from
`notifications.php` said the job "honours only the PUSH switch … it does not
read this one".

**The thing worth copying, with the same qualification: the page said so out
loud.** Rather than hide a switch that did nothing, `auth/account/notifications.php`
carried a standing warning telling the member that switching it off did not stop
the e-mails. That is the right thing to do with a known fault, and it is why this
one was easy to find and easy to trust. The notice was itself imprecise — it
implied the push obeyed this key — so when the fault went, the warning was
**deleted rather than reworded**, because a notice that no longer describes
anything is worse than none.

**Do not write a fifth copy of `notifyPrefAllows()`.** The "a missing key means
yes" idiom is implemented **four** times: `WebPush::notifyPrefAllows()` (public),
`Workflow`'s own private copy, `cron/user-reminders.php`'s plain function, and
`Giving::isOptedOutOfStatements()` (the same rule inverted). All four were
compared and they agree, so there is no latent bug — but there is no one place
either. `ImportNotifier` is **not** a fifth: it already asks `WebPush`, which is
the precedent the reminder job now follows, and `auth/account/save.php` only
writes the column. An earlier draft of this paragraph counted those two as
copies and said six; count the function bodies, not the file names. If a fifth
reader appears, the right move is one `Portal\Core` class that all five ask.

**One mailbox, two accounts, and the order the two rules are applied in.** The
recipient map is keyed by e-mail address, and a couple may share one. A refused
row is dropped **before** the full-detail merge. That gives two properties that
are easy to lose: an address is written off only when *every* account reading it
has said no, so one person's choice cannot silence the other's reminder; and an
account that said no can never raise the other's e-mail to the version naming
the location.

**#616: an `OR u.isAdmin = 1` with no organisation in the query.** The day-of
summary tested "coordinates this event" OR the older portal-wide admin flag, so
every holder of that flag received a morning summary for every event on the
installation — a hosting provider reading each customer's diary, across the
boundary between two parties. The cure is a join to `tblUserSites` for the
event's own organisation, which scopes the coordinators too.

**And the per-organisation flags had to go in with it.** Scoping alone would
have made the ordinary case *worse*: an organisation's own administrator holds
`tblUserSites.isSiteAdmin`, not the legacy flag, so they were already missed and
the join alone would still not have reached them. When you narrow a recipient
set, check who was only ever qualifying through the thing you are narrowing.

**#683 was real and the issue pointed at the wrong code.** It blamed the
reminder job. It could not have been that job: all three reminder bodies are
built as HTML, and `Mailer::send()` wraps a body in the branded base only when
it does **not** look like HTML — so **no reminder e-mail has ever carried a
footer at all**. The live instance is the giving statement, through
`Mailer::sendTemplated()`, which always goes through `renderBase()`.

**`Site::forceContext()` is the trap in it.** It sets the current site id and
reloads the site row, so `PortalAddress` follows it and the footer's *link* was
always right for each organisation. It does **not** re-merge `$SETTINGS`, so the
portal name and the support mailbox stayed with whichever organisation the job's
own request resolved to. Half-right output is the hardest kind to notice: the
link changing per organisation is exactly what makes the footer look correct.

**Read `App::settingForSite()` before writing a two-layer query.** It already
answers "this organisation's value, else the installation's" — the fallback #677
describes. The first draft of `Mailer::footerFactsFor()` wrote its own; that was
a second copy of one rule for no gain, and `Giving.php` next door was already
asking the house way.

**A CHECK THAT PASSED ON THE PRE-FIX CODE, AND THE PLANT THAT WAS NOT A FAULT
AT ALL.** The #616 check was written to prove that the morning summary for one
organisation's event does not reach the installation's global administrator, who
belongs to a different organisation. It passed. It also passed when
`git show HEAD:web/_apps/cron/event-reminders.php`'s own query — the code as it
stood before this package, with no organisation join whatever — was planted back
in. **The check proved nothing.** Part T of `tools/time-zones-selftest.php`
switches every account but one member off, deliberately, so that the clock-change
checks can read what the job *would* have sent without anything being attempted;
and the morning summary's query asks for `u.isActive = 1` where the day-before
reminder's does not. So the administrator was never a recipient of anything, in
either version, and "the administrator was not told" was true for a reason that
had nothing to do with organisations. The check now switches that one account
back on for its own two runs and puts it back as it found it.

**Two things about this are worth more than the fix.** First, the plant I tried
BEFORE the real one — loosening the join to a `LEFT JOIN`, which by reading
should let a global administrator straight through — also passed, and that
looked exactly like "the guard is unnecessary". It was not: the fixture was
dead, so no mutation of the query could have moved the result. **A plant that
fails to go red is as likely to mean the fixture cannot reach the code as it is
to mean the code does not matter, and the two are indistinguishable from the
passing run alone.** The way out was to stop inventing mutations and plant the
actual previous version from git, which is the one plant whose meaning is not in
doubt. Second, the fix is only decisive because the check now asserts the
POSITIVE half as well: the same administrator IS written to about their own
organisation's event the following morning. Without that half, "not told" could
still mean "unreachable", which is the fault this check just had.

**AND THE REPAIRED CHECK STILL PROVED NOTHING ABOUT THE QUERY. This is the
sharpest lesson in the package.** Switching the administrator back on made the
check mean something about organisations, and the independent check then showed
it meant nothing about the query. The summary admits somebody on any of FOUR
grounds — they coordinate the event, or they hold `tblUserSites.isSiteAdmin`, or
`isSiteRootAdmin`, or the portal-wide `tblUsers.isAdmin` — and the administrator
in that made-up world holds **all three ADMINISTRATOR grounds at once**, because
the fixture loop near the top of the file passes one `$isAdmin` value into
`isAdmin`, `isRootAdmin`, `isSiteAdmin` and `isSiteRootAdmin` alike — though the
query never reads `isRootAdmin`.
Measured, one at a time: **each of those three ADMINISTRATOR clauses could be
deleted on its own with all 134 checks green.** Three, not four — and getting
that number right matters, because the first version of this paragraph said four
and the independent check caught it. The COORDINATOR clause was never
deletable-green: that administrator coordinates nothing, so deleting it drops the
coordinator from the expected list. **Claiming a measurement that was never made
is worse than claiming none**, because the next reader has no reason to re-run it.

The REFUSING conditions were worse than the admitting ones, and all three were
inert. `AND us.isActive = 1` on the join, `WHERE u.isActive = 1`, and
`AND revokedAt IS NULL` inside the coordinator sub-select could EACH be deleted
with all 134 checks green, because nothing in the made-up world could trip any of
them — every membership was active, every account that mattered was active, and
the single coordinator had never been stood down. In production that is three
separate leaks: a person removed from an organisation, a person whose account has
been closed, and a coordinator who was stood down, each going on receiving that
organisation's morning diary. **A condition no fixture can trip is not a
condition**, and two of the three took a second and third round of checking to
find because the first round's attention was all on the clauses that ADMIT.

The cure is one person per ground that admits and one per condition that refuses,
seven in all: a coordinator, an `isSiteAdmin` holder, an `isSiteRootAdmin` holder,
and a portal-wide administrator who IS an active member of that organisation, none
of them holding any other qualifying flag; then an ex-member (live account,
membership switched off), a closed account (membership live), and a coordinator
whose appointment is revoked — all three of whom must be told nothing. All six
plants now go red, each caught by the #616 check alone, and each failure names the
person who leaked in or dropped out.
**Note the order the repair went in, because it is the same mistake twice:** the
first attempt added three people and covered three clauses, and the portal-wide
clause stayed deletable, because the person who proved the OTHER half of the same
check still held `isSiteAdmin` as well. **One account holding several flags
cannot tell them apart** — the same shape as a fixture whose two rows differ in
more than one way, and the reason to plant every clause separately rather than
assume a fixture that looks richer is richer.

**A TWO-CHARACTER BRACKET MOVE LIFTS THE WHOLE `WHERE` CLAUSE, AND `php -l`
CANNOT SEE IT.** Round 3 of the independent check found one edit that still left
all 134 checks green: closing the admitting group one disjunct early and opening
a new one, `… isSiteRootAdmin = 1) OR (u.isAdmin = 1`. The parentheses stay
balanced, so the file lints clean, but the condition becomes
`(account live AND address tests AND (coordinator OR isSiteAdmin OR isSiteRootAdmin)) OR (u.isAdmin = 1)`
— and anybody holding the portal-wide flag with a live membership then bypasses
the account test and both address tests. An offboarded administrator would go
back to receiving the organisation's morning diary. It stayed green only because
no fixture held `isAdmin = 1` together with a closed account: the closed-account
person had `isAdmin = 0` and the portal-wide-flag person was fully live.

The cure was one character — give the closed account every qualifying flag, so
the account test is the only thing keeping it out. That **sharpens** its pin
rather than blurring it, which is the question to ask before adding a flag to an
existing fixture person. It is now caught, by the one check that should catch it.
The general lesson: when a condition is a group of `OR`s inside an `AND`, the
grouping is itself a thing that can break, and no amount of pinning the
individual clauses covers it — pin a person who is refused by the OUTER test
while qualifying on an inner one.

**And the rounds themselves are the last lesson.** Three rounds, and each one
found the previous fix incomplete in the same way: round 1 found the fixture
dead, round 2 found three clauses indistinguishable, round 3 found the number
"four" wrong in one place and "stops the e-mails" unqualified in four more.
Every round was wording-or-coverage of the SAME correction, not a new fault.
**When a correction has to be made in more than two places, list the places
first and edit them in one pass** — the cost here was two extra rounds, entirely
self-inflicted, on a package whose code was right from round 1 onwards.

And do not count a neighbouring harness as cover. `tools/mail-queue-selftest.php`
does call `/cron/event-reminders` over real HTTP and does assert on the day-of
summary's recipients, but its check is `count($dayRows) >= 1 && in_array(mailOf('root'), …)`
and `root` holds the portal-wide flag, so it is satisfied by the legacy clause
alone and would not have noticed a per-organisation flag being dropped either.
A claim that this is "the only harness that runs the job" was also simply false,
and is corrected where it was written.

**And `tblEventReminderLog.recipientCount` is not evidence that anything was
sent.** It counts only messages a mail service really took
(`Mailer::lastOutcome() === OUTCOME_SENT`), and part T deliberately points the
portal at an SMTP mailbox with nothing filled in, so every message that goes out
perfectly well is recorded as 0. The first version of all three new checks
asserted on that column; two of them failed on correct code, and the one that
"passed" expected 0 and would have passed on a job that sent nothing at all.
`mailTo()` reads `tblEmailLog.toRecipients` instead, so each check says WHO was
written to — which is both stricter than a count and, unlike a count, actually
about the behaviour. **Asserting on a column the harness cannot populate reads as
a strict check and is really a check of the harness's own missing mail server.**

## Thirty-five tables named a personal column and nothing emptied it (#635)

*2 November 2026.*

**The fault.** `web/_core/personal-data-catalogue.php` names, per table, the
columns that make it personal. `GdprEraser` builds its instructions from that
list — but only ever acted on the names holding an **account number**. A named
column holding an address, a hand-typed name or a note got no instruction and
was never emptied. The list promised to unlink the table; the column stayed.
That was #626 on the activity log, and it was true of thirty-five other tables.

**A NON-LINK `nullCols` ENTRY IS ONLY SAFE WHERE THE MATCHED COLUMN IS THE ROW'S
SUBJECT. This is the whole lesson of the package.** In `processEntry()`, an
account column is emptied with `IF(col = ?, NULL, col)` — scoped to this person.
Any other column is emptied with a plain `col = NULL`, **on every row the
instruction matched**. The comment beside it reads "the row was matched on this
person, so it does belong to them", which is true when `userCol` says who the row
is *about* and false when it says who *acted* on it. Match on an actor and you
delete a third party's name, address or telephone from every row that actor ever
touched, on a request that was never theirs.

**I called four tables "mechanical — the same fault as #626" and was wrong about
two of them, and the same flaw affected a third the owner had already decided.**
In `tblLiveChatMessages`, `tblEventRSVPInvites`, `tblVenues` (caretaker),
`tblKidCheckins` (pickup name) and `tblSmallGroups` (the meeting place), the only
account column is the moderator who approved or hid the message — a chat sender
has **no account at all**, being identified by an anonymous token — or the
coordinator who sent the invitation, whoever added the venue, or the helper who
did the checking. Emptying would have deleted a non-member invitee's e-mail, a
chat visitor's address, a caretaker's telephone and the record of who collected a
child — **while reaching none of the erased person's own data.** All four are kept
now, each with its reason. **"It is the same shape as a fault we fixed before" is
a hypothesis, not a finding**: check which column the instruction actually matches
on before calling it settled. Twice in one package was twice too many.

**A hand-written entry wins over the derived one for the WHOLE TABLE.** That is
why `tblErrors` has both of its instructions written out by hand: the three
diagnostic columns belong to the `userID` one alone, and writing only that one
would have silently stopped `resolvedByID` being detached. The derived route
cannot express "this `nullCols` entry belongs to that instruction", which is the
reason a hand-written entry was needed at all.

**A reason beside the column beats a name in a fixture.** The 35 tables were
pinned by name in `tools/gdpr-coverage-selftest.php`, with no reason attached to
any of them. They are now explained by `notEmptiedHere` in the catalogue itself —
the file a request for somebody's information is answered from — so a person
asking why a column is still there can read the answer. Three checks stop it
becoming the excuse list the pinned list was forbidden from being: a reason must
be long enough to be a reason, an explanation for a column the entry no longer
names fails as stale, and **an explanation for a column that IS now emptied
fails**, which is what makes the list shrink as the work is done. Four plants,
each caught by the one check that should catch it.

**Three honest reasons, and no fourth.** A column an instruction does not empty is
either deliberately kept (the row is the organisation's record of a thing), emptied
elsewhere (and the order matters — the profile images are read to find the file
before the columns are cleared), or genuinely unreachable (the only match belongs
to somebody else). Anything that is none of those three is a bug — and where such a bug is known,
the catalogue records the column with its issue number rather than leaving the
line silent, which is what `tblCareVisit.notes` does today (#709).

**Do not quote SQL in a data file.** A `notEmptiedHere` reason explained the
profile-image columns by quoting `UPDATE tblUsers SET …`, and
`check_account_writes_guarded.py` — which matches on text — read the catalogue as a
file that writes to an account table. The right fix was to reword the prose, not to
add the file to that check's allow-list: the file writes nothing, and widening a
real guard to accommodate a sentence is how a guard stops guarding.

**What this did NOT fix, which is bigger than what it did (#706).** The pinned list
was a list of what the catalogue **admits to**, not of what these tables hold.
`tblAuditTrail`'s `oldValue`, `newValue` and `changeSet` hold `json_encode()` of a
whole row, so a change to somebody's own account leaves their name, e-mail,
and e-mail address in the trail (measured under #707 — NOT a telephone number
or a postal address, which this line claimed until 2 November 2026);
`tblErrors.errorDetail` holds a full
backtrace and `requestURL` the whole query string; and ten more personal columns
appear in **no catalogue entry at all**. None of them is visible to #635, to its
checks, or to an erasure. It is the #645 shape: a guard that reads as complete
because it is only ever compared against itself.

**EMPTYING A FIXTURE KILLED A CHECK, AND THAT IS THE BEST LESSON OF THE round.**
Taking all 35 names out of `$leftBehindOnPurpose` left the check "the pinned
list holds no table that is now clean" **unable to fail** — its only input was
that list — and left the `if ($pinned !== null)` branch as dead code whose only
possible effect, if a name ever went back, was to SUPPRESS a real column. A
check is not just its condition; it is its condition and whatever feeds it, and
**emptying the thing that feeds it is a way of deleting a check without touching
it.** The branch is gone and the list being empty is now pinned directly, which
is a statement that can actually be falsified.

**THE SILENT UNDO.** Every check here compared the erasure routine against the
WRITTEN LIST, so deleting a column from an entry *and* taking its `nullCols`
away passed all of them: the list no longer names it, so nothing is "left
behind". The independent check proved it by undoing this package's own
`tblAuditTrail` fix with all 71 green. The general cure is #706 — compare the
list against the SCHEMA — and the narrow one is here: the five columns #635
empties are pinned by name and must still be named AND still be emptied. **A
guard that reads one document against another can always be satisfied by editing
both.**

**The actor trap is a check now, not a comment.** "A non-account `nullCols`
entry on an instruction matched by WHO ACTED deletes a third party's data" was
written into `processEntry()` as prose. It is a check in
`tools/gdpr-coverage-selftest.php`, and planting proved it: the three diagnostic
columns moved onto `tblErrors`' resolver instruction, and the attendance note
moved onto the coordinator's, are each caught by it and by nothing else. Prose in
the file that has the bug does not stop the bug coming back.

**Three wrong counts in prose, in one package, and one was inherited from the
comment it was correcting.** "Four columns are now emptied" where five are;
"four tables are in this state" where five are; and "migration 192 made exactly
those thirteen nullable" where the migration has fourteen `MODIFY COLUMN` lines —
that last repeated from the stale comment being fixed. This repository's own rule
is that counts in prose go stale within days and that you count from the code.
**Where a number is not load-bearing, the fix is to delete it, not to correct
it** — two of the three are now phrased without a number at all.

**MY OWN FAILURE MODE, THREE PACKAGES RUNNING, AND IT IS NOT THE CODE.** Across
#666/#616/#683, #694/#697 and now #635, the code has been right at or near the
first attempt and every later check round has found the same three things in what
I WROTE about it:

1. **A count in prose.** "Four columns are now emptied" (five). "Four tables are
   in this state" (five). "Four tables keep a personal column" (five again, in
   two more places, after I had already dropped that number from the header for
   exactly this reason). "Migration 192 made exactly those thirteen nullable"
   (fourteen — repeated from the stale comment I was correcting). This
   repository's own rule already says counts in prose go stale within days.
   **The rule I was missing: where a number is not load-bearing, DELETE it; where
   it is, a check must pin it.** Two of #635's three numbers are now phrased
   without a number at all, and the one that matters is pinned.
2. **A correction applied in one place and not the others.** The chat-sender
   claim was fixed in the catalogue and left standing in CHANGELOG and DEV_NOTES.
   **Before editing a wrong sentence, grep the whole repository for its clause,
   list every hit, and edit them in ONE pass** — the hit list is the work item,
   not the first occurrence.
3. **A guard that iterates its own list.** The check I added to catch the silent
   undo looped over `$shouldBeEmptied` and accumulated into one `check()`, so
   deleting a line from that array stopped testing that column without failing
   anything. This is #697's proof-26 lesson verbatim, and I reintroduced it while
   fixing a different instance of the same family. **A check that walks a list
   must pin the list's shape in the same `check()` call.**

The useful conclusion is not "try harder on prose". It is that **the review rounds
on this project are earning their keep on the WRITING, not the code** — so the
cheapest thing I can do is apply the three rules above before asking for a round,
rather than after.

---

## Matching an erasure through a parent table (#709)

**What the problem was.** Every instruction in `GdprEraser::catalogue()` says
"this table, this column, this person's number". A pastoral visit does not work
that way. `tblCareVisit.notes` describes the person being **cared for**, and the
only account numbers on the row are `visitedByID` (the worker who made the
visit) and `followUpAssignedToID` (the worker its follow-up was given to). The
subject is one table up, on `tblCareCase.personUserID`. So until 2 November 2026
that note could not be reached at all, and `personal-data-catalogue.php`
recorded it as "TO BE EMPTIED" with its issue number — the one line ever in that
state.

**The shape of the fix.** An instruction may now carry `subjectVia`, naming four
things: the link on the row (`childCol`), the table one step up (`parent`), that
table's own key (`parentKey`) and the column on it that says who the row is
**about** (`personCol`). `GdprEraser::whereForEntry()` is the ONE place the
"which rows are this person's" clause is written, for both shapes, and three
readers ask it — the probe, the statement that makes the change, and
`inventory()`, which is what a person is shown when they ask what is held about
them. Either shape binds exactly one value, which is what let the binding code
stay as it was.

**The obvious shortcut is the destructive one, and that is why the rule is a
refusal rather than a best effort.** Hanging the notes off `visitedByID` would
empty the safeguarding notes of every visit the erased **worker** ever made —
other people's records, about people who never asked for anything — and would
still reach not one note about the person who did ask. Both halves are bad, and
the second half is why nobody would notice the first. The same mistake is
available one table up: point `personCol` at `tblCareCase.openedByID` and it
empties the notes of every case that worker opened.
`GdprEraser::whyParentMatchUnusable()` is the ONE test of whether an instruction
may match this way, and it is public so the coverage test asks it rather than
keeping a second copy of the rule. It refuses eight things; only one of them
stops real harm (`personCol` must be in `LINK_COLUMNS` and not in
`ACTOR_COLUMNS`), and the other seven stop nonsense.

**`personUserID` was on NEITHER list**, although the database links it to
`tblUsers` and a hand-written instruction had always matched on it — so nothing
could judge whether it named a row's subject or somebody who acted on one. It is
in `LINK_COLUMNS`'s first group now. It is on exactly one table and no catalogue
entry lists it among its own columns, so adding it builds no new derived
instruction; that was checked rather than assumed.

**THE TRAP THE WHOLE FEATURE TURNS ON, and it was live before the feature
existed.** The parent's own instruction empties the very column the child
matches through: the `tblCareCase` step sets `personUserID` to NULL. Run the
child's step after it and the look-up finds nothing, every note stays exactly
where it was, and the sealed audit trail says "nothing held for this person" — a
silent, permanent, complete failure that reads like success. **In the list as it
stood, the parent's instruction came FIRST**, so an instruction added in the
obvious place would have done exactly nothing. Two guards, and both are needed:
`tools/gdpr-coverage-selftest.php` pins the POSITION (it judges the list, where
the mistake is made and where it can be seen before anybody runs an erasure),
and `whyParentLookUpUnsafe()` judges the RUN (the only half that survives the
steps being called in some other order). The run-time guard is deliberately
coarse about WHICH column was emptied — the trail records the table and not the
column, and `tblCareCase` carries two instructions — so it can refuse when the
link it needs is in fact untouched. Refusing is the recoverable direction;
missing is not.

**That guard was wrong TWICE, in opposite directions, and the second one is the
lesson.** Version 1 read the WHOLE request's audit trail. A run with a failed
step is put back to `pending_review` and **run again**, so a second run's trail
already holds the first run's lines — the step refused on every later run and
the request could never be completed. Section 6 of
`tools/gdpr-eraser-selftest.php` went red on exactly that.

Version 2 therefore read only the lines written by the run in hand — **and that
reopened the very fault the guard exists to stop, one step further on.** On a
second run the parent's change is not "from this run", so the step was ALLOWED,
the link was already gone, the look-up found nothing, and the step wrote
"nothing held for this person" while the request closed as **completed** with
the safeguarding note still in it. **No mistake by anybody was needed:** one
transient error on this one step in run 1 is enough, because the walk carries on
and the parent's step still cuts the link. A lock wait while the safeguarding
team edits visits would do it.

**It was the docblock that let version 2 stand.** It said a refusal "leaves
every note in place for a second run, whereas a miss is silent and permanent" —
and that sentence was false, because the second run could not do it and was
itself silent and permanent. DEV_NOTES, `CHANGELOG.md` and both instruction
files carried the same words. The #645 shape again: **a comment stating the
guarantee the code had forgotten to implement.** Worse, **the self-test asserted
the fault as correct** (`$saysClearAfterwards === false`), which is why nothing
caught it.

Version 3 asks all three questions. The parent untouched means the link is
intact. Changed EARLIER IN THIS RUN is an ordering mistake, recoverable by
moving the instruction back. Changed BY AN EARLIER RUN means the link is gone
for good, and the answer then turns on whether this step had already given a
trustworthy answer BEFORE that happened — any line of its own (`anonymise`,
`partial` or `none`) with a LOWER `auditID` than the parent's first change. **A
`none` from before the change really does mean the person held nothing here; a
`none` from after it means only that the look-up could no longer see**, which is
why the comparison is on `auditID` and not on a line merely existing. Where no
trustworthy answer exists the step fails and SAYS the rows must be checked by
hand, because re-running will not reach them. **A request that needs a human
look is worse than one that just works and far better than one that reports
success it has not earned** — and that is a decision about product behaviour, not
a tidy-up, so it is written here beside the code.

`self::$runStartedAfterAuditId` is `MAX(auditID)` as it stood when the run
began, held beside the other per-run state, and it exists only to tell those two
"changed" cases apart. 0 means "nothing is known about where this run began";
every line then reads as belonging to this run, so the guard reports an ordering
mistake rather than letting the step proceed. That is the safe refusal for the
WRONG REASON, so nothing relies on it except as a backstop.

**One more thing the fix round found, by reading rather than by a test going
red.** The "had this step already answered" question was asked of the audit
trail by TABLE NAME — and `tblCareVisit` carries THREE instructions: the note,
and the two that detach the workers. All three write
`tableName = 'tblCareVisit'`, so a line from a different instruction would have
counted as this one having run. Today the pinned order happens to make the two
readings agree, because the only child instruction above the parent's is the
via one. **But nothing pins where the other two sit relative to the parent**,
and moving one of them above it is harmless in itself — neither matches through
the parent — so that edit would silently have made the guard allow a step it
must refuse. Only a parent-matched step writes HOW it reached its rows, so that
sentence is now the discriminator, through `details LIKE`. **It is deliberately
a clause that CAN fail:** `matchedThrough()` builds both the pattern and the
sentence, so case 3 of section 19 reads a REAL via line back through it, and a
pattern that stopped matching turns that check red instead of quietly refusing
everything — measured by planting a pattern that can never match, which failed
section 6's second-run checks.

**ROUND 2 FOUND FOUR MORE THINGS PINNED BY NOTHING, AND THE FIRST IS THE ONE TO
REMEMBER.** Round 1's lesson was "pin the call, not just the behaviour". Round 2
showed that pinning the call is not enough either: **`if (false && isset(...))`
on the line ABOVE switched BOTH guards off — the rule and the run-time guard — in
one word, with all 336 checks across the two files green.** The inner pins
matched text that never ran. **When you pin a call, pin the gate that decides
whether the block containing it is entered**, or you have pinned a label on a
door nobody opens. The rule's own call (`whyParentMatchUnusable()`) turned out to
be pinned by nothing at all; only the look-up guard's had been.

**A CHECK CAN NAME THE RIGHT FAULT AND MEASURE THE WRONG VALUE.** The check
labelled "every refusal is a whole sentence, not a 250-character slice with an
identifier cut in half" measured the sentence the GUARD RETURNS — a literal in
the same file — so putting `mb_substr(..., 0, 250)` back around the audit line,
which is where #709's fault actually was, left it green. **The cut is applied by
the CALLER, and no value inside the guard changes when it is.** Measured, the two
refusals are 261 and 317 characters as stored, so they really would have been cut
again. The cut is now pinned in the source, in the coverage test; the sentence
check is relabelled to say what it can and cannot see.

**AND WIDENING A LIST OF "GOOD" ACTIONS PUT THE WHOLE FAULT BACK.** Adding
`'failed'` to the actions that count as "this step already answered" left both
tests green, and it is live harm: a PROBE failure logs `failed` with details
beginning "could not look for this person (matched through ...)", so **it carries
the very discriminator the `details LIKE` clause matches on**, and its `auditID`
is below the parent's change. Count it and run 2 looks, finds nothing, writes
"nothing held for this person", and closes the request as completed with the note
still there. `'skip'` is excluded for a different reason — it means the rows WERE
found and deliberately left, so "check them by hand" remains the right later
answer. Section 19 now has a case for the `failed` line specifically, one word
apart from the case beside it.

**Two wording faults of the same family as every other round's.** The comment
justifying the unescaped `LIKE` pattern said the identifier rule means "neither
`%` nor `_` can appear" — the rule is `/\A[A-Za-z0-9_]+\z/`, which **allows the
underscore**, and `_` is a single-character wildcard. No harm today, because
neither `tblCareCase` nor `personUserID` contains one, **which is exactly why it
would not have been noticed**; the pattern is escaped now rather than argued
about. And `CHANGELOG.md` said the eraser test had 249 checks when it had 251.

**One more real fault, and it is the silent-success shape yet again.** A
parent-matched step names TWO tables, and error 1146 was handled as though it
named one: `skip`, with the CHILD's name, for "table-missing". If it is the
PARENT that has gone, the child's rows may be sitting there with every word of
the note in them — unmatchable, because the table that says whose they are is
absent — and a skip let the request close as completed having never looked. The
child's absence is still a skip; the parent's is a FAILED step, and which one it
is is asked of the database rather than read out of an error message.

**And the cost of the fix was written up as #710 — now fixed.** A step that
refuses for ever is right, but `closeRequest()` runs only when no step failed, so
such a request sat at `pending_review` with no way to finish it and could not be
cancelled either. `GdprEraser::finishByHand()` closes it now, and the lesson from
building that is below under "Closing a request nobody can finish (#710)". This
paragraph is kept because it records the state #709 shipped in.

**Two smaller things got wrong first, both worth keeping.**

*The "how it matched" clause was at the END of the audit line and the line was
cut to 250 characters*, so on the one instruction that uses this form the reason
ran long and the words `personUserID` were sliced in half — losing exactly the
fact nothing else records. It goes FIRST now and is not truncated: `details` is
a TEXT column, and the 250-character cuts in that method are on FAULT messages,
whose length nobody controls. A reason written in the source is not one of those.

*`['personUserID' => null]` does not give a null column.* `ge_insert()` reads
the people list as `$people[$name] ?? $other`, and `null ?? D` is D — so the
fixture for "a case with nobody named on it" was quietly named after the control
person and proved nothing it claimed to. A null has to go through `$fixed`,
which is read with `array_key_exists()`. Caught by that section's own "the world
is as it should be" check, which is what such a check is for.

**What the child keeps.** `childCol` is never emptied. A visit detached from its
