case is not an anonymised record: it is rubble with every word of the note still
in it. It is `NOT NULL` in the schema as well, so the statement would simply
fail — but the reason it must not be emptied is the first one, and a schema can
be changed. The columns in `nullCols` are therefore the whole of the change,
which is why an instruction naming none is refused: without the account link the
other instructions drop, an empty `nullCols` is a no-op that reads like coverage.

**How the generic world came to exercise it.** Every made-up row in
`tools/gdpr-eraser-selftest.php` is built generically and
`ge_ensureParents()` gives it a parent whose person columns name the
administrator, who is never erased — so the look-up found nothing and the step
reported "nothing held". That was the harness being honest, not the engine being
wrong, but it left the feature covered by nothing. The child's row is now pointed
at the row the PARENT's own instruction already made for this person: nothing new
is inserted, so the row is already allowed and already counted. **Only that
instruction's own rows are re-pointed** — `tblCareVisit` carries three
instructions, and the other two have rows whose notes must stay exactly as they
are; pointing every row of the table at the person's case made all three look
alike and turned three by-name checks red. The side benefit is the valuable part:
the ORDER is now proved by behaviour as well as by position, because moving the
instruction below its parent's brings those rows back with their notes intact.

**What nothing covers, and the first version of this paragraph UNDERSTATED it.**
It named only the three lines in `processEntry()` that act on the guard's
answer. Two more things were covered by nothing, and an independent check found
both by planting: **the guard's CALL** — replacing the whole condition with
`if (false)` left both self-tests and all 46 audit scripts green — and **the
`inventory()` half**, whose reversion to the old "skip an instruction with no
column of its own" was equally invisible, although "what we hold about you
counts these rows too" is listed as delivered. Section 8d of the coverage test
closes both, pinning the whole condition and requiring the refusal to return
`STEP_FAILED`, so neither the condition nor the body behind it can be removed
quietly.

Still covered by nothing: the LIVE path through `processEntry()` with a real
refusal — the audit line it writes, and what an administrator sees afterwards.
Reaching the ordering half needs a list the coverage test refuses outright, and
reaching the earlier-run half needs a trail a correct run does not produce, so
the guard's logic is asked directly over a hand-made audit trail and that is its
only cover. **`$where === ''` in `processEntry()` is also a clause that cannot
fail** — by the time it is reached a non-via entry has a column and a via entry
has passed the rule, so the builder always returns a clause. Its comment reads
like a live safety net and it is unreachable; left in place deliberately as a
backstop, and recorded here so nobody mistakes it for one that is tested.

Count the planted faults from the code and the evidence folder, never from this
paragraph (#671's rule). Tests: section 8c and the new section 8d of
`tools/gdpr-coverage-selftest.php` (no database) and section 19 of
`tools/gdpr-eraser-selftest.php` (a real database).

## PHP 8.6, and the four things worth keeping from supporting it (#705)

Measured on 2 November 2026 against a real **PHP 8.6.0RC4** (the `php:8.6-rc-cli`
image with `mysqli`, `mbstring`, `intl`, `gd`, `zip`, `bcmath` and `exif` added),
alongside the 8.5.11 this machine runs. Everything below was run, not read about.

### A pin that looks stale can be exactly right, and tidying it does harm

`PhpRuntime::PHP2SHELL_FIXED_IN['8.6'] = '8.6.0RC4'` looks like a placeholder
waiting for 19 November 2026, and issue #705 says in as many words that it
"must move from the pre-release to the finished release", calling that a dated
action with a security consequence.

It is wrong, and the whole table of verdicts is what shows it:

| Version | support | security |
|---|---|---|
| `8.6.0RC2` | warn | warn |
| `8.6.0RC3` | warn | warn |
| `8.6.0RC4` | warn (test build) | **ok** |
| `8.6.0` | **ok** | **ok** |
| `8.6.1`, `8.6.10` | ok | ok |

The finished `8.6.0` already passes with the pin untouched, because
`version_compare()` ranks a finished release above its own candidates. And
moving the pin to `8.6.0` flips `8.6.0RC4` from `ok` to `warn` — measured by
planting that exact edit — which is a false alarm in the frightening direction
about a server that is patched. The constant means **the first build carrying
the fix**, and RC4 (21 October 2026) is that build, permanently.

**The general lesson: a dated action with a security consequence deserves
measuring before the date, because the measurement may show there is no
action.** What does fall due as 8.6 matures is unrelated to this list —
`PREFERRED_SERIES` (the owner's decision) and `NEWEST_KNOWN_SERIES` (when an
8.7 appears). Section C4 of `tools/php-runtime-selftest.php` pins all of it and
explains it again at the point of failure, because a reader following the issue
would otherwise "correct" the constant.

### A deprecation survey that lists functions will miss a language change — and I got the version wrong proving it

#705's survey checked 8.6's function and method deprecations individually and
found none in use. It missed a **language** change rather than a function: the
**backtick operator is deprecated**. Two files in the tree use one, both on
purpose — they are fixtures that exist to be *caught* by audit checks looking
for shell execution, and neither is ever executed.

**The version attribution in the first draft of this section was WRONG, and
the way it went wrong is the more useful lesson.** I wrote that 8.6 deprecates
it, having run `php -l` over the tree on 8.6.0RC4, seen the two notices appear,
and attributed them to the version I happened to be measuring. The independent
check measured 8.5 and found it already there. Measured on all three:

| Version | `php -l` on a backtick |
|---|---|
| 8.4.27 | clean, no notice |
| **8.5.11** | **Deprecated: The backtick (`) operator is deprecated** |
| 8.6.0RC4 | the same notice |

So it arrived in **8.5** — the version this project RECOMMENDS and runs
locally — and the notices were already printing before any of this work.
**This is the error the section two above warns about, committed in the same
document: a version claim is only measured if you measured the versions it
distinguishes between.** Seeing a notice on the new version tells you nothing
about whether the old one was quiet.

Two details worth knowing before somebody "fixes" a fixture. `php -l` reports
the deprecation at compile time, so those two files print a notice on 8.5 and
8.6. And `.githooks/pre-push` judges `php -l` by its **exit code**, which is 0
for a deprecation, so nothing fails. No portal code under `web/` uses a
backtick.

### A test function that stops answering and starts throwing

8.6 turns seven filesystem **test** functions into throwers when the path holds
a NUL byte — `is_file`, `is_dir`, `file_exists`, `is_readable`, `is_writable`,
`filesize`, `filemtime` — where 8.4 and 8.5 return `false`. That is a different
shape of change from a deprecation, because every call site is written on the
assumption that a test function answers a question rather than raising one. A
visitor can put a NUL in a path: PHP decodes `%00` into a real NUL and keeps it
in `$_GET`.

Nothing here is reachable, and the reason is a pattern rather than luck —
**every request-derived path is narrowed before it reaches the filesystem**:

| Where | What narrows it |
|---|---|
| `noticeboard/media.php` | `^[a-f0-9]{32}\.(png|jpg|jpeg|gif|webp|mp4|webm)$` before any file call, then re-derived from the database and `basename()` again |
| `ApiRouter` | `^[a-z0-9\-]+$` on both the app and the action, before the path is built |
| `Router` | the target is a `tblRoutes` column; an address with a NUL matches no route and 404s first |
| the backup pages | `DbBackup::isSnapshotName()`, `\A[A-Za-z0-9_\-]+\z`, which throws before `pathOf()` can return |
| `calendar/index.php` | an `in_array($view, $validViews, true)` allow-list with a fallback |
| most download pages | `(int)` on the id, which no NUL survives |
| `giving/statements-download.php` | `strtotime()` does **not** reject a trailing NUL (measured) — but `periodKey` filters the query, so no row matches and the page exits gracefully, and `ZipArchive::open()` already throws on 8.5 |

The tracer that established this is deliberately **not** committed. It is a
textual, single-file trace: it cannot follow a value through a function call or
out of an array element, and a check that blind would give false confidence
rather than cover. What is kept is the table above and the method's limits.

### Checking a close is version-neutral work, and two details bite

`fclose()` has always returned `false` on a failed flush or close; what 8.6
changed is how much of that it reports rather than swallows. That distinction
is written into the code comment on purpose, because it was **not** measured
here — a failed flush cannot be provoked on this machine — and the claim worth
relying on needs no version at all: the old code discarded the result on 8.4,
8.5 and 8.6 alike.

- **`fflush()` is not a substitute.** It pushes PHP's own buffer at the
  operating system, which can still fail afterwards, at close. `BackupArchive`
  checked `fflush()` and then threw the close's answer away.
- **A second `fclose()` throws.** When a close returns `false` the resource is
  closed anyway, and closing it again raises a `TypeError` on both 8.5 and 8.6
  (measured). So the extraction path sets `$handle = null` before throwing, or
  the enclosing `finally` would close it twice and replace an honest message
  about a truncated file with a `TypeError` about a stream.

### What a passing suite does and does not tell you

The whole suite went green with the session hardening in place, which proves
only that nothing **broke**. It says nothing about whether the hardening works.
Section L of `tools/sign-in-limits-selftest.php` is the part that does: it sends
a well-formed session id naming no session and asks what the portal does with
it. With the `ini_set()` removed, that section reports
`the made-up id was ADOPTED` and finds `sess_<the id the request chose>` on
disk — demonstrated rather than argued. Its third check (that the page still
answers normally) passes either way on purpose: it guards the opposite
direction, a hardening that breaks the page.

**Three gaps in this package's own testing, stated because an unstated gap is
worse than a stated one.** First, **the installer's half of the session change
is guarded by nothing**: section L drives the portal's `/login`, and
`installer-selftest.php` sends only the MALFORMED cookie (#509's case), never a
well-formed unknown id — so deleting the `ini_set` from
`web/_install/index.php` would turn nothing red. Second, **neither new
`fclose()` refusal branch is executed by any test, and none can be**: a failed
close cannot be provoked without a custom stream wrapper, and nothing in
`tools/` registers one. They were verified by reading, by measuring the
`TypeError` a double close raises, and by confirming both callers clean up.
Third, the `version_compare` check in section C4 pins PHP's own ranking rather
than anything in this repository, so no edit here can make it fail; the
pre-release test beside it is the one that guards the constant.

## A guard that looks schema-driven and is not (#706)

The personal-data catalogue is the one list behind both of somebody's rights
over their own information: a copy of it, and its deletion. On 2 November 2026
**sixty-six tables were in it nowhere, and thirty-seven columns holding a
person's details were named in no entry at all.**

The interesting part is not the gap. It is that **a hard gate existed to catch
exactly this, it reads the database structure, and it was green over all
thirty-seven.**

### Why it was green

`tools/audit-checks/check_personal_data_coverage.py` decides what counts as a
personal column from a hand-written list of **literal names**, anchored whole:

```python
r"^(firstName|lastName|fullName|…|email|phone|address|postcode|notes|userID|…)$"
```

So it knows `phone` but not `phoneNumber`; `address` but not `addressLine1`;
`visitorIP` but not `createdIP`; nine particular `*Name` columns but not
`walkinName`, `reporterName` or `counterpartyName`. Its own comments record
**eleven separate occasions** on which somebody extended it — "Added by #514
part P7", "Added by #535", "Added by roll-out package A2a", "Added by mail
package M3" — each saying, in effect, "without the name here that entry could
be deleted and this check would still pass."

**It was never a schema-driven check. It was somebody's memory wearing a
schema-driven check's clothes.** That is the #645 shape one level up: the guard
that was supposed to break the circle was itself inside it.

### The rule that replaced it, and why it is narrow

Ask about the **shape** of the name, not the name itself. Split the column name
into words and test whole words:

- a contact word — `email`, `phone`, `address`, `postcode`, `ip`, `dob`, `nhs`;
- or `name`/`names` where the qualifier says **whose** — `reporter`,
  `submitter`, `walkin`, `counterparty`, `external`, `pickup`, `guardian`.

And it only applies to a column that can actually hold text, which is what
keeps `emailOutcome` (an enum), `emailAt` (a datetime) and `emailLogID` (an
integer) out of it.

**The first draft flagged 283 columns across 150 tables** and was useless,
because "contains the word name" matches `categoryName`, `deptName`,
`typeName`, `themeName`, `tuneName`, `eventName`, `locationName`, `groupName`
and `seriesName` — not one of them a person. The same lesson
`check_limit_settings_capped.py` already carries, and #483's: **a check that
cries wolf gets switched off, and then it catches nothing.** As written the rule
finds 37 and every one is real.

**The hand-written list stays beside it.** A shape cannot recognise
`actorUserID`, `giverID` or `decidedByID`, and those account-link columns are
most of that list's present value. The two run together.

**The judgement stays in the catalogue.** The check never decides whether a
column *is* personal or what should happen to it; it insists only that somebody
has written a decision down, in the file a person reads.

### Writing an honest reason is what finds the faults

The work was supposed to be documentation. Four of the sixty-six reasons could
not be written truthfully without recording something broken, and each became
its own issue:

| Issue | What the reason had to admit |
|---|---|
| **#712** | Two tables keep a visitor's network address in full and **nothing ever clears them**. `tblLiveRateLimits` has no clear-out, no foreign key and no cascade — and carries an index named `idx_ratelimit_prune`, for a tidy-up that does not exist. |
| **#713** | `tblWebhookEvent` keeps the **whole** Stripe or PayPal message, and keeps it **before the check on who sent it is acted on** — so anybody's POST is stored for ever, on a table with no foreign keys at all, carrying the payer's name, e-mail and billing address. |
| **#714** | Three places an erasure cannot reach: a recording's transcript and its byte-for-byte search copy; an expense receipt's **original filename** (the uploader's own, so "Jane Smith receipt.pdf"), where the claim above it is deliberately KEPT for HMRC so the cascade never fires; and a workflow's subject label. |
| **#707** | Already open — an audit line *about* the erased person is reachable by nothing. |

**An entry that says "nothing clears this" is a description of today, not a
defence of it.** That is why each carries an issue number in the reason itself.

### Three things the catalogue's own rules taught, the hard way

1. **A column in `notEmptiedHere` must also be named in `columns`** (#635's
   rule). `columns` says what makes the table personal; `notEmptiedHere`
   explains why a named one survives. Adding the second without the first reads
   as a stale explanation left behind by a rename, and the coverage test says
   so.
2. **An entry may not promise an action the code cannot perform** (#535). Two
   drafts said `unlink` and `erase` for tables with no account column anywhere
   on them — `tblExpenseClaimItems` and `tblReadingPlanProgress`. There is
   nothing to find the person by, so both are recorded as kept, with the truth
   in the reason: the first is detached when the claim above it is, the second
   is removed by the database along with the enrolment it hangs off.
3. **`tblErasureAudit` must NOT be in the catalogue** (#510). It is the sealed
   proof that an erasure happened, and rule 7d of the coverage test refuses any
   instruction naming it — **including a `retain` entry, because "keep this" is
   still an instruction.** A deliberate absence looks exactly like the #706
   fault, so the file now carries a comment at that spot explaining why the gap
   is intentional.

### None of the sixty-six could be reached before #709

Not one of them carries a `userID`. They are lists of kinds, settings, and
child tables keyed by a parent (`tblExpenseClaimFiles.claimID`,
`tblEventJobs.eventID`). An erasure instruction needs a person's number to
match on, so they were unreachable **by construction** rather than by
oversight — which is why nobody had written them down.

#709's parent matching changes that for some of them. **But not for
`tblExpenseClaimFiles`**, and the reason is worth keeping: its parent is
deliberately retained for HMRC, so there is no deletion to cascade and no
parent-matched clause to write. A mechanism that reaches rows through a parent
is no help when the parent is the thing being kept.

### Seven things the independent check found, and the first is the best

The package above was NOT CLEAN. Each of these is worth recognising again.

**1. A bracket-counting parser is broken by a comment — and the comment that
broke mine was about this very parser.** `catalogue_named_columns()` walked
brackets from `'tblX' => [`. `personal-data-catalogue.php` line 182 holds,
inside a comment, the text `('tblXxx' => [ \s* 'decision' => '...')` — one
unbalanced `[`. So `tblAnonymousCheckins`' "entry" ran from line 162 to line
2352: **144,494 of the file's 153,340 characters.** Its set of named columns
absorbed every other entry's `notEmptiedHere` keys, sixty of them, so a
contact-shaped column added to that table was invisible whenever its name
appeared anywhere else in the file. Proved by planting: `postcode` on
`tblAnonymousCheckins` passed while `postcode` on `tblVenueRooms` was caught,
in the same run. **This was live on the day it was written, in the guard whose
whole purpose is to close this class of gap.**

**Stripping comments first is the obvious repair and is wrong** — a reason may
legitimately contain `//`, as any URL does. The fix is to stop parsing
structure at all: entries are top-level and uniformly indented, so each runs
from its own header to the next header. Nothing inside an entry can move that
boundary.

**And my stated limit was wrong in the reassuring direction, twice.** The
docstring warned about a `]` inside a *reason string* and said "none does
today" — true, and irrelevant: the break was a `[` in a *comment*, and it was
already happening.

**2. A regex that requires the next thing after `[` misses anything with a
comment there.** `catalogue_decisions()` wanted `'decision'` after the opening
bracket with only whitespace between, so it skipped the two entries that carry
a comment explaining why their decision reads oddly. Measured: the regex saw
226 entries where PHP sees 228 — and the success line printed that wrong
number as though it were the coverage. Both readers now share one splitter.

**3. "Nothing erased them" conflated two different faults.** Of the 37 unnamed
columns, about a dozen were *already* being erased and only the written record
was missing (`git show HEAD:web/_core/GdprEraser.php` — `tblUsers`' nullCols
already held `phoneNumber` and `displayPhone`; `tblPrayerRequests`' already
held its three submitter columns). The rest are genuinely unreached. Both are
faults; one misdescribes the portal to whoever answers a request, the other
leaves personal data in place. **Overstating a fault is the direction this
project keeps calling out.**

**4. Naming a column does not put it in the copy somebody can ask for.**
`GdprEraser::inventory()` reports each table's name, row count, action and
reason — never a column's value — and it iterates instructions, so the
`not-personal` and account-less `retain` entries never appear in it at all.
Three documents claimed otherwise.

**5. A `period` field must be checked against the code that does the purging.**
`tblAssetFoundReports`' new `period` said "nothing clears it on a timer".
`AssetRegister::purgeExpiredFoundReports()` deletes past
`assets.found_report_retention_days` (default 180) and the nightly asset job
calls it. **That method's own docblock records that a note claiming the
opposite was deleted in the #569 sweep** — so this package wrote the same
untruth back, in the one field whose purpose is to let an organisation state
how long it keeps something.

**6. An issue reference must not point at the issue being closed.** Four column
reasons said "Tracked as #706". On closing #706 they would have been recorded
nowhere — the #678 rule. They now point at #715.

**7. Listing a column under an `erase` table reads as "erased", and may not
be.** `externalName` on three event tables is, by its own schema comment, the
"name if person is not a portal user" — so such a row has no account number,
the delete-where-userID-matches never touches it, and the name survives
exactly as a walk-in's does. Naming it in `columns` with no `notEmptiedHere`
said the opposite.

**What the check still cannot do, now stated in its own header:** it cannot
judge free text, it misses a `VARCHAR(10)` postcode (the text-length floor),
and `NAMED_ELSEWHERE_ON_PURPOSE` is empty so its stale-exemption clause cannot
fail today. Nothing in the repository tests the check itself — every mutation
the reviewer tried was invisible to everything but their own eye, which is the
`api-spec-check-selftest.py` shape and the obvious next thing to build.

---

## Reaching a row that nothing says is about anybody (#707)

`tblAuditTrail.userID` is the ACTOR. What was CHANGED is a pair,
`(tableName, recordID)`. There is no column saying who a row is ABOUT — so an
entry reading "somebody edited `tblUsers` id 4211" matched nothing any
instruction could look at. `Logger::audit()` records a creation as the whole
new row and a deletion as the whole old one, so a change to somebody's own
account put their name and e-mail address in there. **Measured, after an
independent check disproved a bolder first draft:** exactly two call sites audit
`tblUsers` and between them they pass `userID`, `fullName`, `emailAddress` and
three yes/no flags — no telephone, no postal address — and nothing audits a
deletion of that table at all. `Logger::audit()` records whatever the caller
hands it; it does not read the row, so "the whole row" is the caller's
convention rather than the function's promise. A name and an e-mail address is
quite enough to matter and did not need overstating.

`GdprEraser::eraseAuditTrailAboutPerson()` empties the three value columns for
such a row. Anonymise, not delete (the owner, 2 November 2026): a change
history is worth having because it shows who changed what and when, and that
survives in full.

### The shortcut reaches third parties and misses the subject

Adding `oldValue`, `newValue` and `changeSet` to the table's ordinary
instruction's `nullCols` looks like the obvious fix. **It is wrong in both
directions at once.** That instruction matches `userID` — the actor — so it
would empty the before-and-after of every change this person made to
**somebody else's** record, and still reach no row about the person
themselves. It is #709's lesson in a new table: the easy route destroys a
third party's data and does not do the job.

One check exists purely to fail if anybody takes it. Planted — swapping the
match to `userID` — it reports exactly that, by name.

### Why it is NOT in DEDICATED_STEP_TABLES, where a reader looks first

Registering a table there makes `fromPersonalDataCatalogue()` **skip** it. So
`tblAuditTrail` would have lost the instruction it already has, the one that
unlinks the actor and empties `ipAddress`. This step is additional, not a
replacement, so it is called directly from the run — exactly as
`eraseProfileImages()` is while `tblUsers` keeps its own instruction. Worth
knowing before somebody "tidies" it into the list.

### A column a dedicated step empties is recorded as emptied elsewhere

The coverage test requires a named column on an `unlink` table to be either in
the instruction's `nullCols` or explained in `notEmptiedHere`. Neither fitted
at first — the step empties it, but not through the instruction. The precedent
is `tblUsers.avatarPath`, which `eraseProfileImages()` handles: it sits in
`notEmptiedHere` with a reason beginning "Emptied elsewhere, on purpose". The
three value columns now do the same, and the reason says why the ordinary
instruction must not do it.

### The ordering trap, for the second time in two packages

Entries about the person's memberships are found by looking their
`tblUserSites` rows up, and the catalogue walk DELETES those rows. So the step
runs before the walk. Run it after and that half matches nothing while the
audit line still says the step ran — silent, and exactly #709's shape. Section
20 of the eraser test has a membership row for this, and moving the call after
the walk turns four checks red.

### Two fixture lessons, both from this section failing first

`ge_user()` does **not** create a membership row — the first version looked one
up, got nothing, wrote the audit row against record 0, and failed loudly. And
`ge_insert()` answers `{table, key}`, where the key is the row's primary key
**by name**: asking for `['id']` gave 0. Both failed noisily rather than
quietly, which is the right way round, but neither was guessable.

### Adding a step shifts every hard-coded count in the test

Six separate expectations had to move: the number of steps a run reports (twice),
the number of audit lines (twice), the list of expected lines in order, and the
position of the first instruction's line. The file keeps a running note at each
one ("CHANGED by mail package M3: + 6 became + 7"), which is what made them
findable — worth continuing.

### Three untrue statements, and the one that teaches most

The independent check of #707 found no behavioural fault — the SQL reaches
exactly the rows claimed, a probe of three collision shapes came back
untouched, and every plant was caught by the check named for it. What it found
was three **untrue statements**, which this project counts as real problems.

**1. The reason I gave for not registering the table was false, and I had
propagated it to four places.** I wrote that putting `tblAuditTrail` in
`DEDICATED_STEP_TABLES` would make `fromPersonalDataCatalogue()` skip it and
lose the instruction that unlinks the actor. It cannot: that instruction is
**hand-written**, and the deriver already skips every hand-written table
through its own `$alreadyHandled` list. The checker registered it and counted:
222 instructions before and after, same entry, same `nullCols`.

**The real reason is better because it is enforced** — with the table
registered, `gdpr-coverage-selftest.php` fails its check that a dedicated-step
table is erased, in time, *and exported*. This step empties three columns of a
**kept** row, so the constant would be claiming something untrue about it.

The lesson: **a plausible mechanism is not a measured one.** I reasoned from
reading `fromPersonalDataCatalogue()`'s skip condition without checking which
list this table was already in — and then wrote the conclusion into a docblock
and three documents, where it reads as established fact.

**2. "Telephone number and home address" was never true, and it was
pre-existing.** Exactly two call sites audit `tblUsers`, and between them they
pass `userID`, `fullName`, `emailAddress` and three yes/no flags. Nothing
audits a *deletion* of that table at all, so "the whole old row" is theoretical
for it too. `Logger::audit()` records whatever the caller hands it — it does not
read the row — so "records the whole row" is the caller's convention, not the
function's promise.

**The wording came from #706's own DEV_NOTES line, so this package propagated
it rather than inventing it** — which means the honest fix reached one line
outside the package's file list. That is declared here rather than buried.
A name and an e-mail address is quite enough to matter and did not need
overstating; the overstatement was in the one sentence a customer reads before
accepting what an erasure leaves behind, which is the #694 round-3 lesson in a
new place.

**3. "Every row about this person" was not true either.** `tblUserDepts`,
`tblUserGroups` and `tblUserRoles` are all audited and none is reached.
Measured, not argued: an audit row for a department membership was added to the
fixture and came back untouched. It costs nothing identifying today — those
payloads carry account numbers and no names (#518) and the account is emptied
by the walk — but the sentence was wrong, and the day a writer puts a name in
one of those payloads #707 returns in a table nothing covers. Tracked as #717.

### Adding a section to a self-test takes TWO registrations, and one is silent

`REQUIRED_SECTIONS` is this test's "a skipped section never reads as a pass"
guard. I added section 20 and did not add `'20'` to it — the checker spotted
that. Adding it immediately exposed a **second** omission: my section printed
its heading with a bare `echo` instead of calling `ge_section('20', …)`, so it
never registered itself as reached either.

So before the fix the section was invisible to that guard **twice over**, and
`EXPECTED_CHECKS` was the only thing standing between a deleted section and a
green run — which it would not survive, because an edit that removed the
section and put the count back would pass. Two one-line fixes; worth knowing
that the `echo` form looks exactly like the real thing.

### A clause can be harmless and still be oversold

`AND (oldValue IS NOT NULL OR …)` carried a comment saying it was what made the
count honest and a second run a no-op. The checker removed it: all 258 checks
still passed. `affected_rows` already counts only rows whose values really
changed, because the connection sets no `CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS`, so `NULL → NULL`
counts zero either way. The clause is kept — it states the intent and narrows
the UPDATE — but the comment now says what it actually earns.

## "No compression preference" means "offer everything" (#716)

CVE-2026-111497 — **HTTP2Shell**, also Node2Shell, Python2Shell and
Broccoli2Shell — is an out-of-bounds write in Google's Brotli decoder
(`c/dec/decode.c`), Brotli 1.0.3 to 1.2.0, fixed in 1.0.10, 1.1.1 and 1.2.1.
Remote, unauthenticated, CVSS 9.8, and on CISA's actively-exploited list since
27 October 2026. It needs nothing but a crafted stream being decoded.

This portal holds no Brotli code. The whole of its exposure was one line.

### The trap, which is the thing to remember

```php
CURLOPT_ENCODING => '',   // looks like "no preference"
```

An empty string tells libcurl to advertise **every** coding it was built with
— Brotli included — and libcurl then **decodes the reply itself**, inside the
web server's process, with whatever Brotli library it links. The comment beside
it said "accept every compression curl understands", which was accurate and
still did not read as a risk.

**Measured** on 2 November 2026: `curl_version()` reported `brotli/1.2.0`,
inside the affected range, with `CURL_VERSION_BROTLI` set. So the portal really
would have accepted and decoded `br` from an address somebody typed.

### Two things that looked like protection and were not

**The size cap.** Its own comment says it counts bytes *after* decompression —
so the decode has already happened by the time the limit applies. A small
crafted stream is decoded regardless. A cap on output is not a guard against a
decoder bug.

**`SafeFetch`'s other defences.** It checks addresses, refuses redirects to
private ranges, follows hops by hand. All of that is about *where* it connects;
none of it is about what the reply is decoded with.

### The first fix did not work, and this is the part to remember

`CURLOPT_ENCODING => 'gzip, deflate'` was committed as the fix (`8dc848a`) and
**still decoded Brotli.** Measured against a server that declares
`Content-Encoding: br` without being asked, on libcurl 8.22.0 / brotli 1.2.0:

| setting | bytes back | decoded? |
|---|---|---|
| option unset | 33 | **no** |
| `''` | 73 | yes |
| `'gzip, deflate'` | 73 | **yes** |
| `'gzip, deflate'` + `CURLOPT_HTTP_CONTENT_DECODING => false` | 33 | no |

**Setting the option to any non-null value switches libcurl's content decoding
on, and libcurl then picks the decoder by NAME FROM THE REPLY.** What we
advertise has nothing to do with it. The `Accept-Encoding` header is a request;
`Content-Encoding` is what actually selects the decoder.

**And the threat model is exactly the case where that matters.** These are
outside calendar feeds at addresses somebody typed — *the server is the
attacker*. "We did not ask for it" is worth nothing against somebody who sends
it anyway. The change reduced the exposure from "any server" to "a hostile
server", which for this threat is close to no reduction at all.

The paradox worth keeping: **every other curl call site in the portal was
already immune**, precisely because none of them sets the option. The one place
that had been "configured" was the only vulnerable one, and the first fix kept
it configured.

### Why the fix still belongs in our code

The portal is installed on hosting we do not control. We cannot know which
Brotli a customer's PHP links, and a version number could not tell a
vendor-patched build from an unpatched one — the rule #640 already records for
PHP. Setting nothing removes the decode path on every installation at once,
whatever the host has. **What it costs is compression on the wire**, accepted
deliberately rather than reaching for a cleverer option immediately after
getting this wrong once. If bandwidth ever matters more, switch libcurl's
decoding off and gunzip in PHP — strictly safer than either, because the size
cap would then count *compressed* bytes.

### A check can pin the wrong invariant and look thorough doing it

The first behavioural check asserted that we do not **offer** Brotli, under the
label *"so no reply is handed to the system Brotli decoder"*. The header fact
was true; the **"so" was false**. That is this repository's own "a check that
pins a reassurance" shape — the comforting half of the sentence becomes
load-bearing, and it was wrong.

The check now serves a reply that **declares** `Content-Encoding: br` without
being asked, carrying plain text, and asserts the bytes come back exactly as
sent. It needs no Brotli library to write the fixture: if decoding were on,
libcurl would try to decode that text and fail. Planted, the withdrawn
`'gzip, deflate'` **fails it** — which the old check passed.

### Two parsing faults in the guard, and the repair that broke it worse

`strip_comments()` matched patterns over raw source, so a `//` inside a string
— any URL — deleted the rest of that line, offence included. A one-line option
array with a URL in it passed while holding `CURLOPT_ENCODING => ''`. A `/*`
inside a string was worse: the block pattern spans newlines.

**Masking every string literal is the repair the repo uses elsewhere, and here
it broke both detectors**, because the thing being read *is* a string — the
option's value and the `Accept-Encoding` header both. Caught by testing
immediately, not by reading. The guard now **walks** the source and steps over
literals, which is the lesson this project already records for brace-matching.

And block comments are now replaced by their own newlines rather than deleted,
because deleting them shifted every reported line number — 666 for a fault on
line 1036, 370 out.

### What was checked and found clean

Every other curl call site leaves the encoding unset, so libcurl sends no
`Accept-Encoding` and decodes nothing — `Hymnal`, `Translation`, `WebPush` and
the rest. The `.woff2` fonts under `assets/fonts/` are decoded by the visitor's
browser. Apache's `mod_brotli` compresses what we send, which is the other
direction and not this bug.

### The part that is not the product

This workstation's Node is **v26.11.1** against a fixed **26.12.1**, and its
libcurl links the affected **brotli/1.2.0**. Both want updating; neither ships
to a customer. And **no workflow pins a Node version** — `grep -rn
"node-version\|setup-node" .github/workflows/` finds nothing — so CI uses
whatever its runner image carries, which is probably patched and is not
knowable from the repository. Left as a recorded finding on #716 rather than
changed here, because pinning CI runtimes is a decision about the build rather
than part of reviewing one CVE.

---

## Take a reserved-word list from MySQL, not from a summary of MySQL (#718)

DreamHost is moving the reference host from MySQL 8.0 to 8.4 on **9 November
2026**. Its notice — **and its help page "Using reserved words in MySQL 8"** —
say 8.4 adds four reserved words: `MANUAL`, `PARALLEL`, `QUALIFY`,
`TABLESAMPLE`, and that "queries using those names will fail".

**Only two of the four are reserved**, settled three ways rather than one. The
decisive source is the server itself, which keeps the answer in a table:

```sql
SELECT WORD, RESERVED FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.KEYWORDS
 WHERE WORD IN ('MANUAL','PARALLEL','QUALIFY','TABLESAMPLE','FULLTEXT','RANK','STATUS');
```

On a real 8.4.13: `FULLTEXT` 1, `QUALIFY` 1, `RANK` 1, `TABLESAMPLE` 1,
**`MANUAL` 0, `PARALLEL` 0**, `STATUS` 0. MySQL's published keyword list agrees,
and so does a parse test — each word given a column and then referenced bare,
with a control to prove the test could tell the difference:

| word | bare reference on 8.4.13 |
|---|---|
| `manual` | works — not reserved |
| `parallel` | works — not reserved |
| `qualify` | **fails** |
| `tablesample` | **fails** |
| `fulltext` | fails — the word behind #276 |
| `rank`, `system` | fail |
| `status` | works — the control |

`manual` and `parallel` are keywords in 8.4 but **non-reserved**, so they are
legal identifiers unquoted. Had the guard been built from the host's wording it
would have failed on a column named `manual` — a thoroughly plausible name —
for no reason, which is #483's rule: a check that cries wolf gets switched off,
and then it catches nothing.

**The durable lesson: when a hosting company and the database disagree about
the database, ask the database.** The documentation was wrong in two separate
places, including the page a developer would go to on purpose. The server's own
`INFORMATION_SCHEMA.KEYWORDS` cannot be stale, and the check records the query
so the list can be regenerated rather than copied.

**None of the four appears in this schema, the migrations or the PHP**, so the
upgrade itself needs nothing from us. The value of the work was the guard.

### What the guard actually asks

Exactly **one** identifier in 229 tables is a reserved word:
`tblTranscript.fullText`, which is `FULLTEXT`. That is #276's column, and every
reference to it today is already backticked or qualified (`t.fullText`) — both
work, because after a dot a reserved word is allowed as an identifier.

So the check has two halves: every reserved identifier in `full_schema.sql`
must be a recorded decision in `RESERVED_ON_PURPOSE` (failing both ways, so a
stale entry is also an error), and every reference to a listed one must be
quoted or qualified. Planted, it catches the original `fullText = ?`.

### Two rules that had to be narrowed, both for the same reason

**An alias rule was written and deleted.** `... AS rank` is the same parse
error by another route, so it looked worth catching. But `AS <word>` cannot be
told from English: "as long as", "as not", "as if", "as is", "as with" all
matched, in help pages and comments — and `CAST(x AS BINARY)` is perfectly
valid SQL that it also flagged. Fifteen reports, not one real. Deleting the
rule is the right answer, not a gap: an alias colliding with a reserved word is
far rarer than a column doing so, which is the fault this exists for.

**"Does this string look like SQL" had to be much stricter.** The first version
asked whether the text contained any of select/insert/update/set/where/from —
which is ordinary English, and matched prose throughout the help pages. The
reliable discriminator in this codebase is the table naming: every table is
`tbl` followed by a capital. A string either names one or begins with a SQL
verb; prose does neither.

**What that costs, stated rather than hidden:** a continuation fragment like
`. 'fullText = ? '` on its own would be missed. In the real fault the bare
reference sat in the same string as `UPDATE tblTranscript SET`, which the check
does see.

### What needed no change

The MySQL 8.0 end-of-life warning the owner asked for already existed, from
#489/#640: `DbServer` classifies 8.0 as "works, but no longer getting security
fixes" and 8.4 as supported, and four callers display it — the installer, the
admin dashboard, Server Information and the health probes. The end-to-end
migration harness already runs against 8.4.11. **Checking before building was
the whole of the work there.**

## When the honest write-up is "nothing writes this", drop the column (#708, migration 235)

`tblAssetStocktakes.notes` and `tblAssetStocktakeItems.notes` were dropped on
2 November 2026. They had been there since the stocktake tables were created
(`4764c06`, Asset Tracker Phase 3), and nothing had ever written to either.

**The interesting part is not the columns; it is how they were found.** Both
columns had an entry in `web/_core/personal-data-catalogue.php` from the day that
file was created (`7a0f203`), and **#635** (`17dce1b`) then required every named
column to carry a written reason. Writing an honest one meant writing, twice, a
paragraph on why a note
that nobody can type is nevertheless kept rather than emptied when somebody asks
to be forgotten. That paragraph is true and useless, and it has a cost: the file
a data subject's request is answered from reads as though the portal held two
more kinds of personal information than it does, which makes the erasure
coverage look **wider** than it is.

So the rule worth keeping: **if the only honest thing you can write about a
column is that nothing writes it, the change is to drop the column, not to write
the paragraph.** A catalogue entry is an instruction about something real.

**How to establish "nothing writes it" — and this is where the real lesson is,
because every attempt at the evidence before this one was wrong, each in its own
way. Four of them are set out below; no count is given in this sentence, because
a draft said "three" above a list of four.** The standing rule says a claim about history carries the command that
proved it. The command has to be one that *could* have shown the opposite.

It takes TWO commands, and the second exists because the first has a blind
spot that a draft of this section papered over with a false claim:

```
# 1. Every statement ever written against either table, anywhere, any quoting
#    style. No path filter; the table name need not follow the verb.
git log --all -p | grep "^+" | grep -i tblAssetStocktake \
  | grep -Ei "insert|update|replace|load data" \
  | sed 's/^+[[:space:]]*//' | sort -u
      -> five statements, across every commit; not one names `notes`.

# 2. Command 1 prints only the LINE carrying the table name, and this codebase
#    builds SQL by concatenating strings, so a SET or ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE
#    clause on a later line is INVISIBLE to it. Ask after the COLUMN instead:
git log --all -p -- web/_core/AssetRegister.php \
  | grep "^+" | grep -w "notes" | sed 's/^+[[:space:]]*//' | sort -u
      -> every line belongs to tblAssetOrgs, an assignment, a kit loan or a
         licence seat. None belongs to a stocktake table.
```

**A draft of command 1 was narrower still** - it required `INSERT INTO` and the
like immediately followed by the BARE table name, under `web/` - and was
therefore blind to the backticked FORM, which is how the rest of `web/_sql/`
is written, and to any writer outside `web/`. (Said as a form and not as a
statement on purpose: `web/_sql/` contains no stocktake INSERT in any style, so
a reader told to look for a backticked one would go hunting for nothing — in the
section whose whole subject is evidence that looks like proof and is not.)

**And the draft justified skipping command 2 with a claim about MySQL that is
simply false:** that `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` "can only name a column the
INSERT list already holds". Measured on a real MySQL 8.0.36, that clause assigns
to **any** column of the table, and a `notes = 'x'` in it really does write a
column absent from the INSERT list. The true statement is about this code and
not about MySQL: *in that upsert as written* the clause names only the four
columns the INSERT list holds. **A false general rule that makes a gap
"harmless by construction" is the most dangerous kind of comment**, because it
stops anybody looking at the gap again.

Three searches that look like proof and are not:

```
git log -S"notes" -- web/_apps/assets/
    Returns the Phase 1 and Phase 2 commits, which predate these tables and are
    about tblAssets.notes - a DIFFERENT column. Match the search to the column,
    not to the word.

git log -S"tblAssetStocktake" -- web/
    BLIND to the very edit being ruled out. -S watches how many times a string
    occurs; adding `notes` to an existing INSERT does not change how many times
    the TABLE NAME occurs, so the count never moves. This was cited as evidence
    in a draft of the migration header.

grep -n "notes" <the stocktake block of AssetRegister.php>
    True - the word is absent - but the conclusion drawn from it ("so nothing
    reads them either") was FALSE. Three of those queries select `st.*` or
    `i.*`, and a wildcard is a SELECT list that names no column, so both values
    really were read back on every call. "The column name is not in a SELECT
    list" does not establish "nothing reads it" in a codebase that uses
    `alias.*`. An independent check caught this one.
```

What actually makes the drop safe on the read side is that nothing **consumed**
the values: the three stocktake pages contain no occurrence of "note", none of
them walks a row's keys generically (no `foreach ($row`, no `array_keys()`, no
`json_encode()` of a whole row), and the scan handler builds its reply field by
field. The wildcards fetched two values and threw them away.

**Two things the drop needed besides the schema and the migration.** The
catalogue entries had to lose the `notes` key from `columns` **and** from
`notEmptiedHere` in the same edit — `gdpr-coverage-selftest.php` fails on an
explanation for a column the entry does not name (#635) and on a named column
the database does not have. And both columns go on `DbBackup::REMOVED_COLUMNS`,
or a snapshot taken before the migration is refused with "Unknown column" by a
database that has run it. That refusal is deliberate for a column nobody has
written down; the list is how a removal somebody thought about is let through.

**BOTH catalogue entries were wrong in the same way, in two sizes, and the
bigger one is the one I nearly left out of this note.**

- `tblAssetStocktakes` named `startedByID` and not `closedByID`, although a run
  records both people and the erasure routine detaches both — so the entry read
  as though the second were somebody else's business. **Half** of what it acts
  on.
- `tblAssetStocktakeItems` named **nothing** it acts on. Its only named column
  was the dead `notes`, so an entry whose decision is "unlink" named no account
  column at all. `scannedByID` was ADDED by this edit, not left behind by it;
  `git show HEAD:web/_core/personal-data-catalogue.php` is where that is visible.

An entry that names half of what it acts on, or none of it, is the same shape as
one that names a column nothing writes: the list and the behaviour have to agree
in both directions. A first draft of this section recorded only the first of the
two and called it "one thing" — understating the lesson in the very place the
lesson is kept, which an independent check caught.

## `is_file()` is true for an empty file, and two permission facts (#711)

`Pdf::create()` decided a write had worked by asking `is_file()`. It is true for
a file that exists and holds nothing, which is precisely what a failed write
leaves behind — so a truncated giving statement was served as a finished one and
nothing recorded a problem. **Compare the byte count:**
`file_put_contents($path, $bytes) !== strlen($bytes)`. The house pattern already
existed — `DbBackup::snapshot()` compares it inline, and so do the installer's
three writers (`install_common.php`, `index.php`'s `installWriteFile()`,
`owner_code.php`) — and this one place did not follow it. (A draft of this
paragraph credited a `DbBackup::writeManifest()` method, which does not exist,
and said "two". Name a method only after opening the file it is in.)

**THE FIRST FIX WAS WORSE THAN THE FAULT, and that is the most useful thing
here.** It wrote straight to the real path and, when the write failed, deleted
whatever was there. But `file_put_contents()` can fail at **open** — the target
file read-only, a read-only mount, the name taken by a directory — and then the
existing contents are untouched. Deleting them turned a working, if stale, PDF
into nothing, while the database row went on naming it: a broken download link
where a moment earlier there had been a working one. These paths use STABLE
names (`_uploads/pdfs/claim_<id>.pdf`, recorded in `tblExpenseClaims.fileName`
and in the HMRC-retained `tblExpenseClaimFiles`), so the damage persisted.

**Write under a temporary name in the same folder and rename into place.** The
real file is replaced only once a complete one exists, in one step, and any
failure leaves what was there exactly as it was. The folder matters: `rename()`
is atomic only within one filesystem. `DbBackup::snapshot()` writes its manifest
this way and its comment gives the same reason — the pattern was two files away
from the code being fixed.

**And the message has to be as careful as the code.** The first version said
"the part-written file was removed" whenever a boolean
`is_file($p) === false || unlink($p) === true` came out true — which conflates
"there was nothing to remove" with "I removed something". A write that failed at
open told the administrator, in `tblErrors`, that a stub had been tidied away
that never existed. Saying nothing is the honest answer when nothing happened.

Three more things from fixing it that generalise.

**1. Hold the bytes in a variable.** Calling the renderer inside the
`file_put_contents()` arguments and again for `strlen()` renders the document
twice and compares the length of the second rendering against the bytes of the
first. For a PDF those differ, because it carries its own creation timestamp.

**2. "Did my `mkdir()` win?" is the wrong question; "is the folder there?" is the
right one.** Two requests can make the same folder at once and the loser gets
`false` for a folder that now exists and is perfectly usable. Report the failure
where it happens, too: the old code let an unmakeable folder fall through to the
write, which then failed and blamed the write.

**3. WRITING TO A FILE THAT ALREADY EXISTS NEEDS PERMISSION ON THE FILE, NOT ON
THE FOLDER — and I got caught by this TWICE, the second time in the fixture
written to guard the first.** A folder's permissions decide only whether a name
may be created or removed in it; an existing file's own mode decides whether it
may be written.

- First time: a fixture meant to show a file existing while nothing was written
  made the FOLDER read-only and put an empty file in it. The write succeeded.
  The check went red and caught it.
- **Second time, and this is the one worth the space.** The regression test for
  the deleted-PDF fault used that same read-only-FOLDER fixture. So the write
  SUCCEEDED there too, and the one check that names the harm — "the file that
  was there is still there" — could never go red; in that fixture nothing can
  delete the file either, because `unlink()` needs the folder. An independent
  check measured the consequence: adding ONE line, `@unlink($filePath);`, to the
  failure branch put the whole original fault back **with every check green**.

The fixture that works needs the write to fail in a **WRITABLE** folder, and
there is a way that needs no root, no quota and no special filesystem: give the
file a basename long enough that the writer's 18-byte `.part-…` suffix crosses
the limit on a name. The real file is created perfectly well and only the
temporary one is refused — the same class of failure as a full disk, where the
open never succeeds. With that fixture the plant above goes red, naming the harm:
"now GONE - DESTROYED bytes, was 57".

**The general lesson, which is not about permissions at all: a regression test
must reproduce the MEASURED fault, not a cousin of it.** Both fixtures look like
"a write that fails with a file already there". Only one of them is.

**And the reason the write path answers a REASON rather than logging** is so that
it can be tested at all: logging needs a database and a request, and dompdf is
not in this repository (`_libraries/` is never committed), so a test that had to
render could not run on this machine or on any runner. The rendered bytes arrive
as an argument and the caller turns the reason into the log line — the same shape
as `ExpenseRules::whyNotEditable()`, and for the same reason.

**IT STILL TAKES TWO GUARDS, and the measurement is the point.** No test on this
machine can force a genuine short write — the open succeeding and the disk
filling part way through — without a quota or a tiny filesystem. Every write
that fails in the self-test fails outright. Measured, with the writer written in
place: replacing the byte comparison with "did anything get written" left EVERY
check in that test green. So `tools/audit-checks/check_pdf_write_verified.py`
pins the whole condition, and the self-test proves the behaviour the filesystem
can actually be made to show. Neither catches the other's half (#646).

**AND PINNING THE COMPARISON WAS NOT ENOUGH, which is #709's lesson arriving in
a new file.** Measured in round 2: `if (false && $whyNot !== '')` at the call
site, and deleting the call while leaving the method intact, EACH left all 23
self-test checks and the whole audit check green — with `create()` handing back
the path of a PDF that was never written. The self-test reaches the writer by
reflection and never goes through `create()`, so it cannot see either. **When you
pin a call, pin the gate that decides whether its block is entered at all.** The
check now pins `$whyNot = self::writeOrWhyNot(...)` adjacent to exactly
`if ($whyNot !== '') {}`. Round 2 also found a **commented-out** copy of the
pinned temporary-name line satisfied the check, because that one branch read the
raw file rather than the stripped source — #569's fault, in a check written with
#569 in mind.

**Finally, one of the same shape is still live elsewhere**, found while checking
this and raised rather than fixed as **#720**: `web/_apps/documents/api/create.php`
accepts `file_put_contents(...) !== false` for an uploaded document, so a
truncated file is recorded as stored. The audit check above is deliberately scoped to
`Pdf.php` rather than widened to catch it, because "a write whose count is not
compared" matches a great deal of harmless code and a check that cries wolf gets
switched off (#483).

## A fingerprint is enough for a limit, and nothing was clearing the log (#712, migration 236)

Two rate-limit tables held a network address unchanged and neither was ever
cleared out. The interesting parts are why it survived so long and what it took
to guard.

**Nothing failed while it was there.** Every page worked, both limits worked, and
the rows simply accumulated. There is no symptom to notice, which is why this is
guarded by reading the code rather than by a test alone.

**A limit only needs a STABLE value, never a readable one.** The throttle has to
recognise the same client coming back after it cycles session tokens; it never
has to know the address. So a fingerprint does the job exactly as well.

Counted rather than asserted, because a draft of this said "three buckets
already hashed" and it was wrong twice. SIX buckets were built from an address.
TWO used it raw — the two-factor code check, which paired it with an ACCOUNT
NUMBER and so made the row a record of which person signed in from where, and
the push sign-up. The other FOUR hashed it (`forms:public-submit`, both
password-reset buckets, `attend:save:`) — and that was not the same as being
safe, which is the next lesson.

**Hashing was only half of it.** `RateLimiter::recordHit()` takes an optional
family prefix, and without one the opportunistic tidy-up matches only the exact
bucket again. A one-off code check or a single push sign-up never produces a
second hit, so those rows were never tidied at all. **A clear-out that only
reaches rows something touches twice does not reach the rows that matter most.**

**`tblLiveRateLimits` had no clear-out of any kind** — no `DELETE` under `web/`,
no foreign key that could cascade in, no scheduled job, no admin page — under an
index named `idx_ratelimit_prune`. And `recordSend()`'s docblock said pruning
"is done incidentally (next call rolls forward via the time window)". The window
only narrows the COUNT. The #645 shape again: a comment stating the guarantee the
code forgot to implement.

**Rename the column, do not just widen it.** `tblLiveChatMessages` has its own
`senderIP`, and that one stays RAW on purpose for the moderation screen. Two
columns of one name in one feature, one to be hashed and one not, is how the
wrong one gets changed. They have different names now, and the index was renamed
too: an index named for an address, on a column that no longer holds one, is a
small lie that outlives everybody who knew better.

**TWO STRING-MASKING TRAPS IN ONE CHECK, and they pull in opposite directions.**
The house remedy for a check that must not be fooled by comments is to blank
comments *and* string contents. But:

- A pin on a LITERAL cannot use the masked source. `hash('sha256', $ip)` becomes
  `hash('xxxxxx', $ip)`, so the pin can never match. Reading the raw file instead
  is the other mistake, because a commented-out copy then satisfies it (#569).
  The answer is a third form: strip comments, keep strings.
- A check for a COLUMN NAME in SQL cannot use the masked source either, because
  the name lives inside the string. Planted, a check for `senderIP` beside
  `tblLiveRateLimits` missed an `INSERT` naming the old column, because both
  words had been masked away.

So which stripper to use is a per-check decision, not a house default, and
getting it wrong fails silently in the green direction both times.

**One more, about judging by file:** the column-name check had to be narrowed to
one statement's worth of text, because `senderIP` is still legitimate on another
table and the personal-data catalogue names both tables in one file. A whole-file
test would have reported that for ever, and a check that cries wolf gets switched
off (#483).

**AND THE PLAIN SHA-256 WAS THE WRONG CALL, measured rather than argued (#712
round 1).** The first version hashed with `hash('sha256', $ip)` and defended it
with `Logger::sessionFingerprint()`'s reasoning (#622). Both halves of that
defence were wrong:

- **An address is 32 bits.** This machine computes about 4.87 million SHA-256 a
  second in single-threaded PHP, so the entire IPv4 space takes roughly fifteen
  minutes. The independent checker recovered a stored value back to
  `192.0.2.44` in under a second by walking one `/8`. A session identifier has
  around 128 bits, which is why #622's plain hash really is one-way. **Citing a
  precedent means checking the thing that made it work carries across.**
- **#622's stated reason did not apply at all.** It keeps a plain hash because
  its clean-out must recompute the same value *in SQL*. This clean-out is
  `createdAt < NOW() - INTERVAL ? SECOND` — purely time-based — and every
  comparison happens in PHP. There was no constraint to honour, so the weaker
  form bought nothing whatever.

`AssetRegister::saltedHash()` had salted an address with the installation's key
since #410, for exactly this purpose, and the first version neither used it nor
mentioned it. `Portal\Core\AddressFingerprint` is now the one place; Asset
Register deliberately keeps its own copy, because its stored hashes are already
on disk and its comment promises they are bit-identical to the pre-#410 values.

**The salt's value is specific and worth stating:** the key is not in the
database, so a database copy — a backup, a dump, a stolen table — no longer
says which addresses the portal has seen. Whoever has the key *and* a candidate
list can still test it. That is why this is a fingerprint and not anonymity.

**Three more things that round found, each one a shape to recognise.**

1. **The hard gate passed the real pre-fix file.** It required the literal
   `clientIp()` inside the bucket assignment; the live code was
   `$clientIp = RateLimiter::clientIp();` then `$rlBucket = 'pushsub:' . $clientIp;`.
   Proved by `git show HEAD:<file> > <file>` and watching the check exit 0.
   **A guard written against the fixed code can miss the shape the fault
   actually had** — test it by restoring the real broken file, not by inventing
   a plant. It follows one hop through a local now.
2. **A check that could not fail, again.** The prune test asked "are any recent
   rows left?" while every row in its fixture was seconds old, so no positive
   horizon could ever remove one. A prune set to wipe the whole throttle log
   passed 15 of 15, three runs running. **Plant rows either side of the horizon**
   — one that must go, one that must survive — rather than asking a question the
   fixture cannot answer.
3. **A removed column has to join `DbBackup::REMOVED_COLUMNS` or a restore
   STOPS.** Not degrades: the unknown column reaches the `INSERT`, `loadTable()`
   throws, and the whole restore ends. This rule was applied correctly two
   entries above in the same session and forgotten here, which is why it is
   written down rather than remembered.

**And one untrue comment with a real consequence.** The prune was guarded by
`if ($prune === false) { return; }` under a comment claiming it failed open.
Under `MYSQLI_REPORT_STRICT | MYSQLI_REPORT_ERROR` — which `DbServer::connect()`
sets — both `prepare()` and `execute()` **throw**, and `@` suppresses a
diagnostic, not an exception. Both measured. So the guard could not fire, and
`recordSend()` is called *after* the chat message is inserted and *before* the
success answer: a lock-wait timeout on the new 500-row `DELETE`, the realistic
failure on a busy chat and one this tidy-up itself introduced, would have given
the viewer a bare 500 with their message already saved. **Failing open takes a
`try`/`catch`; `@` is not a substitute and neither is a `=== false` test.**

**AND THE WHOLE SUITE CAUGHT TWO REGRESSIONS THE PACKAGE'S OWN TESTS COULD
NOT**, which is the clearest argument yet for running all of it rather than the
tests that look related (#695).

**1. A test kept its own copy of the rule — in the very file that lesson came
from.** `tools/sign-in-limits-selftest.php` had:

```php
function bucket(string $kind, string $ip): string
{
    return 'pwreset:' . $kind . ':' . hash('sha256', $ip);
}
```

a second copy of how the two password-reset handlers build their bucket. When
#712 salted those handlers, the test went on computing the old value and **eight
checks failed, every one of them about throttling and not one about anything
that had broken.** This repository already records the remedy, from the
password-reset page: *ask the portal's own function; never keep a second copy of
the rule in a test.* It asks `AddressFingerprint::of()` now.

Two things followed that are worth knowing:

- **The salt has to be the same one the server uses.** That test copies `web/`
  to a scratch tree and writes a NEW RANDOM `enc.key` into it, so the test
  process must point `PORTAL_ROOT` at the scratch tree. Point it at the
  repository and every bucket name differs from the server's — a whole class of
  failure that looks exactly like broken throttling.
- **Its clean-up could no longer work by exact name, and never could have.**
  `removeWorld()` deleted 254 addresses' two buckets each, by name — but with a
  new random key every run, an exact name cannot match a row an EARLIER run left
  behind, which is the only thing a clean-up is for. It ran before the scratch
  copy existed, so there was no key to salt with either. It deletes by the
  `pwreset:` prefix now, which needs no key at all.

**2. A test that loads classes by hand has to load what its dependencies
need.** `tools/gdpr-eraser-selftest.php` requires `_apps/cron/_retention-sweep.php`
directly, with no autoloader. #713 made that sweep ask `WebhookRetention`, so the
whole run stopped at the first line mentioning it — and adding that class alone
was not enough, because `SettingLimit` needs `InstallationSettings`. **Requiring
a file by hand means owning its whole dependency chain, in order.**

Neither fault could have been found by the tests for the package that caused
them: both live in other tests, and both were green before.

## Two columns of one name, and a reserved word in a fixture (#714)

Two mistakes while fixing #714, both more useful than the fix.

**I RENAMED THE WRONG TABLE'S COLUMN.** `tblExpenseClaimFiles` and `tblPhoto`
both have an `originalFilename`, and a search-and-replace matched the photo one.
Their declarations were in fact distinguishable — one carries
`COLLATE utf8mb4_general_ci`, the other does not — but **the search matched on
the column NAME, where they are identical**, so the difference never came into
it. (A first version of this note said they "differ only in whitespace". An
independent check measured that false. It matters because the stated difference
was the whole evidence for how the mistake happened.) `tblPhoto`'s **keeps its
meaning**: `_apps/photos/serve-raw.php` hands it back as the download name, so a
visitor gets the file called what it was called.

`gdpr-coverage-selftest.php` caught the half that mattered to it
(`tblExpenseClaimFiles.fileLabel` does not exist) within seconds. **Nothing would
have caught the other half** — three working photo pages reading a column that
no longer existed — until somebody opened one.

This is the same conflation migration 236 was written to prevent **one package
earlier**, where `tblLiveRateLimits.senderIP` and `tblLiveChatMessages.senderIP`
had to be told apart and one had to stay raw. Writing that lesson down did not
stop me repeating it an hour later. The practical rule: **when a column name
appears in more than one table, confirm which table a match landed in before
replacing anything** — `awk '/CREATE TABLE .*`tblX`/,/ENGINE=/'` answers it, and
`git diff` on the schema afterwards shows exactly which declaration moved.

**AND I WROTE A BARE `fullText` IN A FIXTURE.** `fullText` IS the reserved word
`FULLTEXT` — MySQL ignores case in keywords — so the statement does not parse.
That is #276: the fault that shipped a statement unable to save a transcript,
throwing *after* the outside provider had been called and charged. I wrote it in
the same session as the guard for it, and the test died on its own fixture.

**`check_reserved_words_quoted.py` could not see it, because it read only
`web/`.** It reads `tools/` too now. The reasoning for the widening is narrow and
worth keeping: a self-test writes SQL **by hand against the real schema**, so a
bare reserved word there fails exactly as it fails in the portal, and the
standing rule ("backtick every identifier in hand-written SQL") was never
qualified by which directory the SQL lives in. Planted at the line it missed, the
widened check names it.

The general shape: **a guard's SCOPE is as much a part of it as its rule.** This
one had the right rule and the wrong reach, and the proof is that it passed the
exact identifier it exists for.

## Closing a request nobody can finish (#710)

#709 left a request that could reach no final state: one step refused for ever
and correctly, `execute()` closes only when nothing failed, and cancelling was
refused because earlier steps really had changed records. Three things from
building the way out.

**ASKING "COULD A STEP REFUSE FOR EVER?" IS THE WRONG QUESTION, even answered
correctly.** It says nothing about whether some *other* step still has work left,
so a close based on it would close a request with real work outstanding. The
design that works is blunter: **run the request one final time and close only if
every single failure of that run is permanent.** You cannot close by hand without
the portal having just tried everything it can, and there is no force-close.

**DO NOT RECOGNISE THE REFUSAL BY ITS WORDS.** Reading the audit trail for the
refusal's sentence finds a line from an *older* run too, and would then offer to
close a request whose latest run failed for a quite different reason. The branch
that produces the permanent refusal records the step in a run-scoped list
instead — emptied at the start of every run, the way `$dueAtErasure` is — and
`execute()` reports it. The comparison is then `count($hand) === $failed`, which
is a fact about the run that just happened.

**THE RECORD HAS TO BE UNAVOIDABLE, NOT ENCOURAGED.** The risk is a button that
closes any request nobody has acted on. So `closeRequest()` stays private and
`finishByHand()` is the only other route to it, and the audit line and the close
are written **in one transaction**.

**That last part was a claim before it was a fact.** The line was written before
`closeRequest()` opened its transaction, so it committed immediately — and that
method throws deliberately when a transaction cannot be started or committed. On
that path the sealed trail permanently said "closed after work done outside the
portal" about a request still at `pending_review`, and a second press wrote a
second such line. Three places asserted there was no route to one without the
other; an independent check found the route. **Writing the line first is the
right order; claiming atomicity it did not have was the problem.** The facts are
passed in and the line is written inside the transaction now. And **there is no
free-text box on purpose** — asking an administrator to describe what they did by
hand invites them to describe what they did to a safeguarding note, which would
write that note's content into `tblErasureAudit`, a table deliberately absent
from the personal-data catalogue and never erased. The line is composed from
facts the portal already holds.

**One more thing it forced:** `closeRequest()`'s own audit line said "All N steps
ran and none failed" unconditionally. For a close after hand work that is a plain
untruth, in the one record nobody can correct afterwards. It takes the fact as an
argument now and says which it is.

**And a fixture lesson, because the test passed for the wrong reason first.** The
decisive case needs a SECOND, recoverable failure beside the permanent one. My
first version gave the extra row `startedByID`, where the column is
`triggeredByID` — so the row belonged to nobody, that step matched nothing, the
extra failure never happened, and the check went **green reporting
"closed-by-hand"**, which is exactly what it exists to forbid. A fixture that
cannot produce the condition makes the check agree with the fault. The catalogue
entry names the column; read it rather than guessing.

## A hard-coded list has to be checked against the thing it describes (#719)

`check_reserved_words_quoted.py` carries MySQL's reserved words in code, because
an audit script must run with no database — that is what lets the pre-push hook
run every one of them in about nine seconds. The price is that the list goes stale
silently, and the reserved set moves: 8.4 added `QUALIFY` and `TABLESAMPLE` to
8.0's.

**It was already behind, on both engines, and the verification found that on its
first run.** MySQL 8.0.36 reserves `master_bind` and
`master_ssl_verify_server_cert`, which the list did not carry. MariaDB 11.4
reserves seventeen more — `offset` and `returning` among them, both thoroughly
plausible column names. None of the schema's 1,170 distinct column names is any
of the nineteen, so nothing was broken; **that was luck, not coverage**, and the
difference is the whole reason to measure.

**THE TWO DIRECTIONS ARE NOT THE SAME, AND ONLY ONE MAY FAIL.**

- The server reserves a word the list lacks → the check **cannot catch** a bare
  reference to it, which will then fail to parse on a customer's database. FAIL.
- The list carries a word the server does not reserve → the list is
  conservative, which is **safe**, and happens in both directions as versions
  move. REPORT.

Failing the second direction would mean the test could not run on both MySQL
versions this portal supports — and a test that cannot run is not a guard.

**The list is the union of both engines**, deliberately. The check runs with no
database, so it cannot know which engine a customer has; asking for a backtick
on a word that is legal on the engine in front of it costs nothing, because a
backtick is never wrong. A per-engine list would need the check to choose, which
is exactly what it cannot do.

**MariaDB cannot be asked, so it is tried.** Its `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.KEYWORDS`
has a `WORD` column only, no `RESERVED` flag, and **membership does not mean
reserved**: `FULLTEXT`, `STATUS` and `WINDOW` are all listed, yet only
`FULLTEXT` fails as a bare identifier. So on MariaDB each candidate is used as a
column name in a temporary table. Slower, and the only thing that answers the
question.

**Two details that make it a guard rather than a guard-shaped object.** It reads
the word list **out of the audit script** rather than keeping its own copy —
two copies would agree with each other and with nothing else. And it verifies
its own probe: a bare `fullText` must be refused and a backticked one accepted,
because if the probe stopped working the whole comparison would be measuring
nothing and still passing.

**Where it runs is the design.** A self-test on one version would have found the
8.0 words and missed MariaDB's seventeen entirely. It is wired into
`portal-selftests.yml` (a matrix over 8.0.36 and 8.4.11) and into
`calendar-selftests.yml`, which is the one matrix here that runs self-tests on
all three engines. **Wiring decides what a test can see.**

## Fifteen free-text columns, fifteen decisions (#715)

The useful thing here is not which columns were emptied. It is that **one
decision for all of them would have been wrong whichever way it went**, and the
four groups that fell out are worth recognising next time.

1. **The person's own words, where the row keeps its value without them** —
   emptied. A prayer request's subject and body, a pastoral case summary, a
   prayer partner's note about the person. The request still shows one was made
   and answered; the case still shows care was given.
2. **Text that belongs to the organisation rather than to the person** — kept. A
   presenter's name typed by hand, a licence seat's device label, a group's
   meeting notes.
3. **Text that expires anyway** — kept, because `tblErrors` already has a
   retention rule and the sweep deletes the whole row. Nobody intends an error
   trace to hold a name; it holds one only when a fault quotes a value.
4. **Text nothing can reach** — recorded. A salvation card's prayer request has
   no account link to its subject at all.

**THE HALF-MEASURE IS WHAT GAVE THE FIRST GROUP AWAY.** The portal already
emptied a prayer request's submitter name, e-mail and network address from the
very same row and left what they had said. Look for that shape: a row where some
personal columns are emptied and an adjacent free-text one is not usually means
nobody decided about the text, rather than that somebody decided to keep it.

**AND AN EXPLANATION CAN CONTAIN ITS OWN REFUTATION.** `tblCareCase.summary`'s
catalogue note read: *"The notes of the visits on the case ARE emptied … this
summary is not, so it can still describe them."* That is the argument against
itself, written down and left for a year. When a reason has to describe the
inconsistency to explain itself, the reason is the problem.

**MATCH ON THE SUBJECT'S COLUMN, NEVER ON AN ACTOR'S.** A prayer request has
three instructions — submitter, moderator, assignee. Only the submitter's
empties text. Emptying on the moderator's would destroy somebody else's request
because the person who moderated it left: #709's lesson, in a table #709 never
touched.

**AND SOMETIMES THE GUARD SAYS NO AND IS RIGHT TO.** A room booking's `purpose`
should be emptied by this decision and is not, because `bookedByID` is in
`ACTOR_COLUMNS` and the coverage test refuses `nullCols` there — emptying on an
actor-matched instruction is a blanket `= NULL` over every matched row. For
*this* table the emptying really would be correct, because every row it matches
is the booker's own, and `ACTOR_COLUMNS`' own docblock names `approvedByID`
rather than `bookedByID` as its example. **The right response was to record the
limit and raise the classification as its own question (#723), not to weaken the
guard on my own judgement** — that guard exists because seven tables were once
set to delete a whole row on such a column.

**Finally: "Tracked as #715" is not a decision.** Three explanations still said
it. To the next reader, a record saying somebody will decide later looks exactly
like a record nobody has looked at (#678).

## What the independent check of #710, #715 and #719 found (3 November 2026)

Ten real problems. Three of them are shapes worth recognising, and all three
have happened in this repository before.

**1. A reassuring paragraph was wrong in the one direction that breaks a page.**
Migration 240's header said "every reader prints the column through
`htmlspecialchars((string) …)`, so a NULL shows as an empty string rather than
throwing". `web/_apps/prayer-requests/index.php` printed `$req['subject']` with
**no cast**, twice. Under `declare(strict_types=1)` that is
`TypeError: htmlspecialchars(): Argument #1 ($string) must be of type string,
null given`, and the congregation feed's query filters on site, kind, visibility
and status — **not on submitter** — so an erased person's congregation-visible
request stays in the list and the page really would have met a NULL. The failure
is the quiet kind: the page throws mid-render, the error handler prints the
footer, and the answer is an HTTP 200 ending in an ordinary `</html>` with the
feed missing. `php -l` cannot see it. The same paragraph said there were three
