writers; there are five (`prayer-requests/save.php`,
`prayer-requests/anonymous-save.php`, `prayer-requests/api/create.php`,
`praise/new.php` — a praise report is a row in the same table — and
`care/case-save.php`).

**Establish both halves by reading, one at a time.** Writers:
`grep -rn "INSERT INTO tblPrayerRequests\|INSERT INTO tblCareCase" web/_apps web/_core`.
Readers: `grep -rn --include='*.php' -e "\['subject'\]" … web/_apps web/_core | grep -v '(string)'`
— the `grep -v` is the whole point, because a cast reader is not the question.

**2. The behavioural pin existed, was written for exactly this, and was not
updated.** `MUST_BE_EMPTIED` in `tools/gdpr-eraser-selftest.php` lists, by name,
the columns an instruction must empty, and is kept separate from the
instructions on purpose — its own comment records that an earlier independent
check planted a column quietly dropped from an instruction's list and the test
passed, because the rest of the file works out what to expect from the
instruction itself. #715 added four columns to two instructions and not to that
list. The checker then dropped `body` and `summary` again, each with a plausible
catalogue excuse, and **everything stayed green**: 263 eraser checks, 93
coverage checks, `check_erasure_columns_nullable.py`,
`check_personal_data_coverage.py`. One static check caught a *partial* revert.
Nothing read the columns back out of a database.

**3. A fixture in which a guard's condition can never be true cannot test the
guard.** `closeRequest()` leaves the administrator's account number out of
`tblErasureAudit` when the request is their own, because that table is
deliberately absent from the personal-data catalogue (#510 rule 7d) and is never
erased — writing the number would undo the erasure permanently. Removing the
guard left all 263 checks green: every case in section 21 used an `ADMIN` who
was never the person being erased. Case D exists only to make the condition
reachable, and it checks **both** halves — the number must be absent AND the line
must still record the hand work, so a guard that stopped writing the line at all
would not pass.

### And a check can pin one SPELLING of a write

Section 22 of `tools/gdpr-coverage-selftest.php` counted
`/\$onlyHandWorkLeft\s*\[/` and required exactly one. The same fault written
`self::$onlyHandWorkLeft = self::$onlyHandWorkLeft + [$child => …]` has no `[`
after the name, so adding it to the ordering-mistake branch — or to the
could-not-read branch — left the count at one, left the original write in the
permanent branch for the position check below it, and passed both checks.

The could-not-read plant needs **no second mistake by anybody**: one failed read
of `tblErasureAudit` would then record the step as work only a human can finish,
`finishByHand()` would close the request, and the sealed trail would say no
further run could help — about a step that would have worked on the next try.

The remedy is the repository's usual one: pin the whole surface, not one form of
it. The static may be mentioned in **exactly four places** — the read in
`execute()`, the one write, the reset at the start of a run, and the declaration
— each appearing once, in one spelling. Any edit to those four lines fails the
check on purpose (#697 pins two helper bodies whole for the same reason).

**Comments are removed with `token_get_all()`, never a regular expression.**
Every hand-rolled stripper here has been wrong at least once: a `//` inside a
string literal (a URL is the usual one) eats the rest of the line, and a `/*`
inside one swallows everything to the next `*/` (#716, #675). PHP's own tokeniser
cannot make either mistake.

### Two smaller lessons

**A claim about a count needs the query.** "None of the schema's 1,161 distinct
column names is any of the nineteen" was offered in three documents as the
evidence for #719's safety. The substance is true; the figure is **1,170**
(`SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT COLUMN_NAME) FROM information_schema.COLUMNS WHERE
TABLE_SCHEMA = DATABASE()`, measured on a database built from both the old and
the new `full_schema.sql`). A wrong number beside a true claim is how the next
reader stops trusting the claim.

**And a limitation stated without measuring was false.** A first version of
#719's "what it cannot prove" said no reserved word contains a digit. Measured —
`SELECT WORD FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.KEYWORDS WHERE RESERVED = 1 AND WORD REGEXP
'[0-9]'` on MySQL 8.0.36 — there are **seven**: `float4`, `float8`, `int1`,
`int2`, `int3`, `int4`, `int8`. All seven are already in the hard-coded list and
no column in this schema is named any of them, so the MariaDB parse test's
`^[a-z_]+$` filter costs nothing today. It would cost something the day MariaDB
reserved a new digit-bearing word the list lacked, because that is the one
direction the test fails on.

## A part-written upload is not a stored document (#720)

`file_put_contents()` answers **the number of bytes it wrote**. The documents
API's base64 branch tested `!== false`, so a short write passed as a write. This
is #711's fault in a second file and on a separate code path, and it was found
by #711's own independent check asking whether the shape existed anywhere else.

**Three things worth keeping.**

1. **Two branches, two different kinds of answer, one shared variable.** The
   multipart branch's `move_uploaded_file()` answers a boolean and has no count
   to compare, so `=== false` was right there. Both results went into one
   `$written` boolean, which made the wrong test look like the right one. They
   are judged separately now and both feed one reason string, so neither can be
   "tidied" into the other's shape.
2. **It does NOT need the temporary-name-and-rename shape `Pdf::writeOrWhyNot()`
   uses, and that was checked rather than assumed.** That shape exists to stop a
   failed write destroying a document already on disk, which matters because the
   PDF paths use stable names recorded in the database. Here `$storedFilename`
   is `bin2hex(random_bytes(16))` plus an allowlisted extension — fresh on every
   request, never from the client or the database — and the only other writer of
   `_uploads/documents/` is the legacy `_apps/documents/upload.php`, whose names
   are `date('Ymd_His') . '_' . bin2hex(random_bytes(4))` and always contain
   underscores, so they can never equal a 32-character pure-hex name.
   `_apps/documents/download.php` only reads what `tblDocuments.filePath` names.
   (Established by reading every `_uploads` path under `web/`; the other upload
   folders are many more than that — `pdfs`, `giving`, `expenses`, `mail-queue`,
   `photos`, `recordings`, `venues` and `documents` among them — and an earlier
   version of this note named only three, which an independent check caught: the
   conclusion was right and the enumeration offered as its evidence was wrong, so
   the narrow command is the one to quote,
   `grep -rn "_uploads' . DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR . 'documents'" web/ --include='*.php'`.)
   So a failure has nothing
   to destroy — which is also what makes the clean-up `unlink($destPath)` safe
   here, and what makes the pre-existing `@unlink($destPath)` calls after the
   INSERT safe. Writing in place also avoids the other shape's cost: a
   `.part-…` file left by a killed process is swept by nothing and cannot be
   reached by an erasure (#721). **If stored filenames ever stop being freshly
   generated, that reasoning goes with them.**
3. **No self-test can guard this one, so the guard is static and is itself
   tested.** A genuine short write needs a quota or a tiny filesystem, and
   unlike `Pdf::writeOrWhyNot()` the code is a page that refuses anything but an
   authenticated POST in its first statements — and the destination basename is
   fixed at 36 characters, so the long-name trick `pdf-write-selftest.php` uses
   to force a real failure is not available either.
   `check_document_write_verified.py` therefore pins whole conditions (A–H), and
   `tools/document-write-check-selftest.py` plants each weakening into the real
   file and requires the expected complaint and no other.

**What the pins are, and the two that are not obvious.** Check **E** compares
the gate's position with the INSERT's `prepare`, because moving the gate below
the INSERT leaves every other check green — and the SQL is inside a quoted
string the comment/string masker blanks, so the INSERT is located by
`$stmt = $db->prepare(` rather than by its words. Check **H** counts the
assignments to `$whyNotWritten` (three sets, one append), because one extra
`$whyNotWritten = '';` after the two branches silences the gate for ever while
every pinned line above stays exactly as written. Both were planted and both
are the only thing that catches their fault.

**What was deliberately NOT established:** whether PHP's own copy fallback
inside `move_uploaded_file()` can report success after writing only part of the
file. It answers a boolean and no count, so there is nothing to compare; the
page's comment says that rather than implying the branch is proved. The clean-up
covers the file it leaves on a reported failure either way.

## A room booking's own words, and the list a column is on (#723)

`tblResourceBooking.bookedByID` was in **both** `LINK_COLUMNS` and
`ACTOR_COLUMNS`. The coverage test refuses `nullCols` on an actor column,
because emptying a column on an actor-matched instruction is a blanket
`= NULL` over every row it matches — that is how one person's erasure request
destroys a third party's details, and the guard exists because seven tables
were once set to delete a whole row on such a column.

So the booker's stated reason for wanting the room could not be emptied. **The
fault was the classification, not the guard**, and the owner settled it on
3 November 2026: a booking is made BY the person it is about, so the booker is
the row's subject. `bookedByID` left `ACTOR_COLUMNS` and stayed in
`LINK_COLUMNS`; `purpose` and `declineReason` are emptied; the booking keeps its
times, resource and status, because the room's history belongs to the
organisation.

**`approvedByID` stays an actor column, and the pair is the whole point of the
two lists.** Emptying text on an approver's number would wipe the purpose of
every booking they ever approved. The eraser self-test now holds a booking
somebody **else** made and this person only approved — **without it the
reclassification could have been widened to both columns and every check would
still have passed.** Planted: widening it fails exactly one check, the control.

Rejected and recorded so nobody re-opens it: a separate "who it is for" column.
It models reality better, because a booking can be made on somebody else's
behalf, but it is a schema change plus every writer and reader, and nothing
writes a booking for anybody but its maker. No migration was needed — both
columns were already nullable.

### And be exact about what it empties, because the first version was not

Two overstatements, both found by the independent check and both the shape this
repository keeps meeting — a comfortable sentence in the place a reader checks.

**`tblResourceBooking.notes` IS the booker's own words.** The catalogue said it
was "the organisation's own note about the booking — a caretaker's remark about
access, a charge to be made — rather than anything the booker wrote". False:

    grep -rn "tblResourceBooking" web/ --include='*.php' | grep -iE "INSERT|UPDATE "

finds exactly three writers — the INSERT in `_apps/resources/book.php` and two
UPDATEs in `_apps/resources/action.php` that touch only `status`,
`approvedByID` and `approvedAt`. `book.php` reads `$_POST['notes']` from the
booker's own form and inserts it on the row whose `bookedByID` is that booker.
There is no caretaker's remark and no charge to be made. **The owner was told
exactly that on 3 November 2026 and chose to KEEP the column**, so the reason in
the catalogue is now that decision rather than a description that cannot be true.
The difference between `purpose` and `notes` is a decision, not a principle, and
saying so is what keeps the record honest.

**`declineReason` is written by NOTHING.** The decline branch sets only status,
approver and approved-at, and there is no form field for it anywhere — the only
live `declineReason` writer in the repository is on `tblAssetLoans`. So its place
in `nullCols` can never match. **The limit is recorded in the instruction's own
reason, not in `notEmptiedHere`**, and that is forced rather than chosen: the
#635 check fails a column explained as not-emptied while an instruction empties
it, so the two mechanisms cannot both describe one column. #708's precedent
(`tblCareVisit.followUpAssignedToID`, correct and unable to match) is the model —
record the limit, keep the instruction, so a value stored in future is already
reached.

So what #723 empties of the booker's own words is **`purpose`, and nothing
else**. The headline said "a room booking's own words"; it does not any more.

### A page test can pin the very text the feature erases

The whole suite went red on `erasure-pages-selftest.php` after #723, three
checks, and the diagnosis is the useful part: **the code was right and the tests
were stale, in a way that would have hidden a real failure.**

Both checks found the booking by searching the page for `Welcome team supper` —
the booker's own words. #723 erases those, so after the change finding them
would have meant the erasure had NOT worked. The checks were asserting the
fault.

What they are NAMED for is still true, and that had to be read rather than
assumed:

- `_apps/resources/resource.php` prints `$b['purpose'] ?? '(no purpose given)'`,
  so the slot is still listed with that label and **the room does not look
  free** — which is what the check's own name says it guards.
- `_apps/resources/approvals.php` wraps its "Purpose:" paragraph in
  `if (($r['purpose'] ?? '') !== '')`, so an emptied booking has no purpose line
  while the ROW and its decision controls stay.

Both now require the stable thing AND the absence of the erased text, so they
fail in both directions. **No test in the #723 package could have caught this,
because none of them renders those pages** — the #695 argument for running the
whole set, met for the third time.

## Carrying #711's cost: the part-written statement (#721)

`Pdf::writeOrWhyNot()` writes under a temporary name and renames (#711), which
is what stops a failed write destroying a good file. Its own "WHAT IT COSTS"
note recorded the price: a process killed between the write and the rename
leaves `statement-7-2026.pdf.part-a1b2c3d4e5f6` behind, and
`GdprEraser::statementFilesOf()` globbed `statement-<donorId>-*.pdf`, which does
not match it. A giving statement holds the donor's name, home address and every
gift they have made.

**Before #711 the same crash left a TRUNCATED `statement-7-2026.pdf`, which did
match and was erased.** So this was a narrow regression in erasure reach, taken
knowingly in exchange for not destroying good files — which is worth saying
plainly, because "the fix introduced a privacy gap" and "the fix was wrong" are
different statements and only the first is true.

**Two halves, and they are not interchangeable.** The glob is widened to
`*.pdf*`, which reaches such a file the MOMENT an erasure runs.
`Pdf::sweepPartFiles()` removes stray temporaries older than an hour in the
nightly job, which stops them accumulating. Only the first has a privacy
consequence: an erasure run between the crash and the next sweep would still
miss the file. **Never let the sweep be read as what makes an erasure
complete** — that is the mistake this note exists to prevent.

**One hour, and the check that matters is the one that must NOT fire.** A
statement PDF is written in well under a second, so the margin is thousands of
times over; and the job runs nightly, so a shorter age buys nothing. Section H
of `tools/pdf-write-selftest.php` gives the sweep a file written **this second**
and requires it to survive, because a sweep that took a write in flight would be
worse than the litter it removes.

**`Pdf::PART_MARK` is the ONE place the mark is named**, and the reason is the
failure mode rather than tidiness: the writer builds the temporary name from it
and the sweep looks for it, so two literals would be two places to change — and
the half that broke would be the SWEEP, which would simply stop finding
anything. No error, no log line, no symptom, and a folder with nothing to sweep
looks exactly the same.

**The hard gate went red on that change, and that is the gate working.**
`check_pdf_write_verified.py` pinned the literal `'.part-'`. It now accepts
`$filePath . self::PART_MARK . …` as well, and — this is the part that was added
rather than loosened — **fails when the constant is missing or empty**, because
otherwise renaming or emptying it would leave the gate green while the sweep
matched nothing. Both forms still require the name to be built FROM `$filePath`,
which is the real invariant: the temporary must be in the same folder, because
`rename()` is only atomic within one filesystem.

### The sweep deleted a member's own upload, and the docblock said it could not

This is the worst thing in the package and it was mine. The first
`sweepPartFiles()` walked the whole of `_uploads` and took any name
**containing** the mark, under a docblock reading *"It cannot tell a file this
class left from one named the same way by something else. Nothing else uses this
mark today."* The second sentence was the reassurance, and it was false:

    grep -rn "PATHINFO_EXTENSION" web/ --include='*.php'

`_apps/documents/upload.php` and `_apps/recordings/upload.php` take the stored
file's extension **straight from the client filename with no allow-list** (the
other three callers do check one). `pathinfo('report.part-x',
PATHINFO_EXTENSION)` is `part-x`, so a member who uploaded `report.part-x` had it
stored as `20261103_082700_aabbccdd.part-x` — matching the sweep, deleted an hour
later, while the `tblDocuments` row survived so the portal went on listing and
offering a file that was not there, with nothing logged. `.part` is what download
managers and torrent clients call an unfinished file, so an accident was as
likely as an attack.

**Two guards now, and the owner chose both (3 November 2026) when asked which.**
`Pdf::PART_FOLDERS` is the ONE list of folders the sweep may touch — the four
`Pdf::create()` really writes to, read caller by caller; `documents` and
`recordings` are deliberately absent and must stay so. And the name must **end**
with the mark plus exactly twelve hexadecimal characters, which is the shape
`writeOrWhyNot()` builds, so `notes.part-x` inside a swept folder survives too.

**Why both, when either would have closed the reported fault:** this method
deletes, and a deletion guard resting on one condition rests on nobody ever
editing that condition. Removing the name test alone left **all 31 checks
green** while a day-old giving statement, an expense-claim PDF, an uploaded
document and a recording were all deleted — measured.

### Four of that section's checks could not fail

Every one found by planting, and each is a shape already written down here.

1. **"It leaves a real PDF alone, however old" — the fixture was not old.** It
   was created with `file_put_contents` and never `touch`ed, so the AGE guard
   saved it and the mark test was doing nothing. #645's I7d lesson verbatim:
   when a check exists to prove something ORDINARY still works, check that the
   fixture is actually ordinary.
2. **The symlink check planted a link to a FILE.** `isLink()` skips that
   whatever the iterator flags are, so adding `FilesystemIterator::
   FOLLOW_SYMLINKS` passed 31/31 while the sweep escaped its root through a
   symlinked DIRECTORY and deleted two files outside it. The dangerous case the
   comment named was the one nothing exercised. (The behaviour as written is
   correct — measured on the unmodified file, a symlinked directory is not
   recursed into. What was missing was the pin.)
3. **Nothing exercised the folder list**, which is the guard that stops a
   member losing their own file.
4. **Nothing exercised an unreadable folder**, which without `CATCH_GET_CHILD`
   makes the whole walk throw so the sweep removes nothing at all.

### The glob found the stray statement and the kept test then kept it

The half called the privacy fix did not work on its own, and an independent
check measured it. `GdprEraser::statementFileIsKept()` decides whether a file
found by the glob is tax evidence. For
`statement-7-2026-01-01_2026-12-31.pdf.part-a1b2c3d4e5f6` it failed two ways
round:

- with the keep set to "every gift" its first line answers "kept" for anything;
- with it set to "receipted gifts only", the `-4` chop for `.pdf` leaves the
  period as `2026-01-01_2026-12-31.pdf.part-a1b2c3d4`, which does not parse, so
  the "a name that gives no period is KEPT" fallback applied — to a file that is
  not a statement at all.

Measured on the real private method by reflection: the genuine statement came
back `kept=no` and the part file `kept=YES`. Worse, the step then **counted it
and told the administrator it had been "kept with the donor's giving records as
tax evidence"** — a half-written file holding the donor's name, home address and
every gift they have made.

**A file carrying `Pdf::PART_MARK` is a write that never finished**, so it is
evidence of nothing and is refused before the scope is even looked at.

**Why no check saw it, and the proof was inside the test.** The made-up world
never writes a `tblGivingKeptDonors` row for the erased person, so that whole
branch was dead — and the test's own fixture is `statement-<id>-2025.pdf`, whose
period `2025` does not parse either, so if the branch had run the EXISTING "the
person's file is deleted" check would already have failed. It passed. A fixture
uniform in exactly the way this repository keeps being bitten by.

## Deciding about free text an erasure cannot judge (#724)

**What it is.** Seven columns in this schema hold free text that no automatic
erasure rule touches, because whether it matters depends on the request:

| Table | Column |
|---|---|
| `tblResourceBooking` | `notes` |
| `tblServicePlanItem` | `presenterText` |
| `tblRecording` | `presenterText` |
| `tblAssetLicenseAssignments` | `deviceName` |
| `tblAssetLicenseAssignments` | `seatLabel` |
| `tblSmallGroups` | `meetingNotes` |
| `tblSalvationCards` | `prayerRequest` |

**Three of those are not the names #724 uses, and the database's names are the
right ones.** The issue says `tblServicePlans.presenterText`,
`tblAssetLicenseSeats.*` and `tblSalvationCard.prayerRequest`. There is no
`presenterText` on `tblServicePlans`, and no `tblAssetLicenseSeats` or
`tblSalvationCard` table at all. That is the "name things by the right
identifier" trap, which is why `check_erasure_review_items.py` compares its
pinned list against `full_schema.sql` rather than reading prose.

**The marker, and why it is a marker.** A column is marked by its catalogue
entry's `needsReview` list; the REASON stays in `notEmptiedHere`, so one place
still describes one column. Judging "is this one for a person to look at?" from
the words of a reason would drift the first time somebody reworded one, and it
would drift silently.

**The order is load-bearing, and it is #709's trap in a new place.** The table
walk EMPTIES the account columns these rows are found by (`bookedByID`,
`presenterID`, `userID` …). A check made after the walk would find nothing to
review, every time, and the review page would go blank the moment a run had been
attempted — leaving a request that could never be finished. So the question is
the first thing `execute()` does, and a refusal changes nothing.

**It goes further than "cannot close", on purpose.** The owner's words were
"the request cannot close while an item is unreviewed". Refusing the whole RUN
is stricter, and the paragraph above is why: refusing only at the close would
mean the walk had already cut the links, so the review could never be completed.

**A missing table must not block an erasure.** `tblErasureReviewDecisions`
arrives with migration 242, and files reach a server before anybody presses
"Run migrations" (#694). With the table absent, `whyNotReadyToClose()` answers
"nothing in the way" and the run writes a `skip` line saying the free text was
NOT checked. Refusing instead would be #697's blocked recovery.

**`SHOW TABLES LIKE ?` PREPARES AND MATCHES NOTHING.** MySQL does not take a
parameter for that pattern. The first version of `decisionsTableExists()` bound
the name, so it always answered false — and because a missing table means "not
ready to judge" rather than "not ready to close", THE WHOLE REVIEW SWITCHED
ITSELF OFF SILENTLY: every request ran straight through with its free text
undecided. Thirty-one checks went red the first time the test met a real
database. The name is a constant in the file, checked against
`/\A[A-Za-z0-9_]+\z/`, and written into the query — the
`DbBackup::holdingTableExists()` pattern.

**`GROUP_CONCAT` TRUNCATES EVIDENCE AT 1,024 BYTES.** The check "the emptied
words are nowhere in the audit trail" read the trail with `GROUP_CONCAT`, and a
planted fault that wrote the text straight into the audit line PASSED ALL 87
CHECKS, because the evidence was cut off before it. Read the rows and join them
in PHP. A check whose evidence the database silently shortens is not a check.

**A guard that the strict connection reaches first is not tested by a strict
connection.** `record()` reads the cell back after emptying it, for the NOT NULL
case. On a strict connection the UPDATE itself throws, so the read-back never
gets a turn — and a plant that DELETED it passed all 87 checks. The test now
also runs that case with `sql_mode = ''`, where the server writes an empty
string and warns instead of throwing. The portal's own connection is strict
(`DbServer::connect()`, #593), so the read-back is belt and braces; it is tested
because a guard nothing exercises is not a guard.

**A clause that could not fail, removed before it shipped.** A draft of
`record()` refused a "keep" on a line already recorded as emptied. That branch
can never be reached: an emptied cell is no longer an item, so the "not one of
this request's items" refusal catches it first. The real guard is inside the
transaction, where the row is held and the cell read again — which is also the
only thing that can catch two people deciding at once.

**What the review cannot reach, and it is not a gap that can be closed.** A row
that is ABOUT the person but carries no account number of theirs is not offered.
A response card about the erased person, given to somebody else, is the clear
case: its name, address and prayer request are all typed by hand, and the only
account column on the row is the follow-up worker. Searching the text for their
name was refused on 1 November 2026 (it misses a mistyped name and can match a
different person sharing a mailbox), and nothing here changes that.

**A row reached only through an "acted on it" column is flagged.** The review
offers exactly the rows the table's own erasure instructions match, which
includes rows the person merely approved or was given. The page says which
column matched and warns when every one of them is in
`GdprEraser::ACTOR_COLUMNS`, because emptying such a line takes away a third
party's words. That is a judgement for a person with the row in front of them,
never a rule.

---

## For DEV_NOTES.md — "Counting and showing are two jobs (#724)"

A silent `LIMIT 500` sat in `ErasureReview::rowsHolding()` with no comment, and
`whyNotReadyToClose()` read that list. Measured on a real MySQL 8.0.36: **501 rows, 500 offered, no
problem reported, all 500 decided, the close answered `''` and the request closed with one line of
the person's own words still in it.** Not exotic — somebody who books a room weekly for ten years
has about 520 such rows.

The rules that came out of it:

1. **A display cap may never be able to change a decision.** Anything that decides whether a request
   may close counts in the database, with no limit, and never reads a list that has a size.
2. **A capped page must be a worklist, not a wall.** The list is ordered undecided-first, so
   deciding a page-full brings the next one into view. Without that a page-full of KEPT lines sits
   there for ever and the lines behind them are never seen.
3. **A capped page must not make anything unreachable.** `record()` looks its one line up directly.
   Searching the capped list would have made the 501st line impossible to decide, so the request
   could never be closed — #697's blocked recovery.
4. **One rule, four questions.** `holdingWhere()`/`holdingValues()` is shared by the list, the total,
   the undecided count and the single look-up, so the deciding half cannot drift from the showing
   half.
5. **A plant has to reproduce the WHOLE fault.** Putting only the capped read back left the decisive
   check green, because the undecided-first ordering rescued it; the pre-fix state is the capped read
   AND no ordering, and only then did "THE REQUEST STILL REFUSES TO CLOSE" go red — with a blank
   detail, because the detail is the refusal and the refusal was the empty string.

## For DEV_NOTES.md — "A claim about code checked against a .sql comment (#724)"

`full_schema.sql` said "`grep -rn installFinish web tools` finds nothing", and run today it found
its own comment. **My first two rewordings were untrue in the same way**: scoping the command to
`"function installFinish"` made the comment a hit for that too. The claim is now
`grep -rn installFinish web tools --include='*.php'`, which finds 0 and will keep finding 0 because
the comment lives in a `.sql` file — and it says so. A claim about code has to be checked against
code; writing a claim down can be what makes it false.

## For DEV_NOTES.md — additions to the #724 record

* **`record()` put `$db->error` and `$e->getMessage()` into five page-visible sentences**, thirty
  lines above `rowsHolding()`'s comment explaining why it reports only the error NUMBER ("a database
  message can quote a value, and this one may be reported on a page"). Fixed, and **the fix shipped
  with no guard**: the plant that put the leak back left the self-test 126/126 green. The guard is a
  POSITIVE clause (the refusal must contain `database error 1048` and this class's own reading of
  it), because a clause forbidding some phrase of MySQL's could not fail.
* **Error 1048 is translated in our own words over our own names**, so making the message safe did
  not make it useless on a strict connection, where the UPDATE throws before the read-back runs.
* **A grant that errors inside a transaction on a strict connection refuses the whole transaction.**
  Measured both ways. It takes BOTH `MYSQLI_REPORT_STRICT` and `MYSQLI_REPORT_ERROR`. And the COMMON
  case is different and must be said separately: with no role row, `INSERT … SELECT` inserts zero
  rows and raises nothing at all — which is why "nobody holds the role" was a silent gap rather than
  a visible failure.
* **Granting a role needs a membership.** `fk_user_role_membership` refuses a role for a non-member,
  so `admin/sites/save.php`'s grant reaches nobody on a brand-new organisation and cannot be made to
  — the honest remedy is the sentence on the page, not a cleverer statement.

### A success message over a write that did not happen (#586)

`web/_apps/admin/users/save.php` reported a new password as saved when the account had
never had one. The shape is worth recognising because nothing mechanical could see it:
the write was inside `if ($localRow !== null)` with no `else`, and the flash message was
written unconditionally thirty lines later. `php -l` is happy, every audit script is
happy, and the page answers HTTP 302 exactly as it does on success.

It was that way from the page's first commit —
`git show a443d6c:web/public_html/admin/users/save.php` (7 March 2026) — and was found
on 12 October 2026 by the independent check of the recovery runbook (#488), which had to
carry a warning about it in section 7.4 rather than a fix.

**Three things learned while fixing it.**

1. **An account can have no password for three different reasons, and only one of them
   is a fault to fix.** Nobody accepted the invitation; the person signs in with
   Microsoft or Google (`tblLinkedAccounts`); the person signs in with a passkey
   (`tblWebAuthnCredentials`). Creating a sign-in row for the first is plainly right —
   without it the account can never be used at all. For the other two it is a **product
   decision**, because it adds a second way into the account rather than correcting
   anything, so the page refuses and says so. `Auth::countLoginMethods()` already
   answers "how many ways in does this person have", and it is asked rather than a
   second count being written.
2. **There is no single place that sets a password.** Five files hash and store one —
   `_install/index.php`, `_apps/invites/accept.php`, `_apps/users/api/create.php`,
   `_apps/auth/reset-password/save.php`, `_apps/auth/account/change-password.php` — each
   with its own inline SQL, and `_apps/offboarding/do.php` makes one unusable with
   `passwordHash = ''`. This fix deliberately did NOT add a sixth "one place": that is a
   refactor of an authentication path and belongs to its own issue. What it DID do is
   follow the same route as the rest — `password_hash($password, PASSWORD_DEFAULT)` into
   `tblLocalAccounts.passwordHash`, nothing invented.
3. **"Forgot password" is not the way out, and saying it was would have been untrue.**
   `_apps/auth/forgot-password/save.php` joins `tblLocalAccounts`, so it finds nothing
   for an account with no sign-in row either. The first draft of the refusal message
   advised it. There is no route today for an SSO-only or passkey-only account to gain a
   password, and the message says nothing it cannot stand behind.

**A sign-in row cannot exist without a sign-in name**, and that is the part the obvious
fix forgets. `tblLocalAccounts.username` is `VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL` with a unique key
across the whole installation, while `tblUsers.emailAddress` is `VARCHAR(255)`. So two
more refusals are needed, both honest: an address longer than 50 characters (the
installer has the same limit and the same wording), and an address already in use as
somebody's sign-in name. The length is measured with `mb_strlen`, not `strlen`, because
`VARCHAR(50)` counts characters and counting bytes would refuse an address that fits.
The refusal over a taken name never says whose it is (#521).

**The guard, and what it can see that nothing else can.**
`tools/admin-password-selftest.php` presses Save on the real form over real HTTP, with
nine made-up accounts, and each is without a password for its own reason — a fixture in
which the branch cannot be taken tests nothing. It then proves the person can REALLY
SIGN IN with the new password, both with their e-mail address and with the new sign-in
name, which is the only claim that matters. Part E writes two faults into the scratch
copy and requires each to be caught: `&& false` on the gate that creates the row, and
that plus the read-back switched off, which is the original fault. **Measured on the
real file as well:** planting both into `web/_apps/admin/users/save.php` turns C03, C04,
C05 and C06 red while C01 and C02 stay green — the page still says it worked, which is
precisely why a check on the message alone would prove nothing.

**No audit script can guard this.** The invariant is "no success message over a write
that did not happen", which is about reachability across sixty lines, not about text. So
no check was added to `tools/audit-checks/`: a text-matching one would have gone green
on the `&& false` plant, and a check that looks strong and guards nothing is worse than
none. What carries the fix instead is the read-back inside the transaction — the handler
asks the database whether a password is really held before anything claims it is.

### Gating a feature on a role an organisation created (#727)

**The distribution is what shaped the design — and the first version of this
paragraph got every figure in it wrong, which is the more useful lesson.** It
read: "86 `App::hasRole()` call sites, 62 with a literal key and 24 with a
variable, and `asset_manager` alone accounts for 37 of the 62", presented as
measured. Measured properly on commit `b12ff44`, with PHP's tokeniser and
comments dropped: **65 call sites across 62 files, 61 with a literal key and
four without** — and two of those four pass a class constant, so only **two**
work their key out at run time. 86 was what a `grep` answered, which counts
every mention in a comment and a docblock; 62 was the FILE count standing in for
the literal count; and 24 was the gap between the two. `asset_manager` really
did account for **37 of the 61** literal gates, which is the figure that shaped
the design and the only one that survived checking.

So "make each call site configurable" would have offered a customer sixty-odd
switches, 37 of them the same answer about the asset register repeated. A
capability is coarse on purpose: one door, named in code, covering as many call
sites as it needs to.

**Count them with `php tools/role-gate-count.php`.** That script exists because
four documents quoted a `grep` figure as a fact. It uses the tokeniser, drops
comments, splits literal from run-time keys, and prints the comment-inclusive
`grep` beside its own answer so the gap is visible. **The `grep` does not merely
over-count — it is the wrong shape:** converting a gate leaves a comment behind
naming the gate it replaced, so on 3 November 2026
`grep -rn "App::hasRole('asset_manager')"` returned 19 hits of which **zero were
calls**, while the tokeniser correctly said none were left.

**Two tables, not one, and the second is not tidiness.** "Chosen, and empty"
must be distinguishable from "never chosen": the first means "nobody,
deliberately" and the second means "the role the portal ships with". One table
cannot say both without a sentinel row holding an empty `roleKey` — and a
sentinel could not carry `fk_capmaprole_role`, which is what makes a deleted
role leave every set it was in instead of leaving a door nobody can see is shut.

**There is no "cannot be emptied" flag, and the reason is enforced rather than
asserted.** An empty set is always recoverable because the page that changes a
mapping is gated on `App::isAdmin()` and on no capability.
`check_capability_registry.py` fails if any capability is ever asked from a file
under `web/_apps/admin/roles/`, which is the one edit that would make an empty
set permanent. A flag no test could reach would have read as a protection and
been none.

**`globalAdminPasses()` is a named method, and THE REASON WRITTEN HERE FIRST
BECAME UNTRUE INSIDE THE SAME DOCUMENT.** It said: "No OFFERED capability
declares `globalAdminFallsOpen => true` — there is one, #724's, and it declares
false — so written inline as `$a && $b` the 'true' half would be a branch
nothing could reach." That was true of part one, which shipped `erasure.review`
alone. **Part two made it false and did not revisit it**, so this file
contradicted itself a page later, where its own "THE FIVE" notes say all five
declare `true`. The registry holds **six** offered capabilities and **five**
declare `globalAdminFallsOpen => true`; `check_capability_registry.py` prints
that column on every run, which is where to look rather than at any sentence
here.

That matters because this is the paragraph somebody would read before inlining
the rule or deleting the self-test section that exercises it — a comment stating
a guarantee the code no longer honours, with the correction applied nowhere. The
reasons the method stays named are different and both still hold: the rule is
written ONCE where two opposite answers meet, so no page can keep a second copy
of it, and all four combinations are exercised directly rather than only through
whichever capabilities happen to be declared today.

**Three faults of my own in building this, each worth recognising.**

1. **A pristine copy taken before later edits is not a pristine copy.** The
   copies for the planting round were taken before `globalAdminPasses()` was
   added, so restoring one silently reverted that method — and the next plant
   then reported "could not plant" while four others went red for a reason that
   had nothing to do with them. The machine-wide rule says a backup you made
   yourself is not evidence about the original; it is not evidence about the
   CURRENT state either. Re-take the copies after every edit, and hash them.
2. **A test that renames a table must put it back whatever happens.** Section J
   hides the storage by renaming both tables, to prove a database without
   migration 243 falls back to the shipped roles. A planted fault stopped the
   run between the two renames, so the tables stayed hidden and every later run
   failed in section D. Four plants then looked caught while being caught for
   the wrong reason — **a plant that goes red for the wrong reason is as
   useless as one that will not go red, and the passing run cannot tell you
   which.** The remedy is `brs_tidy()`'s, from #697: a shutdown function that
   renames back only if the hidden name is really there.
3. **A value that runs to the start of the next field includes the comment in
   between.** The audit check reads `CAPABILITIES` by delimiting each field from
   its own key to the NEXT key (#706's remedy — no bracket counting inside an
   entry). Read out of the raw source, `standard` came back as
   `['data_controller'], // ⚠️ FALSE, AND IT IS THE POINT…`, which is not a
   list. The extent is measured on the MASKED text, where comments are blanked
   to spaces of the same length, and the value is then read out of the original
   at those offsets.

**What is not covered.** Nothing drives the roles page over HTTP: the
confirmation box, the global administrator's card and the refused delete are
pinned as text in section M of the self-test and have never been pressed. Two
administrators saving at once is not tested — `save()` replaces the whole set in
one transaction, so the last one wins.

#### The five, converted (#727, part two — 3 November 2026)

*(This used to be a staging block headed "Entries to be folded into
`CHANGELOG.md`, `FEATURES.md` and `DEV_NOTES.md` by the commissioning session.
Nothing here was written into those files." That is a note to a writer, not a
technical lesson, and #678 gives this document one job — so the content is
folded in here and the instruction is gone. The same shape was removed from
`CHANGELOG.md` in the same round.)*

Four things worth keeping, each measured rather than reasoned.

1. **THE FOLDER NAME WAS WRONG ABOUT WHERE A GATE LIVES, TWICE, AND BOTH TIMES
   IN THE DIRECTION THAT LOSES COVERAGE.** `livestream.console`'s own note said
   its gates were in `web/_apps/livestream/` and `web/_apps/admin/livestream/`.
   Measured: the first holds one file, `api/ping.php`, with no role gate at all,
   and the second is gated on `App::isAdmin()` plus the "we are live" push's own
   coordinator rule (#612), which is about ONE event and is deliberately not
   this capability. The real gates are `web/_apps/admin/live/chat.php` and
   `web/_apps/livechat/api/moderate.php`. The same shape the other way:
   `assets.manage` has 37 calls, and THREE of them are outside
   `web/_apps/assets/` — two in `web/_core/AssetRegister.php`
   (`canApproveLoan()` and `canManageMaintenance()` each fold the manager
   bypass in themselves, #398) and one in `web/_apps/calendar/event.php` (the
   Unassign button beside an event's assets). Converting the folder and
   stopping would have let a customer's own role open every asset page and then
   be refused the one action on an individual asset. **Find a gate by searching
   for the role key, never by reading a folder name** — but use
   `php tools/role-gate-count.php <role>`, not `grep`. A `grep` was what found
   these three, and it worked only because nothing had been converted yet:
   afterwards each converted file keeps a comment naming the gate it replaced,
   so on the working tree of 3 November 2026
   `grep -rn "App::hasRole('asset_manager')"` returned 19 hits of which ZERO
   were calls. The same command, run twice a day apart, means two different
   things.

2. **A MISSING `use` LINE IS INVISIBLE TO `php -l`, TO EVERY ADMINISTRATOR, AND
   TO EVERY SELF-TEST HERE.** Most of the 49 gates read
   `App::isAdmin() === false && App::can(…)`, so PHP never evaluates the
   right-hand side for an administrator. Planted (the `use` line deleted from
   `web/_apps/care/case.php`): `php -l` clean, the 199-check self-test green,
   and the first ordinary member to open the page would have got a fatal error.
   Check O of `tools/audit-checks/check_capability_registry.py` is the only
   thing that catches it — #536's lesson, in a new place.

3. **MASKING STRING LITERALS IS THIS REPOSITORY'S USUAL REMEDY AND IT WOULD
   HAVE BLINDED THE NEW GUARD COMPLETELY.** Check M has to find
   `App::hasRole('asset_manager')`, and the thing it reads IS a string literal:
   `mask_php()` would hand it `App::hasRole('xxxxxxxxxxxxx')`. A separate
   `without_comments()` blanks comments and leaves strings alone, still walking
   the source rather than using a regular expression. Exactly the fault that
   broke both halves of #716's guard.

4. **THREE OF THE FOUR `treasurer` MATCHES WERE NOT GATES.** `App::hasRole(` was
   counted with the role key beside it and the count was four for `'treasurer'`;
   two of those were in COMMENTS, and of the remaining ones `Giving::canManage()`
   opens the GIVING records — donors' names and home addresses — which is not
   the expenses treasury. `ExpenseRules::EXPORT_ROLE` is the `approver` role,
   `ReportRegistry` passes a role key as a variable, `ExpenseMailer` uses the
   key in SQL to build an AUDIENCE. Only three were the capability. **Count
   function bodies and gates, not matches.** The deliberate leftovers are named
   in `HAS_ROLE_ON_PURPOSE` with a reason, and that list fails both ways.

**And a wording fault of my own, which the new section N of the self-test now
forbids.** The first draft of all five `emptyMeans` sentences said "Only a
global administrator will be able to…". That is wrong twice: every one of these
gates ALSO lets an ordinary administrator of the organisation in through
`App::isAdmin()`, and for the asset register the people an individual asset
names as responsible keep their access too. An empty set shuts the ROLE out and
nothing else. Nothing can judge how an assembled sentence reads, so what is
pinned is that it does not make the claim that was false.

**What is NOT covered.** `App::can()` runs over real HTTP for
`expenses.treasury` (the treasury pages ask the capability FIRST, so everybody
evaluates it) and for `livestream.console` (a member is refused by it in
`tools/live-chat-moderation-selftest.php`). For `assets.manage`,
`care.register` and `kids.checkin` the only HTTP exercise is by an
administrator, who short-circuits before the call — so the behaviour of those
three gates for a non-administrator is proved by `Capabilities::allows()`
against a real database (section O) and by the static checks, not over HTTP.


**Three questions, three sources, one rule.** `Portal\Core\SettingLimit` now
answers the three-tier rule from three different places, and the difference
between them is only WHERE the two numbers come from:

| method | the organisation's figure comes from | what it is for |
|---|---|---|
| `effective()` | the merged `$SETTINGS` | drawing a page for the organisation being served |
| `cappedForSite()` | a figure the caller read for one NAMED organisation | a job that walks every organisation (#685) |
| `whyNotAllowedFor()` | the posted number, judged against a ceiling read LIVE and locked | a save (#687) |

All three end in one private `smallerOfTwo()`, which is the only place the
arithmetic — including the zero rule — is written. `installationAllows()`,
`installationAllowsForEver()` and `whyNotAllowed()` are now thin wrappers that
take the value out of the installation layer. **Adding a fourth source means
adding a reader, never a second copy of the rule**: two readers that disagree
about what a job will do is the fault `MailQueue::numbers()` had to fix.

**The caller keeps its own meaning of a stored value, and that is deliberate.**
`cappedForSite()` takes a figure rather than a key to read, because what a
stored value MEANS differs per setting and those decisions are already written
down beside each one: `AnonymousCheckins` reads a negative number of days as
"keep for ever" (for a clear-out, doing nothing on a number nobody meant to type
is the safe direction), `TranscriptRetention` reads the same negative as "not
chosen". Both are right for their own setting and folding them into one rule
would silently change one of them.

**`installationAllows()` NEVER ANSWERS 0 for a zero-is-largest key**, and
believing otherwise cost two live faults in one package. It hands back the hard
maximum, because what a form's `max` and a comparison need is a number of days.
Two places had worked their own arithmetic out against it:
`TranscriptRetention::daysForSite()`, where `if ($ceiling === 0)` was dead code
and "for ever" could never survive even where the installation allowed it; and
Admin, Transcription, where `$installDays === 0 ? 'Kept for ever.'` could never
print and the box prefilled 3650 over a stored 0. **Ask
`installationAllowsForEver()` for the other half — a page needs both, and they
are different questions.**

**A save-time cap is not a cap, measured.** With the installation allowing 90
days and organisation 1 holding 1000 put in by SQL, `readRetentionDays(1)`
answered 1000 before and 90 after; a stored 0 ("for ever") answered 0 before and
90 after; a stored 30 answered 30 both times, which is what stops the cap being
a clamp. The full before/after table is in
`.claude-work/evidence/p685/measure-685-{before,after}.txt`.

**The lock, and what proving it needs.** `TranscriptRetention::saveForSite()`
re-reads the installation's row `FOR UPDATE` inside the transaction that writes,
because #687 measured two overlapping ordinary web requests storing fifty years
under a ceiling of seven, 60 pairs out of 60. Proving that needs two connections
at once, so it cannot be an HTTP test: the page harnesses run the built-in server
with one worker, and such a test passes on the broken code. Section D of
`tools/retention-caps-selftest.php` starts a second PHP process to hold the row.
With ` FOR UPDATE` deleted, measured: **3000 days stored under a ceiling of 7,
and the save reported as successful.**

**Two things that section cannot catch, both measured by planting:**

- **"It waited" is not the proof.** With ` FOR UPDATE` deleted the save still
  took over a second, because the holder's `UPDATE` on `uq_settings_key_site`
  locks the gap beside its own row and the saver's INSERT blocked there instead.
  The discriminators are the three checks after it.
- **Moving the locked read OUTSIDE the transaction leaves every check in that
  section green.** A `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` still blocks and still reads the
  committed value; what is lost is that the lock is released at once by the
  implicit commit, leaving a window between reading the ceiling and writing the
  figure (#697, "a lock outside a transaction is decoration"). Only the ORDERING
  check in section E catches that. Both are needed and neither covers the
  other's half.

**And the hard gate cannot see a save that has stopped refusing.**
`check_limit_settings_capped.py` asks whether a per-organisation writer MENTIONS
the rule. Two of its six writers are now core classes that both resolve the limit
and write the row, and such a class satisfies the test with its own
`self::installationAllows()` — measured by deleting every `SettingLimit::` call
from `TranscriptRetention.php` and watching the gate stay green. Tightening the
token to `::installationAllows` was tried and changes nothing, because `self::`
carries the `::` too. That is the check's own limitation 2 in its sharpest form,
and the answer is a behaviour test: section C of
`tools/retention-caps-selftest.php` asks the method to store a figure above the
ceiling and requires nothing to be written. Planted (`if (false)` on the
refusal), the gate stayed green and section C went red on eight checks.

### A retention period that is read per organisation, and the rows that belong to nobody (#491)

Both log tables carry a `siteID`, which is what made the per-organisation fix
possible at all — read out of `full_schema.sql` rather than assumed. Three
things are worth keeping:

1. **A loop over `tblSites` is only two thirds of the answer.** `siteID` is
   nullable on `tblActivityLogs` and `tblErrors` ("nullable for pre-bootstrap
   logs"), and both foreign keys are `ON DELETE SET NULL`, so a deleted
   organisation's rows become nobody's. A per-organisation loop alone would
   have kept every one of them for ever — and for the activity log that means
   the sender's address, the browser description and the session facts. They
   follow the installation's own figure, which is also the right party: those
   rows are not any customer's.
2. **Zero is not "for ever" for these two settings**, and that is the opposite
   of `attend.detailRetentionDays`, `webhooks.payload.retentionDays` and the
   transcript period. The code this replaced read
   `if ($activityDays < 1) { $activityDays = 365; }`, so a stored 0 has always
   meant "nothing usable, fall back to a year". Reading it as "for ever" would
   stop a log row ever being cleared; handing it to `SettingLimit`'s ceiling
   machinery as a number of days would clear **every** row on the next run.
   So `log_retention_installation_days()` refuses a 0 before any comparison,
   and says why.
3. **No page can create a per-organisation row for either key.**
   `_apps/settings/save.php` counts the installation's own row as a clash, so
   such a row can only arrive by hand-written SQL or a whole-database restore
   — which is exactly why the cap lives in the reader the clear-out uses and
   not on a form.

### A help page is the one document nothing here reads (#583)

`tools/backup-restore-selftest.php` already said it, in the "what this cannot
show" list of proof 28: *"Nothing in this repository reads
`_apps/help/disaster-recovery.php`, and its sentence about this feature has
already been turned false once and corrected."* That was measured again for
#583 and is still true: the only help page any test reads is
`help/calendar-imports.php`, pinned by check W50 of `feed-admin-selftest.php`.

So the in-app help is the one body of customer-facing text in this repository
with **no guard of any kind** — and it is the text somebody reads at the worst
moment of their year. #583 is what that costs: the page kept giving advice for
#582's unbuilt tools for three weeks after the runbook had been rewritten to
say those tools do not exist, and it kept telling people to delete files the
database points at.

**Two shapes worth recognising.**

1. **An anchor can be corrected while the words are not.** The stolen-credentials
   link's `href` already ended `#7-after-a-break-in` while its visible text
   still read "runbook section 4.4". Whoever fixed the anchor fixed the half a
   machine can follow and left the half a person reads. Nothing compares the
   two, and nothing ever will unless a check is written for it.
2. **Advice that names a feature request reads exactly like advice that names a
   feature.** "clear every session, force password reset, rotate `enc.key`" is
   the three bullets of #582 transcribed as instructions. The issue was raised
   *because* the tools do not exist; the help page was written *as if* they did.
   Before quoting a capability in customer-facing text, grep for it: there is no
   `revokeSessions`, no `signOutEverywhere`, nothing of the kind under `web/`.

**The cheap guard that is still owed, and why it was not built here.** The
narrow class of fault — a help page citing a runbook section number that is not
a heading in `docs/disaster-recovery-runbook.md` — is mechanically checkable in
about thirty lines, fails both ways, and would have caught "section 4.4" the day
the runbook was reorganised. It was not built in this package because a new
script in `tools/audit-checks/` is picked up by the pre-push hook's glob and so
becomes a hard gate for everybody, which is a decision for the owner rather than
a tidy-up. Raised as a follow-up instead.

### Claims in an issue go stale too (#583)

Two of #583's seven claims were **wrong when measured on 3 November 2026**, and
both pointed the reassuring way for the wrong reason:

- "links to a GitHub address a customer cannot open". The repository is
  **public** (`gh repo view --json isPrivate` → `false`) and
  `https://github.com/MWBMPartners/WebMS-Intra/blob/main/docs/disaster-recovery-runbook.md`
  answers **200**. A customer can open it. What they get is the **old** runbook,
  because the rewrite lives on `claude/alpha-wip` and has not merged — which is
  a timing matter that fixes itself on merge, not a broken link.
- "cites runbook section 4.4, which no longer exists". On the branch, true. On
  `main` — which is the page the link actually opens today — section 4.4 **is**
  still there, headed "Stolen credentials". So for a reader today the section
  number was right and the anchor was wrong; after the merge the anchor is right
  and the number is wrong. Either way the link contradicted itself, which is the
  real fault and is what was fixed.

The lesson is the repository's own: a claim about what something "does not have"
or "cannot do" needs the command that establishes it, and an issue written three
weeks ago is as capable of being out of date as the page it complains about.

### A `.php` address hidden inside a PHP string is seen by neither check (#583)

Found by planting, and reported rather than fixed. Written as a literal,
`<a href="/admin/users.php">` is caught by **both**
`check_no_php_in_urls.py` and `check_site_aware_addresses.py`. Written as

```php
<a href="<?php echo htmlspecialchars('/admin/users.php', ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8'); ?>">
```

it is caught by **neither**, and `check_registered_addresses.py` does not see it
either, because it judges `Site::url()` calls rather than strings. That is the
exact shape somebody produces by "simplifying" a built address away, and
`.htaccess` answers 404 for it. Raised as a follow-up.

### Whose record is it? Three reclassifications in one week (#723, #492 parts 2 and 3)

`GdprEraser::LINK_COLUMNS` and `ACTOR_COLUMNS` answer one question: is this
column the person the row is ABOUT, or somebody who acted on it? The answer
decides whether free text on the row may be emptied, because `processEntry()`
empties a non-account column in `nullCols` with a plain `= NULL` on EVERY row the
instruction matched. On a subject column that is the person's own row; on an
actor column it is a third party's record destroyed on a request that was never
theirs.

Three columns were on the wrong side of that line, and all three were found the
same way — by asking what the column HOLDS rather than what it is called:

| Column | Looked like | Really is |
|---|---|---|
| `tblResourceBooking.bookedByID` (#723) | who made the booking | the person the booking is about |
| `tblAssetLoans.counterpartyUserID` (#492 part 2) | a party to a transaction | the person the loan is about |
| `tblEventRegistrations.submittedByUserID` (#492 part 3) | who the registration is for | **only who typed the form in** |

The third is the interesting one, because it goes the other way. The first two
were subjects misfiled as actors, and the cure was to reclassify. The third was
an actor misfiled as a subject — there was no subject column at all — and
reclassifying would have fixed nothing: the cure was a NEW column
(`registeredForUserID`, migration 246). **So "the classification was the fault"
is not a general answer; the general question is which real person each column
names, and sometimes the answer is that nobody records the one you need.**

Two things worth keeping about the guards:

- **A limit cannot be recorded in two places.** `counterpartyName` is named by
  the loan instruction and can never match it. Writing that in the catalogue's
  `notEmptiedHere` AND leaving the column in `nullCols` fails the #635 check,
  because a column may be explained as not-emptied or be emptied, not both. The
  limit goes in the INSTRUCTION's reason. #723 learned this for `declineReason`
  three days earlier and it had to be learned again in the same sitting — the
  comment saying so was written and then broken two edits later.
- **The control row is the half that stops real harm, and the coverage test
  cannot supply it.** Widening the reclassification to `approvedByID` and
  `requestedByID` left `gdpr-coverage-selftest.php` entirely GREEN (93 of 93 at
  the time the plant was run) and failed only the two real-row checks on loans
  somebody else borrowed. Without a loan the erased person only APPROVED, the
  widening would have shipped.

### A migration that "looks idempotent" and is not (#492 part 3, migration 246)

Migration 246 copies `submittedByUserID` into the new `registeredForUserID` once.
The obvious guard is `WHERE registeredForUserID IS NULL`, and it is WRONG: an
empty value is the honest answer for "this registration is for somebody else", so
once the form starts recording that, a replay would fill it in from the submitter
and put the original fault back one row at a time. The installer replays every
numbered migration over `full_schema.sql` and ignores `tblMigrations`, so the
replay really happens. The guard is `@col_exists` as read BEFORE the column was
added, so the copy runs only on the run that creates the column.

Measured on MySQL 8.0.36 (3 November 2026). With the correct guard, a row holding
`submittedByUserID = 777001` and `registeredForUserID = NULL` survived a second
run untouched. With `WHERE registeredForUserID IS NULL` planted instead, the
same row came back with `registeredForUserID = 777001` — the volunteer's number
written into the subject column, which is exactly the harm the column exists to
prevent.

Also: **no foreign key on the new column, deliberately.** `submittedByUserID` has
none, so it can hold the number of an account that has since been deleted;
adding a key to the new column would make the migration refuse with error 1452 on
any database where it does. Measured: a row with a dangling submitter copied
through without complaint.

### `docker run --rm` does not always remove the anonymous volume (3 November 2026)

The standing rule reads "Start test containers with `docker run --rm`, or remove
them with `docker rm -v`". Measured on Docker Desktop on this Mac, those are not
equivalent and the difference is in how the container ENDS:

- `docker run --rm …` then `docker stop <name>` — the anonymous data volume IS
  removed.
- `docker run --rm …` then `docker rm -f <name>` — the anonymous data volume is
  LEFT BEHIND, and it is a full MySQL data directory.

Identified by content: the leftover held exactly this package's `selftest_*`
databases. Use `docker stop`, or `docker rm -v`.

### Whether a snapshot was really read at one moment (#581)

`DbBackup::snapshot()` reads the tables one after another inside one
transaction. Two lines give it a single consistent view of all of them, and
**the first is the one that does the work on a host whose own isolation level is
READ COMMITTED**:

```sql
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ
START TRANSACTION WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT, READ ONLY
```

**Measured on 3 November 2026, on `mysql:8.0.36 --transaction-isolation=READ-COMMITTED`:**
deleting the first line alone made every snapshot stop being taken at one
moment. A parent row saved into a table the snapshot had already read, and its
child into one it had not, gave a snapshot holding the child and not the parent;
the snapshot still answered `success`; and the restore then refused it with "a
row of tblUserSites points, through its column siteID, at the row of tblSites
whose siteID is 970481, and that row is not in the snapshot". **On a server
whose own level is REPEATABLE READ — MySQL's default, and what every self-test
in this repository runs on — the same deletion changes nothing and proof 11
stays green.** That is the #646 shape: a correct guard over a fault that has
already happened, with nothing able to run it.

**`@@transaction_isolation` IS A DECOY, and it is the obvious thing to reach
for.** Measured on the same server: inside a transaction the SET line had
already put right, and which really did give a consistent view, that variable
still answers `READ-COMMITTED` — because `SET TRANSACTION` with no scope word
sets the NEXT transaction only and never touches the session value the variable
reports. A guard or a check built on it would condemn a working snapshot on
every such host.

**The statement's own warning is what answers the real question.** MySQL says
`Warning 138: InnoDB: WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT was ignored because this phrase
can only be used with REPEATABLE READ isolation level.` A clean server says
nothing at all, and `START TRANSACTION WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT` **clears the
warning list** (measured: a `SELECT 1/0` immediately before it leaves
`@@warning_count` at 0 and `SHOW WARNINGS` empty), so a leftover warning cannot
be mistaken for this one. Hence three answers and not two: no warnings is
`yes`, a warning naming the phrase is `no`, and any other warning is
`cannot tell` — because a check that cries wolf gets switched off (#483).

**MariaDB 11.4.13 prints no warning at all** when it ignores the phrase
(measured). So there the answer is always `yes` and means only "nothing was
said". What was **not** measured is whether MariaDB's read is really
inconsistent in that case.

A fourth word, `ONE_MOMENT_NOT_RECORDED`, is never written into a manifest and
exists only for the restore: "it looked and could not tell" and "it never
looked, because it was taken before snapshots looked" are different facts about
different snapshots, and the first draft of the sentence said "an older one
never looked" for both — untrue, in the reassuring direction, of a snapshot that
really did look.

Guards: `tools/audit-checks/check_snapshot_one_moment.py` (a hard gate; 17
plants, each caught) and proof 29 of `tools/backup-restore-selftest.php`, which
reaches the fault **on one server** by taking the isolation level away from the
backup's own connection. Its section A proves, with the test's own two
connections and none of the class's code, that doing so really does destroy the
isolation — so section B is not testing nothing.

### Is anything actually calling the scheduled backup job? (#581)

The portal could take a backup on a timer (`cron/backup-run`, #569) and could
offer the choices on a page, and **nothing anywhere could say whether the
hosting company's scheduler was calling it.** The page's only words were
conditional — "this only happens if your hosting company's scheduler is calling
the portal" — which is true and no use to somebody deciding whether their data
is safe. `backup.schedule.frequency` ships as `daily`, so that is the state
every new installation is in.

`DbBackup::recordScheduledCall()` writes the moment into
`_backups/.backup-run-last`. **A FILE, NOT A SETTINGS ROW OR A COLUMN, and the
reason is the whole design:** every table goes into every snapshot, so a value
kept in one travels backwards whenever a snapshot is put back — restore a
snapshot taken while the scheduler was working and the portal would say the
scheduler is working, on a server where it has since stopped. That is a false
reassurance about backups. `cron/backup-run.php` already drew the same line for
working out whether a snapshot is due.

**Where the call is recorded is three decisions, all load-bearing:** after the
token check (a stranger who guesses the address must not be able to make the
page claim the scheduler is working); before the "switched off" answer (an
installation that has chosen `off` must still be able to find out, or the only
way to find out would be to switch backups on); and before the
one-run-at-a-time lock (a second overlapping call still counts).

The check for that last one was **deleted after planting proved it could never
fail on its own** — the lock sits after the switched-off answer, so the earlier
clause always fires first. What is checked instead is that the lock still comes
after that answer, which is what makes the lock ordering follow, and that clause
*can* fail. A clause that cannot fail makes a check look stronger than it is.

`DbBackup::scheduleIsRunning()` is the ONE test of "recently" (two days, so one
missed night does not read as "nothing is calling it"), asked by
`scheduleWords()` and by the Backup page for its colour. The page's first
version chose the colour by looking at how the sentence **started**, which would
have gone wrong the first time anybody improved the wording — and would have
drawn "your scheduler is calling but backups are switched off" in green.

**Never say a backup was taken.** Being called and taking one are different
things: a call that decides nothing is due answers in one query and takes
nothing, which is correct. Proof 29 has a computed check that none of the six
sentences blurs them — computed, because the first version ended in an
unconditional `brs_check(true, ...)`.

### #472 is finished, and every number in its title was stale

Measured on a real MySQL 8.0.36 loaded from `web/_sql/full_schema.sql`:

| The issue said | Measured on 3 November 2026 |
|---|---|
| 209 tables | **232** (`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM information_schema.TABLES`) |
| 71 cannot be restored | **0**. All 232 come back identical through `restoreAll()` |
| 71 named in a foreign key | **76**, of which the database really refuses `TRUNCATE` on **74** |
| — | `restoreTable()` refuses **78** of 232, by design and in plain words |

The two the `REFERENCES` grep over-counts are `tblAssetLoans` and `tblTasks`,
whose only foreign key is to **themselves** — MySQL allows `TRUNCATE` on such a
table. So a grep of the schema cannot give this number; the database can.

A failed restore no longer destroys anything. Measured: a snapshot taken, the
live data then changed, a column added to `tblRoutes` that must have a value, so
the refill is refused after all 232 tables have been emptied and about half
refilled — **0 rows lost, every table's row count unchanged, and the one test
row still holding its pre-restore value.** The old shape is still demonstrable
in two lines: `TRUNCATE` inside a transaction followed by `ROLLBACK` leaves 0 of
3 rows; `DELETE` leaves 3.

The one acceptance criterion that is **not** met, and is documented rather than
fixed: a whole restore can still delete rows from a table it is not restoring,
through the database's own cascade rules. Measured — a table named outside
`tbl*` with a link into `tblSites` lost its row — and the restore counts it,
names it and says a snapshot cannot bring it back. No table in the portal's own
schema is in that position: all 232 are `tbl*`.

## One `${{ }}` in a long script stops a whole workflow file (#745)

**The shortest version: a workflow step's script that holds a `${{ ... }}` must
stay under 21,000 characters, or GitHub refuses the entire file and starts no
job at all.** A script is one value, so the ceiling applies to the whole of it,
not to the expression inside it.

### What happened

Commit `c61211e` (27 October 2026) took the "Heuristic anti-pattern scan" script
in `.github/workflows/pr-security.yml` from 14,910 characters to 24,525. That
script held two `${{ ... }}` on its ninth and tenth lines. From the next push
onwards, every run of "PR Security Checks" failed with **no jobs**, for a week,
while all thirty-five of that file's hard gates sat doing nothing
(`grep -c "^      - name:.*hard gate" .github/workflows/pr-security.yml`).

### Why no check here could see it

| What was asked | What it said |
|---|---|
| Ruby's YAML parser | Valid |
| actionlint 1.7.12, locally and in `lint.yml` | Valid — green on every failing day |
| `php -l`, the audit scripts, the pre-push hook | Not their business |
| GitHub | A run with **zero jobs** and "This run likely failed because of a workflow file issue" |

**The ceiling is enforced by GitHub's own service, not by the workflow schema**,
so no local tool knows about it. That is the whole trap: every parser that can
be run here accepts the file.

### How to recognise it in thirty seconds

Ask the API for the run and look at its **name**:

```bash
gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/actions/runs/<run_id> -q '{name,path,conclusion}'
```

```json
{ "name": ".github/workflows/pr-security.yml", "conclusion": "failure" }
```

**`name` equal to `path` is the giveaway.** GitHub falls back to the file path
when it cannot read the file, so a run that should be called "PR Security
Checks" and is called `.github/workflows/pr-security.yml` has never been parsed.
A second tell: the run's `event` is `push` for a workflow whose only trigger is
`pull_request` — GitHub cannot know whether the file matches the event, so it
reports the error against the pushed commit regardless.

### The ceiling, honestly

21,000 is the figure in GitHub's own error message ("Exceeded max expression
length 21000"). **The exact boundary was not measured.** What was measured, on
this repository against the real service: **14,910 characters with an expression
was accepted; 24,525 with an expression was refused.** 21,000 lies between them.

### The fix, and why it is the better shape anyway

Pass the value in as an environment variable and read it as an ordinary shell
variable:

```yaml
      - name: Heuristic anti-pattern scan
        env:
          PR_BASE_SHA: ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}
        run: |
          BASE_SHA="$PR_BASE_SHA"
```

The script then holds no expression and has no ceiling on it. **This is also
GitHub's own hardening advice:** a `${{ ... }}` pasted into a shell script
becomes part of the script, so whatever the value holds runs.

### The guard, and where it had to live

`tools/audit-checks/check_workflow_expression_length.py`. It fails on a script
over the ceiling that carries an expression, on a workflow file over GitHub's
500 KB file limit, and on a script over the ceiling with no expression that is
not listed in `LONG_SCRIPTS_ON_PURPOSE` with a reason — that list fails both
ways, so it cannot go stale the way the migration harness's exceptions did.

**It cannot be a step in `pr-security.yml`, and that is the point: a workflow
cannot run from a file GitHub will not read.** It lives in
`tools/audit-checks/`, which `.githooks/pre-push` globs, so it runs before the
push that would break things, and it is also a hard gate in `lint.yml` for the
push made with `--no-verify`.

**What it cannot see**, said plainly: a long `${{ ... }}` in a `with:`, `env:`
or `if:` value hits the same ceiling and is not measured — nothing here is
remotely near it, and measuring those needs a real YAML parser, which this
machine has not got (no pyyaml, and an audit script must run with no
dependencies so the hook can run all of them in about nine seconds). It is also
not a YAML parser: it finds `run:` by indentation, so a workflow written in flow
style would be measured short.

### Two things this does NOT establish

**The file is readable again; the gates have not run.** `pr-security.yml`
triggers on `pull_request` only, there is no open pull request, and its last
completed run was 26 October 2026. So nothing here shows that the thirty-five
gates pass — only that GitHub will read the file. In a repository where this
package exists *because* checks looked wired and were not (#646), that is not a
quibble.

**And the loss was the GitHub half, not all of it.** `.githooks/pre-push`
arrived on 29 October (`1e4da0e`) and globs `tools/audit-checks/*.py`, so from
the outage's second day every audit-check script still ran locally before every
push. What really went unrun for the week is what only GitHub does: the PHP lint
on a clean runner, gitleaks, the inline heuristic greps, and the pull-request
comment — plus everything, the audit scripts included, for the first two days.

### The lesson worth keeping

**A service-side limit is invisible to every local validator, so "the linter is
green" says nothing about whether the file will run.** The thing to check is not
whether the file parses but whether the run that should exist exists — and when
a run reports zero jobs, read its `name`, because GitHub has already told you it
could not read the file.

Planting also taught something about the guard: putting an expression back into
the long script produced the real complaint **and** a second one telling the
reader to delete an allow-list entry that was still perfectly correct. **A
check that cries wolf beside a true finding teaches the reader to skim both.**
