## What a customer is told is tested must be derived, not written (#475)

**The shortest version: `Portal\Core\DbServer` showed customers a hand-written
sentence about which database versions the automated tests run on, and two of
those sentences were untrue.** They are derived from a constant now, and a hard
gate compares that constant with the workflow that does the running.

### What was wrong

| Where | What it said | Why it was untrue |
|---|---|---|
| Every MariaDB answer | "this portal's own automated tests only ever run against MySQL … no test here proves it" | The migration harness had been replaying every database change on MariaDB 11.4 since 28 October 2026 (#487) |
| Every supported-MySQL answer | "tests run against the MySQL 8.0 line, so if you are on something newer you are ahead of what is routinely tested here" | 8.4 and 9.7 are tested, so somebody on a tested version was told nobody had tested it |
| The class docblock | the same "only ever run against MySQL" | as above |
| The MySQL 8.0 message | "this is the version everything here is tested against" | It is one of five tested lines, not the only one |
| `tools/db-server-selftest.php` comment | "MySQL, the line everything here is tested against" | as above |

All five were stale in the **modest** direction, which is the safer one. That is
not a defence. A customer-facing sentence that is untrue is a fault whichever
way it points, and the next one to go stale could as easily tell somebody a
version is tested when nothing has ever been run against it.

### How it was found, which is the transferable part

**Not by reading the code — by printing what the code actually says to a
customer:**

```bash
php -r 'require "web/_core/DbServer.php";
  foreach (["8.0.41","9.7.4","10.6.21-MariaDB","11.4.13-MariaDB"] as $v) {
    $r = Portal\Core\DbServer::classify($v);
    printf("%-22s %-5s %s\n\n", $v, $r["state"], $r["detail"]);
  }'
```

Reading `judgeMariaDb()` would not have shown it: the sentence is correct
English, assembled correctly, from a variable whose contents nobody had reason
to re-read. **It is only wrong against the world.** The same applies to any
message built from a constant that describes something outside the file.

**A warning about reading that output in a hurry.** The first look at it was
truncated to 96 characters and read as "MariaDB 10.6 is accepted with a
reassuring message and no mention that its support has ended" — which was
wrong; the message says so plainly, further along the line. Print the whole
sentence, or the finding is about the truncation.

### The cure, and why a constant alone would not have been enough

`DbServer::TESTED_LINES` names the release lines the migration harness really
runs on, and `testedLinesCaveat()` is the one place the sentence is built. It
differs **by line**, because that is what is true: the harness runs on MySQL
8.0, 8.4 and 9.7 and on MariaDB 11.4 and 12.3, and on **none** of MariaDB 10.6,
10.11 or 11.8 — all of which the portal still accepts.

**A constant on its own just moves the staleness one step along.** So
`tools/audit-checks/check_tested_db_lines.py` compares it with the `include:`
matrix in `.github/workflows/e2e-migrations.yml` and **fails both ways**:

* a line the harness tests that the constant does not list — the portal
  under-claims;
* a line the constant lists that the harness does not test — **the portal tells
  a customer a version is tested when nothing runs on it.** That is the
  dangerous direction and the reason it is a hard gate.

**No exception list, deliberately.** There is no honest reason for the two to
differ: if a line leaves the workflow, the sentence must stop claiming it the
same day. Four plants, each caught by the message that should catch it: the
constant over-claiming, the workflow dropping a claimed line, the workflow
gaining an unclaimed line, and the constant renamed so it cannot be read (which
fails rather than comparing two empty lists, because two empty lists agree).

### What `TESTED_LINES` deliberately does NOT describe

**The migration harness and nothing else.** The calendar self-tests run on their
own set of engines, and `portal-selftests.yml` on another. Folding them together
would overstate what the sentence means — "replays every one of its database
changes on it" is a specific claim about a specific body of work. A line tested
only by the calendar self-tests is correctly absent.

And the wording never says "supported". For a tested line it says the project
"really runs against" it, and then says out loud that this is **not** the same as
somebody running it in production — which, for MariaDB, nobody does.

### The decision beside it

**MySQL 8.0 and MariaDB 10.6 stay accepted, with a warning** (the owner,
3 November 2026), although their support ended on 30 April and 6 July 2026. So
`MIN_MYSQL` stays `8.0.0` and `MIN_MARIADB` stays `10.6.0`. Do not raise them as
a tidy-up. It also means the warning is the only protection, which is why its
truthfulness stopped being cosmetic.

### The fix round, and the two faults worth carrying forward

An independent check of this package found nine real problems. Two are general.

**A new script in `tools/audit-checks/` is not wired up until
`pr-security.yml` NAMES it.** That file lists every audit script
**individually**; there is **no folder glob in any workflow in this
repository**. `.githooks/pre-push` *does* glob the folder — and that is exactly
what misled me. The gate described above was written, called "a hard gate" in
four documents, and was **the only one of 56 scripts in no workflow at all**:
the #646 shape re-created inside the package that cites #646. A hook that is
turned on per clone and that `git push --no-verify` skips is not a gate. The
test takes a second:

```bash
for f in tools/audit-checks/check_*.py; do
  grep -rqs "$(basename "$f")" .github/workflows/ || echo "NOT IN ANY WORKFLOW: $f"
done
```

**A check that takes the FIRST match in a file can be switched off by a
comment — and the house style asks for exactly that comment.** `.claude/CLAUDE.md`
says to "record what was tried and rejected", so a note showing the constant's
previous value is ordinary good practice. The gate read it instead of the real
constant, and a release line the portal claimed while nothing tested it passed
with `OK` and exit 0 — the direction the check's own header calls the dangerous
one. Comments are blanked now, in both readers, **keeping every line and column**
so reported line numbers stay right (#716 put its numbers 370 out by deleting
them instead).

**And blanking them broke the next line immediately.** The blanked comment lines
became pure whitespace, and `^(\s*)include:` matched *across* them — the
"indentation" came out as 1,918 characters and the check failed with "could not
read the matrix". **Use `[ \t]`, never `\s`, for indentation: `\s` matches a
newline.** It failed loudly, which is the only reason it cost minutes; in a
check that defaulted to passing it would have been silent.

Three more worth recognising, each a repeat of something already written down:

* **The behaviour this package exists to produce was pinned by nothing.**
  `return '';` at the top of `testedLinesCaveat()` removed the caveat from every
  answer with 36 of 36 checks green — because the one clause that claimed to
  guard it tested `$got['untested'] !== true`, which `$base` sets for every
  MariaDB answer, so it **could not fail**, and it was never about the sentence
  anyway.
* **"The ONE place" was untrue, and the exception was the line the gate cannot
  protect.** `judgeMySql()`'s 8.0 branch hand-wrote its own version. #475's
  direction is to stop accepting MySQL 8.0 — and the day 8.0 leaves the matrix,
  the gate *forces* it out of `TESTED_LINES` and goes green while a hand-written
  sentence goes on telling every 8.0 customer their version is tested.
* **A watch that closed its own issue on the day the event happened.** PHP 8.4
  answers `soon` on 30 December 2026 and `fine` on the 31st, because its
  security fixes run to 2028. The close step would have fired with the words
  "Nothing this portal says it supports is now within the warning window", and
  the only durable record of the finding would have gone, at the moment of the
  event. `security-only` is its own reportable state now — as is `unknown`,
  whose exclusion had made the header's "silence is not success" a promise the
  code did not keep.

## A check can be sound by accident, and a string can hide an address (#742, #743)

Two checks that proved less than their names claimed. The lessons are different
and both transfer.

### #742 — "safe by accident of spacing" is not safe

`tools/capabilities-selftest.php` proved a gate really refuses with:

```php
'/<condition>\{.{0,900}?exit\(\);\s*\}/s'
```

With the `s` modifier `.` crosses newlines, and
`web/_apps/admin/roles/save.php` holds **22** `exit(` calls, **21 of them
followed by `}`**. So in principle the search can run past the block being
checked and find the next refusal's `exit();`.

**Measure the stronger claim before repeating it.** Deleting the `exit();` from
either of the two blocks made the old pattern go **red** — correctly. The
nearest other refusal was 2,011 and 1,181 characters away, both beyond the 900
limit. **They were sound by accident of how far apart the refusals happened to
sit, not by design.** The issue said they were already broken; they were not.

The plant that shows the real risk is the one a developer actually performs —
delete the `exit();` **and** add an ordinary new refusal just after that block:

```
    old idiom (bounded dot, /s) : says the refusal is THERE  <-- WRONG
    new brace walk              : goes RED  <-- correct
```

So the fix is right and the reason given for it has to be the true one.

**`cap_blockFrom()` is the one way a block is cut in that file now.** It walks
the braces and **steps over string literals** — #647 records a walk that did
not, where one `{` inside a log message swallowed the rest of a function and the
check passed on a removed gate. It also replaced a *second* helper, newer and
better, that cut at "the closing brace at N spaces": that worked, but it trusted
the read file's indentation and made the caller supply N, and both blocks in
question contain braces of their own. **Two ways of doing one thing in one file
is the fault, even when both happen to work.**

Two checks that look identical and are not: the two in
`tools/expense-rules-selftest.php` pinned on `ExpenseRules::isOwnClaim(...)`
**anchor** their pattern at the start of a slice cut from the gate itself and
spell out the whole block, so a deleted `exit()` cannot be satisfied by a later
one. Left alone — and proved by planting, not merely by reading.

**And "the other 54 apparent matches are the harness's own router" was wrong
twice over, which is the lesson.** The figure could not be reproduced from any
search (53 is the natural one: `exit('403')` 27 plus `exit('404')` 26), and the
remainder are NOT all router shims — there are at least **seven** other genuine
refusal pins across `tools/`. **Cite the command, not the answer** — #727's own
rule, broken in the package that quotes it.

Two of the seven needed action: a **sixth** pin in `capabilities-selftest.php`
still cut by indentation, which made "one way of cutting a block in this file"
untrue; and `gdpr-coverage-selftest.php` asked for an `exit();` **within 1,100
characters** of its question, on the guard that stops an erasure request being
cancelled after it has already changed records. The question sits at byte 1,500
and the write at 2,391, so the window reached 209 characters past it. It asks
the meaningful question now — **is the refusal before the write?** — and **no
plant was found that fooled the old form, so the change rests on the arithmetic
and on the better property, not on a demonstrated failure.**

### #743 — the form a check cannot see is the form the codebase uses

Planted into a real page:

```php
<a href="<?php echo htmlspecialchars('/admin/users.php', ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8'); ?>">
```

**All three checks written to catch a `.php` address stayed green.** The same
address as a plain `href="/admin/users.php"` is caught by two of them. The
checks expect the address to sit directly in the attribute — and
`htmlspecialchars()` round an address is the house style for anything built in
PHP, so **the shape they could not see was the shape most of the codebase
uses.**

The remedy is the #716 one: **look inside the literal, do not strip it** — the
value being judged *is* a string, so masking literals is precisely what blinds
you. And decide by context, because a bare `.php` string is usually innocent
(`require`, a route target, a comment, a fixture) and a check that cries wolf
gets switched off (#483). Nine plants, both directions.

**One limit kept rather than fixed, and the reason is worth repeating:** a
*trailing* comment quoting such an address is reported. The patterns that were
already there have the same exposure. Stripping a trailing `//` would cut a line
at the `//` inside any `https://` string — a fault this repository has already
paid for (#716). Nothing in the tree trips it; if something ever does, rewrite
the comment rather than loosen the check.

### The sibling finding, measured and left for its own package

The blindness is wider than `.php`. A **bare** address hidden the same way is
invisible to `check_site_aware_addresses.py`, which is #536's guard — and that
harm is quieter, because a bare `/page` drops the organisation's part of the
address and the page still looks normal.

A probe over every `.php` file under `web/` found **no real instance today**.
Its two candidates were both false positives, and the second is the trap to
avoid: `'/href="(https?:[^"]+)"/i'` — the probe matched **`/i`**, a regular
expression's own delimiter and modifier, on a line that contains `href`, so a
marker test does not save you. Raised as its own issue because that check is a
hard gate with `--strict` and an empty pending list.

---

## The in-app help, and two ways a check about it goes wrong (#744)

**Thirteen of the twenty help pages were loaded by nothing until 4 November
2026** — and the first version of this note said "nothing loaded any help page",
which was untrue and carried no command, against this repository's own rule.

**Thirteen of the twenty help pages were loaded by nothing.** The other seven
were already fetched over HTTP, for their *words*, by `feed-admin-selftest.php`
(`/help`, `/help/calendar`, `/help/approvals`, `/help/calendar-imports`),
`mail-pages-selftest.php` (`/help/admin`, `/help/admin-first-steps`, both
asserting HTTP 200), `mail-queue-pages-selftest.php` (`/help/admin`),
`channel-selftest.php` and `page-head-selftest.php` (`/help`), and
`portal-address-selftest.php` (`/help/support`, `/help/admin`). **None of the
seven was checked for whether the page finished**, which is the gap that
remains.

```bash
git grep -nE "(req|pw_req|[$]get)[(].*'/help" 55b0f78^ -- tools
```

Twenty pages read by end users, on code that can throw, and not one of them
checked for finishing.

### Two guards, and what neither does

| | What it does | What it does NOT do |
|---|---|---|
| `tools/audit-checks/check_help_page_references.py` (hard gate) | Every runbook section number a help page shows must be a real heading in `docs/disaster-recovery-runbook.md` | Judge whether any advice is correct. **No check can** |
| `tools/help-pages-selftest.php` (50 checks, HTTP) | Every help address answers a WHOLE page to an administrator, and a whole page or a clean refusal to a member | Judge the words, the layout, or whether the help is complete |

Both say that in their own headers. A green run means the pages open and their
pointers resolve — it is not a statement that the help is right. #583's fault
was advice that would have destroyed a customer's data, on a page that loaded
perfectly.

### Trap 1 — collapsing code pulls distant text together

The reference check reads only the text outside `<?php … ?>`, which is what the
reader sees. The first version replaced each PHP block with **a single space**,
and that cried wolf three times in my own planting: "Version 4.4 of the
portal", "About 4.4 million records" and the date "4.4.2026" were each reported
as a stale runbook reference, because collapsing a long PHP region pulled a
"runbook" hundreds of lines away into the same 60-character window.

**When you remove a region to read what is left, replace it with a FENCE the
window cannot read across, not with whitespace.** A space makes two distant
things adjacent, which is exactly what a proximity rule is reading for.

### Trap 2 — "A or B" is satisfied by all B

The HTTP test asks that every help page answer a member with **a whole page or
a clean refusal**. Twenty refusals satisfy that completely. So if every help
page turned an ordinary member away, all twenty checks would pass while proving
nothing about a page opening for the person most likely to read it.

B99 counts how many the member really read — **20 of 20** today — and fails if
it is none. This is the I7d lesson (#645) in a new place: *when a check exists
to prove something ORDINARY still works, check that the fixture is actually
ordinary.*

### Two things worth knowing about the help itself

**All seven live runbook references are correct**, so the check is a tripwire
rather than a repair. And `help/disaster-recovery.php` still contains "section
4.4" twice — **inside a PHP comment** that records the #583 correction. A check
reading the whole file would fail on the very comment documenting the repair,
which is why only the reader-facing text is read.

### And a fault of mine, caught by running it rather than by reading

The first version queried `tblRoutes.routePath`. The column is **`routeKey`**,
and the test died on its first run. That is CLAUDE.md's "name things by the
right identifier" trap: check a name against the thing that actually uses it —
here `web/_sql/full_schema.sql` — not against what looks similar. Writing the
query from memory and running it cost one minute; writing it from memory and
*not* running it is how a test ships broken.

### What a reader should take from the numbers

`tools/help-pages-selftest.php` makes 50 checks: 20 pages as an administrator,
20 as a member, B99, two reachability checks, four on the disaster-recovery page
and three planted faults. **Count them from the run, not from here** — a number
in prose goes stale the day somebody adds a help page, which is the fault this
whole package is about.

## One place hashes and stores a password (#728)

**Eight writers, each correct, and that was the problem.** The installer,
`invites/accept.php`, `users/api/create.php`, `auth/reset-password/save.php`,
`auth/account/change-password.php`, two sites in `admin/users/save.php`, and
`offboarding/do.php` each hashed a password and wrote it with their own SQL.
None of them was wrong about hashing. What no one could do was enforce a rule
about passwords in one place — and #586 was such a rule.

`Auth::setPassword()` / `setUnusablePassword()` own the storing;
`storeHash()` behind them is the only writer. They do **not** own who may set a
password: that stays with each caller, which has its own gate.

### The empty string is the unusable marker, and it is ENFORCED

Five places depend on it — **four read it and one writes it**, which is why a
random hash was wrong:

| Where | What it does with `''` |
|---|---|
| `Auth::loginLocal()` | **reads** — refuses the account *before* `password_verify()` |
| `_apps/auth/account/change-password.php` | **reads** — refuses on `($row['passwordHash'] ?? '') === ''` |
| `_apps/auth/2fa/disable.php` | **reads** — the same test, and now says "no password" rather than "wrong password" |
| `docs/disaster-recovery-runbook.md` | **reads** `passwordHash <> ''` as "has a password" |
| `_apps/offboarding/do.php` | **writes** it, to take a sign-in away |

**A first version of this table said "three places read" and cited
`admin/users/save.php`'s #586 read-back as one of them — which this very change
DELETED.** So it offered as evidence the thing it had removed, missed two real
readers, and described the one writer as a reader. (No line numbers here on
purpose: this package moved code inside `Auth.php`, and the repository's own
rule is to cite issues and commits, which do not move.)

`users/api/create.php` wrote `password_hash(bin2hex(random_bytes(32)))` — nobody
can match it, but **nothing can recognise it**, so every account created through
that API read as having a working password. The claim that an empty marker
"could be made to succeed by a caller that got its own logic wrong" is false,
measured on PHP 8.5: `password_verify()` answers false for `''`, `'0'`, `'x'`
and `'*'`, against both a real password and an empty one.

Before adopting it, measured that `_apps/auth/forgot-password/save.php` joins
`tblLocalAccounts` with **no condition on the hash**, so the reset route stays
open for such an account — which is the only route it has.

### I claimed a race was impossible, and it was not

`storeHash()` said "nothing in this portal creates a second one", in five
places. **Measured false** on MySQL 8.0.36: two connections, each in its own
transaction, both setting a password for the same account with *different*
sign-in names — **both reported success, and the account ended with two rows.**
Under REPEATABLE READ neither transaction can see the other's insert, so
neither `COUNT(*)` finds a clash.

The harm is not the duplicate row; it is what follows. That account can never
have a password set through the one writer again — it refuses, correctly — while
**both** old passwords keep working. So the member who most needs to change
their password, because they fear their account is compromised, is the one who
cannot.

**The unique key does not cover it.** It is on `username`, so it catches the
case where the two names *match* — one administrator double-clicking Save, which
rolls back — and nothing where they differ.

The fix is a lock on the account's own `tblUsers` row before the count. The
parent is locked because the row being guarded against does not exist yet, so
there is nothing else two requests can both wait on. **That lock is real only
inside a caller's transaction** (#697), and every caller that can create a row
is inside one; the only caller without a transaction passes no sign-in name and
can therefore only update. If a future caller creates a row outside a
transaction, this protection is not there for it and nothing can tell.

Making the lock real made a new path reachable that the broken version never
could — the #694 round-3 shape. A lock-wait timeout throws
`mysqli_sql_exception`, which would escape with the caller's transaction open;
checked rather than assumed, every creating caller catches it and rolls back
(the app pages catch `\Throwable`, the installer catches
`\mysqli_sql_exception`).

**Section I takes two real processes**, because two connections driven one after
the other from a single process simply deadlock — measured while building it.

### Refusing beats choosing, and a draft chose

`tblLocalAccounts.userID` carries a plain `KEY`, not a unique one, so the schema
does not stop one account having two rows. A draft read `MIN(localID)` — at
least deterministic, where `LIMIT 1` with no ordering is not even that. **But
deterministic is not safe:** setting the password on one row leaves the other
row's old password working, so a member who resets because they fear their
account is compromised is still signable-in with the password they just
replaced. It refuses now, and says why.

`offboarding/do.php` is the counter-example that settled it: clearing the hash
with `WHERE userID = ?` reaches **every** row, which is right for taking a
password away. That is why it is a stated exception rather than a conversion.

### The installer has no autoloader, and `php -l` cannot see it

`web/_install/index.php` requires every class by hand — its own comment says it
"can't autoload `\Portal\Core\Migrator`". So `\Portal\Core\Auth::setPassword()`
there would have been a fatal "class not found" **on every installation**. Found
by asking what loads the class, not by reading. Safe to require, measured:
`Auth.php` loads standalone, and `setPassword()`, `setUnusablePassword()` and
`storeHash()` reference no class but `self` — which section A of the self-test
pins, because that is what the one `require_once` rests on.

### A test that could not tell the read-back from LENGTH()

**Sections A–G of `tools/password-writer-selftest.php` passed 49 of 49 with the
read-back weakened** to `if ($stored === null)` — exactly the question the old
`admin/users/save.php` asked with `LENGTH(passwordHash)`, and the thing the
whole section was written to prove was stronger.

They all check the database before and after, so they prove the write *landed*.
The read-back only matters in the state they never produce: the write lands, a
row exists, and the value is not the hash we made. **Section H makes that state
with a `BEFORE UPDATE` trigger** that overwrites the column — standing in for a
truncation, a stale replica, or a column altered underneath. It goes red on the
weakened read-back (51 of 53) and skips honestly where the database will not
allow a trigger.

The transferable part: **when a check exists to prove one question is stronger
than another, build the one case where the two answers differ.** Everything
else passes on both.

**Two faults in the test itself came out of this, and both are named shapes.**
Its brace walk stepped over string literals but read a `//` comment as ordinary
code, so the apostrophe in "a caller's transaction" opened a quote that never
closed; the walk ran three methods past `storeHash()` and reported it reaching
`App::settings()`, which lives in `validatePassword()`. That is the fault
`check_page_head_tags.py` and `check_no_outside_qr_service.py` each had, found
here the only way it can be — by a comment in the code under test gaining an
apostrophe. Comments are blanked before the walk now.

And check I2 first demanded that one of the two racing requests be **refused**.
That is the pessimistic answer: with the lock in place the loser waits and then
correctly **updates**, so nobody is turned away. A check demanding a failure the
fix removes has to be weakened the day the code improves, which is how a test
ends up fighting its own subject. It asserts that at most one of them *created*
a row.

### The guard, and what it cannot see

`tools/audit-checks/check_one_password_writer.py`, a hard gate in
`pr-security.yml`. It fails both ways. It replaces comments with spaces of the
same length while **keeping** string literals — the opposite of the masking
checks in that folder, because the SQL it looks for lives inside them.

**Its first version used distance windows and three shapes got past it**, each
measured by the independent check: `REPLACE INTO` (a verb it did not know); a
joined `UPDATE tblUsers U JOIN tblLocalAccounts LA … SET LA.passwordHash` (the
table named is not the one it looked for, and the column is reached through an
alias); and an INSERT whose column list runs past 300 characters before the
column — **which defeats the window, not the pattern**, so the guard's own
"cannot see a name built by joining pieces" admission did not cover it.

There are no windows now: it splits a file at each SQL write verb and flags any
span naming both the table and the column, so a long column list, an alias and a
join are all inside reach. The cost is a possible false alarm — a span that
writes some other table and merely *reads* this column — which no file here
does, measured. A check that cries wolf gets switched off (#483), so if that
changes the answer is to narrow it with evidence, never to put the windows
back.

It still cannot see a name built by joining pieces or held in a variable, a
write with no SQL verb of its own, or whether `Auth::setPassword()` is correct —
only that it is the only thing doing the job.

## Adding a password to your own account (#731)

### The gap, measured

An account that signs in only through Microsoft, Google or a passkey had **no
route to a password at all**:

| Route | Why it could not help |
|---|---|
| Admin, edit a user | refuses it on purpose (#586) |
| "Forgot password" | joins `tblLocalAccounts`, and `Auth::createUser()` — the first-time single-sign-on path — creates no row there |
| Change password | there is none to change |

So a lost identity provider, a lost Microsoft or Google account, or a lost
passkey device meant the member was out, and the disaster-recovery runbook's
server-level operation was the only way back — for what is one person's problem.

### What proving yourself means here, and what it cannot mean

**Not an e-mail link**: for such an account the e-mail address may *be* the
single-sign-on account, so a link to it proves nothing a lost provider has not
already taken away. The person re-signs-in by a method they really hold, and
that is recorded as a proof carrying the moment and the method.

**`/login` cannot be used for it.** It redirects away whenever `Auth::check()`
is true, so a signed-in person sent there bounces straight back having proved
nothing. The add-password page therefore offers the methods itself, which costs a
**third inline copy of the passkey browser plumbing** — not of the ceremony:
`login/webauthn.php` is still the one place an assertion is verified, and the
challenge is session-bound, compared and cleared, so nothing can be replayed.

**The proof is recorded ABOVE the two-factor gate**, deliberately: that gate
takes the sign-in away and redirects, so a proof written below it would never
exist for a two-factor account and such an account could never add a password.
Nothing can *use* one while the session is still waiting for the code, because
the check compares it against the signed-in person, who at that moment is
nobody. (For the password route that gate lives in
`_apps/auth/login/index.php`, **not** below in `loginLocalOneAtATime()` — a
copied comment claimed "below" and was wrong of that one function.)

### Three guards that nothing pinned, and the one of them that was my own

Each of these left the suite at **88 of 88 green**:

1. **The form-token gate deleted.** Every other check fetches a real token
   first, and the check that posts "anyway" uses a *good* token with no proof —
   the opposite case. So the only thing standing between a member and a page
   that posts this form on their behalf, inside the five-minute window, was
   guarded by nothing.
2. **The page renewing the proof's moment.** A sliding window turns five minutes
   into "five minutes after you stop looking". **And the check written for it
   could not fail either:** the whole run happens inside a second, so a renewal
   writes back the same `time()` and compares equal. **Age the proof first,
   still inside the window** — then a renewal is visible because the moment
   jumps forward.
3. **The second rule check inside the transaction deleted.** Which exposed an
   untrue sentence of the reassuring kind: the test claimed two simultaneous
   adds are protected by "the transaction and the lock `Auth::setPassword()`
   takes". **The lock makes them sequential; it does not refuse the second.**
   `storeHash()`'s existing-row branch would UPDATE and answer success, so the
   second password would silently replace the first and both members would be
   told theirs was set. What refuses it is that second ask, on facts read inside
   the lock. The lock is what makes the read trustworthy; the refusal does the
   work.

### The setting's organisation half is not reachable, and three places said it was

`auth.password.selfAdd` follows D-026: the stricter level wins, `false` being
stricter. The class implements that correctly. **But an organisation cannot
express its own "no" through any page** — measured: nothing under `web/` writes
the key outside the class, and `_apps/settings/save.php` refuses to *add* a
per-organisation row for any key the installation already holds, the four
`mail.queue.*` numbers being the only exception via `$onlyOwnRowClashes`.

This is exactly the shape #668 recorded — *"all 32 limit-shaped candidates are
seeded INSTALLATION-WIDE … so almost none of them is overridable whatever its
name suggests"* — re-created by a package that then documented the layer as
usable. The control is #755. Section G of the test inserts that row with raw
SQL and now says so, because otherwise the next reader believes a control is
there.

### And a docblock went to the wrong function, for the second time in a day

The new `comeBackAfterSignIn()` was inserted **between**
`Auth::safeRedirectUrl()`'s docblock and `safeRedirectUrl()` itself. So
`safeRedirectUrl()` had no docblock, and its `@param mixed $url` tags — plus
**the "do not narrow this back to `string`" warning that is the whole lesson of
the 27 October sign-in bypass** — sat above a function that takes no arguments.
Any tool reading docblocks would attribute it wrongly.

**#728 made the same mistake in the same sitting**, putting a block between
`RESET_LINK_FORM`'s docblock and the constant. The remedy both times is to put
a new member *after* the one below it, never between a docblock and its subject —
and the tell is two `*/` … `/**` pairs with no declaration between them.

## Phase two of the capability conversion (#739)

### What moved

Hard-coded role gates: **16 call sites → 3**. Capability gates: 51 → 64.
Counted with `php tools/role-gate-count.php` (PHP's tokeniser, comments
dropped). **Never `grep`** — it counts comments, and converting a gate *leaves
a comment naming the gate it replaced*, so the `grep` figure went **up**, to 73.

The three that remain, each for a stated reason: two take their key from a row a
customer filled in (a guided tour's `forRoles`, a report's own gate list), so
neither is a page gate; and `Photos.php`'s `volunteer` rung is a **no-op** —
both branches return the same rank — so a switch for it would open nothing
(#756).

Thirteen gates became **six** capabilities, grouped by the door and not the
role. `groups.manage` alone is six gates. `giving.records` is deliberately
**not** folded into `expenses.treasury` although both ship with `treasurer`:
folding them would hand the donor list to whoever a customer later made
responsible for paying claims, without telling them.

### Why access changed for nobody, and why that sentence was worthless until it was pinned

With no stored choice, `App::can(C)` is
`globalAdminPasses(isRootAdmin, true) || Roles::hasAnyOf([shipped key])`, and
`Roles::hasAnyOf([key])` uses the same three joins, the same `us.isActive = 1`
and the same `normaliseKey()` as `Roles::has(key)`. Every call site kept its own
`App::isAdmin()` ground, so an organisation's administrator is never shut out and
the Roles page itself is always reachable — **no capability can be emptied
unrecoverably.**

**But that guarantee was pinned by nothing, and it passed on broken code.**
Changing one word in the registry — `giving.records` shipping with
`['approver']` instead of `['treasurer']` — left **all 60 scripts in
`tools/audit-checks/` green**. Reproduced independently before anything was
changed.

The harm is concrete. On upgrade that one word hands donors' **names and home
addresses** to whoever decides expense claims. `photos.staff => ['volunteer']`
opens the staff photo tier to every signed-in member, because the volunteer rung
is a no-op.

**The cause is a naming habit.** The per-capability pin was
`$fiveShouldShipWith` while **eleven** capabilities existed, beside a second
list of fixture people called `$fiveHolders`. Neither was extended when six more
capabilities arrived, and nothing noticed, because
`check_capability_registry.py` only requires the shipped key to **exist** in
`Roles::STANDARD`, and section A of the test asserts that every capability ships
with **a** role, never **which**.

**A list named after a number is the shape that goes stale.** Both are now named
for their job, cover every offered capability, and the test is 287 checks (from
227). Planted, that one word fails two of them, and the telling one reads
*"capability says true, the old gate said false"* — which is access changing for
somebody, said in those words.

**Add a capability to `$shouldShipWith` and `$capHolders` in the same change
that adds it to the registry.** Nothing else will tell you.

### Two holes in the new guard, both of which existed in this repository already

`tools/audit-checks/check_no_new_role_gates.py` is the hard gate that stops the
conversion being undone one feature at a time. It had two:

1. **A heredoc containing an apostrophe made it report "Nothing wrong" over a
   real hard-coded gate.** `mask_php()` had no heredoc branch, so
   `<p>Don't change this</p>` opened a bogus string literal that swallowed the
   `App::hasRole(` that followed. **That is the exact fault the function's own
   docstring claimed to have closed.** It was latent rather than live only
   because the repository's single nowdoc happens to hold an *even* number of
   apostrophes; it would have fired the first time anybody wrote ordinary
   English prose in a heredoc. Fixed in both checks that share the walk, and the
   control case — the call appearing *only* inside a heredoc — must stay green.
2. **It matched two of the four `Roles` methods that answer a role question.**
   `Roles::hasAnywhere()` and `Roles::keysHeldBy()` walked straight past, and
   **both are live here** — `Gatekeeper.php` and `Workflow.php`. The check's own
   argument for covering `has()` and `hasAnyOf()` is that without it "the whole
   check is one search-and-replace away from being decorative"; that argument
   applies word for word to the other two methods on the same class.

What it still cannot see, measured by planting each: a class alias, a variable
class name, and a key built by concatenation. **A fully qualified
`\Portal\Core\App::hasRole()` IS caught** — the pattern is
`\bApp\s*::\s*hasRole` and a backslash is a word boundary — and an earlier
version of the list claimed otherwise. Untrue in the *modest* direction still
misleads the next reader about what is covered.

### Six untrue sentences, and where they came from

| Claim | Measured |
|---|---|
| `canSee()` is the read-only test | the method is `canView()`; `canSee()` does not exist |
| "22 files name `tblUserRoles` in a query" | its own command answers **25**; two of those name only `tblUserRolesUnplaced`; two mentions are prose or a comment |
| that paragraph's own breakdown | summed to **21**, leaving four files uncategorised — `Workflow.php` among them |
| "12 remaining gates naming 6 role keys" | **14** fixed-key gates naming **7**; `Photos.php`'s staff rung, a real conversion, was in no bullet |
| "six offered capabilities and FIVE declare `globalAdminFallsOpen`" | **12 and 11** — written one paragraph below that same docblock's lesson about stale counts |
| "The seven added by #739" | six |

The stale-count sentence now **names no number at all** and points at the
registry, because re-numbering it would only reset the clock.

## Making content translation reachable (#485, #761)

*4 November 2026. The technical record; `CHANGELOG.md` says what shipped and
`.claude/CLAUDE.md` holds the standing rule.*

### The transferable lesson

**Making an unreachable handler reachable is the act that makes its faults
live.** `_apps/api/translate.php` had sat in the repository since #278 with three
serious faults, and none of them was exploitable, because `ApiRouter` resolves
`api/{app}/{action}` under `_apps/{app}/api/` and that address had two segments.
Every audit check was green over it. The temptation when finishing such a feature
is to move the file to the convention path and seed its switch — twenty minutes'
work — and that single act would have published all three.

So the order matters: **read the handler as though it were already live, before
making it live.** The same applies to AI Assist (#277, #658), which is the same
shape and still unreachable, and that is now recorded on #485 and in FEATURES.md.

### The three faults, and why fault 2 catches no test by accident

1. **`lookupCached()` asks nothing about who is reading.** It is keyed on
   `(sourceTable, sourceID, sourceField, targetLanguage)` alone. The old handler
   passed whatever row number was posted, so any signed-in person could read back
   any organisation's translated words.
2. **The text came from `$_POST['text']`.** The allow-list of tables therefore
   constrained the *label*, not the words — and `persist()` then cached the result
   against a real row's number. **This is the one that survives testing**, because
   the feature keeps working: the button translates, something comes back, the
   cache fills. Only a reader comparing the cached text with the row would notice.
   Section C of the self-test posts a `text` field carrying something else and
   requires the answer to be a translation of the *row*.
3. **Nothing checked the caller could see the row.**

**The cache key needed no change, and that is worth saying because adding a
`siteID` column looks like the obvious fix.** `sourceID` is the primary key of a
row in one of the source tables, and those keys are global, so a cache row already
identifies exactly one source row in exactly one organisation. The key was never
ambiguous; the gate in front of it was missing. A denormalised `siteID` on
`tblContentTranslation` would have been a second copy of a fact that can
disagree with the first.

### What the fixture had to contain for section D to mean anything

D02 asks whether a member of organisation A can read back organisation B's
cached translation. **A world in which nothing had ever been translated would
pass on the broken code**, because there would be nothing for the cache to hand
over. So B's announcement is put into `tblContentTranslation` first, and D01
asserts that it really is there before D02 runs. The row is inserted with SQL
rather than earned by B's own member, because the harness serves one
organisation; that is stated at the point it matters, and the state is one
production reaches the moment B's member presses the button — a fixture in a
state production can never reach tests nothing.

### Three faults of mine, all found by running it rather than reading it

**An HTML comment put the control's own attribute into every page the portal
served.** `footer.php` explained the script in an HTML comment that named
`data-portal-translate`. Two costs: a developer's note shipped to every visitor,
and four checks became wrong, because searching a page for the attribute found
the comment on pages that have no control. That is #647's shape — a check
answered by a comment mentioning the thing — in a new place. Notes for developers
belong in PHP comments, which are not served.

**A clause that could not fail.** The gate's "no language was asked for" test
read `Translation::normaliseLocale($facts['targetLanguage'])` and compared it
with `''`. `normaliseLocale('')` answers `'en'`. So a press with no language was
read as English, got as far as the database, and came back "already in that
language" with HTTP 200. Caught by a check that asserted the refusal.

**`Translation::detect()` read an English sentence as Welsh.** "We are raising
money for a new boiler in the church hall" — `' a '` is one of its Welsh markers,
the English markers scored the same 1, and a tie goes to whichever language the
list reaches first, which is Welsh. The press then translated nothing. The
detector is a cheap guess and `api-spec.json` says so; the fixture was reworded.

### Two measured limits left behind, each with an issue

**The monthly limit cannot bite on the `libre` route (#762).**
`libreTranslate()` returns `costPence => 0` — honest for a self-hosted
LibreTranslate, which is free — and `monthSpendPence()` sums that column. So
nothing is ever added to the spend and the cap is inert for that provider. The
four paid providers all report a figure. The self-test therefore makes spending
happen by writing a row's `costPence` directly, and says so in its header.

**A member's saved interface language is applied nowhere (#763).** Established
with commands rather than reasoned: `I18n::init()` is called at
`web/_core/bootstrap.php:891`; the session starts at
`web/public_html/index.php:67`, after bootstrap is required, and index.php's own
comment says start-up leaves no session started; and
`grep -rn "I18n::init\|resolveLocale" web/` finds no second call anywhere. So
`resolveLocale()` can never reach source 1 (the member's row) or source 2 (the
language switcher), and the block at `bootstrap.php:924` that would read
`tblUsers.locale` cannot run. Measured: a member whose row says `cy` was served a
control asking for `en`. `ContentTranslation::readerLanguage()` therefore reads
that column itself — which is also simply the right source, because the
translation is made *for one person*. Fixing `I18n` changes the language every
page is drawn in on every installation, so it is the owner's decision.

### What the tests cannot do, said once here as well

No outside company is called: the run starts a stub on its own port and points
the `libre` provider at it. So nothing proves a paid provider's own cost figure
is right. One worker means two members translating the same piece at once is
untested, and such a test would pass on broken code. And **no request can tell
the engine's internal order from the handler's gate** — both ask
`translation.enabled` and the handler asks first — so the reorder of
`Translation::translate()` (switch before cache) is defence in depth, exercised
by nothing. That was found by planting the old order and watching the check stay
green; an earlier label claimed it caught the reorder, which was a reassurance
the check could not support.

### What the first independent check found, and the three shapes worth keeping

**ONE FORM TOKEN PER SESSION MEANS ONE PER PAGE, NOT ONE PER BUTTON.**
`Auth::csrfToken()` returns the session's single token and `Auth::verifyCsrf()`
replaces it on every acceptance. So a page carrying several controls — and
`/projects/view` carries one per update, up to 21 — plus an ordinary form, has
them all stamped with the same string, and the first accepted press invalidates
the rest. Measured: press Translate, then pledge, and the pledge is refused with
a bare "Bad request" with what the member typed gone. **A refused form token is
the ONE refusal that carries no replacement**, because
`ApiAuth::requireWrite()` answers it before recording the rotation — so a stale
control could never recover and showed a member the words "CSRF check failed" on
every press. The rule, which #625 states and this missed: *a page that writes
more than once must be handed the replacement token and must keep it* — keep it
for the PAGE. `shareToken()` writes every replacement into every control and
every `input[name="csrf_token"]`.

**"NOTHING HAS BEEN CHARGED" IS A CLAIM ABOUT SOMEBODY ELSE'S MONEY, AND THE
PORTAL CANNOT MAKE IT.** A provider call answering HTTP 200 with an unexpected
shape, or timing out after the provider has accepted the request, returns null
and has still been billed. The sentence stood in three places — the member's
refusal, api-spec.json and the help page — while the script's own comment said
the opposite correctly. **Two halves of one package contradicting each other,
and the half a customer reads was the reassuring one.** What is certain is that
nothing was added to the portal's own record of the spend, so that is what the
words now say.

**A CONDITION NO FIXTURE CAN TRIP IS NOT A CONDITION — and it took TWO rounds to
find all five, which is the lesson.** Round 1 found that the project statement's
organisation test and its `isPublic` could both be deleted with all 66 checks and
all 61 gates green, because the world held organisation B's ANNOUNCEMENT and no
project of B, no update of B and no unpublished project. Three rows and four
checks closed those two — **and the note written beside them claimed the class
was closed.** Round 2 then found three more of exactly the same kind: the
project-UPDATE's own `isPublic` (the only update in the world had a public
parent), and the announcement statement's `isDeleted` and `publishAt` clauses
(every announcement fixture had `isDeleted = 0` and `publishAt` NULL).

**Five, not two.** The transferable part is not "add fixtures" — it is that a
fix round which closes the instances it was handed will write a sentence saying
the class is closed, and that sentence is wrong unless somebody enumerated the
whole class first. Here the enumeration is mechanical: every clause in every
`SOURCES` statement needs a fixture that fails it.

**And "five" was itself a false completeness count, in the paragraph about false
completeness counts** — round 3 found it. Five was the number of previously
UNTRIPPABLE clauses, written as though it were the number of clauses. Beyond the
three primary-key tests there are **nine**: the announcement's `siteID`,
`isPublished`, `isDeleted`, `publishAt` and `expiresAt`; the project's `siteID`
and `isPublic`; the update's `p.siteID` and `p.isPublic`. Round 3 planted all
nine and every one turned at least one check red, so the class really is covered
— but the sentence telling the next reader how to check that would have stopped
them at five, and three of the four it omitted are organisation tests. **The
honest form of such a sentence names the METHOD, not a total**, because the total
is the part that goes stale.

**AND TWO OF MY OWN FIXES FAILED FOR THE SAME REASON WITHIN AN HOUR OF EACH
OTHER, which is the most useful thing here.** Both were checks that could not
fire:

* `"$_SERVER['HTTP_"` searched in a MASKED copy. Masking turns string contents
  into `x`, and that name is half code and half string literal, so it could
  never match — and the planted header reading the text went on passing. **A
  pattern that spans the boundary between code and a string cannot be searched
  for in a copy where one side has been blanked.** Ask for `$_SERVER`.
* `"shareToken(" not in script` was satisfied by `function shareToken(payload)`.
  **A definition is not a use.** Deleting the only call left the check green
  while the whole fix was gone. The same shape as the QR guard's version 1,
  which passed on a commented-out function, and #739's check that passed on a
  renamed one. Pin the call, excluding the definition.

**The script was read by nothing at all.** Deleting the token sharing and
changing `textContent` to `innerHTML` left 61 audit checks and 66 self-test
checks green — and the `innerHTML` rule is what stops an outside translation
company putting markup into this portal's pages. Check F of the gate reads both
rules as text now. **Nothing exercises that script's own behaviour**, so the
toggle, the deadline and the abort path are exercised by nothing, and the
self-test's header says that rather than implying coverage.

> **Corrected 5 November 2026 (#768).** This said "No test in this repository
> drives a browser", which was already untrue: `tools/layout-audit.mjs` has
> driven Edge over the DevTools protocol since `0186531` (30 October 2026), and
> `tools/csrf-carriers-selftest.mjs` does now too. Neither runs *that* script,
> so the conclusion stands; the reason given for it did not. Established with
> `grep -rln "remote-debugging-port" tools/` — a command nobody ran before
> writing the claim, which is the habit the rule about "never worked" exists to
> enforce.

**An empty box is a value somebody submitted.** `(float) ''` and `(float) 'abc'`
are both `0.0`, and `0` means "no limit" for this setting — the LARGEST value.
So an administrator clearing the monthly limit to start again, and pressing Save,
switched the cap off with no refusal and no activity-log line. `min="0"` does not
stop an empty field being submitted. An unreadable figure is refused now, which
leaves a deliberate `0` as the only way to say "no limit" — and the comment that
had claimed zero was "tested for separately" says where it is really handled
(`SettingLimit`, through `$zeroIsLargest`).

### Round 2: the same fault one step on, three times

**THE TOKEN HAS THREE CARRIERS, NOT TWO.** Round 1's fix shared the replacement
with every control and every `input[name="csrf_token"]`. `header.php` also puts
`<meta name="csrf-token">` on **every** page, and five scripts read the token
from there rather than from a form — `portal.js` (which `Portal.apiRequest`
uses), `portal-tour.js`, `push-subscribe.js`, `report-builder.js`,
`event-hub-upload.js`, the first two on every page. Measured: after a Translate
press, a guided-tour post answered 403 "Invalid CSRF token" on the same page
where the pledge fault had been measured. **And the portal already had the
pattern** — `event-hub-upload.js`'s `syncCsrf()` writes the meta tag and every
field, and `Portal.rememberCsrf()` does the meta half — so this was a third copy
of one rule with a half missing. **When you find yourself writing a third copy of
something, go and read the other two.**

**PINNING A CALL IS NOT ENOUGH, TWICE OVER.** Check F went through three
versions, each bypassed:

* v1 asked whether `shareToken(` appeared — satisfied by `function shareToken(`.
  A definition is not a use.
* v2 asked for a call that is not the definition — satisfied by
  `if (false) { shareToken(…); }`. **#709's round-2 lesson exactly: when you pin
  a call, pin the gate that decides whether its block runs.**
* v3 asked whether two selector strings appeared — satisfied by changing the
  write loop to `index < 0`. The selector is still there and the fix is gone.

The remedy is the one `check_table_name_comparisons.py` already uses: **pin the
whole body and the call line**, so any edit fails on purpose and has to be read.
That is deliberately annoying, and it is the only thing standing in front of a
fault measured to break a payment form, on a script no test in this repository
runs.

**A FIX'S OWN GUARD IS PART OF THE FIX.** Round 1's money fix — refusing a
monthly limit that cannot be read — was correct and was pinned by nothing:
deleting the whole refusal block left 73 checks and 61 gates green, because
nothing in `tools/` had ever posted to `/admin/translation/save`. The behaviour
was right and the next edit would have taken it away silently.

**A NEW MESSAGE CAN BE UNTRUE THE MOMENT IT IS WRITTEN.** "This page has been
open a while, please reload" was shown for every 403 carrying no replacement —
but `ApiRouter` answers 403 "This API endpoint is disabled" before any rotation,
so with the endpoint switched off a member was told to reload for ever while the
portal's own accurate words were thrown away. The same shape in the abort path:
"press Translate again — if the first attempt did get through, the second is
free" is a dead end precisely when the first attempt got through, because its
token was spent. **Advice has to be checked against the states that really
produce it, not the state it was written for.**

### Round 4, and the only lesson that generalises: I kept closing instances

Four independent check rounds, and **every one found a one-edit change that left
the previous round's pin green while the script's token sharing was dead or
partial:**

| round | the bypass |
|---|---|
| 2 | the call deleted; the call inside `if (false)`; the form loop made `index < 0` |
| 3 | the call wrapped but keeping its assignment; a `return` above it; the line moved into a dead function; a SECOND `function shareToken()` |
| 4 | `shareToken = function () {…}` — a reassignment, the round-3 case written differently; `&&` → `||` in the reload guard, one character; three weaker ones |

Each round I read the plants, closed those spellings, and wrote a comment saying
the class was shut. **The comment was wrong four times.** Round 3's even named
#709's lesson — *when you pin a call, pin the gate that decides whether its
block runs* — while leaving the binding and the condition unpinned.

**The remedy was not a fifth cleverer pattern.** It was to stop probing for
spellings and pin the file: its code, comments stripped and whitespace
normalised **with its line breaks kept**, must equal a committed copy. Any
change to a statement fails, including a harmless rename, and `--repin`
regenerates it as a deliberate separate act. That is a
heavy instrument and it is right in exactly one circumstance, which holds here:
**nothing runs the file**, so there is no behavioural test behind the pin, and
the faults it stands in front of were measured — a pledge form refused with the
member's typing lost, a guided-tour post answering 403, a member told to reload
when reloading cannot help.

**When to reach for a whole-file pin, then:** when the thing is small, nothing
executes it, and a wrong edit is both invisible and costly. Otherwise write a
test.

### The same shape in the test harness, twice

Round 3 found that section J posted no `libre_base`, so each save rewrote the
provider's address to a real outside URL; the fix was to post that field. Round
4 found `translation.anthropic.model` and `translation.openai.model` being reset
to the handler's defaults by the same eleven presses, and never put back — with
the run reporting 88 passed and its clean-up check green, because that check
counts rows in the test's own number range and a settings row is not one.

**The class: it is not enough to track the settings a test WRITES. Track every
setting anything the test PRESSES can write.** A save handler that upserts from
`??` defaults changes every key it knows about, whether or not the form carried
it. `rememberSetting()` records a key without changing it, and the measurement
that proves it is marker values in all six rows surviving a full run — not the
absence of a complaint.

### Round 5: the pin's own hole, and it was whitespace

**IN JAVASCRIPT A NEWLINE IS A SEMICOLON.** Automatic semicolon insertion ends a
statement after `return`, `throw`, `break`, `continue` and `++`/`--`. The first
whole-file pin normalised *all* whitespace to single spaces, so

    return
        box.querySelector('[data-portal-translate-output]');

normalised to the same text as `return box.querySelector(…);` — and that one
added newline made `outputBlock()` answer `undefined`, so a translation that had
arrived and been paid for was discarded while the member was told nothing came
back. **It still parses**, which is what makes it the dangerous kind. Measured
by executing the file in node against a stub DOM, not reasoned.

So the fifth round found the same class of one-edit bypass as rounds 2, 3 and 4
— reached through the NORMALISER rather than through a spelling. The lesson that
generalises: **when you normalise before comparing, enumerate what the
normalisation throws away and ask whether the language cares about any of it.**
For JavaScript the answer is yes for line breaks and no for indentation; for
Python it would be the opposite; for SQL, case.

`normalised_code()` keeps line breaks, frees indentation, blank lines and
comment text, and is used by both the comparison and `--repin` — one function,
because two copies would let the generator and the checker disagree and the pin
would then certify whatever the generator produced. Checked both ways: three
newline plants go red, and re-indenting, a blank line and an edited comment all
stay green. The residue is stated in the header, and round 6 showed the first
statement of it was understated: it is ANY whitespace inside a string literal,
in either direction, and one string did depend on it (see below).

### Round 6: the invisible character, and a residue understated in the direction that bites

**JAVASCRIPT ENDS A `//` COMMENT AT FOUR CHARACTERS**, not one: LF, CR, U+2028
LINE SEPARATOR and U+2029 PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR. The comment blanker ended one at
`\n`. Python's universal-newline read folds a lone CR, so that case was safe by
accident; U+2028 and U+2029 came through untouched, the blanker ran past them to
the end of the physical line, blanked the real code after them, and
`splitlines()` then had nothing to split on, so the whole line was dropped as
blank.

One added line therefore put `output.innerHTML = String(data.translation || '')`
live with the gate green and every audit check green — proved by executing the
file in node, where the planted markup ran. **It defeated both guards at once**:
the whole-file pin, and the `innerHTML` search which is the only security rule
in that check.

**The accident is worse than the attack.** U+2028 is what text pasted out of a
PDF or a word processor carries. A `//` comment whose *text* contains one, with
no code after it at all, makes the whole file fail to parse — so the control
silently does nothing on every page, while the gate says OK. That is precisely
the fault class the pin exists for.

**The transferable rule, which is the one from round 5 sharpened:** when you
blank or split on a delimiter, use the delimiter set THE LANGUAGE uses, not the
one your own language's library offers. `str.find("\n")` is Python's idea of a
line ending; JavaScript has four, SQL has its own comment forms, and a CSV has
quoting. Enumerate them from the target language's specification.

**And a residue I had written down was understated.** "A double space inside a
string literal collapses to one" is true and incomplete: a tab and a
non-breaking space do too, and the direction that bites is turning one space
INTO two. `'CSRF check failed'` is matched against the exact words `ApiAuth`
sends, so any of the three silently shows a member the raw words "CSRF check
failed" on every press. Writing "no string in the pinned file depends on that"
beside it made it a reassurance the check could not support — this repository's
own named shape. That one comparison is checked separately and un-normalised
now; the residue remains, honestly stated, for strings that do not have to match
anything exactly.

### Round 7: "it does not parse" is a third thing a pin cannot see

The U+2028 fix closed one route to the worst outcome — the file fails to parse,
so nothing in it runs, the Translate control silently does nothing on every
page, and the gate says OK. Round 7 found two more, and the first is an accident
rather than an attack:

* **A `/*` that is never closed, after the last statement.** `blank_comments()`
  treats an unterminated block comment as "comment to the end of the file" and
  blanks it; JavaScript refuses the whole file with "Unterminated comment". With
  no statement after it, the normalised code is unchanged, so the pin matched.
  A comment begun and not finished, or a paste cut short at the end of a file,
  does this.
* **U+001F in a statement.** `str.split()` counts it as whitespace and removes
  it; JavaScript rejects it as an illegal character. It is the ONE C0 control
  Python strips without splitting — U+0085, U+001C, U+001D and U+001E all broke
  the pin by accident, which is why only this one got through.

**The lesson, and it is the third form of the same one.** A pin compares what it
can see after normalising. Rounds 5, 6 and 7 were each a thing the normalisation
threw away: a line break (semicolon insertion), a Unicode line terminator
(comment ending), and now a control character and an unclosed delimiter. So the
question to ask of any normalise-then-compare guard is not only *"what does the
language care about that I discard?"* but also **"could the input be something
the language refuses outright, which my reader accepts?"** `js_will_not_parse()`
asks that first, before the comparison, because a file that does not run cannot
be guarded by comparing its code.

Two smaller things worth keeping. `repin()` was the one read that did not fold —
so the generator and the checker could disagree about a U+2028-bearing file,
which is precisely what sharing one function is meant to prevent. **It failed
safe**, which is why it is a note rather than a fault: the gate stayed red and
nothing was blessed. But the failure message said "run `--repin`", and on that
input `--repin` could never make it green, with nothing explaining why — advice
that cannot work is its own kind of untrue. And `\v`/`\f` used as whitespace made
the pin go red over perfectly legal JavaScript, because Python's `splitlines()`
splits on them; both are folded to spaces now. **Crying wolf gets a check
switched off (#483), so the two directions have to be checked together.**

---

## A question asked too early (#763)

**5 November 2026.** A member's saved interface language was applied nowhere.
Not sometimes — nowhere, on every request, since the translation framework
landed in March 2026.

**Nothing was broken.** `I18n::resolveLocale()` consults four sources in order:
the member's own saved language, the language switcher's choice, the browser's
`Accept-Language` request, and the installation's default. The first two live in
the session, and both are guarded by
`session_status() === PHP_SESSION_ACTIVE`. `I18n::init()` is called from
`bootstrap.php`; the session starts in `index.php`, with
`Auth::ensureSession()`, **after** bootstrap has been required. So both guards
were false every time, both sources were skipped, and the block in bootstrap
that would have read `tblUsers.locale` was behind the same test and could not
run either. `init()` latches `$initialised`, so nothing asked again.

**The shape worth recognising: no condition was wrong and no statement was
unreachable in the ordinary sense.** Each guard is correct, the code it guards
is correct, and the whole thing is in the wrong order relative to one line in
another file. `php -l` cannot see it, no audit script could see it, and the
feature fails silently and completely. The one tell was in
`ContentTranslation::readerLanguage()`, whose author had hit the same wall,
written it down, and deliberately not fixed it.

**The switcher half was worse than the applying half.** `I18n::switchLocale()`
is the ONLY thing that has ever written `tblUsers.locale`, and it writes only
when a session is active. Its one and only caller sat in `bootstrap.php` —
established with `git log -S"switchLocale" -- web/`, which answers `fe2b3fb`
(7 March 2026) and `bd1ef12`. So `?lang=cy` applied the language to the request
that carried it and lost it in its own redirect, and the column was never
written on any installation.

**Which is what made the fix dangerous, and is the part to remember.** The
column was declared `DEFAULT 'en'`, so every account row held `'en'` — put
there by the database, not by anybody choosing. Obeying the column as it stood
would have **pinned every signed-in member to English**: somebody whose browser
asks for French and gets a French portal today would start getting an English
one, with nothing on any page explaining why. (A draft added "and no control
anywhere to change it", which is false and is finding 1 below.) `isSupported()` reads a built-in list of **thirteen** languages rather
than a setting, so browser detection is live on every installation and that
regression is real rather than theoretical. (Drafts of this said twelve. Count
them from the code: en, cy, fr, de, es, pt, ar, he, fa, ur, zh, ja, ko.) **A default value and a deliberate choice are
indistinguishable once stored, and the moment a column starts being obeyed is
the moment that stops being harmless.** Migration 251 empties the rows still
holding the default and changes the default to NULL; the measured ground for
calling that safe is the `git log -S` above. D-060.

**Two guards, and neither can prove the thing that matters.**
`tools/i18n-member-language-selftest.php` drives the class over a real MySQL,
reproducing the real order — `init()` with no session, then a session carrying
a member whose row says `cy` — and with the fix removed the answer stays on
`Accept-Language`. `check_member_language_applied.py` fails when either call
goes missing, when either drifts back above `Auth::ensureSession()`, and when
start-up makes either call again. Neither tells you whether a page RENDERS in
Welsh; that needs HTTP and a seeded installation, and both say so in their own
output.

**Three smaller lessons from building it.**

* **The probe must buffer its output**, or `session_start()` refuses and source
  1 is skipped for the WRONG reason — the test then reports a false failure on
  correct code, which is the hardest kind of red to diagnose.
* **A check that masks string literals cannot look at an array key.** Masking
  turned `$_GET['lang']` into `$_GET['xxxx']`, so the clause requiring the
  `is_string()` gate could never match: a clause that cannot fail, dressed as
  the strictest check in the file. It reads a comments-removed, strings-kept
  view for that one question, and says why at the point of the call.
* **The second fixture must differ in only one way.** Section F's "unknown
  language is refused" check is only worth anything because the row already
  holds `cy`: starting from an empty column, "nothing was written" passes
  whether the refusal works or not.

**And the first independent check found twelve problems, none in the fix
itself.** The worst two are the lesson.

**I told the owner there was no control for choosing a language anywhere in the
portal, and there is one on every page.** `I18n::languageSwitcher()` renders a
globe dropdown printed from `nav.php` twice -- once for a signed-in person,
once for a visitor -- and `header.php` always requires `nav.php`. One
`grep -rn languageSwitcher web tools` would have shown it. The owner declined
to build a picker on the strength of my sentence (D-061), which D-062 now
supersedes. **A claim that something does not exist anywhere needs the search
that establishes it, exactly as a claim about history needs its `git log`** --
this file already says so for history and the same rule was broken for the
present tense.

**And "nothing anybody sees changes on the day this ships" was untrue in two
ways, one of which costs money.** The globe menu starts working. And
`ContentTranslation::readLanguage()` reads the same column and falls back to the
browser's language when it is empty -- so emptying it turns the Translate button
from "asks for English, sees English, charges nothing" into a real, charged
translation for anybody on a non-English browser. **Ask of any column you are
about to empty: who else reads it, and what does their fallback do?** The owner
accepted the change deliberately (D-063).

**Five more were guards that passed on broken code**, three of them in the hard
gate: the call wrapped in `if (false)`; the call with its argument dropped,
which is legal PHP because the parameter defaults to null and which restores
half of #763 in full; and `&& false` appended to the `?lang=` condition, which
stops a language ever being chosen again. The remedies were this repository's
usual ones -- compare brace depth against `Auth::ensureSession()`, require the
argument, pin the whole condition as one string. **Three self-test clauses could
not fail** because the browser header and the default locale were both `'en'`,
so the right answer and the wrong answer were the same string.

**The migration's own comment argued for the worse of its two orders.** It put
the row-emptying first and claimed the reverse order would leave a row behind;
walking both showed the opposite, and the window is now closed. Its "safe to
run twice" was also MySQL-only: MariaDB reports `COLUMN_DEFAULT` as a literal
expression, never SQL NULL, so the `ALTER` re-runs on every replay. Same end
state, measured twice -- just not free.

**A SECOND ROUND FOUND SEVEN MORE, SIX OF THEM IN ROUND 1'S FIXES, AND THE
HEADLINE IS ONE SENTENCE: I CLOSED THE SPELLINGS I WAS HANDED.** Round 1's plant
was "the argument dropped", so the gate was taught to ask whether the brackets
held anything -- and `reconsiderNowSessionExists(null)` passed it, one word, the
same harm, with the check printing "the reconsider call is passed a connection"
while it was not. The account-page checks were presence-only, so `false &&` in
front of the save gate left a member picking a language, pressing Save, being
told it worked, and nothing stored, ever. **This is #485's four-round lesson
re-made inside a single round**, and the remedy is the same one that closed it
there: pin the whole statement, not a substring of it. Five statements are
pinned now.

**The worst live bug was the control I had just built, and it DELETED things.**
The select was filled from `enabledLocales()` -- readable `web/_lang/*.php`
files, two on a stock installation -- while a choice is accepted by
`isSupported()`, a hard-coded list of thirteen. So a member who had stored `ar`
matched no option, and because `$langStored !== ''` the "Follow my browser"
option got no `selected` either: the whole `<select>` carried no `selected`
attribute, every browser pre-selected the first option, `value=""`, and pressing
"Save Changes" **to correct a telephone number** posted an empty language and
wiped their choice. Measured on the real class. **A `<select>` with no
`selected` option is not neutral -- it is a vote for option one**, and if option
one means "forget my choice" then every unrelated save is a deletion. The stored
language is always offered now, labelled "not translated yet, so pages read in
English" rather than hidden.

**And the label was wrong for exactly the people who would read it.** "Follow my
browser (X today)" was built from `I18n::locale()` -- the language the page is
being DRAWN in, which after this very fix IS the member's stored choice. The
option exists only to undo a choice, so it was shown only to people with one,
and for every one of them it named the wrong language. `I18n::browserLanguage()`
exists for this. **When a label describes an alternative, build it from the
alternative, never from the current state.**

**Two sentences were untrue in the reassuring direction, again.** "Both offer
the same languages, from the same list" -- the top-bar menu additionally hides
any language below `portal.i18n.minimum_coverage_for_switcher`, a real seeded
setting, and `coverage('cy')` measures 0.30, so at the threshold the menu's own
comment suggests the menu vanishes entirely while the account page still offers
Welsh. And **D-060, written in the very commit that corrected "no control
anywhere" and "twelve languages" everywhere else, contained both of them** --
the register's permanent record of the decision in force, stating the falsehood
with no correction beside it. It has a note now. **Writing the correction is not
the same as applying it to the thing you are writing.**

**And a third reader of the column was missed, after I had written the rule for
finding it.** `ReportRegistry` offers `u.locale` as a displayable, filterable
column of the Members report, and report definitions are SAVED. Before the
migration every row held `'en'`; afterwards a saved report showing Locale prints
blanks and one filtering `Locale = en` -- which matched every member -- matches
nobody. The commit's own transferable lesson was "ask of any column you are
about to empty: who else reads it, and what does their fallback do?" It reached
two of three. **Enumerate with a command** --
`grep -rnE "SELECT .locale.|'expr' => 'u\.locale'" web/_apps web/_core` answers
exactly those three -- **not from memory, and not from the sweep you did before
you wrote the rule.** #780.

**And the first command I cited for that did not return what the sentence
claimed.** It was `grep -rn "u\.locale\|\`locale\`" web/_apps web/_core`, and
it answers ELEVEN lines: six comments, the WRITER, and the three reads. The
sentence introducing it was the transferable rule itself. **Citing a command that
does not return what you say it returns is worse than citing none**, because the
next reader runs it, counts eleven, and stops trusting the sentence -- and this
repository's own record already says `grep` counts comments.

**A THIRD ROUND FOUND SIX MORE, FIVE OF THEM IN ROUND 2'S GUARD WORK, AND THE
PATTERN IS NOW THE FINDING.** Round 1 handed me `if (false) { ... }`, so I
answered with a brace count -- and `if (false)` with NO BRACES walked through,
and so did `false &&` glued in front. Round 2 handed me "the argument dropped",
so I answered "are the brackets empty" -- and the literal `(null)` walked
through. Round 2 pinned the gate CONDITIONS, so emptying the block BODY walked
through, and so did `chooseLanguage(null)` (every profile save deletes every
member's language) and `$langStored === false` inside the option loop. Six
spellings, one fault: **the statement is still there and does nothing.**

**The remedy was not a fifth pattern. It is the one #485 took four rounds to
reach: pin the whole region as TEXT.** Three regions now --
`index.php` from `Auth::ensureSession()` through the `?lang=` block, the account
page's control, and the account handler's language block -- held in
`tools/audit-checks/member-language.pinned.txt` and regenerated by `--repin`, so
a deliberate change is a separate visible act. The four substring pins and the
brace-depth test came OUT: two guards over one fact drift apart, and a pattern
left as dead code under an authoritative comment is one somebody will edit
believing it works.

**And a whole-region pin has THREE holes, not the "exactly one" an earlier
version of this paragraph claimed — the fourth check round measured the other
two.** The first: it cannot see something glued IN FRONT of its first
statement. `if (false)` on the line above, no braces, makes the entire region
the body of a conditional that never runs while the region's own text is
untouched -- measured, the gate green while a member's language could never be
stored. Moving the start anchor one statement earlier only moves the hole, so
**a pinned region must BEGIN A FRESH STATEMENT** — the last thing before it,
whitespace aside, `;`, `}` or an opening `<?php`.

**THAT RULE CALLED ITSELF GENERAL THREE TIMES AND WAS DEFEATED THREE TIMES, AND
THE FIFTH CHECK ROUND DIAGNOSED IT BETTER THAN ANY OF MY FIXES HAD.** Its words
are worth keeping: "`;`/`}` is not a weaker allow-list than `;{}:>`, it is the
same KIND of rule. Nothing about the last character can distinguish 'a fresh
statement at the level the region belongs to' from 'a fresh statement inside a
dead block'." Measured: `if (false) { ;` and `switch (0) { case 1: {}` both end
in an allowed character and both wrap the whole region in dead code, `php -l`
clean, gate green — and combining one with a differently-spelled live copy
defeated the uniqueness rule too, because the anchor then matched only the dead
copy.

**So the question is NESTING, not the preceding token, and that is what is
pinned now.** `structure_at()` records three numbers beside each region's text:
how many `{` are open where it starts, how many alternative-syntax blocks
(`if (…):` … `endif;`, which change no brace count), and how many `return` /
`exit` / `die` sit at its own level before it — because a bare `return;` above a
region changes neither count and makes it unreachable just the same. Nine
wrapping spellings now go red, including five nobody handed me
(`while (false) { }`, `else if (false) {`, `foreach ([] as $x): … endforeach;`,
`do { } while (false);`, and the bare `return;`). **That is the test the lesson
demanded: try the spellings nobody gave you.**

**AND THAT ENUMERATION WAS UNTRUE IN THE REASSURING DIRECTION, which the sixth
round found.** It listed only things a static check genuinely cannot prove — a
conditional `require` of the file, a `goto`, an exception above it — and read as
though every remaining escape needed that excuse. It did not: five more PLAIN
wrappings were still getting through, because **the hand-written reader was
