wrong about PHP**, which is a different thing from the rule being too narrow.
The sixth round measured `$endif = 1;` cancelling the hand-rolled `endif`
counter; a `}` inside a heredoc body cancelling the brace counter;
`#[Deprecated]` read as a `#` comment and hiding a `{`; `'?>'` inside a string
ending the PHP span early so a `/* } */` counted as code; and
`<!-- <?php if (false) { ?> -->`, which **PHP executes** and the reader blanked.
Plus one in the other direction: `$exit = false;` — a variable name this
repository uses twelve times — counted as an exit, so the guard cried wolf on
correct code.

**SO THE SEVENTH VERSION STOPPED HAND-PARSING PHP AND ASKED PHP.**
`tools/audit-checks/member-language-structure.php` reads the three regions with
`token_get_all()` and reports their text, nesting, anchor count and the token
before them; the Python check is a wrapper that refuses loudly when PHP is
missing and has **no fallback to reading the PHP itself**, because six rounds
proved there is no second-best reading to drop to. After that, `$endif` is a
`T_VARIABLE` and `endif` is `T_ENDIF`; `#[` is an attribute; a brace in a
heredoc is part of an encapsed string; a `'?>'` in a string is a string; and PHP
in an HTML comment is PHP. **None of the six spellings is expressible any
more**, because the distinctions were never in the text — they are in the
grammar.

**A FIRST VERSION OF THAT SENTENCE ADDED "and neither are the ones nobody has
thought of", AND THE SEVENTH ROUND MEASURED THREE THAT ARE.** Each is one
ordinary statement, one line above a region, `php -l` clean, killing the region
with the probe reporting no change at all:

    if (true) { exit; }
    { exit; }                 (a bare block — it runs unconditionally)
    while (true) { }

The first two are braced, so the `exit` sits a level deeper than the region and
the own-level test skipped it. **They are caught now**, by a second count of
exits at ANY depth above the region, whose cost is stated rather than hidden:
adding a new guard above the region needs a `--repin`, which is a visible act,
and an exit newly placed above the code that stores somebody's language is worth
having to acknowledge.

**The third is not caught and cannot be.** "Does this loop finish" is not a
question a parser answers, and neither is "can this condition be false" — which
is why a legitimate `if (badRequest) { exit; }` above a region must not read as
a kill. That is the honest end of what a static guard does here, and exactly why
#781 exists: all three of those wrappings fail a test that drives the page.

**The seventh round also found three ways this guard CRIED WOLF on correct code,
and under #483 those are what get a check switched off.** The anchor was found
and counted in the RAW source — the one path left that did not ask PHP, in a
file whose whole argument is that raw text cannot be trusted — so a comment
quoting it reported "appears 2 times, so this pin is worthless" and sent the
reader hunting for dead code that does not exist. `index.php` already carries
two such comments and was saved only by their missing semicolon; a string
quoting it was worse, relocating the whole region inside the string. `else:` and
`elseif:` were counted as alternative-syntax OPENERS, so adding an ordinary
`else` branch to a balanced block eighty-five lines above the region reported
the region had MOVED. And `die` as a plain name was counted as an exit "to be
safe" — measured on PHP 8.5, `die` is `T_EXIT` in every context where it exits
and a plain name only as a method, so the branch caught no exit and fired on
`$log->die()`. **"Counting both to be safe" was the cry-wolf direction.**

**Two things were also dead under authoritative comments:** a `HEREDOC_MARK`
constant that a comment named as the mechanism refusing a heredoc, when the
refusal is the probe's own token flag, and a sixty-line `block_end()` helper
nothing called. That is the second time in this package a comment has named a
heredoc safeguard that did not do the work — the first named one that had never
been written at all. **Name the thing that does the work, and delete what does
not.**

Fourteen wrapping spellings go red, and the three cry-wolf cases stay green.

**AND THEN MOST OF THE GUARD WAS DELETED, WHICH IS THE REAL LESSON OF THE WHOLE
PACKAGE.** Eight independent review rounds went into it: 12, 7, 6, 6, 3, 3, 6, 9
findings — **52 in all, every one after the first round in the GUARD and not one
in the fix**, which every round confirmed correct. Six rounds each found a new
way to wrap a region in dead code, each answered with a sharper pattern; the
eighth found the guard still REFUSING correct work — a passing comment that
merely mentioned the guarded call made it report the pin "worthless", and an
ordinary helper above the region made it report that the region had "moved".
**A check that cries wolf gets switched off (#483)**, so by then the rounds were
not buying protection at all.

**The instrument was the mistake, not the sharpening.** "Is this code reached"
is behavioural, and the forms no source-reading check can ever see —
`while (true) { }` above it, `trigger_error` at `E_USER_ERROR`, a conditional
`require` of the file — are not edge cases but the same question asked again.
On the owner's decision (**D-065**) the guard was cut from roughly 1,235 lines
to 521: what stays is presence and ORDER, which in eight rounds produced no
finding and cannot cry wolf. What replaced the rest is
`tools/i18n-member-language-http-selftest.php` — 24 checks that sign a member
in, load the real account page, choose a language, save, and read the column
back. **Every wrapping the pin caught also fails it, and so do the four classes
it could not see.**

**The transferable rule: where the property is "this code RUNS", drive it; where
it is "this code LOOKS like this", pin it.** (#485's pinned script is the
closest relative and stays, because its justification is the opposite situation
— nothing executes that file, so there is nothing to drive.)

**Two checks in the new test are driven by nothing else**, and both are shapes
this repository has paid for before: a post carrying NO `locale` field must
leave the stored language alone (#677's cleared-portal-address shape), and
exactly ONE option must carry `selected`, because a `<select>` with none is a
vote for option one — which here means "forget my choice". Section F plants the
fault and proves the test goes red, which is the thing the static pin could not
do for the forms it could not see.

**And the review rule itself changed** (**D-064**): a round whose findings are
all in checks, tests or tooling now counts towards the three-round cap, while
the protected arm stays open for anything touching money, personal details,
authentication, erasure, backups or stored data. Judge each ROUND by where its
findings landed, never the package by where it started.

**The rule that got us to the tokeniser, still true as far as it goes:** when a
guard has to understand a language, use that language's own parser. Six rounds
of regular expressions lost to `$endif`, a heredoc, an attribute, a string and
an HTML comment — and the author of the fix was the one being outwitted each
time, not an attacker.

**And writing that file broke it in the most fitting way available.** A comment
explaining the HTML-comment case wrote the example out in a `//` comment — and
**a closing PHP tag inside a single-line comment ENDS PHP MODE**, so everything
below became markup and PHP reported an unclosed brace sixty lines later. The
argument for the file is that PHP's grammar holds surprises a reader will not
guess. It holds them for the author too.

**What it STILL cannot see, now that the enumeration is honest:** it reports
where a region SITS, not that the region RUNS. A conditional `require` of the
whole file, a `goto` over it, an exception thrown above it, or an `exit` inside a
function called above it all leave the numbers unchanged. **Proving reachability
needs a test that drives the page**, which is owed and is its own issue — six
rounds went into inferring statically what one HTTP request would have measured.

**And the structure check nearly shipped inert.** It looked for the anchor in a
copy whose string literals were masked — and the anchor contains `'locale'`, so
it was never found, and the function returned a neutral sentinel which I then
pinned: a check that could not fail, dressed as the strongest guard in the file.
**The only tell was the negative numbers in the sidecar.** It uses two views
now, offsets shared because masking preserves length, and a not-found anchor
returns a value that cannot equal any real measurement.

**The first version of that rule also allowed `:` and `{`, and both let
something reach across** — `if (false): ...region... endif;` and
`function neverCalled() { ...region... }`, each measured with `php -l` clean and
the guard printing "nothing is glued in front of any of them" while no member's
language could ever be stored. `switch (0) { case 1:` has the same shape. **An
allow-list written from the spellings you were handed is not a rule**, which is
the lesson of this whole file arriving one level up. (And the first version
cried wolf the other way, on the account page's own `<?php`, so both directions
have to be checked together — #483.)

**The second hole: the region is found by its FIRST match, so a dead duplicate
above the live code satisfies the pin while the live code is gutted.** Measured:
a copy of the handler block inside `if (false) { }` above the real one, the real
one replaced by a block that does nothing, guard green, and the only surviving
`chooseLanguage()` call the dead one. The start anchor must appear exactly once.

**The third: a heredoc inside a region.** Its internal whitespace is
significant and the normalisation frees whitespace, so two genuinely different
regions compare equal. Refused outright. An earlier comment claimed
`readable_code()` already refused one, citing a `NO_HEREDOC` that had never been
written — so **the enumeration #485's rule asks for was itself unsupported**,
which is the worse kind of wrong, because it is the sentence the next reader
relies on.

**Say the cost out loud: a pure reformat fails a text pin.** Whitespace runs are
freed, but PHP needs a space where a re-wrapped call previously had none, so
splitting a call across lines really does change the normalised text. Taking
whitespace out altogether is not available -- `new Foo` would become `newFoo`.
The failure message says this, and the justification is the same one #485 gave
for `portal-translate.pinned.js`: **nothing EXECUTES this code in any test**, so
a text pin is the only guard there is.

**The sixth finding was a data-loss path my own round-2 fix brought into view.**
`storedChoice()` answered null for BOTH "has not chosen" and "could not be
read", under a docblock asserting that "nothing a caller could do differs". The
account page could: after a failed read it drew "Follow my browser" as the
selected option, and the member's next Save -- for any unrelated reason, a
telephone number -- posted an empty language and wrote SQL NULL over the choice
they still had. Silently. **A reassuring sentence in a docblock is how that
survived two review rounds.** It answers three things now -- a code, null for
"has not chosen", **false for "could not be read"** -- and the page leaves the
control out and says why, because a member who cannot see their language is far
better off than one whose language is quietly deleted.

**Three documents were wrong, and one was the guard's own failure message.** It
still said the account page and the top-bar menu "can never offer different
languages" -- the menu also hides anything below
`portal.i18n.minimum_coverage_for_switcher`, and `coverage('cy')` measures 0.30,
so at the 0.95 that setting's own comment suggests the MENU VANISHES while the
account page still offers Welsh -- and it still said the list "keeps a
right-to-left language with no translation file off", which is the behaviour
round 2 deliberately removed. **That is the sentence whoever hits the failure
will act on.**

**Still open**, each recorded rather than guessed at: a restore from a snapshot
taken before this migration puts `'en'` back in every row with the migration
already marked as run, and the portal then reads it as a deliberate choice of
English (noted in the migration header, on #763); `?lang=` is a state-changing
GET with no form token, so a third-party page can set a member's language with
an `<img>` tag -- nuisance rather than data loss, and the top-bar dropdown is a
GET link by design; there is still no setting for which languages an installation
offers, because `isSupported()` reads a hard-coded list and `enabledLocales()`
reads the filesystem (#779); and a globe click made while signed OUT writes the
session key, so for that one session a member's own stored language is never
read -- no cross-member leak, because `Auth::logout()` empties and destroys the
session.

## A time on a clock is not a moment (#777, part one)

**5 November 2026.** Four pages displayed a stored clock reading with
`date('g:i A', strtotime($clock))`. Measured in Europe/London on a stored
`01:30`:

    28 March 2026   ->  1:30 AM    right
    29 March 2026   ->  2:30 AM    WRONG
    25 October 2026 ->  1:30 AM    right

`strtotime('01:30')` resolves a bare reading against **today**, in PHP's
**default** zone. On the spring-forward morning that reading does not exist, so
PHP moves it an hour — and `01:00` and `01:30` both came out as `2:00`/`2:30`,
two different stored times reading as one.

**The round trip was correct on every other day because both halves used the
same zone.** `strtotime()` and `date()` both take PHP's default, so they
cancelled out.

⚠️ **AND THAT ZONE IS NOT THE FAULT. This paragraph said "the same WRONG zone"
and "which has nothing to do with the organisation's", and both were withdrawn
in round 3 of the check — in `web/_core/I18n.php`'s own docblock, in
`.claude/CLAUDE.md`, and in `.OpenAI/CONTEXT.md` (that one only in round 16).
It survived HERE for fourteen rounds**, in the file `.claude/CLAUDE.md` names as
the technical record for this package, which is the worst place of the four for
it to survive. `web/_core/bootstrap.php` runs
`date_default_timezone_set(Site::timezone())` during start-up, so on any page
reached through the router PHP's default zone IS the organisation's. **The fault
is the DATE that `strtotime()` supplies without being asked** — today's —
because on one morning a year the hour the reading names does not exist. Same
fix, different reason, and a wrong reason sends the next reader to change the
zone.

**The transferable part is how it survived.** Round 16's finding 5 was this
exact pattern and its stated lesson was "when a finding says 'both files', DIFF
THE TWO AGAINST EACH OTHER afterwards" — and **two files was not the set.** The
claim lived in four places; fixing the two that were named left the
authoritative one standing. Round 16 is also the only round in this package to
change no line of DEV_NOTES (rounds 12 to 15 changed 45, 15, 71 and 13), which
is how a file stops being checked at all. **Enumerate every place a claim
lives, by searching for it, before calling a correction done.**

`I18n::formatClockTime()` is now the one place a clock reading becomes words,
and it builds no moment: hours and minutes come off the digits. `web/_apps/rota/`
already did the right thing by slicing the text, and is the model.

**THE MOST USEFUL THING HERE IS THAT THE TEST FOR IT CANNOT WORK.** With the old
`date('g:i A', strtotime(...))` put back inside the formatter,
`tools/clock-change-selftest.php` stayed at **40 of 40**. Of course it did: the
two agree on every ordinary day, they differ only inside the hour that does not
exist, and PHP offers no way to tell a script that today is that morning. **That
is #549's own recorded trap — "a test written in December passes in London
whatever the code does" — arriving one level up, in the test written to close
it.**

So the formatter's BODY is pinned by
`tools/audit-checks/check_clock_time_not_a_moment.py`, which fails if it ever
contains `strtotime`, `date(` or `DateTime` again. Planted, that goes red where
the behavioural test does not. **The rule being applied is D-065's, in the other
direction: where no test running today can tell, pin the source — and say why,
or the pin reads as belt and braces.**

The column names come out of `full_schema.sql` rather than a list typed in the
check (#706's lesson), so a new `TIME` column is covered without anybody
remembering. Sixteen are declared; eleven distinct names.

**AND THE GATE ITSELF WAS WRONG BOTH WAYS, which the independent check
measured.** It cried wolf because `[^;]{0,200}` blocks a semicolon but **not a
newline**, so the search walked out of the call and across the rest of a
multi-line statement: a date and a time side by side in one array literal —
ordinary, and already the shape of `calendar/feed.php` and
`venues/schedule-pdf.php` — was reported as a fault. And it passed on broken
code because `new\s+DateTime` did not allow a **leading backslash**, which is
live in this codebase — `attendance/api/create.php`, one of the files this
package fixed, writes `\DateTimeImmutable`.

**And the figure I gave for that was wrong, which is its own lesson.** I wrote
"the MAJORITY style under `web/`: 87 occurrences against 79", and those counts
had no word boundary, so they counted `DateTimeZone` too. For the class the
sentence is about:

    grep -rEo 'new[[:space:]]+\\DateTime(Immutable)?[^A-Za-z0-9_]' web | wc -l   # 51
    grep -rEo 'new[[:space:]]+DateTime(Immutable)?[^A-Za-z0-9_]'   web | wc -l   # 55

so the backslashed form is the **minority**. Allowing it is still right — 51
places is not a corner case — but the evidence was not what the command
returned, in the very commit whose lesson was "write what the command returned,
and quote the command". **A word boundary is not a detail when you are
counting**, and the figure appeared in three places before anybody checked it.

**AND DO NOT STATE THAT RATIO AT ALL — round 6 showed a third way this bites.**
The figures move with every commit, including the ones that cite them: this
round's own fixes added `new \DateTimeImmutable` uses, so for that class alone
it went from minority to MAJORITY (47 backslashed against 46 bare, measured)
while the corrected sentence still read "minority". **A ratio between two live
styles is not a stable fact; it is a moving number.** The only load-bearing
point is that BOTH forms are live, so both must be matched. Today's figures:

    grep -rEo 'new[[:space:]]+\\DateTime(Immutable)?[^A-Za-z0-9_]' web | wc -l
    grep -rEo 'new[[:space:]]+DateTime(Immutable)?[^A-Za-z0-9_]'   web | wc -l


It also skipped **every** `createFromFormat`, where the header claimed only the
date-AND-zone form was skipped — so the no-date-no-zone form was invisible, and
that form was live in the two files above. The right construction is now
recognised by its format string carrying a date part, which `'H:i'` does not.

Eight cases are measured each way now: four real faults red (`strtotime`, both
`new DateTime` spellings, `createFromFormat('H:i', …)`) and four correct
constructions green (a date and a time in one array literal, `createFromFormat`
with a date and a zone, slicing the text, a column name appearing only inside a
SQL string).

### The verdicts, including the ones already right

#777 asks for every place checked, because a sweep that lists only faults cannot
be told from a sweep that stopped early.

### The scale of what remains, measured rather than guessed

    486 time-shaped columns in full_schema.sql (402 DATETIME, 66 DATE, 16 TIME, 2 TIMESTAMP)
    125 of them carry ANY comment at all

Established with
`grep -cE '\`[A-Za-z0-9_]+\` +(DATETIME|TIMESTAMP|DATE|TIME)\b' web/_sql/full_schema.sql`
and the same per type. **The commit message for part one printed the breakdown
as "402 DATETIME, 66 DATE, 16 TIME", which sums to 484 under the 486 two lines
above** — it dropped the two `TIMESTAMP` columns. Quote the command, and make
the parts add up to the whole.

**And then the commit that corrected that one said "`php -l` clean on all six
changed PHP files" where five changed** — a wrong count inside the section
headed FIGURES CORRECTED.

**AND THE COMMIT THAT CORRECTED *THAT* SAID FIVE WHERE SIX CHANGED.** Four
consecutive commits, four wrong counts of the same kind, the last one inside a
paragraph whose heading is "THREE WRONG NUMBERS IN THREE CONSECUTIVE COMMITS"
and whose closing line is "the habit that fixes this is not care — it is running
the command and pasting its answer". I wrote that line and then did not do it.

    $ git show --name-only --pretty= 61eebfc | grep -c '\.php$'
    6

The sixth is `tools/clock-change-selftest.php`, which I had been counting as a
test rather than as a PHP file — so each time the number was not guessed, it was
derived from a category in my head instead of from the command.

**The transferable rule, stated as a sequence rather than an intention: run the
command, read its answer, paste its answer — in that order, before the sentence
around it is written.** Four rounds of "be careful about numbers" produced four
wrong numbers; the ordering is what fixes it, because a figure written before the
command is run is a guess however carefully it is phrased.
    338 strtotime( under web/_apps and web/_core
     54 new DateTime(Immutable)?(
    479 date( / gmdate(

So "does the column comment say which kind of value it holds?" is answered **no**
for three quarters of them before any reading starts. That is the bulk of #777
and it is not done.

### I WROTE "NONE ANYWHERE" OVER A LIVE FAULT, AND IT WAS A WRITE PATH

The first version of the table above said **"NONE anywhere — neither the PHP
form nor `CONCAT()` in SQL"** for date-plus-clock-time concatenation. The
independent check found `web/_apps/resources/book.php` doing exactly that, and
it is the worst instance in the package because it does not merely DISPLAY the
wrong hour — **it stores it.**

    $startAt = $date . ' ' . $start . ':00';   // $start came from the form
    $startTs = strtotime($startAt);            // resolved in PHP's DEFAULT zone

Measured in Europe/London on 2026-03-29, before the fix:

    asked 01:00-01:30  ->  STORED 02:00-02:30
    asked 00:30-01:30  ->  STORED 00:30-02:30   (a one-hour booking became two)
    asked 01:30-02:00  ->  REFUSED, "End time must be after start time"

So a member booked a room for an hour they had not asked for, or was turned away
for a reason that was not true — and the conflict check then used the moved
values, so the booking could also collide with something it should not.

**The fix keeps everything on the wall clock**, which is what the column holds
and what the conflict query compares. The posted reading is stored exactly as
given; start-before-end is compared as TEXT (#435's own fix); the buffer either
side is added arithmetically through `shiftWallClock()`, in UTC precisely
*because* UTC has no transitions; and the one question that genuinely needs a
moment — "is the start in the past" — is the one place a zone appears, and it is
the organisation's, through `Site::timezone()`.

**The transferable part is about the record, not the code.** The table exists
because "a sweep that lists only faults cannot be told from a sweep that stopped
early". A row reading **NONE anywhere** over a case that exists is worse than no
row at all: it tells the next reader to stop looking, in an append-only
technical note. **Write what the command returned, and quote the command** —
`grep -rniE "CONCAT\(...\)"` really does return nothing, and that is the claim
that was safe to make; the PHP form was never searched for with a pattern that
could find a differently-named variable.

### And two more of the same class, found by looking where the gate admits it is blind

`attendance/api/create.php` and `update.php` validated a posted session time
with `\DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat('H:i', $timeRaw)` and then compared
`format('H:i')` with what was posted. With no date and no zone that means
"today, in whatever zone this server uses" — measured,
`createFromFormat('H:i','01:30')` really does answer today's date — so on the
spring-forward morning the reading is moved, the comparison fails, and the API
answers **400 "sessionTime must be a valid H:i time" for every valid time from
01:00 to 01:59.** Whether a session time was accepted depended on today's date
and the server's zone, neither of which has anything to do with the session.

Both validate the TEXT now, with a pattern that accepts all 1,440 real times and
refuses `24:00`, `23:60`, `1:30`, `01:3` and the rest — the same set the old code
refused, so nothing else changes.

**The gate's own header says it cannot see "a reading pulled into a variable
several lines earlier and converted there", and that is exactly where these
were.** A stated blind spot is a place to go looking, not a place to stop.

### The schema can say which kind of value a column holds, and then a check can read it

The three reader pages above were fixed and **guarded by nothing.** Planted,
putting `date('D j M, H:i', strtotime($r['startAt']))` back into
`my-bookings.php` left all 65 audit scripts and the clock-change test GREEN:
`tblResourceBooking.startAt` is a `DATETIME`, which the gate deliberately does
not sweep because a `DATETIME` may legitimately hold a moment, and section H of
the test drives `I18n` directly without touching a page.

**The fix is not a list of two column names in the check.** That is the #706
shape -- somebody's memory wearing a schema-driven check's clothes. Migration
252 gives both columns a comment saying they hold a WALL-CLOCK reading, and the
gate now sweeps every `DATETIME` whose own comment says so. A new such column
is covered the day it is declared, the declaration is useful to anybody reading
the SQL, and nothing has to be remembered.

Proved by planting: the reverted `my-bookings.php` now fails the gate on the
exact line, and the restore is byte-identical.

**And reading the schema immediately found four columns nobody had been
reading.** `tblEvents.startDateTime` and `endDateTime`, and
`tblEventSnapshots.snapStart` and `snapEnd`, have said "wall-clock local
(venue/site local); NOT UTC" since long before #777, and **28 files put one of
them through `strtotime()` or a DateTime constructor.** An event's zone is
`tblEvents.timezone`, which need not be the organisation's at all, so those are
suspect twice over -- the wrong zone for an event in another country, and the
wrong hour on the change morning even when the zone is right. Each needs a
person, because a few pass a zone a line or two later where this check cannot
see it.

They are in `tools/audit-checks/clock_wall_clock_datetime_pending.txt`, **not
fixed here**: part one was about the `TIME` columns, and a sweep that quietly
widened to 28 files would be a different package wearing part one's name. The
list fails BOTH ways -- nothing new may join it, and a listed file that has
stopped doing it also fails -- and `--strict` fails while it holds anything.
That is the `site_aware_addresses_pending.txt` pattern (#536): a backlog made
visible rather than permanent.

### Round 10: a widening caused silent data loss, and my gate's spelling list was not a rule

**Seven findings, six in round 9's work. And one observation worth more than
any of them, from the checker:** every earlier round moved the code from
"stores something wrong" to "refuses". Round 9 moved a refusal to "stores
something wrong" — **the first widening in this package to lose data** — and
that is the direction to check first on any shape accepted from here on.

**(1) A legal ISO 8601 decimal time was accepted and silently truncated.**
Round 9's bare-hour branch ran after the fractional-second strip, and the strip
matched a fraction on ANY component. In ISO 8601 a decimal fraction on the
lowest component is legal, so `T10.5` means **half past ten**:

    2026-06-01T10.5     before round 9: refused   after: stored 10:00:00
    2026-06-01 23.9     before round 9: refused   after: stored 23:00:00
    2026-06-01 10.5Z    before round 9: refused   after: 11:00 (means 11:30)

**Up to 59 minutes lost silently, HTTP 200, on a live API and a public form**,
where it had been an honest 400. Measured against
`3d753a4:web/_core/I18n.php`. The strip is anchored to follow `:MM:SS` now —
and to the SECONDS, not the minutes, because a fraction on the minute means
seconds (`T10:00.5` is 10:00:30), which is the same truncation one component
up. `api-spec.json` says "fractional seconds", so that is now what it means.

**(2) The write-path gate was bypassed by ONE WORD.** `date_create_immutable()`

    weekly,  AFTER round 10   first occurrence 2026-04-04 00:30   a week late

### The test depends on auto-increment landing on particular IDs, which nothing said

Adding three checks broke the file outright: `Duplicate entry '960470' for key
'tblEvents.PRIMARY'`. Later blocks INSERT with explicit `eventID` values from
960470 up, while earlier ones let MySQL choose — so **every row an earlier check
creates shifts what comes next**, and round 7's six checks had consumed the last
two spare slots.

`$withoutConsumingIds()` puts the counter back, so a check that creates and
deletes its own rows is ID-neutral. **A real fault in the test, found by adding
to it rather than by reading it** — and the sort that would have cost the next
person an afternoon, because the error names a line 600 lines away from the
cause.

### Round 7: the write-path fixes were pinned by nothing, and the test that posts to them used an ordinary day

**Five findings. The first is round 6's own finding 4 one level up, and the fix
is the most useful thing in the package.**

Reverting all three write paths at once — the events API's create and update,
and the public submission form — left `php -l` clean, **all 65 audit scripts
green, `clock-change-selftest.php` at 71 of 71, and `time-zones-selftest.php`
entirely green.** Round 6 had recorded exactly this hole and not closed it: its
section I pins `I18n`, and nothing pinned the CALLERS.

**Why the behavioural test could not see it.** `time-zones-selftest.php` DOES
post to `/api/events/create`, `/api/events/update` and `/calendar/submit-save`
— W08, W09, W09b, W09c, W06. Every fixture is `clockIn(25..30, '19:00:00')`:
an ordinary evening, 25 to 30 days from whenever the test runs. **On an
ordinary day the old round trip and the new code agree exactly**, so those
checks passed on the broken code. #549's own trap — a test written on an
ordinary day passes whatever the code does — reappearing inside the file
written to close it.

**The fix drives the real endpoints over an hour that does not exist** (D-065's
rule: where the property is "this code RUNS", drive it). Six new checks,
W09d–W09h:

  * `2028-03-12 02:30` is skipped in `America/New_York`, the test's event zone.
    A FIXED date, so it cannot rot, and far enough ahead to stay a future event.
  * **W09d asserts the hour really is skipped before anything else is checked**,
    or every check below it would be vacuous and would pass on anything.
  * **The submission form needed a DIFFERENT hour, and getting that wrong would
    have made its check vacuous.** That form stores the ORGANISATION's zone and
    the old code read the posted value through PHP's default, which start-up
    sets to the same one — so the skipped hour has to be `Pacific/Auckland`'s,
    not New York's. `2028-03-12 02:30` is an ordinary time in Auckland.
    `2028-09-24 02:30` is the one that does not exist there, and W09h0 pins that
    too.
  * **W09g is the opposite direction**: a value carrying its own offset must
    STILL be converted, or the fix breaks every integration sending an instant.

Measured with all three write paths reverted: W09e, W09f and W09h go red;
W09d, W09g and W09h0 correctly stay green. Restored: 140 of 140.

### And my own round 6 fix was new data loss

`import.php`'s fallback was `str_replace('T', ' ', trim($text))` before
`strtotime()`. **It replaces every capital `T`, not just the ISO separator**,
and the old code passed the cell untouched. Measured in Europe/London, old
against what round 6 shipped:

    "Tuesday, 3 March 2026 19:00"  ->  REFUSED   (was 2026-03-03 19:00:00)
    "Tue, 3 Mar 2026 19:00"        ->  REFUSED   (was 2026-03-03 19:00:00)
    "2026-03-03 19:00:00 GMT"      ->  REFUSED   (was 2026-03-03 19:00:00)
    "2026-03-29 01:30 UTC"         ->  10:30     (was 02:30)

`"Tue,"` became `" ue,"`; `"UTC"` became `"U C"`, which `strtotime()` read as
half past TEN — **eight hours out, a value the old code could not produce.**
Excel's default long date format begins with a weekday name, so the commonest
spreadsheet in the world stopped importing — under a comment promising "the old
round trip, deliberately" and a commit message saying "measured unchanged".

**And only the START was guarded.** A row whose start was plain and whose end
was `"Tue, 3 Mar 2026 20:30"` imported with `ok => true` and the message
"Imported as event #N" **with no end time at all**, bound as SQL NULL. Of the
three harms, that was the one nobody could see afterwards: the preview screen
prints the cell raw, so the administrator reviewing the file sees exactly what
they typed and nothing warns them. The old code could not reach this state,
because the upstream check guaranteed `strtotime($end) !== false`.

Fixed: the fallback takes the raw text (`wallClockFromInput()` already handles
the `T` form, so by then the text is something it must not touch), and an
unreadable end refuses the row. **A refused row is visible and recoverable; a
silently emptied column is neither.**

### The API's published contract said the opposite of what the code did

`api-spec.json` promised *"Any date text PHP can read is accepted, not only ISO
8601"*. After round 6 a value with no offset had to match a strict shape or the
request was a 400 — and the CHANGELOG said "an integration in another country is
unaffected", which was not true. Three of the refusals were wrong rather than
merely stricter:

  * **A lower-case `z`.** RFC 3339's own ABNF note allows `t` and `z` in lower
    case, so a standards-conforming client was rejected — and it sat in the
    branch round 6 called identical, because the offset pattern had no `i` flag.
    The value is a genuine instant; refusing it is a fault.
  * **Fractional seconds.** JavaScript's `toISOString()` sends `.000` as a
    matter of course. The column holds whole seconds, so the fraction is simply
    not expressible — dropping it is right, refusing it is not.
  * **A date with no time.** The API has an `isAllDay` field and a bare date
    used to store `00:00:00`, so every all-day integration broke with a 400.

All three accepted now, none of which needs a moment to be built. The loosening
**stops there**: `June 1 2026 10:00`, `2026-6-1T10:00`, a day-first date and a
double space still need `strtotime()` to read them, which is the very thing that
moves the hour — so they stay refused and **the description now states the
accepted shapes exactly** instead of promising the opposite. Ten checks
(I21–I30) pin both halves.

### A third blind spot: a reading reaching a conversion through a function parameter

`calendar/manage/series-repattern.php:1140` did
`createFromFormat('Y-m-d H:i:s', $reading)` with no zone, where `$reading` is a
`tblEvents.startDateTime` value passed in as a parameter. Measured: a stored
`2026-03-29 01:30:00` was shown as `Sun 29 Mar 2026, 02:30` — **on the one
screen whose entire purpose is comparing a date's current time with the time the
new pattern would give it.** Display only.

**Nothing could have reported it.** The gate needs a column name within 200
characters on the same line; the published one-hop sweep looks for
`$x = $row['<column>']`. A hop through a parameter defeats both. So the
backlog's header now names three blind spots, and admits that its promise —
"a file not on it that does this fails the check" — holds only **for the shapes
the check can see.** That is worth having and it is not the same sentence.

The em-dash the old helper printed for an empty cell is deliberately kept:
`formatClockDateTime()` answers `''`, and dropping it would have blanked the
table's empty cells — a change to the page made by accident inside a fix for
something else.

### Two comments round 6 blamed, still saying the thing it fixed

`import.php:213` still read *"Each row's start and end are read below with
strtotime() and written with date()"* — **quoted in round 6's own commit message
as part of the fault, fixed in code, and left standing in the comment.** And
`submit-save.php:222` still read *"The start and end were read just above on
PHP's clock"*, a read round 5 had deleted.

Both conclusions (`Site::timezone()` is the right zone to store) were correct
throughout. The stated REASON was gone — and in this repository the reason is
what the next reader checks the design against, so a reader asking "why is the
organisation's zone right here?" was sent to a mechanism that no longer exists.
Both now give the real reason: the form, and the spreadsheet, belong to that
organisation.

### Round 6: the SAME fault in the events API, with my own gate declaring it correct

**Nine findings. The first is the one to remember, because it inverts the rule
the package is built on.**

`events/api/create.php:85` and `events/api/update.php:105` wrote
`tblEvents.startDateTime`/`endDateTime` like this:

    $startAt = (new \DateTimeImmutable($startDateTime, $zone))->setTimezone($zone);

That looks safe, and it was reviewed as safe five times, because **the zone is
the right one** — the event's own. It is not safe. Measured:

    2026-03-29T01:30 in Europe/London     ->  2026-03-29 02:30:00
    2026-03-08T02:30 in America/New_York  ->  2026-03-08 03:30:00

**"We passed the correct zone" is not a defence. Building a moment AT ALL is
what moves it.** #777's own rule — "a reading becomes a moment when something
gives it a date AND A ZONE" — cuts the other way for a value about to be STORED
as a reading: there, giving it a zone is precisely what must not happen.

**And my gate actively declared it correct.** `CORRECT_WITH_DATE_AND_ZONE` and
the constructor exemption added in round 4 exist so that a genuine READ which
needs a moment stays green — `Livestream.php`, `calendar/event.php`'s
schema.org JSON-LD. The exemption is sound for a read and wrong for a write,
and nothing in the check knew the difference. Planted, removing the zone
argument from `create.php:85` makes the gate name the line, so **the only thing
keeping it green was the zone.** A check that passes on broken code, in the
round that added it.

Both endpoints are seeded live (`api.events.create.enabled` and
`api.events.update.enabled`, `full_schema.sql:3750-3751`) and the documented
request example is exactly the affected shape. An integration creating an event
for 01:30 that morning got 02:30 stored for ever, with no error.

**The fix keeps the feature that made the old code look reasonable.** An OFFSET
in the value (`+02:00`, a trailing `Z`) is a zone written into the value, so
such a value really IS an instant and must be converted onto the event's clock —
which is what the old comment promised and what an integration abroad needs. So:

  * no offset → a reading; store the text, build nothing.
  * an offset → an instant; convert it, exactly as before.

Measured each way: every offset-bearing value behaves identically to before,
`2026-06-01T10:00:00` (the documented example) is unchanged, and
`2026-02-31T10:00:00` is now refused where it used to roll silently to 3 March.

### And a third write path, carried on the backlog as a display item

`calendar/manage/import.php:238` did
`date('Y-m-d H:i:s', strtotime($r['startDateTime']))` into `INSERT INTO
tblEvents`, **and its own comment at 210-219 described that round trip as the
design.** It was on the part-two backlog — a list whose prose describes its
entries as files needing a DISPLAY fix — so a fault that corrupts stored data
was queued behind cosmetic work, and the per-column exemption forgave it.

Fixed, and the backlog's header now says that every entry is a reader and that
a write path must be labelled if one is ever added. **A reader shows a wrong
hour until somebody fixes it; a writer is wrong for ever.**

A spreadsheet column carries no offset, so every value is a reading on the
import's chosen zone — which is why a moment was never needed. Loose formats a
person might type (`1/3/26 7pm`, `March 3 2026 10:00`) fall back to the old
round trip deliberately, because the upstream check only asks whether
`strtotime()` can read them and refusing here would break imports that work
today. Measured: those behave exactly as before.

### THE RULE MOVED, because four handlers had four copies of it

Each of the four fixes started as its own closure, which is #768's shape — five
copies of one rule, no two agreeing — and this repository's own lesson is that
**a test holding its own copy of the logic it tests is not testing anything**
(#647). So `I18n::wallClockFromInput()` and `I18n::inputCarriesOffset()` are
the ONE place for each, all four handlers call them, and section I of
`clock-change-selftest.php` calls THE REAL METHODS rather than a copy.

Each caller needed its own `use Portal\Core\I18n;` line, and `php -l` is happy
without it — #536's trap, which only fails when the line runs.

### Round 5's fix was pinned by NOTHING, and section I exists because of it

Putting the old round trip back into `submit-save.php` left `php -l` clean, all
65 audit scripts GREEN and `clock-change-selftest.php` at 51 of 51. The one
test that posts to that handler (`time-zones-selftest.php` W06) uses a fixture
24 days ahead at 19:00, where old and new code agree exactly — **#549's trap, a
test written on an ordinary day passing whatever the code does.**

Section I (20 checks) drives the real methods over the hour that does not exist
in two zones that resolve differently, and pins the OLD behaviour beside each
so no check can be vacuous. Planted: the round trip back inside
`wallClockFromInput()` fails five of them.

### `--repin` still wrote a wrong pin silently — the exact shape its own comment cited

Round 5 added refusals for an empty set and a shrinking set, citing #697. **The
test was on `len()`, so an equal-sized swap walked through.** Measured: reword
`startAt`'s comment away, add `WALL-CLOCK` to another column, and `--repin`
reports success while `tblResourceBooking.startAt` — the column round 2 fixed
three reader pages for — loses its only guard. It compares the SETS now.
`--repin-shrink` also printed `FAIL:` and then exited 0, so a successful run
read as a failure.

### A new silent refusal, and EIGHT error codes that were never shown

`submit-save.php` gained `if ($endUtc <= $startUtc)`. The admin handler for the
same column says the opposite in as many words: *"An equal end and start is
allowed … the comparison below is deliberately 'before', not 'before or
equal'."* Two handlers writing one column must not disagree about what it may
hold, and the decision was already taken. Now `<`.

Worse, `calendar/submit.php` read only `?submitted`. **The handler emits eight
error codes and the page showed none of them** — every refusal was a bounce to
a blank form with no message and everything the visitor had typed gone. Seven
were already silent before #777; round 5 made the eighth reachable by ordinary
user error. All eight are worded now, from an allow-list, never from the posted
value.

### Finding 8: the stored value is right and the screens are now visibly wrong

Round 2's recorded lesson is *"a fix on one side of a stored value makes the
other side's fault VISIBLE — look at both sides."* Round 5 fixed a writer and
checked no reader. `admin/calendar/moderation.php:111` — the screen a submission
is reviewed on — is on the part-two backlog:

    date('j M Y, H:i', strtotime('2026-03-29 01:30:00'))  ->  29 Mar 2026, 02:30

So after round 5: member submits 01:30 → the database correctly holds 01:30 →
**the reviewing administrator sees 02:30.** Before round 5 the two agreed, both
wrong. The stored value being right is the correct trade, but **part two is not
cosmetic: 24 listed files now disagree visibly with correct data**, and the one
a submission passes through is among them.

### Two wrong counts, and a wrong specification

**#785's specification was wrong in all three parts**, which matters because it
is what the guard would be built from. I wrote that the fingerprint
`date('Y-m-d H:i:s', … strtotime …)` "matches seven files, five legitimately, so
a narrow idiom check would have caught both faults and would cry wolf nowhere".
Measured: it matches **four**; it would have caught **neither** fault (in both,
the `strtotime()` and the `date()` are 7 and 15 lines apart); and one of the
four was a real fault. The specification that works follows the VALUE — a moment
assigned to a variable, then that variable reaching `date('Y-m-d H:i(:s)', …)` —
and catches both, measured at `05a8097^`. Recorded on #785 with the commands.

My first attempt at measuring even that reported `submit-save.php` as missed,
because `[^)]*` cannot cross the `)` in `(int) $startDt`. I nearly wrote that
down as the design's limit when it was my regex's.

**And the published one-hop sweep typed its own column list.** It named 17 and
the gate derives 17 — which hid that **five were wrong in each direction**: it
missed `eventTime`, `overrideStartTime`, `overrideEndTime`, `parsedStartTime`
and `parsedEndTime`, and invented `closeTime`, `cutoffTime`, `openTime`,
`reminderTime` and `serviceTime`, which are not clock columns at all. Both
totals being 17 was coincidence. #706's named shape — somebody's memory wearing
a schema-driven check's clothes — in the paragraph that calls itself mechanical.
It imports `clock_columns()` from the gate now.

### And a data-loss bug in the file round 5 rewrote

`submit-save.php`'s `bind_param` type string was `issssssiiiss`. The 8th
parameter is `$locArg`, the location name, and the 8th character was `i`:

    bound 'i': locationName => '0'
    bound 's': locationName => 'Main Hall'

So **every public submission that named a venue stored `'0'`**, and the
moderator saw `0`. The comment on the line above has always described the right
string (`isssssssiiss`). A comment stating what the code had forgotten to do —
this repository's named worst fault — and it survived because `php -l` cannot
see a type string and nothing posts to this handler with a location.

It came in with #604, not with #777 (`git log -S"issssssiiiss"` → `d8177e4`).
Fixed here because round 5 rewrote 87 lines of this file and read this very
INSERT to establish that `isAllDay` is a literal `0`.

### Round 5: a PUBLIC form was still storing the moved hour, and four rounds had missed it

**The worst finding of the package, and it was found by reading the form rather
than by any check.** `web/_apps/calendar/submit.php:120` is an ordinary
`<input type="datetime-local" name="startDateTime">`, open to anybody the
installation lets submit an event. Its handler did this:

    $startRaw = trim((string) ($_POST['startDateTime'] ?? ''));
    $startDt  = strtotime($startRaw);
    $startUtc = date('Y-m-d H:i:s', (int) $startDt);
    // ... bound into INSERT INTO tblEvents (…, startDateTime, …)

Measured in Europe/London:

    posted 2026-03-29T01:30  ->  STORED 2026-03-29 02:30:00
    posted 2026-03-29T01:00  ->  STORED 2026-03-29 02:00:00
    posted 2026-03-28T01:30  ->  STORED 2026-03-28 01:30:00   (right)

`tblEvents.startDateTime` declares itself "Event start — wall-clock local
(venue/site local); NOT UTC". The variable was called `$startUtc`, which was
wrong twice over: not UTC, and not a moment.

**This is worse than the reader faults the package found first, because nothing
cancels it out.** A member submits an event for half past one, the diary holds
half past two **for ever**, and every later reader shows half past two
perfectly faithfully. The fix is the one `resources/book.php` already uses: keep
the value on the wall clock, validate the TEXT for shape AND range, store the
text, build no moment at all.

It is stricter than what it replaced, which is worth stating rather than
leaving to be discovered: `2026-02-31` is refused where it used to roll silently
forward to 3 March, and arbitrary English that `strtotime()` happened to
understand is refused.

**This paragraph also said a bare date was refused, and that stopped being true
within hours.** Round 7 loosened the shared helper to accept a date with no
time, because the events API needs one for an all-day event — and all four
callers share it, so the public form inherited the change while both this note
and the handler's own comment still said `?err=date`. Round 8 found it. The
cost of sharing one rule is now stated where the rule lives: **a change made
for one caller reaches all four.**

### Why nothing could see it, and the sweep that should have

**The gate matches a column being READ.** A write path builds its value from
`$_POST`, converts it, and names the column only in the `INSERT` — so there is
nothing for the pattern to match on, and the whole class of "store the moved
hour" is invisible. Both instances of that class in this package
(`resources/book.php`, `calendar/submit-save.php`) were found by eye. **That is
#785.** The first step recorded there follows the VALUE: a moment assigned to a
variable, then that variable reaching `date('Y-m-d H:i(:s)', …)`.

**ROUND 5 SPECIFIED THE SAME-LINE IDIOM INSTEAD AND IT WAS WRONG IN ALL THREE
PARTS**, which round 6 measured — four files not seven; it would have caught
NEITHER fault, because in both the `strtotime()` and the `date()` are 7 and 15
lines apart; and one of the four it does match was a real fault, not a
cry-wolf. The corrected specification, with the commands, is on #785. **A
number written before the command is run is a guess however carefully it is
phrased — and a SPECIFICATION written that way sends somebody to build the
wrong thing.**

And the OTHER blind spot — a reading copied into a variable and converted
later — is now swept mechanically rather than by eye, because it has yielded a
real fault twice:

    # One hop: $x = (string) $row['<a clock-reading column>'];  then a moment
    # function applied to $x within the next 40 lines.
    #
    # ⚠️ THE COLUMN LIST IS IMPORTED FROM THE GATE, never typed here. The first
    #    version of this sweep typed its own, and round 6 measured the result:
    #    it named 17 columns and the gate derives 17, which hid the fact that
    #    FIVE were wrong in each direction -- it missed eventTime,
    #    overrideStartTime, overrideEndTime, parsedStartTime and parsedEndTime,
    #    and invented closeTime, cutoffTime, openTime, reminderTime and
    #    serviceTime, which are not clock columns at all. Both totals being 17
    #    was coincidence. #706's named shape -- somebody's memory wearing a
    #    schema-driven check's clothes -- in the paragraph that calls itself
    #    mechanical. The conclusion happened to hold (re-run with the real set,
    #    the same four sites come back) but that was luck.
    python3 - <<'PY'
    import os, re, importlib.util
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(
        "gate", "tools/audit-checks/check_clock_time_not_a_moment.py")
    gate = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); spec.loader.exec_module(gate)
    root = gate.repo_root()
    cols = gate.clock_columns(open(os.path.join(root, gate.SCHEMA)).read())
    assign = re.compile(r"\$(\w+)\s*=\s*(?:\((?:string|int)\)\s*)?\$\w+\[[\'\"](" 
                        + "|".join(map(re.escape, cols)) + r")[\'\"]\]")
    moment = re.compile(r"(?:strtotime|new\s+\\?DateTime(?:Immutable)?"
                        r"|\\?DateTime(?:Immutable)?::createFromFormat)\s*\(")
    for folder, _, files in os.walk("web"):
        if "vendor" in folder: continue
        for n in files:
            if not n.endswith(".php"): continue
            p = os.path.join(folder, n)
            lines = open(p, errors="replace").read().split("\n")
            for i, l in enumerate(lines):
                for mm in assign.finditer(l):
                    var, col = mm.group(1), mm.group(2)
                    for j in range(i + 1, min(i + 40, len(lines))):
                        if moment.search(lines[j]) and re.search(r"\$" + var + r"\b", lines[j]):
                            print(f"{p}:{j+1}  [{col} via ${var}]"); break
    PY

Four sites today: two faults on the part-two backlog
(`_core/Newsletter.php:682`, `calendar/zoom-create.php:94`) and two that are
CORRECT, each passing a real zone on purpose — `_core/Venues.php:3590` with the
venue's own, and `_core/Events.php:590`, which compares one reading in two zones
deliberately to detect an old-form migration. **The pending file's header said
round 4 "found two" there; it had found two of four by eye.**

### An explicit `null` zone defeated round 4's new rule, in one word

Round 4 taught the gate that a value plus a zone in one call is correct, and
counted it by commas at the call's own bracket depth. **It counted the
separator, not the zone.** All three of these were green:

    new \DateTimeImmutable((string) $r['sessionTime'], null)
    \DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat('Y-m-d H:i', $d . ' ' . $r['sessionTime'], null)
    new \DateTimeImmutable((string) $r['sessionTime'],)      // trailing comma

And `null` really does the harm:

    $ php -r 'date_default_timezone_set("Europe/London");
              echo (new DateTimeImmutable("2026-03-29 01:30", null))->format("Y-m-d H:i:s P");'
    2026-03-29 02:30:00 +01:00

So the whole #777 fault, with the hard gate green. `null` is legal and means
PHP's default zone — the thing the check exists to forbid. **An explicit
`(null)` is one of the shapes that already walked through #763's guard**, so
this repository had paid for the lesson once. The last argument is read now, not
counted. What it still cannot see, stated: a variable that happens to hold null,
which needs to know what a variable holds — not a question a source-reading
check answers (D-065).

### The backlog forgave SIX columns where three places said FOUR

Round 4 narrowed the exemption from forgiving a FILE to forgiving a COLUMN —
and then forgave every column in `wall_clock`, all **six** declared wall-clock
columns, where the backlog is about **four**. So `tblResourceBooking.startAt`
and `endAt` — the pair migration 252 declared, the pair round 2 fixed three
reader pages for — were forgiven in all 25 listed files. Planted one line in
the listed `venues/booking.php`:

    $planted = date('g:i A', (int) strtotime((string) $ev['startAt']));

**Gate exit 0, output byte-identical.** Three statements were untrue at once,
and all three were the note describing the narrowing: the pending file's "IT
FORGIVES THESE FOUR COLUMNS … AND NOTHING ELSE", the gate's success message, and
the code comment at the exemption itself.

**That is round 4's own finding 1 one level on: the narrowing was right, the
note overstated it, and the overstatement was exactly where the hole was.**
Round 4 even wrote the right framing — "a `TIME`-column fault in a listed file
still fails" — tested that case, and never tested a `startAt` one.
`BACKLOG_COLUMNS` names the four now; both directions are planted.

### Three more sentences that were untrue

**`.OpenAI/CONTEXT.md` still asserted the withdrawn "87 against 79" figure** at
line 3229, twenty-eight lines above its own correction. Introduced by `04a6226`,
survived rounds 2, 3 and 4 — and `1bfd057` added 73 lines to that very file for
the stated purpose of bringing both instruction files into line. `.claude/CLAUDE.md`
was fixed; its mirror was not. **The fifth repeat of "a correction recorded in
one place and not applied to the others", inside the finding that names the
pattern.** When a finding is "both files", diff the two against each other
afterwards instead of editing them in sequence.

**The constructor-with-zone trio named the wrong third file.** The gate and
DEV_NOTES both said `calendar/event-attendance.php`, `calendar/event.php` and
`_core/Venues.php`. `Venues.php` does use the spelling, but it reads the column
into a variable first, so the gate **never saw it** and never reported it — it
cannot have been told to rewrite anything, and was never on the backlog. The
real third is `events/api/create.php`, which the sentence omitted and which the
diff shows is one of the two actually removed from the list.

**"Gains no hit" gains one.** The gate said re-running the pattern without the
newline restriction "gains no hit, so nothing live is hidden today". Verified
independently by running both patterns over all 912 files and diffing the match
sets: it gains exactly one, `_core/Livestream.php:99`, whose `createFromFormat`
is split over five lines with its zone on line 102, and is the correct
construction. The
conclusion holds; the premise the "so" rested on did not — in the paragraph
whose own rule is to paste what the command returned.

### And `--repin` wrote a degraded pin and reported success

With every `WALL-CLOCK` comment reworded away, `--repin` wrote a pin holding
**zero** columns and printed "Repinned 0 wall-clock column(s)", exit 0. **That
is #697's lesson about this exact shape:** a `--repin` that writes the fault
into the sidecar and prints success is the one way a text pin fails silently.
Today an ordinary run still goes red afterwards through the stale-entry rule —
but round 4 itself recorded that the protection vanishes the day the backlog is
emptied, which is precisely when somebody will be editing those comments. It
refuses an empty set outright now, and refuses a shrinking one without an
explicit `--repin-shrink`, so the intent is in the command and not only in the
diff.

### Round 4: eight findings, and two were guards that passed on broken code

Every one of the eight landed in a previous round's fix rather than in the
build. Two mattered.

**(a) The backlog exempted the FILE, not the column, so part one's own rule was
switched off in 28 of 912 files.** The pending list skipped a file by path:

    if relative in pending:
        seen_pending.add(relative)
        continue

So a file listed for part TWO stopped being checked for part ONE. Planted: one
extra line in `calendar/event.php`, a listed file —
`date('g:i A', strtotime($event['meetingTime']))`, a brand-new fault on a `TIME`
column — left the gate **green with its output unchanged.** Two of the listed
files already handle `TIME` columns (`attendance/record.php`, and
`venues/booking.php`, which is a booking form with four of them); both are
correct today, so nobody was shown a wrong hour, but they had left the guard
entirely.

**The pending file's own header promised the opposite** — "a file not on it that
does this fails the check, so the hole closes behind us" — written in the same
commit, by the same hand, as the code that did not do it. That is the #645
shape: a note stating the guarantee the code had forgotten to implement. It
forgives a COLUMN now, so a `TIME`-column fault in a listed file still fails,
and the matched column name is printed beside each line number.

**(b) Nothing pinned WHICH columns say WALL-CLOCK, so the whole of round 3's fix
rested on an English word in a comment.** Planted: reword only
`tblResourceBooking.startAt`/`endAt`'s comment from "WALL-CLOCK local to the
organisation" to "Local clock reading for the organisation" — a plausible
documentation tidy — and put the reader fault back into `my-bookings.php`. Every
check stayed green, this one included, while the column count silently fell from
17 to 15.

The remedy is the one this repository settled on in #485 and #763 after four and
six rounds of cleverer patterns respectively: **pin the set**, in
`clock_wall_clock_columns.pinned.txt`, regenerated only by an explicit
`--repin`. Changing a column's comment is fine; doing it without noticing that a
guard reads it is not. The pin covers the NAMES, not the wording — a column
whose comment is reworded but still says WALL-CLOCK passes, because the word is
the contract.

Worth recording: the MECHANISM was accidentally pinned all along. Changing the
gate's own matcher from `"WALL-CLOCK"` to `"WALL CLOCK"` does go red, because
the 25 listed files then stop tripping and the stale-entry rule fires. **That
accidental protection disappears the day the backlog is emptied**, which is
precisely when somebody will be editing these comments.

`CORRECT_WITH_DATE_AND_ZONE` matched `createFromFormat` only. A constructor
given a date **and** a zone is equally correct by the gate's own stated rule:

    new \DateTimeImmutable($row['sessionDate'] . ' ' . $row['sessionTime'], $tz)

That was reported as a fault, with a message telling its author to rewrite it or
add the file to `ALLOWED`. Three live files use that spelling **and were reported for it**:

anything, and it was never on the backlog. That is a fact about the blind spot,
not a file this fix rescued, and mixing the two overstated what the fix did.
So the check was crying wolf and miscounting its own backlog in one breath, and
under #483 crying wolf is the direction that gets a check switched off.

Both forms are recognised now, by the same `has_a_zone_argument()` with a

so **every short-echo block followed anywhere later in the file by a `<?php`
block was blanked.** Planted and measured: a

but `<?=` is ordinary PHP. It takes the earliest of the two openers now.

The gate's header said **"two do today"** where six do, naming only the pair
migration 252 declared and omitting the four its own backlog is about — the

And the comment split was stated as **123 of 486** in six places. The commands:

    grep -cE '`[A-Za-z0-9_]+` +(DATETIME|TIMESTAMP|DATE|TIME)\b' web/_sql/full_schema.sql           # 486
    grep -cE '`[A-Za-z0-9_]+` +(DATETIME|TIMESTAMP|DATE|TIME)\b.*COMMENT' web/_sql/full_schema.sql  # 125

**125, so 361 carry none.** The fifth wrong count in this package, and it sat in

`ca19f73` touched `CHANGELOG.md`, `DEV_NOTES.md`, the gate, the pending file,

round 3 corrected everywhere else, left standing in the two files that ARE the

against 79" figure **and its own correction**, in the same bullet.

**This is the third time in two months that a correction was recorded in one
