### Comparing a wall-clock column with `NOW()` (#783)

Two queries filter `tblResourceBooking` by `NOW()`:

    my-bookings.php:30   AND b.endAt   > NOW()
    resource.php:60      AND b.startAt >= NOW()

`NOW()` is the **database server's** clock in the connection's time zone, which
is `SYSTEM` by default -- the database host's own setting, which has nothing to
do with the organisation's zone. The columns hold the organisation's wall clock.
So "my upcoming bookings" is cut at a boundary that can be hours out for an
organisation in another country, and an hour out on either change morning.

Raised rather than fixed: the right answer is to pass the organisation's own
wall-clock "now" as a parameter, and that changes which rows a member sees, so
it is a behaviour change and not a tidy-up.

### Round 14: the import closure was churning, and the remedy was a committed matrix

**Four rounds running found their faults in the previous round's fixes, and
rounds 13 and 14 were the worst of them.** Round 14: 8 findings, 5 in the
portal, every one inside round 13's own work, and three of them faults round 13
itself NAMED and then re-made.

**THE ROOT CAUSE, which is a shape rather than a slip.** `$fmtClock` in
`calendar/manage/import.php` has to be strict about ISO values and permissive
about whatever a spreadsheet holds. Twice I wrote a strict rule and it **leaked
into the permissive path**, refusing formats only that path ever handled:

    round 12  refused every offset-bearing ISO value -- `toISOString()` output
    round 13  refused RFC 2822 (an e-mail `Date:` header, an RSS `pubDate`),
              three unpadded or basic ISO forms, and -- through a `date_parse()`
              rule -- a legal ISO ordinal date

**The cure is structural: steps 1 and 2 are ATTEMPTS, not GATES.** Each takes
the value if it recognises it and otherwise falls through. **Nothing in that
closure may refuse a value for the SHAPE it is written in**; the only refusals
are for a value that is genuinely wrong — an impossible calendar day, and the
one fractional shape PHP misreads.

**`date_parse()` IS A DIFFERENT PARSER FROM `strtotime()`, and that broke my
"ask PHP what it parsed" reasoning.** It reads `2026-152` as day 152 of month 1
and reports "The parsed date was invalid", while `strtotime()` correctly reads
the ISO ordinal date as 1 June. So refusing on any warning refused a value the
fallback handles — a check crying wolf inside the rule written to stop a check
crying wolf. The test is the HARM, stated exactly: **a day somebody could have
typed (1 to 31) in a month that does not have it.** Day 152 is not such a day.
**Ask the function that does the work, not a neighbouring one.**

**THE REMEDY FOR THE CHURN IS THE PART TO KEEP.** Every one of those
regressions was found by an independent checker building a MATRIX of formats,
and every one had been missed by me probing the cases I happened to think of.
**A list of cases you chose yourself cannot tell you about the class you
forgot.** So the matrix is committed: section K of `clock-change-selftest.php`,
26 formats that must store and 12 that must be refused, each annotated with the
round that broke it, lifting the real closure out of the page source so it
needs no database or server. Both earlier regressions were planted and both
turn K01 red. Its stated limit: `Site::timezone()` is stood in for, so K proves
what the closure does with a zone and nothing about the zone being the right
one.

**A TEST HOLDING ITS OWN COPY TESTED NOTHING, and its comment said the
opposite.** Round 13 decided the moved-date branch inline in `save.php` and
re-implemented the same arithmetic in check J14, whose comment claimed "a wrong
branch is caught without a database or a web server". Measured: changing ONE
WORD in the page left all 65 audit scripts green, J14 green at 75/75,
clock-change at 100/100 **and `event-repeat-pages-selftest.php` at 251/251 on a
real database** — because that test's M02 asserts only the DATE substring,
which every branch produces. `EventRecurrence::whyFirstDateMoved()` is the ONE
place now and J14 asks it.

⚠️ **AND "planted, the same one-word change goes red" WAS UNTRUE, which round
15 measured.** Moving the arithmetic into one method pins the RULE; it does not
pin **which answer the page branches on**. One word in `save.php` — `=== 'gap'`
to `=== 'pattern'`, giving every clocks-moved-it date the "to match the repeat
you chose" sentence, which is round 12's original fault restored — left all 65
audit scripts, 75 recurrence checks, 104 clock checks AND 251 HTTP checks green.
The three sentence pins survive any mis-mapping, so they could not see it
either. The mapping is pinned now, as `$why === 'gap'` and
`$why === 'pattern and time'` in `FLASH_BRANCHES`, and that plant goes red.
**Pinning a rule is not pinning its use.**

**AND I MADE THE DOCBLOCK MISTAKE AGAIN IN THE COMMIT THAT WROTE THE LESSON.**
Round 13 reported a docblock stranded from its method, fixed it for
`pastTheHourThatIsMissing()`, added a comment telling the next reader to insert
a method **above a docblock or below its method, never between the two** — and
inserted `readingPastTheGap()` between `readingIsReal()`'s docblock and its
signature. Reflection reported `readingIsReal` as undocumented. **Writing a
lesson down is not the same as applying it to the edit you are making while you
write it**, and the check that catches it is `ReflectionMethod::getDocComment()`
rather than reading the file.

**One more untrue sentence, in the branch built to be truthful.** The
clocks-moved-it message said the typed time "does not exist on that date" while
naming the MOVED-TO date — and in the two Greenland zones this branch exists
for, it exists perfectly well on that date: 23:30 on 29 March 2026 in
America/Nuuk is a real reading; it is the 28th that has no 23:30. The sentence
names the typed date and time now, where the claim holds.

### Rounds 15 to 17: the import reader, and what finally closed it

Three more rounds on one closure, `$fmtClock` in `calendar/manage/import.php`.
It has to be strict about machine-written ISO values and forgiving about
whatever somebody typed into a spreadsheet, and **every attempt from round 12
to round 16 broke something legitimate.** What closed it was not a cleverer
pattern.

**Round 15 — the impossible-date rule stepped over a zero.** Round 14's test
required the day to be 1-31, the month 1-12 and the year to be a number, so any
cell whose broken component was a ZERO, or which had no year, fell to
`strtotime()` and was rolled silently: `2026-06-00` to 31 May, `2026-00-10` to
December 2025, `Feb 31 10:00` to 3 March. **And `0000-00-00` — the zero date a
legacy MySQL dump exports — rolled to `-0001-11-30`, which a DATETIME column
refuses**, so the insert threw and the whole import stopped part-way with
earlier rows already written. The range test now covers anything a day or month
COULD be, zero included, with the year `strtotime()` itself assumes.

**Round 16 — "measured" meant the two cases I picked.** Round 15's fraction
rule refused **189 machine formats** that had imported since the page was
written: fractional SECONDS with anything after them, such as
`2026-06-01 10:00:00.000 UTC`, which is what a database or log export contains.
The comment above it said "Legitimate fractional SECONDS are unaffected,
measured rather than assumed" — and the measurement had covered the only two
shapes where the claim held, which were then added to the test as if they proved
the general case. **Writing "measured" over a set you chose yourself is worse
than writing nothing**, because it removes the next reader's reason to look.
Third occurrence in this package.

**Round 17 — the premise itself was wrong, and PHP settled it.** For four
rounds the rule rested on "`10.5` means 10:30 and `strtotime()` reads it as five
past". True — for ONE digit. **`strtotime()` does not read a decimal hour at
all: it reads the dot as a MINUTE SEPARATOR**, and the proof is that it refuses
minutes above 59:

    10.5  -> 10:05        10.59 -> 10:59
    10.30 -> 10:30        10.60 -> FALSE       10.75 -> FALSE

So for two digits PHP's reading matches what a spreadsheet writer INTENDS:
`19.30` is half past seven to PHP and to whoever typed it.

⚠️ **IT DOES NOT MATCH THE DECIMAL-HOUR READING, and saying it did was round
18's finding 2.** Measured over all 100 two-digit fractions, 60 are parseable
and the two readings agree in just TWO of them (`.00`, and `.01` by rounding):
`10.30` is 10:30 to PHP and 10:18 as a decimal hour, twelve minutes apart.
**The honest ground for storing them is intent, which is a product judgement,
not arithmetic** — and presenting it as arithmetic matters, because a reader
applying the stated rule literally ("refuse where the readings differ") would
refuse all 58, which is round 16's fault restored.

**And the round attribution was wrong, which round 18 established by running
every committed closure over the same cells.** `2026-06-01T19.30` was first
refused by ROUND 12; `2026-06-01 19.30` and `2026-6-1 19.30` by ROUND 15; only
`Tue, 3 Mar 2026 19.30`, the Excel form, by round 16. So round 16 widened an
existing refusal rather than introducing it, and "all five earlier versions
stored it" is true of the Excel form alone. Section K's precedent labels said
"round 16" for all of them — **the field whose whole purpose is naming the
round that broke a format, giving the wrong one.**

⚠️ **AND THE SENTENCE THAT USED TO SIT HERE WAS BROKEN BY MY OWN CORRECTION.**
Round 18 spliced "Round 16 had generalised the one-digit case…" down to the two
words "Round 15 had", leaving a subject with no verb — and, as it then read,
crediting **round 15** with pushing the refusal into every date spelling and
with breaking Excel's long date. Both are round 16's, which the paragraph
immediately above states correctly, so the correcting paragraph was followed by
a restatement of the error it corrects. Round 19 found it. `.claude/CLAUDE.md`
and `.OpenAI/CONTEXT.md` got the same edit and both read correctly, so **the two
mirrors agreed with each other and disagreed with this file** — which is why
diffing the mirrors is not enough.

**The lesson is about the edit, not the fact.** This project's own note says
never to slice between two markers, because that style has already deleted
working code once and duplicated a block once. Replacing a verb phrase by a
subject is the same mistake in prose. **Rewrite the sentence; do not splice
it.**

To state it plainly, measured by running every committed closure over the same
cells: **round 12** first refused `2026-06-01T19.30`; **round 15** first refused
`2026-06-01 19.30` and `2026-6-1 19.30`; **round 16** widened the refusal to
every other date spelling and so broke `Tue, 3 Mar 2026 19.30`, Excel's long
date format. Round 16 was also internally inconsistent: `19.30` refused while
`19.30:00` stored.

The rule is now one digit, non-zero, on the hour or the minute — the case where
the cell is genuinely ambiguous, because `10.5` reads as naturally as five past
ten as it does as half past.

⚠️ **NOT "the only case where the two readings genuinely differ", which is what
this line said until round 19.** That sentence is the one round 18's own
finding declared measurably false and removed from `import.php` — and it
survived HERE, twenty-five lines below this file's own correction of it, and
below its own round-17 lesson "enumerate every place a claim lives". Measured:
of 100 two-digit fractions, 60 are parseable and the two readings agree in just
TWO. **Two-digit fractions are stored because PHP's reading matches what a
spreadsheet writer intends, which is a product judgement, not because the
readings agree.**

**And that dissolved the OTHER fault in the same breath.** Round 16's rule
needed a trailing set to decide what counted as a zone, and it allowed letters,
`/` and `_` but not digits, `+` or `-` — so any zone whose NAME holds one of
those (`GMT+1`,

`Etc/GMT+1`, `America/Port-au-Prince`, `Asia/Ust-Nera`) fell through and stored
the wrong hour, under a comment saying a fraction "followed only by a zone or an
offset" was refused. **A date-spelling list had been replaced by a zone-spelling
list.** Narrowing the rule to one digit removed the need for any trailing set,
so there is nothing left to be missing from.

**THE LESSON ACROSS ALL THREE, which is the only part worth carrying.** Every
one of these faults was found by a checker building a MATRIX, and missed by me
probing the cases I had thought of. The remedy was not a sharper pattern each
time; it was:

1. **Measure what the library actually does** before writing a rule about it.
   One `strtotime()` sweep would have settled the premise in round 12.
2. **Commit the matrix.** Section K of `clock-change-selftest.php` holds cells
   that must store and cells that must be refused — **the two counts are pinned
   in the test as K04/K04b and are deliberately not written here**, because this
   line carried a stale pair twice over, and the second time the stale figure
   was sitting inside this very clause saying it was not repeated. Read them
   from the file that fails on them. Each cell is annotated with the round
   that broke it, lifting the real closure out of the page so it needs no
   database. **Both counts are pinned** (K04/K04b), because round 17 measured
   that deleting ten entries left 104 of 104 green.
3. **Name the rule after the thing it is about.** Every version that mentioned
   a DATE spelling was defeated by a date spelling; every version that
   enumerated a ZONE was defeated by a zone. The rule is about the TIME and now
   says nothing else.

**One more shape, from round 17's finding 7.** The withdrawn "same wrong zone"
explanation lived in FOUR places. Round 16 fixed the two that its finding named
and recorded the lesson "when a finding says 'both files', diff the two against
each other" — **and two files was not the set.** It survived here, in the file
named as this package's technical record, for fourteen rounds, and round 16 is
the only round in the package to change no DEV_NOTES line at all. **Enumerate
every place a claim lives, by searching for it, before calling a correction
done.**


### Rounds 18 to 21: what each round measured, and the claim round 21 withdrew

**⚠️ "THE READER HAS CONVERGED … TEN ROUNDS OF CHURN ARE OVER" WAS WRITTEN HERE
AND IS WITHDRAWN.** Round 21 found the fault in it, and it is worth keeping
because the sentence read as a measurement and was a prediction.

The measurement it cited was round 18-versus-19 — the two versions BEFORE round
20's own edit — and it was presented as round 20's verdict on round 20. Round 20
then widened the reader, by thousands of cells. So the round asserting the churn
was over was itself a round of churn. Every one of rounds 16, 17, 19 and 20
repaired an over-refusal in this closure; round 21 newly stored nothing (the
table below). Round 22 had added "and 21" here, which the table contradicts.

**What was actually measured, each time, and nothing beyond it.** Round 21 swept
round 19 against round 20; round 22 swept round 20 against round 21. **Both
report the same SHAPE, which is the finding — the absolute counts are not,
because each depends on a cell list nobody committed:**

| direction | r19 → r20 | r20 → r21 |
|---|---|---|
| newly REFUSED (an over-refusal, the harmful direction) | none | thousands, every one a sub-1000, negative or 5+ digit year |
| newly STORED | thousands | none |
| both store, DIFFERENT value | none | none |

So each change was clean in the direction that matters, and nothing a customer
could plausibly have in a spreadsheet changed either way — round 22 checked that
separately against two-digit years, both Excel epochs, written-out months and
offsets, and found two cells changed, both improvements.

**And round 22 found me writing FOUR MORE unreproducible figures while removing
three** — one of them in `import.php`, under the very paragraph saying such a
figure "reads as evidence". That is why this table gives directions and not
totals.

**The transferable part: a sweep comparing two OLD versions cannot be the
verdict on a NEW one, and "the churn is over" is not a measurement at all.** No
cell count is written in PROSE in `import.php`, the self-test or these notes any
more — section K's two counts are pinned in the test as K04/K04b, which is code
that fails when they move — for the reason
in the next section.

Rounds 18 to 21 also found the *record* wrong about the reader, repeatedly, and
that is the rest of this section.

**THE REFUSAL HAD SWALLOWED A CASE THAT IS NEVER AMBIGUOUS.** The one-digit
fraction rule is about an hour or a minute, where `10.5` could mean five past
ten or half past ten. **A fraction on the SECONDS has no such problem, and the
reason is the column:** a `DATETIME` holds no fractional part, so both readings
of `10:00:05.5` store the identical value. The rule was refusing it anyway, so
`2026-06-01 10:00:05.5` — an ordinary database or log export — was turned away
with a message about an ambiguity that does not exist. It is **exempt** now
(`/:\d{1,2}:\d{1,2}\.\d/` tested first), not refused, and the third refusal
sentence, which existed only to explain the seconds case, is deleted.

**AND THE REFUSAL BLAMED THE WRONG THING WHEN THE CELL WAS SIMPLY UNREADABLE.**
`1.6. 10:00` is a dotted European date PHP cannot read at all, and the fraction
rule reached it first, so the administrator was told it "writes the hour with a
single digit after a decimal point" — about a cell with no hour in it. The
readability test (`strtotime`) runs **ahead** of the fraction rule now, so an
unreadable cell says "cannot be read" and only a readable one is judged for
ambiguity. **Order the refusals so each one is only ever reached by a cell it
can describe truthfully.**

**SECTION K PASSED ON BROKEN CODE A FOURTH TIME, AND ALL FOUR WERE ONE
MISTAKE.** Each time, the matrix held one representative of a dimension the rule
ranges over, so narrowing the rule along that dimension left every cell green:

| the narrowing | why K could not see it |
|---|---|
| `\d{1,2}` → `\d{2}` on the hour | every one-digit-fraction cell used a two-digit hour |
| dropping the `:SS.` exemption | every fractional-second cell used three or six digits |
| `[1-9]` → `[359]` on the digit | only three of the nine digit values appeared |
| requiring a padded component | every cell was zero-padded |

**The rule: cover the DIMENSION, not an example of it.** A matrix is only a
matrix along the axes you varied. Section K now varies hour width, minute width,
fraction digit value, fraction length and whether the year is given, and all
four narrowings go red.

**THE REST WERE FIGURES AND SENTENCES, and two are worth keeping.** "89 zone
spellings" had been taken from a review report and written down without being
re-derived; round 19 replaced it with "91", **which round 20 could not reproduce
either** — the sweep answers anything from 82 to 146 depending on whether an
offset family is generated, so the number is a property of the list you sweep
and not of the code. **No count is given now.** A figure nobody can reproduce is
worse than none, because it reads as evidence — and this was the second attempt
at the same sentence, in the paragraph whose own thesis that is.

And the comment above section K said **"nothing POSTS a CSV"**, which is false:
`tools/time-zones-selftest.php` posts six to `/calendar/manage/import`. Round 19
said it had corrected this and corrected a different sentence. The replacement
claim — that every cell those six send is a clean ISO value — **is also false**,
because W07e and W07f send `24 September 2028 3:15am`. The accurate narrowing,
stated once and in the test itself: **none of the six sends an impossible date, a
decimal fraction or an offset**, so they cover the round trip and not the rules
section K is about. That is #787.

**ROUND 23 WAS THE LAST ROUND (D-066), because every finding was in a test, a
check or a written note.** Two are worth carrying forward. The guard round 22
pinned by counting assignments was switched off by five other spellings of an
assignment, each with section K at 112 of 112 — the spelling-list mistake one
level up, and the reason the fix is to DRIVE the real import with out-of-range
cells (#796, D-065). And round 22 corrected "a `DATETIME` holds 1000-01-01 to
9999-12-31 and NOTHING ELSE" in ONE comment while the same sentence stood in
the same file, the self-test and both mirrors — so the mirrors agreed with each
other and were both wrong, and diffing them could not catch it. **Search for a
withdrawn claim by its words, everywhere, before calling the withdrawal done.**
Outside its scope the round also found a real storage fault older than round
22: a cell with no date, such as `2026`, is stored as today at 20:26 (#797).

**#797, fixed straight after.** The import's last reader is `strtotime()`, which
fills in whatever a cell leaves out from the moment the import runs. The fix is
step (a2) of `$fmtClockRaw`: read the cell against two reference moments that
differ in every field IN UTC (2001-02-03 04:05:06 and 2010-11-12 13:14:15, a
Saturday and a Friday) and refuse it when the two answers differ. **Not in every
zone, and the first version said otherwise:** the page reads them in the
organisation's zone, and in 118 zones both land on the same local weekday. The
independent check found no gap (a cell that takes its weekday from "now" takes a
date from it too), but the stated reason was wrong. **And its message was
untrue of a real cell:** "does not give a full date" was said of `01.06.26`,
which IS a full date with a two-digit year that PHP reads as the time 01:06:26.
The message now says what is true of every cell reaching it — it could not be
read as a complete date — with an example. **It sits before the
impossible-date test on purpose**, because that test judged a year-less cell
against the year `strtotime()` assumed — the very assumption now refused — and
its `(int) date('Y')` fallback, unreachable as a result, was removed rather than
kept as a clause that cannot run. **K06 had pinned the fault as correct:** round
21 made it year-proof by asserting "stored in a leap year, refused otherwise",
which was right about the time bomb and wrong about the behaviour; it now asserts
one answer in every year. Two cells deliberately still store: `Jan 2026` and
`June 2026 10:00`, because PHP always supplies the 1st, so the result does not
depend on when the import runs. And the bare-year cell met the #669 trap in the
test: the array key `'2026'` became an INT and the closure threw a TypeError
under strict types.


### Part two (a): the 24 pages, one formatter, and bookings on the right clock (#777, #784, #783)

**Four methods, one job each, and the rule for choosing.** Words:
`I18n::formatClockDateTime()` is the ONE place a wall-clock date and time
becomes words — `FeedAdmin::showWallClock()` calls it and keeps only "(all
day)" and naming the event's zone, and the reminder job's `eventClockText()`
calls it too (it had been a THIRD copy of the same UTC build). Walking a
reading across days: `wallClockReading()`, built in UTC because UTC has no
transitions — it is NOT a moment and must never be compared with a real "now".
Comparing with now: `wallClockNow($zone)` on the EVENT's clock
(`Site::zoneFor($event['timezone'])`), compared as `Y-m-d H:i:s` text. A real
instant: `wallClockInstant($reading, $zone)`, which moves a skipped-hour
reading forward by the gap (RFC 5545 §3.3.5; 02:30 New York on 2027-03-14 is
07:30 UTC) and, in the hour that happens twice, takes PHP's own pick, which
differs by zone — accepted for a countdown and said in its docblock.

**The calendar grids had to convert BOTH sides.** `_day_columns.php` compared
each event with a column's midnight built in PHP's zone; with the event now a
UTC-built reading, that compares two clocks. The columns are readings too.
**And `formatDate()` is handed the DATE only** on the event page and list view,
because it runs `strtotime()` itself and, handed the time, moved a Greenland
23:30 reading onto the next day.

**#783: "still to come" means the organisation's clock.** For a resource page,
this organisation's, bound as a parameter, never SQL `NOW()`. For My Bookings,
each booking's own organisation's, because a member's bookings can be at
several: the query takes a loose floor (UTC now less one day — no clock on
Earth is more than twelve hours BEHIND UTC; fourteen is the furthest ahead) and
each row is judged exactly in PHP. The reminder job's `UTC_TIMESTAMP()`
prefilter needs NO change: it is a −1 to +2 day net, and with every zone
between −12 and +14 hours the margin is **more than nine hours** either way
(9h45m at UTC+14, because its 24-hour window accepts starts up to 24h15m away —
the builder's draft said "at least ten", which round 1 measured false).

**Three hand-written class lists had to gain `I18n.php`**
(`feed-admin-selftest.php`, `import-notifier-selftest.php`, the job runner in
`feed-importer-selftest.php`) — the #775 lesson again: tests that load classes
one by one break silently the day a dependency is added.

**Testing, and its honest limit.** The gate stops a PAGE going back to
`strtotime()` of the column; section L of `clock-change-selftest.php` drives
the four methods on fixed skipped hours (London, New York, Auckland, and Nuuk
at 23:30) with the premise asserted first and the old behaviour beside each;
part X of `time-zones-selftest.php` drives the real pages over HTTP. **None of
them can see a page that keeps the new methods but passes the WRONG ZONE**:
the independent check undid three fixes that way (countdown feed, list
past/today, day columns) with everything green. That is #805 — and the day
columns' check could not fail because its event was at 02:30, inside its own
day whichever way the columns are built, the exact shape the builder had fixed
in L10 and left in X03.

**Review closed at round 1 under D-066**, because every finding was in a test
or a document; the ordinary-day sweep (old formatter against new, every 15
minutes through 2027 in nine zones) found differences only inside skipped
hours. Left on issues: #804 (thirteen other `NOW()` comparisons, seven of them
in files this package changed — the countdown feed still picks its "next" event
on the database's clock), #805, #806.

### Raised rather than bundled

**#782 — eighteen hard-coded `Europe/London` literals across ten files, and two
columns that DEFAULT to it.** The exact command matters, because the independent
check re-counted and got a different figure from a wider search:

    grep -rnE "'(Europe|America|Asia|Africa|Australia|Pacific)/[A-Za-z_]+'" \
      web/_apps web/_core | grep -v WindowsTimeZones | grep -v giving-retention

answers **18 lines across 10 files**. `WindowsTimeZones.php` is excluded because
every literal in it is a mapping entry, and the giving-retention JSON because it
is data. A search across all of `web/`, or one that counts comments, answers
more — so the issue now carries the command rather than only the number. The standing rule is explicit ("never hard-code a
zone… a customer in another country is the ordinary case"). The two defaults are
#763's shape exactly — a default that cannot be told from a choice — with one
real difference: unlike `tblUsers.locale`, those columns ARE written by their own
pages, so some rows genuinely are choices, and the answer needs reading rather
than D-060's one-liner. The measured cost: a livestream schedule with no zone set
resolves to London, so "next: Saturday 11:00" is eleven hours out for a church in
Sydney.

### And a mistake of mine worth recording, because it was the second time

Backing files up to `/tmp/$(basename $f)` **collided**: `small-groups/index.php`
and `attendance/index.php` share a basename, so the second backup overwrote the
first and the restore put the attendance page inside the Small Groups file. It
was caught by `check_capability_registry.py` going red — the file had lost its
`App::can(Capabilities::GROUPS_MANAGE)` gate — and `git checkout --` put it back.
**This repository's memory already records that trap from earlier the same day.
Use distinct backup names, or better, use git.**

### A cache cannot count calls (#762)

`tblContentTranslation` looked like the obvious place to count translations: one row per
translation, with `costPence` on it, and the money limit already summed it. It is a
CACHE — one row per (table, row, field, language), written by an upsert — so it answers
"how many pieces have been translated", never "how many requests were made". Today the two
differ three ways: two simultaneous presses pay twice and leave one row; a failed request
leaves no row though it may have been billed; and nothing invalidates a cached row when its
source is edited (`grep -rn tblContentTranslation web/` on 6 November 2026: no DELETE
anywhere; the only writers are migration 250's backfill and `persist()`, reached only on a
cache miss). That last one is also a live fault of its own: an edited announcement keeps
showing the translation of its old words. The day somebody fixes it by translating afresh,
a count of cache rows would silently fall behind the bill.

So both limits are counted in `tblTranslationUsage`, at the moment a request is made.
**When a limit is about money, count the thing that costs money, where it is spent — not
a by-product of it.**

Two further points worth keeping:

- **A counter must count only what it says it counts.** The first version took the slot
  before asking whether the request could be sent at all, so a portal switched on before
  its key was typed exhausted its month on requests that never left the server, and the
  admin page called them "sent". Ask "can this be sent" before counting; keep counting a
  request that was sent and failed.
- **A sentence about a per-provider property must not be phrased as a per-organisation
  one.** "With LibreTranslate the money spent stays at £0.00" was untrue whenever money had
  been spent earlier in the month on a paid company, because the record is per
  organisation; it then contradicted the money banner above it. Say what the provider
  ADDS, not what the figure IS.
- **A guard checked only for being PRESENT is half a guard.** The "not set up" warning was
  proved to appear when it should; nothing proved it was absent on a working set-up, so a
  condition showing it on every portal passed. Every warning needs its negative case.
- **A substring pin on unreachable code is not enough; pin the whole region.** Two
  substrings around `return self::settle(` let one inserted line zero the cost. The
  repository's settled remedy (#485, #763, D-065) — compare the whole region as code —
  closed it.
- **A cost path no test can reach should be coupled to one it can.** Recording the cost
  was a separate line, reached only by a provider reporting more than 0, which no test
  can call; deleting it left every check green. Now the words come back through the
  method that records the cost.
- **A count can be reserved; money cannot.** The cost is known only after the provider
  answers, so money is check-then-add and can overshoot by one call per simultaneous
  press. The count is one conditional UPDATE (`... SET calls = calls + 1 WHERE ... AND
  (? = 0 OR calls < ?)`, `affected_rows === 1`), which InnoDB serialises. Money is asked
  FIRST so a money refusal uses no slot (F01d pins that order).
- **Two fail-closed reads mask each other.** With the usage table missing, both
  `monthUsage()` and `reserveCall()` refuse. Planting a fail-open in `monthUsage()` alone
  left the press refused (the reservation still refuses) and only the admin page's
  "could not be read" check went red; it took both planted together to turn F2-09 red.
  Defence in depth is real here, but say it: each guard alone is not proved by the press.
- **A check that a value "stayed the same" cannot tell a refusal from a clamp to the same
  value.** J11 (money, "stays at 100000" after J10 stored exactly 100000) passed with a
  planted clamp; so did the new number check until a smaller value was saved between them.

### Pinning code no test can reach: eight rounds, and where it ended (#762)

No test here can reach a paid translation company, so whether a PAID translation is checked
against the limits could only be guarded by pinning the code. Every round from 3 to 7 found
the same thing one step further out — a single line, outside whatever was pinned, that
switched the limits off for paid providers while every check stayed green:

| round | what was pinned | the one line that got past it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | two substrings | `$result['costPence'] = 0;` above the return |
| 2 | from the provider call to the return | `$month = '1999-01-01';` above it |
| 3 | from the provider choice; start "exactly once" | a paid-provider shortcut above it; a dead copy plus a respelled live one |
| 4 | the whole of `translate()` | the shortcut moved into a method it calls; a second `Translate()` (PHP ignores case) |
| 5 | the whole FILE, as tokens | `function ceil()` in ANY other `Portal\Core` file — an unqualified call is looked up in the namespace first |
| 6 | every built-in written `\ceil`; the gate refusing unqualified ones by a list of positions to skip | the skipped positions hid real lookups (a ternary's middle, a `switch` case) |
| 7 | refuse in EVERY position except the four that can never be a lookup | — (round 8 clean) |

**Three lessons, each already recorded once here and needed again.** (1) **Pin the unit PHP
loads, not a region of it** — #485 and #763 ended the same way. (2) **A pinned line can
still change MEANING if a name in it is resolved somewhere else**: inside a namespace, PHP
looks an unqualified function or constant up in that namespace first, so write built-ins
fully qualified wherever a guard depends on what a line does (#807 carries this to the
other money paths). (3) **A rule that lists the shapes to skip is a spelling list; refuse by
default and allow only what the grammar proves harmless** — the #763 lesson, met by the
guard that was written to close #763's own kind of hole.

**Where it honestly stops:** the code of the classes the engine calls by design
(`SettingLimit`, `App`, `Site`, `ContentTranslation`) and the endpoint that calls it. Any of
them could be edited to treat paid providers differently; review of a change to them is what
covers that, and the gate says so rather than pushing its edge outwards again.

### #804, #805, #806: the event's own clock in SQL, and which days an event is on

**`Events::nowOnItsOwnClock($db, $alias, $siteId)` is the ONE place a query asks whether an event is still to come, under way or today.** Each event has its own zone (`tblEvents.timezone`), so no single bound "now" fits every row (#783 could bind one for a resource page only because a resource belongs to one organisation). The database cannot convert a zone NAME reliably either: `CONVERT_TZ()` with a name needs the time-zone tables, which shared hosting rarely loads, and then answers NULL. So the zone texts in use are read first (`SELECT DISTINCT`, a handful), PHP works out each one's clock, and the answer is `CAST(CASE e.timezone WHEN ? THEN ? … ELSE ? END AS DATETIME)` with every value bound. That is exact row by row INSIDE SQL, which is why it was chosen over #783's "loose bound in SQL, exact test in PHP": the calendar list COUNTs and PAGES its rows and the countdown feed takes `LIMIT 1`, and a PHP filter after the fetch cannot keep either right. `Events::looseUtcBound('-1 day')` sits beside it only so the `startDateTime` index can still be used — the CASE differs per row and cannot use it. The ELSE is the organisation's clock, which is also what `Site::zoneFor()` gives every page for a zone PHP cannot open; the one case it can be wrong is a row saved with a brand-new zone in the instant between the two statements.

**With no events at all there are no zones, and a `CASE` with no `WHEN` is not SQL.** The first version built exactly that, so `/dashboard` answered HTTP 500 on every installation or organisation with no events yet. Nothing in the time-zones test could see it, because that test always has events; ten other self-tests that load the dashboard on an empty database went red, which is how it was found. The method now returns `CAST(? AS DATETIME)` (the organisation's clock) for that case.

Where the expression is written twice in one statement (dashboard, reminder preview, newsletter), its values are bound twice, in the order the marks appear.

**Four sites were left, each with its reason beside the code** — they are windows with deliberate slack, not decisions about one event: the sitemap (search engines, cached an hour), the attendance-recording picker (±30 days), the asset page's picker and `Events::volunteeringFor()` (both "since a day ago"). **That bound is the DATABASE's session clock, not UTC, and clocks span 26 hours (UTC-12 to UTC+14)**, so it never drops an event still to come only while the database clock is at most 12 hours ahead of UTC; on a server set to UTC+13 an `Etc/GMT+12` event is dropped in its last hour. The builder's draft and both code comments said "no clock is more than fourteen hours from UTC", which the independent check measured untrue; the harm is small and rare and is now stated.

**`I18n::wallClockDaySpan()` / `wallClockDays()` are the ONE place a page asks which calendar days an event covers** — the month grid, the year grid and the attendance register. Days come off the readings (built in UTC, so nothing can move) and are compared as DATES. Two faults closed: the register made a moment in the event's zone then set midnight, which in Nuuk put a 23:30 event on the next day; and the grids walked from the start reading while `<=` the end reading, so an event ending earlier in the day than it began lost its last day. **An end of exactly 00:00:00 does not occupy its own day** — walking by date alone would otherwise put every evening-to-midnight event on the next day too. Imported all-day events end 23:59:59 on their last day, so they are unaffected.

**#805's three guards exist now, and each was planted:** X03 has a 23:30 event beside the 02:30 one (02:30 falls inside its own day whichever clock the columns are built on — a check that could not fail); X12/X13 drive the list's past and today with a New York event that is still to come on its own clock and past on Auckland's; X14 is the first test ever to fetch `widget/countdown.json`. Premise first (X10), with the old answer each way stated. #804's other fixed sites are driven over HTTP too: X11 (list upcoming), X15 (reminder preview), X16 (Host Console today), X17 (newsletter preview's events block), X18 (discipleship sweep, read back from `tblPathwayProgress`), X19 (the dashboard's count, measured three times so other events in the run cannot blur it). **Not driven: the "all upcoming" calendar subscription in `calendar/export.php`** — reverting it to `NOW()` left every check green (#814), along with the pathway-scoped discipleship sweep and two grid windows.

**`tools/my-volunteering-selftest.php` had been red since `3f29995`**: that commit made the page call `I18n::formatClockDateTime()`, and the test's own page runner has no autoloader, so every case died with "Class I18n not found". The runner now requires `I18n.php`.

**Review closed at round 1 under D-066** (findings only in tests and a comment; the SQL was run on MariaDB 11.4.13, MySQL 8.4.11 and 9.7.4 with identical rows, every bind order checked, and the day-span edges probed). Left on issues: #810 (the registration clear-out deletes personal data on the database's clock — protected arm), #811 ("next" sorted across zones, a midnight sliver, an unreachable widget loop), #812 (discipleship rule 3 not scoped to the pathway's organisation), #814.

### The registrations clear-out and the event's own clock (#810)

- `registration_sweep_where($db, $siteId, $days)` returns `['sql','types','params']`;
  `registration_sweep(bool $reallyDelete)` is the ONE function behind both the count (preview) and
  the delete, the `log_sweep()` shape. Prepared once per organisation, because each organisation's
  clock values differ.
- **`Events::nowForADeletionDeadline($db, $alias, $siteId, $lookBackDays)`** is new and is what the
  sweep asks. For each zone it binds "UTC now + the LOWEST offset the zone has had in the last
  `$lookBackDays` + 2 days" as a reading m, and the row is deleted when `reading < m − n days`
  (exact 24-hour days, because m stands for a clock with no changes). That is never earlier than
  n days on the event's clock (m ≤ the clock now) and never earlier than n × 24 real hours (the
  event's offset when it ended is one of those m's minimum was taken over, provided the window is
  the caller's LONGEST period — the sweep passes `MAX(COALESCE(own days, organisation's))` for the
  organisation). The `ELSE` is `Etc/GMT+12`. So do a zone with no list of changes
  (`getTransitions()` answers false: `EST`, `BST`, `+05:00`) and a look-back over 36,500 days — that
  limit is the code's own, not PHP's. The extra days are load-bearing — one is needed and the second is margin (one gave no early deletion in any zone; none gave 151,225): the later
  meaning of a skipped-hour reading uses the offset in force just before the change, which a window
  of exactly n days misses for an event near its start (up to two hours early in ~200 zones, per the
  round-2 simulation). The lowest offset is over EVERY state in the window, not its two ends.
- **`Events::deadlineReadingFor($zone, $lookBackDays, $nowUtc)`** is the per-zone rule, public and
  given the moment, so section G drives it at fixed dates (a skipped hour at the window's start, a
  winter in a summer-to-summer window, `EST`/`+05:00`). `nowForADeletionDeadline()` passes `time()`.
- **Lateness, stated properly:** up to the gap between the zone's offset at the event's end and its
  lowest offset in the window — one hour normally, about two hours (2 h 0 m 1 s measured) for Antarctica/Troll and America/Nuuk, and up to a day where a zone jumped the date line (Pacific/Apia, 2011). The window is
  the organisation's longest period.
- `nowOnItsOwnClock()` keeps its three-argument signature and meaning for pages; both methods share
  one private builder, `perZoneReading()`. (Round 0 added a fourth argument to it; that is gone,
  replaced by the dedicated method.)
- **Byte-for-byte zone comparison:** the zone list is `SELECT DISTINCT CAST(`timezone` AS BINARY)`
  and the expression is `CASE CAST(`e`.`timezone` AS BINARY) WHEN …`. The column is
  `utf8mb4_general_ci`, which folds accents, so `Europe/Zürich` and `Europe/Zurich` were one value.
  No form can store such a text today (`Site::isZoneName()`); old, hand-written or restored rows can.
  Round 1 used `COLLATE utf8mb4_bin`, which is PAD SPACE (`'Europe/London '` = `'Europe/London'`),
  so "exact" was untrue; behaviourally the two are identical here because `Site::zoneFor()` trims.
- **A failed read throws; it does not come back empty.** `bootstrap.php` sets
  `MYSQLI_REPORT_STRICT | MYSQLI_REPORT_ERROR`, so `prepare()`/`execute()` throw and nothing is
  deleted. The `=== false` guards in the builder, the look-back query and `registration_sweep()`
  are marked as backstops for a caller without strict reporting. (Round 0's notes claimed a failed
  read made every row take the `ELSE`; that path is unreachable here — #694's lesson again.)
- **Direction trap:** a reading on a clock behind the server's is a smaller number for the same
  moment, so it crosses the deadline early. The old docblock was right; the issue text was not.
- "Now" comes from PHP (the web server's clock) instead of the database's. Stated in the code.
- Other date limits in the sweep and `_core/` retention code are on the database's own clock at
  both ends: activity log `timestamp`, error `createdAt`, `offboardedAt`, webhook `receivedAt`,
  webhook delivery `createdAt`, transcript `generatedAt`, anonymous check-in `checkedInAt`.
- Test: section G of `tools/retention-caps-selftest.php` (36 checks; the file expects 116). It
  includes the organisation's own figure for events with none (20 days, and 0 = keep), a real
  recent spring-forward zone (found among every zone PHP knows, so its name changes with the date),
  the `Europe/Zürich` collision, and the `ELSE`. Anybody requiring `_retention-sweep.php` without
  the autoloader must load `Site`, `I18n` and `Events`; `tools/gdpr-eraser-selftest.php` does now.
- `tools/audit-checks/check_event_visibility.py`: the two `_core/Events.php` LINE_ALLOWLIST entries
  moved 491/492 -> 681/682 and their text is now `SELECT DISTINCT CAST(`timezone` AS BINARY) AS `zone` …`.

**Review: three rounds by fresh Claude agents, the third CLEAN** (protected arm — it deletes personal data). Round 3 drove the real method over 5.67 million cases in all 598 zones, 2008–2028, on PHP 8.4, 8.5 and 8.6, with zero early deletions — and showed the simulation can fail (151,225 early deletions with the extra days removed); `CAST(... AS BINARY)` was measured on MySQL 8.0, 8.4 and 9.7 and MariaDB 11.4 and 12.3. Left open: the race where an event's own figure is raised between the longest-period read and the delete, and the installation ceiling on the figures themselves (#816, D-074).

### Frequent jobs get allowances from their own timing (#793, D-076)

**The rule, written once beside the constants in `web/_core/ScheduledJobs.php`:** three times the longest gap the
job's own page header states, never under 30 minutes. Where a header gives a range, the longer end is the gap,
because a customer following that page may choose it.

| job | its own words | allowance |
|---|---|---|
| `cron/push-golive` | "every 5 minutes" | 30 minutes (the floor; 3 × 5 = 15) |
| `cron/webhook-retry` | "every 5-15 minutes" | 45 minutes |
| `cron/user-reminders` | "every 15 minutes" | 45 minutes |
| `cron/asset-reminders` | "every 15-60 minutes" | 3 hours |
| `cron/venue-reminders` | "every 30-60 minutes" | 3 hours |
| `cron/workflow-timeouts` | "called hourly" | 3 hours |
| `cron/health` | silent; the staff health page prints `0 * * * *` | 3 hours |
| `cron/discipleship-sweep` | silent; "a convenience, not a dependency" | 36 hours (nightly) |

- **Why three times:** a job is reported only after two missed runs in a row, so one slow or skipped run on a busy
  shared host says nothing (#483), while a stopped job is still reported the same morning.
- **Why the 30-minute floor:** it is the owner's own example for a five-minute job in D-076, and a shared-hosting
  scheduler can run several minutes late. The mail queue keeps 15 minutes although it too runs every five, because
  that figure is `MailQueue::jobIsRunning()`'s window, which decides how mail is SENT; the page must agree with it.
- **One constant per job, not per figure**, so changing one job's allowance cannot move another's.
- **An allowance a customer is never told is a false alarm waiting to happen.** The new figures assume each job is
  called as often as its header says, and until this change nothing a customer reads said so for most of them — and
  the one place that did (`venues/settings.php`) said "daily" for a job whose header says every 30-60 minutes, both
  written in `37bf418` (`git log -S"daily schedule" -- web/_apps/venues/settings.php` and
  `git log -S"every 30-60 minutes" -- web/_apps/cron/venue-reminders.php` each answer only that commit). So
  `docs/INSTALL.md` step 6 now carries a table of all fifteen, and check E8 of `scheduled-jobs-selftest.php` holds its
  last column to the hand-typed figures.
- **The test types the figures, never asks for them (#795).** E4 compares every job's `overdue` with a literal map,
  and H0c3 (scheduled-jobs) and P4 (portal-check) compare the all-clear's reason with a sentence written out by hand.
  The old H0c3 looked for `allowancesInWords()`'s own answer on the page, so the page and the test agreed whatever
  that method said; planted, doubling every minute figure inside `lengthInWords()` now turns H0c3 and P4 red.
- `allowancesInWords()` now writes "45 minutes (2 jobs)" rather than "45 minutes for 2 of them": with eight figures
  the old form said "for one job" five times in one sentence.

---

**Round 3 (the last under the three-round cap, D-051) found the job's WHERE clause is not its whole selection**: `cron/giving-statements` calls `Site::forceContext()` per row, which refuses an inactive organisation, so a statement queued for one is never sent — and counting it made the page report a PROBLEM that could never clear, on the very set-up the guide recommends. `PortalCheck::JOB_WORK_WAITING_ACTIVE_ONLY` now adds that condition; Q8 compares the job's WHERE with everything before it and Q8b pins it; Q9c/Q9d drive it (planted out, both go red). That fix and the guide's giving row were made by the commissioning session AFTER the capped review, and were not independently checked. Left on #820: Q8 is a text comparison a JOIN or an extra condition can slip past; two schedule sentences (DbBackup, the retention page) are not held; and the giving job's own skipped rows and unretried failures. Review: three rounds by fresh Claude agents; Codex has not reviewed it.

### Page findings left from the widened audit (#569)

- **A "JavaScript error" in the browser audit can be a missing icon link.** With no
  `<link rel="icon">` the browser asks `/favicon.ico`, gets a 404 and logs it as a
  console error. It shows only on the FIRST page in a run that lacks the link, because
  the browser remembers the failure — so fixing one page moves the error to the next
  (fixing `/api-docs` exposed it on `/assets/kiosk`). Find the address before guessing:
  the audit prints only the text, so a probe that logs `Network.responseReceived` with
  status >= 400 is what named it.
- **`check_page_head_tags.py` now reads `web/public_html/` too.** It used to read only
  `web/_apps/`, so `/api-docs` was never examined (an issue comment called it
  "exempt"; it was out of reach). The web-root no-network page
  `offline/index.php` is exempt with a reason. Section G of
  `tools/page-head-selftest.php` checks `/api-docs` over both ways in (router and
  direct) and the kiosk screen, with a planted fault.
- **A long dotted setting key in a flex row cannot shrink**, so it widens the page.
  `<wbr>` after each dot gives it break points without changing the copied text;
  `text-break` alone cut "requireUppe / rcase".
- **A page reachable at more than one address names its own canonical path** (`$pageCanonicalPath` in `head-meta.php`): building it from the request path gave `/api-docs/index.php` a `.php` canonical address. `/settings` vs `/admin/settings` and `/` vs `/dashboard` still give one page two (#823).
- **Review:** two rounds by fresh Claude agents (three-round cap). Round 1 found the `.php` canonical; round 2 confirmed the fix across 15 pages and in multi-organisation path mode (the organisation's part never printed twice), and found only an untrue comment (corrected). Left on #821, #822 (the top bar over 3,000px wide for a root administrator with every app on), #823. Codex has not reviewed it.

### Outside services in three tiers (#778)

- **`Portal\Core\OutsideServices` is the ONE place** the answer is worked out and the ONLY file
  under `web/` that may hold the Gravatar or Google-photo host in code. `Avatar` asks
  `gravatarUrlIfAllowed()` / `providerPhotoIfAllowed()`, which return null rather than an address
  when the answer is no, so an outside address cannot exist without the decision. `header.php`
  widens `img-src` only from `cspImgSources()`; with everything off it answers '' and the header is
  byte-identical to before #778 (pinned by C14 of the self-test).
- **Values per level:** `no` < `off` < `on`; anything else, missing or unreadable is `no`. An
  organisation with no row follows the installation; with a row it can only lower the answer (a
  minimum). A member's `off` always wins; `on` counts only where the ceiling is not `no`; with no
  choice the service is on only if the ceiling is `on`.
- **Point 4 is why `$SETTINGS` is never read here.** It holds the open organisation only, merged.
  The facts reader takes the installation from `InstallationSettings::layerOrNull()` and EVERY
  organisation in `{Site::id()} ∪ OutsideServices::membershipsOf($user)` from its own rows, in one
  statement.
- **`membershipsOf()`, NOT `Site::organisationsFor()` — round 1 of the independent check.**
  `organisationsFor()` answers "which organisations may this person USE", so it requires
  `tblUsers.isActive = 1` and returns nothing for a switched-off account. `admin/users/save.php`
  switches `isActive` alone and the directory still shows such a person, so organisation B's "no"
  was dropped for exactly that person (measured: 0 rows against 1 on the profile query). For this
  rule every membership row still switched on counts (`tblUserSites.isActive = 1`), whether or not
  the account or the organisation is; a switched-off membership row still means "no longer a
  member". A global administrator counts as a member of every organisation, so their own picture is
  held to the strictest on the installation — the conservative reading, stated rather than hidden.
  Pinned by G09/G10 (a switched-off member of A and B, B saying no, with a control); the
  global-administrator clause by H01/H02.
- **Maps are capped by the SERVICE, not only by the levels (D-072, round 1).** `SERVICES[...]
  ['maxLevel']` is `off` for maps: `levelValuesFor()` is what both admin cards offer, both writers
  refuse anything else with the reason (recorded), and `decide()` reads every stored level through
  `capFor()`, so a hand-written or restored "on" cannot put a member's home on a map before that
  member chose it. The organisation writer has TWO guards here (the service limit, and the
  installation's value read through `capFor()`); removing either alone is caught by the other, so
  the plant that proves D17 removes both. An organisation going looser than the installation for
  maps ("off" under "no") is refused at the writer (H13). The pure `effectiveFrom()` knows nothing of
  services.
- **Who touches `tblUserOutsideServicePref`:** written only by `OutsideServices`; also read by the
  member's own data download and deleted by an erasure (`GdprEraser`). The table comment says so
  (round 2 corrected "read and written only by").
- **Any read that throws makes the whole answer "unreadable", which is `no`**, never "not chosen"
  (which for a ceiling of `on` would be yes). Section B renames `tblUserSites`, `tblSettings` and the
  preference table away to prove it, each with a positive control.
- **D-072 asks two DIFFERENT questions**, by the owner's words: the member shown, the ordinary rule;
  the person looking, only "allowed for them and not switched off". `allows($service, $subject)` is
  the one place both are asked. The plan said "both must allow" and implied the full rule for both;
  D-072's own text ("the viewer has not switched it off") is what was built.
- **The writers judge only what CHANGED (#687).** A value an organisation stored before the
  installation tightened is offered, selected and labelled "held down", and an untouched Save keeps
  it without a refusal; the reader holds it down. A `<select>` with no selected option is a vote for
  its first option (#763), which here would delete the organisation's row.
- **The reader is the enforcement; the writers give the honest refusal.** A looser organisation
  value is refused with the reason, never clamped (#668), with the installation's rows read live and
  `FOR UPDATE` inside the writing transaction (#647, #687), using `siteScope = -1` so the lock is on
  the unique key. A member's `on` row that outlives a later "no" is ignored by the reader (E05c).
- **Member choices are one row per service** (`tblUserOutsideServicePref`), upserted or deleted one
  at a time; never a rebuilt list (#667, pinned by E02).
- **"You can always switch it off" is kept true (round 2).** A member who chose "on" and whose
  organisation then said "no" used to get NO control, so the recorded choice could not be withdrawn
  and came back by itself when the organisation relaxed. Whenever a choice is stored, the member
  page now draws a control offering "Off" and "Follow my organisations" (never "On" above what is
  allowed), whose first, selected option is "Keep my earlier choice" (`OutsideServices::KEEP`),
  which the writer reads as "leave alone" — a `<select>` with no selected option is a vote for its
  first option (#763). Pinned end to end by H14-H19, including that an "off" set while not allowed
  holds after the organisation relaxes.
- **The member writer judges only what CHANGED too (round 3).** A page drawn before an
  organisation said "no" still holds the member's earlier "on", and the browser re-posts it
  untouched; refusing that refused the WHOLE save, so switching another service OFF in the same
  press was lost with a message about switching Gravatar ON. An "on" equal to the stored choice is
  now neither refused nor written (the reader holds it down). So "switching off is never refused" is
  true in the writer, the handler's header and on the page. Pinned by H20-H23, which draw the page,
  tighten B, then post.
- **A withdrawal of consent is never lost (round 4; the stronger reading of D-058, chosen by the
  coordinator).** A member's press is no longer all-or-nothing: every "off" and every "follow" is
  applied, and only a real change to "on" above the ceiling is refused — that service is left exactly
  as it was. The message says what was saved and what was refused and why; a mixed press records
  both `OutsideServicePrefsUpdated` and `OutsideServicePrefsRefused`. "Is this a change?" is read
  from the member's STORED choices on their own (`memberChoices()`), so it is still answered when
  the ceiling cannot be read — then withdrawals are applied, every real "on" is refused, and the
  message says the settings could not be read. An untouched "on" is in no activity record (a record
  of it would be a false consent record). The refusal sentence names EVERY refusing level, and the
  member page says "if those changed" when more than one refuses. Pinned by H22b and H24-H30.
- **Two saves at once are serialised (rounds 5 and 6; the #728 shape).** The member writer used
  to read the stored choices OUTSIDE any transaction and skip writing an "off" it believed was
  already stored, so two tabs saving at once could end with BOTH services on while each was told
  "saved" — measured by the independent check. Now: ONE transaction whose first act is
  `SELECT … FROM tblUsers WHERE userID = ? FOR UPDATE` (the PARENT row, because the preference rows
  may not exist yet); the stored choices are then read with an ORDINARY read, which is fresh because
  of the ORDER — InnoDB takes a transaction's snapshot at its first plain read, and that comes after
  the lock; and, as a belt, an "off" is ALWAYS written (listed as a change only when it was not
  already stored).
- **Round 5 first used a LOCKING read there, and it was wrong (round 6, measured).** A locking read
  of "every row for this member", and a DELETE of a row that does not exist, both take GAP locks
  reaching the NEXT member's rows, so two DIFFERENT members saving at once deadlocked 36-40 times in
  40 and one member's withdrawal was refused because of somebody else. The read is ordinary now and
  the DELETE is skipped when nothing is stored. **Lesson: a lock taken to serialise ONE member must
  not be a range lock that reaches OTHER members.**
- A lock wait that runs out (1205, or a deadlock 1213) is rolled back and told plainly: "Another
  change to your account was being saved at the same moment … try again" — "your account", because
  the other writer may be a profile edit rather than another save of these choices. Refused "on"
  lines are kept in that message when the wait happens at a write.
- Pinned by section T of the self-test, which uses REAL SEPARATE PROCESSES (one process cannot block
  itself): T01 (premise: tab A really was held), T03 (the one order T01 proves, on/off), T07 (tab B
  read what A stored — its record lists its withdrawal), T04-T06 (the lock-wait message; the parent
  lock is taken first), T08 (refused lines kept), T09 (after a failure the SAME connection's next
  write is committed — the rollback, because `Logger::db()` shares the connection), T10 (two
  adjacent members withdrawing at once, 12 runs in two shapes, no refusal). With the lock in place
  the belt is not observable on its own (plant V03 stays green) — a second defence, said so.
- **Round 7 pinned the three things the fix depends on.** T11: two tabs of ONE member released
  together BEFORE either has written — the window T07 cannot reach, because there a write's
  foreign-key check already holds the member's row — must end in one serial order with exactly one
  tab's record naming both services (a lock taken outside the transaction gave off/off in 16-18 of
  20). T12: a failure AFTER an "on" was written is ROLLED BACK, so "Nothing was saved" is true
  (committing in the catch left Gravatar on). And the "both were held" premises of T01, T10 and T11
  now ASK THE DATABASE — rows in `information_schema.innodb_trx` with `trx_state = 'LOCK WAIT'` —
  because "the process is still running" passed with a wait of 0.
- **And round 7's version of that premise read a STALE CACHE (round 8, measured).** InnoDB rebuilds
  `innodb_trx` only when nobody has read it for 0.1 s, and every read resets that clock; the helper
  read FIRST and slept after, so its first read returned the previous call's snapshot — 17 of 18
  calls answered true at once from T10's FIRST run, a T11 with no hold at all stayed green, and on
  MariaDB T10b stopped catching round 6's deadlock. Now it sleeps 0.15 s BEFORE every read and counts
  only connections (`trx_mysql_thread_id`) not seen by any earlier call. **A premise read from a
  cache is only a premise if you know when the cache was filled.** T10 now runs 24 times — and even so, on MariaDB T10b catches round 6's deadlock in MOST runs, not every one (5 of 6 and 4 of 6 measured in rounds 8 and 9), because there it is a matter of timing; on MySQL it caught 3 of 3. T12 gained
  a premise too: while the save waits it has already modified a row (`trx_rows_modified >= 1`), so
  the rollback really has something to undo.
- `memberChoices()` is read only by the writer (its docblock had said the member page too), and its
  unused `$lock` parameter is gone, with the reason written beside the method.
- The read's freshness holds at REPEATABLE READ and READ COMMITTED (for different reasons, both
  written beside the code), measured by the independent check on MySQL 8.0/8.4 and MariaDB
  11.4/12.3. Under SERIALIZABLE, which the portal promises nothing about, one neighbour deadlock in
  60 was measured on MySQL 8.0; the docblock says so.
- **A database failure keeps the refused lines in the member's message**, as the Refused record
  does. Not covered by a test: no test here can make the write fail part-way.
- Also pinned in round 5: a "follow" beside a refused "on" is applied and listed (H32-H34); the
  stored-choices read failing is said exactly and never reported as saved (H35-H36); the Refused
  record's text (H26b); a mixed press shown as a warning (H25b).
- **"Did it change" is asked of the value as the card SHOWS it (round 2).** Both admin cards fill
  their boxes through `capFor()`, so both writers now compare `capFor($service, $stored)` with the
  posted value. Comparing the raw row made a stored map "on" (shown as "off") read as changed on an
  untouched Save, judged against an installation "no", and refused the WHOLE save, losing a picture
  change made on the same form. The card now says what was STORED and what it counts as, instead of
  claiming the organisation chose what it shows. Pinned by H05-H12.
- **`Avatar::localPath()` is an allow-list (round 2).** A stored value is a local path only if it is
  an optional single `/`, then `[A-Za-z0-9_]`, then only `[A-Za-z0-9_./-]`, never `//`. Everything
  else is another website and goes to the decision (an https:// address on the photo hosts, or the
  silhouette). The old "starts with http(s):// or //" test, a list of bad spellings, missed
  `/\host/x`, `\\host/x` and `/<TAB>/host/x`, all of which a browser reads as another host — and
  `/\lh3.googleusercontent.com/…` would have skipped the decision while the page rule allowed that
  host. Pinned by C15 and H03/H04.
- **The sign-in photo is drawn only from `https://…googleusercontent.com`**, because the page rule
  is widened only for that family; any other stored outside address now draws the silhouette instead
  of a picture the browser would refuse. (Microsoft ID tokens carry no `picture` claim in practice;
  a stored Graph address would have needed a token anyway.)
- **The OSM tile host stays named on four pages whose map is of a BUILDING** (venue, event venue,
  organisation address, small-group meeting place) and in the shared map script, each counted in
  `check_outside_services_gated.py`; only the member directory had to change. A small group's meeting
  place may be a host's home — that is #809, not covered.
- **Two known, fail-safe imperfections, left as notes (round 1):** (1) capitals — the settings
  layer is read case-SENSITIVELY by key while `storedAt()` and the organisation reader compare
  case-insensitively, so a hand-written installation row in different capitals can make the admin
  card show "on" while the reader says "no" (only hand-written SQL reaches it; the reader is the
  stricter side); (2) `saveMemberChoice()` reads the member's ceiling without a lock, so a member
  "on" can race an organisation tightening to "no" — harmless, because the reader ignores such a row
  (E05c).
- **The data download carries the choices** (`outsideServiceChoices`), pinned by E07, which reads
  the real download. `tblUserTranslationPref` is still not in the download — noted, not changed.
- Guards: `tools/audit-checks/check_outside_services_gated.py` (hard gate in `pr-security.yml`;
  presence and counts only, D-065) and `tools/outside-services-selftest.php` (real HTTP; in
  `portal-selftests.yml` and `tools/run-all-selftests.sh`). Count the checks from the file's output,
  never from here.
